Rather than adopting existing algebraic tools, GCC formulates coded computing through a natural end-to-end mean-squared error loss that directly measures the discrepancy between the desired computations and their recovered estimates. By deriving suitable upper bounds and restricting the encoder and decoder to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with mild smoothness constraints, we show that both the encoder and decoder admit specific representations as linear combinations of RKHS kernel functions. This representation allows the corresponding coefficients to be computed efficiently. Moreover, this framework enables us to establish theoretical performance guarantees for GCC under two complementary straggler regimes. In the worst-case setting with $N$ worker nodes, and at most $S$ stragglers, we show that the end-to-end loss decays at least at rate $O(S^3N^{-3})$ for standard configurations. We then study a probabilistic setting in which each worker independently straggles with probability $p$. We prove that the expected loss can still converge at rate $O(\log_{1/p}^3(N)N^{-3})$.

AI.tldr: GCC introduces a learning-theoretic approach to coded computing that uses RKHS optimization with end-to-end MSE loss, enabling efficient approximate computation for modern ML workloads like DNNs with provable convergence rates under different straggler regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing coded computing schemes are limited to exact recovery of highly structured computations (polynomial evaluation, matrix multiplication) with strict recovery thresholds, making them unsuitable for modern ML workloads like DNNs which lack rigid algebraic structure and often require only approximate rather than exact results.
AI.method: GCC formulates coded computing as an end-to-end mean-squared error loss minimization problem. It restricts encoder and decoder to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with mild smoothness constraints, showing they admit representations as linear combinations of RKHS kernel functions, enabling efficient computation of coefficients.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees show end-to-end loss decays at O(S^3N^{-3}) in worst-case setting with N worker nodes and at most S stragglers, and at O(log_{1/p}^3(N)N^{-3}) in probabilistic setting where each worker independently straggles with probability p.
AI.conclusion: GCC provides a principled learning-theoretic framework for coded computing that extends applicability to modern ML workloads like DNNs by enabling approximate computation with provable performance guarantees under different straggler models, overcoming limitations of existing algebraic approaches.

title: The Race between Agentic AI Capabilities and Data Quality Control in Online Surveys
summary: Online surveys are a foundational data collection instrument in a variety of fields, with attention checks serving as critical guardians of response quality. However, the rapid emergence of agentic AI (goal directed systems powered by a large language model (LLM) brain and/or a multimodal processing unit with tool-augmented capabilities) raises new questions about the robustness of these safeguards. We investigate how well agentic AI architectures can complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks. We evaluate a single-agent architecture capable of multimodal input processing and tool-based web interaction on a controlled survey sandbox. We analyze the problem from two perspectives. From an attack perspective, we demonstrate how structural vulnerabilities such as exposed DOM metadata and predictable option encoding allow agents to resolve attention checks through structured parsing only. From a defense perspective, we implement a mitigation strategy of DOM metadata obfuscation to remove semantic cues in text-based questions. We evaluate multiple open-source language and multimodal models to study capability and orchestration effectiveness. Based on our evaluations, we offer perspectives on how to simultaneously meet the needs of empiricists and agentic AI researchers.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI systems can bypass traditional attention checks in online surveys by exploiting DOM vulnerabilities and predictable question encoding, requiring new defense mechanisms.
AI.motivation: The emergence of agentic AI (LLM-powered, multimodal, tool-augmented systems) raises concerns about the robustness of attention checks in online surveys, which are critical for maintaining response quality in research fields.
AI.method: Evaluated single-agent architectures with multimodal input processing and web interaction tools on a controlled survey sandbox. Analyzed from attack and defense perspectives: identified structural vulnerabilities (exposed DOM metadata, predictable option encoding), and implemented DOM metadata obfuscation as a mitigation strategy. Tested multiple open-source language and multimodal models.
AI.result: Agentic AI can successfully complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks by exploiting structural vulnerabilities. DOM metadata obfuscation shows promise as a defense mechanism by removing semantic cues from text-based questions.
AI.conclusion: Traditional attention checks are vulnerable to agentic AI attacks due to structural weaknesses. New approaches are needed that balance the needs of empirical researchers (ensuring data quality) and agentic AI researchers (enabling effective system testing), with DOM obfuscation offering one potential solution.

title: Asynchronous Cooperative Online Learning for Multi-Robot Control under Computational Delays
summary: Ensuring the safe operation of multi-agent systems (MASs) under uncertain environments is crucial for cooperative robotic, where external disturbances and inaccurate dynamic models can significantly compromise performance and reliability. To address this challenge, calibrated machine learning models, particularly Gaussian process (GP) regression, are extensively employed due to their interpretable performance quantification. As the interconnected communication of MASs facilitates cooperative learning, agents are able to enhance learning performance by exchanging local GP inferences with their neighbors and aggregating the received information via distributed GP strategies. However, variations in computational power and prediction tasks among agents inevitably lead to heterogeneous computational delays and differences in query points, which are often overlooked in existing aggregation methods. To overcome these limitations, this work proposes an asynchronous cooperative learning strategy that explicitly accounts for prediction accuracy, query point variations and delay effects. Additionally, a distributed control law based on an adjoint MAS is developed to ensure the desired control performance. Simulations on unmanned surface vehicles validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, demonstrating substantial improvements in both learning and control performance compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an asynchronous cooperative learning strategy for multi-agent systems that addresses heterogeneous computational delays and query point variations, combining distributed Gaussian process learning with control based on an adjoint MAS.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent system (MAS) cooperative learning methods overlook heterogeneous computational delays and query point variations arising from differences in agent computational power and prediction tasks, which compromise safety and performance in uncertain environments.
AI.method: 1) An asynchronous cooperative learning strategy accounting for prediction accuracy, query point variations, and delay effects. 2) A distributed control law based on an adjoint MAS to ensure desired control performance. Both use distributed Gaussian process regression where agents exchange and aggregate local inferences.
AI.result: Simulations on unmanned surface vehicles show substantial improvements in both learning and control performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, validating the effectiveness of the proposed asynchronous strategy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed asynchronous cooperative learning framework successfully addresses computational heterogeneity in MASs while maintaining learning accuracy and control performance, representing an advancement over existing synchronous aggregation methods.

title: SemKV: Semantic Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization Guided by the Quality Cliff for Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: The key-value (KV) cache is the dominant memory bottleneck of long-context large language model (LLM) inference, growing linearly with context length. We show that uniform KV quantization on a fractional-bit grid does not degrade gracefully: under a prespecified multi-seed statistical protocol, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with an affine quantizer is statistically indistinguishable from FP16 KV down to 2.322 code bits/value and collapses at 2.0 bits - a quality cliff in (2.0, 2.322] that reappears in generation-time quantization and multi-turn dialogue and transfers to Mistral-7B. The cliff reframes importance-aware mixed precision: above it, eight model-internal importance indicators are statistically interchangeable, so the benefit of mixing is grid interpolation, reaching average precisions uniform quantization cannot realize. SemKV preserves every token, ranks tokens by a model-internal score, and assigns two adjacent above-cliff precisions, achieving a measured 6.0x storage reduction with no statistically detectable quality difference from full KV (n=900, three seeds), and outperforming FP16 token pruning granted a 1.5x larger memory budget. Replacing the affine base with a distortion-optimized quantizer (TurboQuant-MSE) lowers the cliff in every protocol tested, raising the no-detectable-loss operating point to 7.9x. The recipe: measure the cliff for the target deployment setting, then interpolate above it.

AI.tldr: Uniform quantization of KV cache hits a "quality cliff" around 2 bits, but SemKV uses mixed precision based on importance scores to achieve 6-8x storage reduction without quality loss.
AI.motivation: The KV cache is the dominant memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference, growing linearly with context length. Current uniform quantization approaches degrade quality ungracefully.
AI.method: SemKV preserves all tokens, ranks them using model-internal importance scores, and assigns two adjacent above-cliff precision levels to different tokens. This achieves storage reduction through grid interpolation rather than importance mixing.
AI.result: SemKV achieves 6.0x storage reduction with no statistically detectable quality difference from full FP16 KV cache, outperforming token pruning even with larger memory budgets. Using optimized quantizers pushes this to 7.9x reduction.
AI.conclusion: The key is to first measure the quality cliff for specific deployment settings, then use mixed precision quantization above that cliff through grid interpolation rather than traditional importance mixing.

title: CDPR: Counterfactual Advantage-based Credit Assignment for Cost-Aware Sequential Medical Diagnosis
summary: Clinical diagnosis is a step-by-step, cost-aware process: a physician orders examinations one at a time, observes the results, and updates the diagnosis before reaching a final conclusion. Most medical language models instead treat diagnosis as a one-pass classification task and ignore the trade-off between a test's value and its cost. We model diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process and train the policy with reinforcement learning. The main difficulty is credit assignment: the only reliable signal comes once at the end of a long trajectory, so it scores a wasteful workup the same as an efficient one. We propose CDPR (Counterfactual Diagnostic Process Reward), which needs no expert labels and no learned critic. CDPR first finds the states where the policy hesitates, using the uncertainty of its action distribution, and then scores the chosen action by its advantage over the alternatives the policy itself would consider, estimated with short rollouts under a utility that balances correctness against test count, cost, and infeasible requests. A rollout cache reuses within-batch trajectories to keep the cost low. We integrate CDPR into GRPO and test it on one in-domain (MIMIC-IV) and two out-of-domain (ClinicalBench and a private hospital dataset) benchmarks. CDPR improves diagnostic accuracy while clearly reducing the number and cost of examinations.

AI.tldr: CDPR is a reinforcement learning method that models clinical diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process, using counterfactual reasoning to score actions without expert labels, leading to more efficient and accurate diagnostic workflows.
AI.motivation: Current medical language models treat diagnosis as one-pass classification tasks, ignoring the sequential, cost-aware nature of real clinical practice where physicians order tests incrementally and consider cost-value tradeoffs. Traditional methods lack proper credit assignment for efficient diagnostic workflows.
AI.method: Models diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process using RL. Introduces CDPR (Counterfactual Diagnostic Process Reward) which: 1) identifies hesitation states using policy action distribution uncertainty, 2) scores chosen actions by comparing them to alternatives via short rollouts under a utility function balancing correctness, test count, cost, and feasibility, 3) uses rollout cache for efficiency, and 4) integrates with GRPO framework.
AI.result: Tested on MIMIC-IV (in-domain), ClinicalBench, and a private hospital dataset (out-of-domain). CDPR improves diagnostic accuracy while significantly reducing both the number and cost of examinations compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: CDPR successfully addresses the credit assignment problem in sequential clinical diagnosis by using counterfactual reasoning without needing expert labels or learned critics. It enables more efficient and cost-effective diagnostic workflows that better mimic real-world clinical practice.

title: Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security
summary: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face reliability, context consumption, and execution stability bottlenecks when deployed on complex, long-horizon tasks. While monolithic prompt engineering and stateless tool-calling paradigms struggle to scale, the field is rapidly converging toward \emph{agentic skills}: modular procedural abstractions that externalize execution knowledge into reusable, executable, and portable artifacts. This paper establishes a unified systems foundation and reference architecture for the agentic skills ecosystem. We formalize skills as externalized procedural knowledge bridging high-level cognitive planning with deterministic execution environments, and systematically delineate the architecture across a nine-stage lifecycle: autonomous discovery, authoring and representation formats, memory storage, dynamic retrieval and routing, composition and orchestration, execution and repair, lifelong adaptation, empirical evaluation, and security governance. We further examine marketplace dynamics, public registries, and emerging adversarial threat vectors, alongside runtime verification and defense mechanisms. Finally, we categorize system implementations across software engineering, operating system navigation, embodied robotics, and scientific discovery, while highlighting critical open challenges in continual learning and benchmark realism. This work establishes agentic skills as a foundational paradigm for building scalable, robust, and verifiable autonomous language agents.

AI.tldr: Agentic skills as modular procedural abstractions that externalize execution knowledge to overcome reliability and scalability bottlenecks in autonomous LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM agents face reliability, context consumption, and execution stability bottlenecks on complex, long-horizon tasks. Monolithic prompt engineering and stateless tool-calling paradigms struggle to scale, necessitating a new approach for building scalable, robust autonomous agents.
AI.method: Establishes a unified systems foundation and reference architecture for agentic skills ecosystem, formalizing skills as externalized procedural knowledge bridging high-level planning with deterministic execution. Proposes a nine-stage lifecycle covering discovery, authoring, representation, storage, retrieval, composition, execution, adaptation, evaluation, and security governance.
AI.result: Provides a comprehensive architectural framework for agentic skills, examining marketplace dynamics, public registries, adversarial threats, and defense mechanisms. Categorizes system implementations across software engineering, OS navigation, robotics, and scientific discovery domains.
AI.conclusion: Establishes agentic skills as a foundational paradigm for building scalable, robust, and verifiable autonomous language agents, while highlighting open challenges in continual learning and benchmark realism.

title: RankShift: In-Database Detection and Explanation of Categorical Shifts
summary: A login service can receive its usual number of failed sign-ins while one source grows from 2% to 30% of them. The same pattern appears in system logs when a rare event template becomes common while the message rate stays stable. These events change which categories are active without changing how many events occur. RankShift detects such changes inside the analytical database that stores the data. It compares each window's category shares with a benign reference using a Pearson score whose terms identify the categories responsible for the change. The same query returns the score, calibrated alert, and largest increasing contributions. We evaluate RankShift on HDFS, BGL, and Thunderbird. It matches the count-vector autoencoder within 0.001 AUROC on HDFS (0.999 versus 1.000) and leads on Thunderbird (0.983 versus 0.949). In a controlled fixed-volume experiment, RankShift detects rare-category shifts that are invisible to event-count monitoring, reaching 0.787 AUROC compared with 0.771 for the autoencoder. Across all three corpora, observed false-alarm rates track the requested operating levels. RankShift requires no model training or inference service, and the autoencoders deployed state is 137x larger.

AI.tldr: RankShift is a lightweight method that detects subtle shifts in category distributions within log data without requiring model training, outperforming or matching autoencoder-based approaches while being significantly more efficient.
AI.motivation: Traditional log monitoring focuses on event count changes but fails to detect subtle shifts where rare categories become common while overall event rates remain stable. This is a critical blind spot in anomaly detection for login services and system logs.
AI.method: RankShift operates directly on analytical databases, comparing category share distributions across time windows against benign references using Pearson scores. It identifies responsible categories through contribution analysis and provides calibrated alerts with minimal computational overhead.
AI.result: On HDFS, BGL, and Thunderbird datasets, RankShift performs comparably to autoencoder methods (0.999 vs 1.000 AUROC on HDFS) while being 137x smaller. It successfully detects rare-category shifts invisible to count-based monitoring, achieving 0.787 AUROC vs 0.771 for autoencoders in fixed-volume experiments.
AI.conclusion: RankShift provides an efficient, training-free solution for detecting distributional shifts in categorical log data, addressing a critical gap in existing monitoring systems while maintaining low resource requirements and reliable false-alarm control.

title: SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning
comment: accepted to The 3rd AI for Math Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, yet the mathematically meaningful skills underlying their reasoning remain underexplored. We introduce \texttt{SHAPE}, a framework that analyzes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories through two lenses developed in mathematics education: (1) semantic spaces: the model's evolving mathematical interpretations of a problem (e.g., algebraic, geometric), and (2) heuristics: the specific mathematical actions taken within those spaces (e.g., simplifying the problem, working backward). We first use \texttt{SHAPE} to analyze the reasoning patterns of various models. Our findings reveal that the mathematical heuristics employed by a model better explain final answer correctness than traditional CoT features. Furthermore, models are likely to reach correct solutions by concentrating their reasoning effort within a few semantic spaces rather than exploring many disparate ones -- a pattern consistent with human behavior. Next, we utilize the \texttt{SHAPE} lens to evaluate whether post-training truly enhances mathematical proficiency. We find that reinforcement learning induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. Lastly, we post-train LLMs by promoting diverse heuristics and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving accuracy. Overall, \texttt{SHAPE} provides a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework for decoding LLM reasoning and offers a new path toward post-training LLMs for math reasoning. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/holi-lab/SHAPE-of-CoT

AI.tldr: SHAPE is a framework that analyzes LLM mathematical reasoning by examining semantic spaces (mathematical interpretations) and heuristics (specific actions), showing that heuristic usage better predicts correctness than traditional CoT features, and that concentrating reasoning within few semantic spaces leads to better performance.
AI.motivation: While LLMs perform well on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, there's limited understanding of the actual mathematical skills underlying their reasoning. The authors aim to provide a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework to decode LLM reasoning patterns in mathematics.
AI.method: The SHAPE framework analyzes Chain-of-Thought trajectories using two lenses from mathematics education: semantic spaces (model's evolving mathematical interpretations like algebraic or geometric) and heuristics (specific mathematical actions like simplifying or working backward). The approach includes analyzing reasoning patterns, evaluating post-training effects, and post-training LLMs to promote diverse heuristics.
AI.result: 1) Mathematical heuristics better explain final answer correctness than traditional CoT features. 2) Models succeed by concentrating reasoning within few semantic spaces rather than exploring many disparate ones (consistent with human behavior). 3) Reinforcement learning induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. 4) Post-training LLMs by promoting diverse heuristics improves accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SHAPE provides a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework for decoding LLM reasoning and offers a new approach for post-training LLMs for mathematical reasoning, with potential applications in improving mathematical proficiency through targeted heuristic promotion.

title: Detect Before You Attribute: Cascade Failure Attribution for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown strong potential in solving complex tasks through multi-step reasoning, yet they remain vulnerable to execution failures. Accurate failure attribution is therefore critical for improving agent reliability. Existing topology- and spectrum-based methods exploit trajectory structures but often overlook fine-grained semantics, while LLM-based attribution methods capture semantic cues but suffer from long-context degradation over lengthy trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose DUOTRACE, a plug-and-play detection filter for LLM-based failure attribution. DUOTRACE follows a detect-before-attribute paradigm: it first detects anomalous executions and then supplies focused trajectory evidence to downstream LLM-based attribution methods. For effective VAE-based anomaly detection on agent trajectories, DUOTRACE integrates dual-view semantic-structural node representations, a Tree-LSTM-based trajectory encoder, and prefix-chain- and LLM-based data augmentation to handle heterogeneous nodes, hierarchical execution structures, and limited failure data. Experiments with six LLM-based attribution baselines show that DUOTRACE improves agent-level and step-level attribution accuracy by 8.7% and 7.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: DUOTRACE is a plug-and-play detection filter that improves LLM-based agent failure attribution by detecting anomalous executions first and providing focused trajectory evidence to downstream attribution methods.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are vulnerable to execution failures, and accurate failure attribution is critical for improving agent reliability. Existing methods have limitations: topology/spectrum-based methods overlook fine-grained semantics, while LLM-based attribution methods suffer from long-context degradation over lengthy trajectories.
AI.method: DUOTRACE follows a detect-before-attribute paradigm. It integrates: 1) dual-view semantic-structural node representations for VAE-based anomaly detection, 2) Tree-LSTM-based trajectory encoder for hierarchical execution structures, and 3) prefix-chain- and LLM-based data augmentation to handle heterogeneous nodes and limited failure data.
AI.result: Experiments with six LLM-based attribution baselines show that DUOTRACE improves agent-level attribution accuracy by 8.7% and step-level attribution accuracy by 7.0%.
AI.conclusion: DUOTRACE effectively addresses the limitations of existing failure attribution methods by combining semantic-structural anomaly detection with focused evidence supply, significantly improving attribution accuracy for LLM-based agents.

title: Revisiting the Provable-Auditable Privacy Gap of DP-SGD
comment: The code for this paper can be found here: https://github.com/pineappleEnthusiast/empirical-privacy-defense
summary:
Differential privacy (DP) has traditionally been used to provide theoretical upper bounds on an algorithm's stability to changing its training data. In modern private machine learning applications, achieving strong tradeoffs between utility and theoretical privacy is challenging, and thus one may optimistically hope that existing theoretical privacy analyses are loose. Recent work on privacy auditing has adopted a dual viewpoint, instead lower bounding the true privacy of an algorithm by constructing empirical distinguishing events. The auditing literature has thus far yielded a pessimistic outlook on the looseness of theoretical privacy bounds for DP-SGD, the de facto private training method in modern ML, as nearly-matching empirical lower bounds have been achieved under various threat models [NHSBTJCT23, AC24, CBP25].
  In this work, we propose the empirical privacy lower bound of an algorithm as a concrete metric to optimize for, complementary to the theoretical upper bound. We give a lightweight defense framework that generically augments optimization methods in the ML pipeline to have significantly-improved empirical privacy on standard benchmarks. Moreover, we show that our framework comes at no theoretical privacy cost when augmenting DP-SGD, unlike previously-proposed defenses against membership inference attacks. We evaluate our defense against a broad range of audit constructions, models, and datasets to demonstrate its flexibility.

AI.tldr: A defense framework that improves empirical privacy lower bounds for ML algorithms while maintaining theoretical privacy guarantees, particularly effective for DP-SGD with no privacy cost.
AI.motivation: Traditional differential privacy provides theoretical upper bounds, but recent auditing work shows these bounds may be loose for practical algorithms like DP-SGD. The paper aims to bridge this gap by optimizing for empirical privacy lower bounds rather than just theoretical bounds.
AI.method: Proposes a lightweight defense framework that generically augments optimization methods in ML pipelines to improve empirical privacy. The framework maintains theoretical privacy guarantees when applied to DP-SGD, unlike previous defenses against membership inference attacks.
AI.result: The defense framework significantly improves empirical privacy on standard benchmarks across various audit constructions, models, and datasets. It achieves this without compromising theoretical privacy when augmenting DP-SGD.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully introduces a practical approach to optimizing for empirical privacy lower bounds, providing a defense framework that enhances real-world privacy while preserving theoretical guarantees, particularly for the widely-used DP-SGD algorithm.

title: Leveraging Generative AI to Design Accessible Interactive Visualizations for Undergraduate Mathematics: A Six-Phase Workflow
summary: Interactive visualizations support conceptual understanding in undergraduate mathematics, but building them has required programming expertise most instructors lack. Using a design-based research approach, we develop, deploy, and evaluate a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control) that uses generative AI to build WCAG~2.2 Level~AA compliant visualizations without programming. The six phases structure every prompt, scaffold the AI's code generation, and define where human verification is applied. We ask whether the structure reliably yields correct and accessible tools, whether it runs both backward (reverse-engineering prompts from a finished tool) and forward (generating a tool from a plain-language idea), and what verification each phase requires. Across four deployed tools spanning calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, we evaluate mathematical correctness against closed forms, accessibility through automated and manual screen-reader testing, and the errors that recurred. The structure produces structurally complete first-pass tools, but human verification remains mandatory at every phase: each output must be checked for mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical fit before the next phase begins. The workflow is platform-independent and serves both instructors and students.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a six-phase workflow using generative AI to create accessible mathematics visualizations without programming, requiring human verification at each phase for correctness and accessibility.
AI.motivation: Interactive visualizations help with math understanding but require programming skills most instructors lack. Current barriers include technical expertise needed to build accessible tools, limiting adoption in undergraduate mathematics education.
AI.method: Design-based research approach with a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control) using generative AI to create WCAG 2.2 Level AA compliant visualizations. The workflow includes human verification at each phase and was tested across calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations tools.
AI.result: The structure produces structurally complete first-pass tools but requires mandatory human verification at every phase. The workflow works both forward (generating from ideas) and backward (reverse-engineering from finished tools), but each phase output must be checked for mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical fit before proceeding.
AI.conclusion: The AI-assisted workflow enables non-programming instructors to create accessible mathematics visualizations, but human verification remains essential throughout. The approach is platform-independent and serves both instructors and students in undergraduate mathematics education.

title: SimCRAFT: Distilling Remote Sensing Agents via Synthetic Trajectories and Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning
summary: The unprecedented surge in Earth observation data volume and diversity has exposed a critical bottleneck for traditional manual workflows, catalyzing the emergence of Remote Sensing (RS) Agents. However, the practical deployment of these advanced agents is severely hindered by their heavy reliance on large-scale general-purpose LLMs, which lack deep domain expertise and impose prohibitive infrastructure demands. To resolve this, we propose SimCRAFT, a model-agnostic framework that distills sophisticated RS orchestration capabilities into a compact 7B-scale model. Addressing data scarcity, we first pair a multiagent synthesis engine with a Mock Execution Engine that checks schema correctness, inter-tool dependencies, and sensor/tool compatibility, producing SimRS-14k, a large-scale, constraint-validated workflow planning corpus. Second, we propose Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (CRAFT) that finetunes the model to reason analogically by adapting retrieved Standard Operating Procedures to novel queries under a noise-robust objective, generalizing RAFT to multi-step RS workflow planning without mechanical copying. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SimCRAFT-7B significantly outperforms openweights LLMs and rivals advanced closedsource models and specialized RS agents, while reproducing across three 7B backbones. This work contributes a competitive open-weights baseline for lightweight RS intelligence, enabling efficient autonomous deployment under resource-constrained or resource-conserving conditions.

AI.tldr: SimCRAFT is a framework that distills remote sensing orchestration capabilities into a compact 7B model using synthetic data generation and contextual retrieval-augmented fine-tuning, enabling efficient RS agent deployment without large general-purpose LLMs.
AI.motivation: The surge in Earth observation data has exposed limitations of traditional manual workflows, but current RS agents rely too heavily on large general-purpose LLMs that lack domain expertise and have prohibitive infrastructure demands, hindering practical deployment.
AI.method: 1) Created SimRS-14k dataset using multiagent synthesis engine with Mock Execution Engine to validate workflow constraints; 2) Developed Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (CRAFT) that adapts retrieved procedures to novel queries with noise-robust training, extending RAFT to multi-step RS workflow planning.
AI.result: SimCRAFT-7B significantly outperforms open-weights LLMs and rivals advanced closed-source models and specialized RS agents, while demonstrating reproducibility across three different 7B backbones.
AI.conclusion: SimCRAFT provides a competitive open-weights baseline for lightweight RS intelligence, enabling efficient autonomous deployment under resource-constrained conditions, advancing practical RS agent deployment.

title: From the Loss Landscape to Diverse Feature Learning in Neural Networks
comment: PhD dissertation. This article draws from arXiv:2408.11804
summary:
Over the course of the last decade, neural networks have grown from an academic curiosity to moving the markets of nations. Despite this explosion in both research and deployment, relatively little is understood about how they achieve the solutions they do. This is both scientifically relevant, and pressing for society. When neural networks make decisions across self-driving, construction, law, hiring and health, there have been and will continue to be unintended consequences.
  However, attempting to generalize the failures of the largest and most important production systems makes for a very difficult task. Yet signs of these failures exist at all scales of neural networks, so we should be able to study a much more tractable setting. All neural networks must undergo an optimization process, called training, to be useful. To a great degree, understanding neural networks is understanding their optimization: through what process and exposure to which data did they arrive at their results. Yet our knowledge on this topic as a field is quite imprecise. In particular, a curious phenomenon called mode connectivity, the ability to connect neural networks in the loss surface, defies explanation entirely.
  This dissertation elucidates, explains and exploits this special structure in the loss landscape...

AI.tldr: This dissertation investigates mode connectivity - the ability to connect neural networks through low-loss paths in the loss landscape - to better understand neural network optimization and behavior.
AI.motivation: While neural networks have achieved remarkable success, their decision-making processes remain poorly understood, which is scientifically relevant and socially pressing as these systems are deployed in critical domains like healthcare, law, and autonomous vehicles. The field lacks precise understanding of neural network optimization, particularly the unexplained phenomenon of mode connectivity.
AI.method: The dissertation approaches the problem by studying mode connectivity as a tractable setting to understand neural network failures and optimization processes. By analyzing the ability to connect neural networks through low-loss paths in the loss surface, the research aims to elucidate the special structure in neural network loss landscapes.
AI.result: The dissertation elucidates, explains, and exploits the special structure revealed by mode connectivity in neural network loss landscapes, though specific experimental results from the full dissertation are not provided in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: Understanding mode connectivity provides crucial insights into neural network optimization and behavior, offering a more tractable approach to studying neural network failures and decision-making processes that could ultimately improve their reliability and transparency in real-world applications.

title: Integrating Triaxial IMU Sensors and Ensemble Learning for Effective Parkinson Disease Severity Classification
summary: Parkinson disease PD is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that can have a significant impact on motor performance resulting in the appearance of symptoms such as tremors rigidity postural instabilities and bradykinesia. Timely clinical treatment disease management and quality life of the patients are closely linked to early and appropriate identification of PD. Over the past few years the growth of wearable sensor technology and artificial intelligence AI have made it possible to create noninvasive and data driven disease detection methods. This paper proposes a comparative system using artificial intelligence to detect Parkinsons disease by analyzing the motion and tremor data captured by an inertial measurement unit IMU. The data comprises the signals of the acceleration and gyroscope sensors measuring movement in three directions X Y and Z. The signs and symptoms provide helpful information about subtle motor deficits associated with PD. Several classification models like Support Vector Machine SVM Logistic Regression LR KNearest Neighbors KNN Decision Tree DT Extreme Gradient Boosting XGBoost and Light Gradient Boosting Machine LightGBM were used to compare their effectiveness. The Logistic Regression model had a performance around 75 percent in all evaluation metrics and KNearest Neighbours KNN around 90 percent. The support vector machine SVM performed almost 94 percent whereas the performance of classifiers such as Decision Tree and XGBoost was close to 96 percent and overall classification efficacy respectively. LightGBM model performs consistently at the best rank among all of the evaluated methods having Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1score of around 97 percent. The results show that the proposed machine learning approach offers an accurate and effective predictive capability in the classification of PD severity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-based system using IMU motion data to detect Parkinson's disease severity, comparing multiple machine learning classifiers where LightGBM achieved the best performance at 97% across all metrics.
AI.motivation: Early detection of Parkinson's disease is crucial for timely treatment and quality of life improvement, and recent advances in wearable sensors and AI enable non-invasive, data-driven detection methods.
AI.method: The study uses IMU sensor data (acceleration and gyroscope in X, Y, Z directions) to capture motion and tremor patterns, then applies multiple classification models including SVM, Logistic Regression, KNN, Decision Tree, XGBoost, and LightGBM for comparative analysis.
AI.result: LightGBM performed best with ~97% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Decision Tree and XGBoost achieved ~96%, SVM ~94%, KNN ~90%, and Logistic Regression ~75% across evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed machine learning approach using IMU data offers an accurate and effective predictive capability for classifying Parkinson's disease severity, with LightGBM demonstrating superior performance among all evaluated methods.

title: HiRS-Agent: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent System for Reliable Long-Horizon Remote Sensing Task Solving
summary: Recent advances in large language models and multimodal models have pushed remote sensing (RS) processing from simple perception models to agentic systems designed to tackle complex, long-horizon RS tasks. However, existing systems often rely on monolithic decision-making frameworks, which fail to accommodate the multi-stage, interdependent nature of RS tasks. This centralized approach leads to challenges such as unstable task execution, incorrect tool usage, and error propagation across stages. To address these issues, we propose HiRS-Agent, a hierarchical multi-agent system for long-horizon RS task solving. HiRS-Agent adopts a two-level collaborative architecture: the Manager Layer handles dynamic routing, step-level verification, replanning, and termination control, while the Specialist Layer organizes domain-specific tools according to the RS workflow and is responsible for subtask reasoning and tool execution. To further enhance the system's capability, we introduce a two-stage supervised tuning strategy and a verification-guided hierarchical reinforcement learning stage to jointly optimize coordination and tool-use policies. Experiments on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo show that HiRS-Agent substantially improves long-horizon tool-use capability and final-task correctness, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured multi-agent collaboration for reliable RS agents. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/IntelliSensing/HiRS-Agent.

AI.tldr: HiRS-Agent is a hierarchical multi-agent system for long-horizon remote sensing tasks that uses a two-level collaborative architecture with Manager and Specialist layers, optimized through supervised tuning and reinforcement learning, achieving improved task correctness and tool-use capability.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing systems use monolithic decision-making frameworks that fail to handle the multi-stage, interdependent nature of RS tasks, leading to unstable execution, incorrect tool usage, and error propagation across stages.
AI.method: Proposes HiRS-Agent with two-level architecture: Manager Layer handles dynamic routing, verification, replanning, and termination; Specialist Layer organizes domain-specific tools and handles subtask reasoning/tool execution. Uses two-stage supervised tuning and verification-guided hierarchical reinforcement learning to optimize coordination and tool-use policies.
AI.result: Experiments on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo show HiRS-Agent substantially improves long-horizon tool-use capability and final-task correctness, demonstrating effectiveness of structured multi-agent collaboration for reliable RS agents.
AI.conclusion: HiRS-Agent's hierarchical multi-agent approach effectively addresses limitations of monolithic systems in remote sensing, providing a structured solution for complex, long-horizon RS tasks with improved reliability and correctness.

title: Continuity-Free Near-Minimax Leading-Order Regret for CVaR-UCBVI
summary: For finite-horizon tabular CVaR reinforcement learning, prior work proves a $\widetilde{O}(τ^{-1}\sqrt{SAK})$ leading regret bound for arbitrary normalized return laws and the sharper $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{SAK/τ})$ rate under a density lower bound. We show that the same Bernstein CVaR-UCBVI algorithm attains the sharper rate without continuity assumptions. The key is a selected-budget self-bound: the conditional variance of the episode shortfall is at most $τ$ plus the value-estimation width. Substitution into the original Bernstein decomposition yields, with high probability, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{SAK/τ}+(SAHK^{1/4}+S^2AH)/τ)$ regret for arbitrary normalized return laws, including atomic, mixed, and continuous laws. The $τ^{-1/2}$ leading term matches the expected-regret minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Thus Bernstein CVaR-UCBVI is minimax-optimal over the full return-law class in the leading-order regime; the lower-order terms retain their $τ^{-1}$ dependence.

AI.tldr: Bernstein CVaR-UCBVI algorithm achieves minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{SAK/\tau})$ regret for CVaR reinforcement learning without requiring continuity assumptions or density lower bounds, matching the expected-regret minimax lower bound.
AI.motivation: Prior work had two regret bounds for finite-horizon tabular CVaR RL: $\widetilde{O}(\tau^{-1}\sqrt{SAK})$ for arbitrary normalized return laws and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{SAK/\tau})$ under a density lower bound. The authors aim to achieve the sharper rate without requiring continuity assumptions.
AI.method: The authors use the Bernstein CVaR-UCBVI algorithm with a key innovation called "selected-budget self-bound": showing that the conditional variance of the episode shortfall is at most $\tau$ plus the value-estimation width. This is substituted into the original Bernstein decomposition to derive the improved bound.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{SAK/\tau} + (SAHK^{1/4} + S^2AH)/\tau)$ regret for arbitrary normalized return laws (atomic, mixed, and continuous). The leading $\tau^{-1/2}$ term matches the expected-regret minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: Bernstein CVaR-UCBVI is minimax-optimal over the full return-law class in the leading-order regime. The algorithm achieves the sharper regret rate without continuity assumptions, though lower-order terms retain their $\tau^{-1}$ dependence.

title: C3-UniMM: Causal Cycle-Consistent Unified Multimodal Modeling via Super Alignment and Shared Decoding Space
summary: Unified Multimodal Models aim to achieve any-to-any understanding and generation across arbitrary modalities. However, existing methods primarily rely on modeling implicit statistical correlations and lack cross-modal structural consistency constraints. This deficiency leads to profound issues, including semantic drift, poor compositional generalization, and instability under interventions. In this paper, we propose C3-UniMM, a unified multimodal modeling framework based on Causal Cycle Consistency and Super Alignment. Specifically, we introduce a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) as a shared cross-modal semantic space and design unified multimodal encoding blocks, enabling understanding and generation to be synergistically optimized within the identical causal semantic structure. Furthermore, we propose a Unified Decoding Space to enforce structural preservation and semantic invertibility during the cross-modal generation process. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances both the invertibility and mechanism invariance of cross-modal mappings. Extensive experimental results across multiple understanding, generation, and compositional generalization tasks indicate that C3-UniMM substantially outperforms existing unified multimodal baselines.

AI.tldr: C3-UniMM is a unified multimodal model framework that uses causal cycle consistency and structural alignment to address semantic drift and improve cross-modal understanding and generation.
AI.motivation: Existing unified multimodal models rely on implicit statistical correlations without structural consistency constraints, leading to semantic drift, poor compositional generalization, and instability under interventions.
AI.method: Proposes C3-UniMM framework based on Causal Cycle Consistency and Super Alignment. Introduces Structured Latent Causal Graph as shared semantic space, unified multimodal encoding blocks, and Unified Decoding Space for structural preservation and semantic invertibility.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows enhanced invertibility and mechanism invariance of cross-modal mappings. Extensive experiments across multiple understanding, generation, and compositional generalization tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements over existing unified multimodal baselines.
AI.conclusion: C3-UniMM effectively addresses structural consistency issues in unified multimodal models through causal modeling and alignment, achieving superior performance across various multimodal tasks while maintaining semantic stability.

title: V2TATC: A Joint Voice-Trajectory Embedding Framework and Dataset for Air Traffic Controller Situational Awareness
summary: As air traffic volumes in the National Airspace System continue to expand, in particular in the low altitude airspaces, the need for scalable decision support tools used by air traffic controllers will also require more development. This article introduces Voice-to-Trajectory for Air Traffic Control, a joint voice communication-flight trajectory data embedding framework, that can be a component of situational awareness in congested airspaces, and assist the development of tools for ATC as they reason in real-time over Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast trajectories, or the intent expressed by pilots in natural language. We show that these data modalities are not independent and represent a common physical referent: an aircraft flying through the airspace. V2TATC maps a voice instruction and the trajectory of the addressed aircraft to nearby points in a single latent space that can be queried in both directions. It combines a self-supervised trajectory encoder, a frozen large-scale speech encoder, a contrastive joint embedding, and a bijective lifting via normalizing flows. We demonstrate V2TATC's effectiveness on the San Francisco Bay Area, for its concentration of major airports, and its mix of commercial and general aviation low altitude traffic. Lastly, we release a novel paired voice-trajectory dataset, and report experiments on cross-modal retrieval, ablations, and latent-space analysis.

AI.tldr: V2TATC is a voice-to-trajectory embedding framework for air traffic control that combines voice communications with flight trajectories in a shared latent space, enabling cross-modal retrieval between controller instructions and aircraft trajectories.
AI.motivation: With increasing air traffic volumes in low altitude airspaces, there's a need for scalable decision support tools for air traffic controllers. Current systems treat voice communications and flight trajectory data as separate modalities, but they both refer to the same physical reality of aircraft movement.
AI.method: V2TATC uses a joint embedding framework combining: 1) a self-supervised trajectory encoder, 2) a frozen large-scale speech encoder, 3) contrastive joint embedding, and 4) bijective lifting via normalizing flows. This maps voice instructions and aircraft trajectories to nearby points in a single latent space that can be queried bidirectionally.
AI.result: Demonstrated effectiveness on San Francisco Bay Area airspace with its concentration of major airports and mix of commercial/general aviation traffic. The paper includes release of a novel paired voice-trajectory dataset and reports experiments on cross-modal retrieval, ablations, and latent-space analysis.
AI.conclusion: The V2TATC framework successfully integrates voice communications and flight trajectories, showing these data modalities are not independent but represent common physical referents. This can enhance situational awareness and support development of real-time ATC decision tools.

title: MedTVL: Harnessing Vision and Language for Medical Time Series Classification
summary: Recent advancements in multimodal learning for medical time series (MedTS) classification highlight the benefits of integrating complementary modalities for clinical decision. However, existing methods typically focus on bi-modal interactions (e.g., time series and text), leaving the tri-modal synergy between time series, vision, and language largely unexplored. Inspired by diagnostic practice synergizing numerical assessment, visual inspection and clinical context, we introduce MedTVL, a text-guided dual-pathway architecture tailored for MedTS classification. Specifically, it synergizes a convolution-based temporal pathway for fine-grained temporal dynamics from raw numerical sequences and a transformer-based visual pathway for holistic morphological structures from time-series-derived images. Such combination of cross-modal and architectural heterogeneity provides a comprehensive diagnostic perspective. To further resolve potential diagnostic ambiguity, both pathways are guided by adaptive medical textual semantics. Finally, a Mixture-of-Experts mechanism dynamically routes each instance to specialized fusion experts, capturing instance-specific reliance on the temporal and visual pathway outputs. In addition, MedTVL supports multimodal contrastive learning to mitigate the clinical label scarcity challenge. Extensive experiments across multiple medical datasets and tasks, spanning supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings, demonstrate the superiority and transferability of MedTVL, highlighting its potential for robust clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedTVL introduces a tri-modal fusion framework for medical time series classification that combines temporal data (numerical sequences), visual representations (time-series-derived images), and textual guidance (clinical context) using a dual-pathway architecture with adaptive routing and contrastive learning.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal medical time series methods focus on bi-modal interactions (time series + text), leaving tri-modal synergy (time series + vision + language) unexplored despite diagnostic practice synergizing numerical assessment, visual inspection, and clinical context.
AI.method: Text-guided dual-pathway architecture with: 1) Convolution-based temporal pathway for fine-grained temporal dynamics from raw numerical sequences, 2) Transformer-based visual pathway for holistic morphological structures from time-series-derived images, 3) Adaptive medical textual semantics guidance, and 4) Mixture-of-Experts mechanism for dynamic instance routing to specialized fusion experts. Also supports multimodal contrastive learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple medical datasets and tasks demonstrate superiority and transferability in supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings, showing robust clinical decision support potential.
AI.conclusion: MedTVL successfully explores tri-modal synergy for medical time series classification, providing comprehensive diagnostic perspectives through heterogeneous cross-modal integration and adaptive routing, effectively addressing clinical label scarcity and diagnostic ambiguity challenges.

title: Effective Graph and Rank-based Contextual Embeddings for Textual and Multimedia Data
comment: Published in International Joint Conference on Neural Networks, 2025 (IJCNN 2025)
summary: In a data-driven world, efficiently organizing and mapping relationships between objects is crucial. Graphs are powerful tools for modeling these connections, being widely used in social networks, telecommunications, and biology. However, graph-based methods often face high computational costs, particularly in memory and space usage. To address this, graph embedding techniques, also referred to as Network Representation Learning, encode graph information into lower-dimensional representations while preserving structural aspects. Traditional methods, however, lack interpretable dimensions. RaDE (Rank Diffusion Embedding) introduces a new approach using rank-based information, with a key step being the selection of a representative subset of nodes to provide interpretability for its dimensions and improve retrieval tasks. Despite its potential, RaDE's original proposal did not fully explore the effectiveness of representative subset selection across different classes or evaluate embeddings in tasks like classification and clustering. Inspired by RaDE, this work introduces GRaCE (Graph and Rank-based Contextual Embeddings), a fully unsupervised framework that generates interpretable embeddings by leveraging robust rank-based measures for representative subset selection and node embedding. GRaCE surpasses RaDE and Original Features across diverse datasets, including textual and image collections, excelling in retrieval, classification, and clustering tasks, considering state-of-the-art Transformer models as feature descriptors and Graph Convolutional Networks models in classification tasks.

AI.tldr: GRaCE is a fully unsupervised framework that generates interpretable graph embeddings using rank-based measures for representative subset selection, outperforming previous methods in retrieval, classification, and clustering tasks across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional graph embedding methods often lack interpretable dimensions and face high computational costs. While RaDE introduced rank-based embeddings, it didn't fully explore representative subset selection effectiveness or evaluate embeddings in classification/clustering tasks.
AI.method: GRaCE uses robust rank-based measures for both representative subset selection and node embedding generation in a fully unsupervised framework. It builds upon RaDE's concepts but enhances them with better subset selection and broader task evaluation.
AI.result: GRaCE surpasses both RaDE and Original Features across diverse datasets (textual and image collections) in retrieval, classification, and clustering tasks, even when compared against state-of-the-art Transformer models as feature descriptors and Graph Convolutional Networks.
AI.conclusion: GRaCE provides an effective, interpretable graph embedding framework that addresses limitations of previous methods, demonstrating superior performance across multiple tasks and dataset types while maintaining unsupervised operation.

title: RegDivergence-101: An LLM Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdiction Regulatory Contradiction Detection in Life Sciences
summary: Pharmaceutical sponsors developing a drug for both the United States and the European Union must reconcile guidance issued independently by the FDA and the EMA. Where the two agencies require substantively the same thing, a sponsor can file once; where they diverge, a single trial design risks rejection in one region; where one agency is silent on a point the other regulates, the sponsor must infer obligations. Today this reconciliation is performed manually by regulatory-affairs experts. We introduce cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection: given an FDA requirement and an EMA requirement on the same topic, classify their relationship as AGREE, DIVERGE, or SILENT. SILENT is inherently directional (SILENT_FDA vs. SILENT_EMA); we record direction per pair and report per-direction F1 alongside the collapsed label. We release RegDivergence-101, a 101-pair expert-grounded pilot evaluation benchmark (labels grounded in three peer-reviewed FDA/EMA comparison studies and primary FDA/EMA/ICH guidance text; dual-annotation inter-annotator kappa = 0.85), and systematically characterise a four-method baseline hierarchy: lexical heuristic (0.511 macro-F1, 95% CI [0.411-0.605]), NLI cross-encoder (0.233), obligation-level Graph-RAG (0.663 [0.570-0.747]), and flat LLM judge / Claude Haiku (0.830 [0.747-0.908]). Three directional observations emerge at pilot scale (n = 101): SILENT is semantically detectable but invisible to entailment-only formulations; pair-level obligation graphs improve over lexical methods but trail flat-LLM context (CIs partially overlapping); and corpus-level graph construction is the indicated architectural target for large-scale silent-detection. RegDivergence-101 is a pilot release establishing the task formulation and baseline hierarchy; four unrepresented regulatory domains and an expansion roadmap are described in Section 7.

AI.tldr: A framework for automatically detecting regulatory divergence between FDA and EMA requirements using NLP techniques, with a pilot benchmark showing LLMs outperform other methods.
AI.motivation: Pharmaceutical companies face challenges reconciling FDA and EMA regulations manually; automated detection of agreement, divergence, or silence between requirements would streamline drug development across jurisdictions.
AI.method: Created RegDivergence-101 benchmark with expert-grounded labels; tested four baseline methods: lexical heuristics, NLI cross-encoders, obligation-level Graph-RAG, and flat LLM judges (Claude Haiku).
AI.result: LLM judges achieved best performance (0.830 macro-F1), followed by Graph-RAG (0.663), lexical heuristics (0.511), and NLI cross-encoders (0.233). SILENT relationships are detectable but require more than entailment-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: Flat LLM context outperforms specialized architectures for this task, but corpus-level graph construction is the promising direction for large-scale silent-detection, with RegDivergence-101 establishing foundational task formulation.

title: Context-Aware Interpretable Representations for Retrieval and Graph Convolutional Network Classification
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Multimedia Retrieval (ICMR 2026)
summary: The advances in visual information modeling and representation during the last decades are remarkable, mainly supported by Convolutional Neural Networks, Transformer-based, and Foundation Models. Despite this progress, critical challenges regarding the nature of similarity assessment and model transparency have been neglected. A primary concern is the Geometric Gap, where traditional pairwise measures fail to capture the intrinsic geometry of the dataset manifold. Furthermore, the Interpretability Gap persists, as representations often lack alignment with human cognition. Therefore, how to provide interpretability to representations while maintaining low dimensionality and high effectiveness in downstream tasks remains an open challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised framework that integrates Manifold Learning strategies with Rank-based Interpretable Graph Embeddings. Our approach effectively bridges these gaps by first characterizing the contextual information of the dataset through manifold analysis and subsequently generating sparse, self-explainable embeddings. The proposed approach employs a flexible formulation, allowing different Manifold Learning and Representation Learning strategies. Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets and features demonstrates that our Context-Aware representations not only provide intrinsic interpretability and dimensionality reduction but also maintain or enhance effectiveness in downstream tasks, specifically in image retrieval and semi-supervised classification using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs).

AI.tldr: A novel unsupervised framework integrates manifold learning with rank-based graph embeddings to address geometric and interpretability gaps in visual representation learning.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in visual modeling, critical challenges remain: the Geometric Gap (pairwise measures fail to capture dataset manifold geometry) and the Interpretability Gap (representations lack alignment with human cognition). There's a need for interpretable representations that maintain low dimensionality and high effectiveness in downstream tasks.
AI.method: Proposes an unsupervised framework integrating Manifold Learning strategies with Rank-based Interpretable Graph Embeddings. First characterizes contextual information through manifold analysis, then generates sparse, self-explainable embeddings. Uses flexible formulation allowing different Manifold Learning and Representation Learning strategies.
AI.result: Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets and features demonstrates that Context-Aware representations provide intrinsic interpretability and dimensionality reduction while maintaining or enhancing effectiveness in downstream tasks (image retrieval and semi-supervised classification using GCNs).
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively bridges geometric and interpretability gaps by generating interpretable, low-dimensional representations that perform well in downstream applications, offering a solution to the open challenge of interpretable representation learning.

title: TPvG: A Moral Decision Framework for Large Language Models from One-Shot to Sequential Feedback
summary: Existing LLM moral evaluations typically present models with isolated moral vignettes and elicit a single-shot decision, neglecting a factor known to profoundly influence human moral behavior: consequence feedback. We introduce TPvG (Text-based Pain-versus-Gain), adapted from a human moral paradigm, which embeds consequence feedback into an everyday moral dilemma of not harming others versus maximising self-gain. TPvG comprises five moral decision tasks, progressing from minimal-context one-shot choices to sequential decisions with explicit consequence feedback. Our results show that LLM moral decisions were strongly affected by decision format (one-shot versus sequential), and explicit receiver feedback produced heterogeneous effects across models. Furthermore, LLM responses to explicit receiver feedback diverged from the human reference pattern, suggesting potentially different decision processes. These findings highlight the need to evaluate whether LLM moral behavior remains stable in high-stakes interactive settings.

AI.tldr: LLM moral evaluation needs to include consequence feedback, not just one-shot decisions. A new test (TPvG) shows LLM decisions change with feedback and differ from human moral patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM moral evaluations typically present isolated moral vignettes with single-shot decisions, neglecting consequence feedback which profoundly influences human moral behavior.
AI.method: Introduced TPvG (Text-based Pain-versus-Gain), adapted from human moral paradigms, embedding consequence feedback into everyday moral dilemmas. TPvG comprises five moral decision tasks progressing from minimal-context one-shot choices to sequential decisions with explicit consequence feedback.
AI.result: LLM moral decisions were strongly affected by decision format (one-shot vs sequential), and explicit receiver feedback produced heterogeneous effects across models. LLM responses to explicit receiver feedback diverged from human reference patterns, suggesting potentially different decision processes.
AI.conclusion: These findings highlight the need to evaluate whether LLM moral behavior remains stable in high-stakes interactive settings, as current evaluation methods may not capture how LLMs behave in realistic moral contexts.

title: Hybrid Semantic Context-Enhanced Ensemble Learning for Wind Power Ramp-Event Forecasting and Uncertainty-Aware Evaluation
summary: Wind power ramp events which are sudden, large swings in turbine output over short windows are difficult to estimate, and standard models often miss them. Hybrid forecasting approach is built which augments semantic context to ramp-event forecast. Rather than applying an extensive language model directly to predict turbine operating data, we have implemented a pipeline where turbine operating data is converted to simplified text, which is then converted to dense embeddings to be used as inputs for ensemble models incorporated with other features. Testing runs are performed at multiple intervals within the SDWPF dataset, including 10-minute, 30-minute, and 60- minute horizons, with ramp events constituting the highest change in future power output. We check robustness against autoregressive, LSTM, and GRU baselines plus several ensemble configurations, using Diebold-Mariano tests and bootstrap confidence intervals, and we vary the ramp threshold, compress the embeddings with PCA, and validate externally on Kaggle SCADA and NREL data with uncertainty-aware scoring. The semantic-context features produce negligible yet statistically significant gains over the baselines in multiple paired ensemble runs, most clearly at the 30- and 60-minute horizons where these gains hold across different ramp-threshold definitions, and PCA compression helps in some longer-horizon cases. The best context- augmented ensembles rank near the top overall, though the GRU model still posts the lowest ramp-event RMSE at 30 and 60 minutes. External tests confirm the error reduction generalizes across datasets, but the size of the gain depends on both model and dataset. Prediction intervals cover most test cases well but weaken during ramp events, pointing to a localized shift in the data distribution.

AI.tldr: A hybrid forecasting approach uses semantic context features from turbine data converted to text embeddings to improve wind power ramp event prediction, showing statistically significant but modest gains over traditional models at 30-60 minute horizons.
AI.motivation: Wind power ramp events (sudden large swings in turbine output) are difficult to estimate and standard forecasting models often miss them, creating a need for improved prediction methods.
AI.method: Developed a pipeline that converts turbine operating data to simplified text, generates dense embeddings from the text, and uses these as semantic context features in ensemble models combined with other features. Tested at 10-, 30-, and 60-minute horizons on SDWPF dataset, compared against autoregressive, LSTM, and GRU baselines with Diebold-Mariano tests and bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Semantic-context features produced statistically significant but modest gains over baselines, most clearly at 30- and 60-minute horizons across different ramp-threshold definitions. PCA compression helped in longer-horizon cases. GRU still had lowest ramp-event RMSE at 30 and 60 minutes. External validation on Kaggle SCADA and NREL data confirmed error reduction generalizes across datasets, though gain size varies. Prediction intervals cover most cases but weaken during ramp events.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-context features provide measurable but limited improvement in wind power ramp event forecasting, with gains most evident at longer horizons. The approach shows promise for enhancing ensemble models, though traditional GRU models still achieve best absolute performance for ramp-event RMSE.

title: InternReviewer & InternAdvocate: Objective Reward and Evaluation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning in Peer Review and Rebuttal
summary: Generating professional scholarly content, such as peer reviews and rebuttals, requires an intricate synergy between domain reasoning and factual grounding. This work presents a comprehensive framework for the development and evaluation of specialized scholarly agents, InternReviewer and InternAdvocate. We first establish a large-scale, high-quality scholarly dataset and integrate a high-efficiency arXiv retrieval tool to enable active evidence gathering. To optimize these agents, we implement an agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm driven by a unified objective metric and reward system. This system avoids the biases of subjective model-based judging by employing multi-dimensional criteria, including reference-anchored semantic alignment, structural compliance, and a strict verification mechanism that cross-checks citations against real-time interaction logs to eliminate hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that agents trained within this closed-loop framework exhibit significant improvements in reasoning depth and citation accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for developing scholarly agents (InternReviewer and InternAdvocate) that generate professional academic content like reviews and rebuttals through domain reasoning, factual grounding, and an agentic RL paradigm with real-time citation verification.
AI.motivation: Generating professional scholarly content requires complex integration of domain reasoning and factual grounding, but current approaches may lack proper evidence gathering and verification mechanisms, leading to potential hallucinations or biased outputs.
AI.method:
1. Created a large-scale, high-quality scholarly dataset
2. Integrated high-efficiency arXiv retrieval tool for active evidence gathering
3. Implemented agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm with unified objective metric and reward system
4. Used multi-dimensional criteria to avoid subjective bias: reference-anchored semantic alignment, structural compliance, and strict verification mechanism
5. Cross-checks citations against real-time interaction logs to eliminate hallucinations
AI.result: Experimental results show that agents trained within this closed-loop framework exhibit significant improvements in reasoning depth and citation accuracy compared to previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: The comprehensive framework for scholarly agents effectively integrates domain reasoning with factual grounding through active evidence gathering and rigorous verification mechanisms, producing more reliable and professional scholarly content generation.

title: Flow-JEPA: Flow Matching for Robust Latent Dynamics in JEPA World Models
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have shown strong potential for learning compact predictive representations, and LeWorldModel (LeWM) extends this paradigm to reconstruction-free latent world modeling from pixels. However, its deterministic autoregressive predictor generates future states through repeated one-step transitions, which can accumulate errors and remain sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations. In this work, we propose Flow-JEPA (F-JEPA), a conditional flow matching dynamics model that jointly generates a sequence of future latent states conditioned on the current observation and actions. A Gaussian distribution serves as the flow source, exposing the vector field to perturbed latent trajectories as it learns to transport them toward clean future representations. This formulation retains the reconstruction-free JEPA framework while replacing point-wise transition regression with stochastic trajectory-level prediction. F-JEPA raises mean success from $86\%$ to $92\%$ under clean observations and from $67\%$ to $86\%$ under noisy conditions, suggesting that conditional flow matching provides a promising alternative to deterministic autoregressive dynamics in JEPA world models.

AI.tldr: F-JEPA replaces deterministic autoregressive prediction in JEPA world models with conditional flow matching for stochastic trajectory-level prediction, improving robustness to noise.
AI.motivation: Current JEPA-based world models like LeWorldModel use deterministic autoregressive predictors that accumulate errors and are sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations, limiting their robustness.
AI.method: Proposes Flow-JEPA (F-JEPA), a conditional flow matching dynamics model that jointly generates sequences of future latent states conditioned on current observations and actions. Uses Gaussian distribution as flow source, learning to transport perturbed latent trajectories toward clean future representations.
AI.result: F-JEPA improves mean success from 86% to 92% under clean observations and from 67% to 86% under noisy conditions, demonstrating superior robustness compared to deterministic approaches.
AI.conclusion: Conditional flow matching provides a promising alternative to deterministic autoregressive dynamics in JEPA world models, offering better noise robustness while maintaining the reconstruction-free framework.

title: Preference Elicitation for Policy Optimization and Application to Aligning Heart Transplantation with Human Values
summary: Preference elicitation is essential for aligning AI systems with human values. Prior approaches (e.g., for organ allocation) often ask stakeholders to compare the decisions of an algorithm (e.g., patient A vs. patient B). Such a decision-level approach conflates the means with the ends. Instead, we elicit preferences directly over allocation outcomes to learn a utility function for policy optimization. We construct a novel preference elicitation algorithm for linear utilities that outperforms prior techniques in practice. Our algorithm has two phases. The first phase learns cutting planes through pairwise comparisons to rapidly shrink the space of possible attribute weights and warm-starts the second phase by eliminating dominated regions. The second phase then provably converges to the user's utility function. We apply our technique to heart transplant allocation where a policy must balance competing objectives such as post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geographic ease, and equity. Using our algorithm, we conduct a user study to learn and aggregate a community-aligned utility function, and use it to optimize heart transplant policies that are significantly better aligned with human values. Compared to the hindsight optimum, the status quo policy achieves a competitive ratio of just 0.54, while our method is near-optimal with a competitive ratio of 0.95.

AI.tldr: A novel two-phase algorithm for preference elicitation that learns utility functions directly from allocation outcomes, then optimizes policies - applied to heart transplant allocation with near-optimal results (0.95 competitive ratio).
AI.motivation: Current preference elicitation methods conflate means with ends by asking stakeholders to compare algorithm decisions. The authors argue for eliciting preferences directly over allocation outcomes to learn utility functions for better policy optimization in AI alignment with human values.
AI.method: Two-phase algorithm for linear utilities: 1) First phase uses pairwise comparisons to learn cutting planes and rapidly shrink attribute weight space, eliminating dominated regions. 2) Second phase provably converges to user's utility function. Applied to heart transplant allocation balancing objectives like post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geography, and equity.
AI.result: The algorithm outperforms prior techniques in practice. In heart transplant allocation, conducted user study to learn community-aligned utility function. Achieved near-optimal 0.95 competitive ratio compared to hindsight optimum, while status quo policy only achieves 0.54 competitive ratio.
AI.conclusion: Direct preference elicitation over allocation outcomes enables learning better utility functions for policy optimization. The proposed two-phase algorithm provides practical improvement over prior methods and enables significantly better alignment with human values in critical applications like organ allocation.
