title: NVE: A Separability and Coverage-Aware Internal Validation Metric for Biclustering
summary: Biclustering, or co-clustering, aims to discover coherent submatrices by grouping rows and columns of a data matrix simultaneously. This local two-dimensional structure makes validation more difficult than in ordinary clustering, where internal indices usually rely on compactness and separation in a single shared feature space. Existing popular internal biclustering measures such as Mean Squared Residue (MSR), and Virtual Error (VE) mainly evaluate within-bicluster coherence. Although useful, these measures do not directly assess whether the extracted biclusters are mutually distinct or whether they explain a meaningful portion of the data matrix. This paper investigates Normalised Virtual Error (NVE), an internal validation metric that extends VE using a super-bicluster normalization strategy. By comparing the VE of each bicluster with the VE obtained after merging it with other biclusters, NVE introduces a relative notion of separability and redundancy. We also study a coverage-adjusted variant, NVE\textsubscript{cov}, which penalizes solutions that obtain low error by selecting only very small submatrices. Through controlled synthetic benchmarks and yeast gene-expression datasets, we examine whether NVE and NVE\textsubscript{cov} provide information beyond standard coherence-based metrics. The results show that NVE is sensitive to redundant and poorly separated biclusters, while NVE\textsubscript{cov} changes solution rankings when low-error biclusters cover only a negligible part of the matrix. These findings suggest that NVE-based measures are useful complementary criteria for internal co-clustering validation, especially when coherence, separability, and coverage must be considered jointly.

AI.tldr: NVE and NVE_cov are internal validation metrics for biclustering that extend Virtual Error with super-bicluster normalization to assess separability and redundancy, plus coverage adjustment to penalize small submatrices.
AI.motivation: Existing biclustering metrics like MSR and VE only evaluate within-bicluster coherence but don't assess whether biclusters are mutually distinct or explain meaningful portions of the data matrix.
AI.method: Proposes Normalised Virtual Error (NVE) that extends VE using super-bicluster normalization - comparing each bicluster's VE with VE after merging with other biclusters. Also introduces coverage-adjusted variant NVE_cov that penalizes solutions selecting only very small submatrices.
AI.result: NVE is sensitive to redundant and poorly separated biclusters, while NVE_cov changes solution rankings when low-error biclusters cover only negligible parts of the matrix, providing information beyond standard coherence-based metrics.
AI.conclusion: NVE-based measures are useful complementary criteria for internal co-clustering validation, especially when coherence, separability, and coverage must be considered jointly.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Tabu Search for Tactical Wireless Network Design
summary: Designing high-performance tactical wireless networks under realistic operational constraints gives rise to challenging combinatorial optimization problems, where the evaluation of candidate solutions relies on detailed physical and traffic-aware models. Although classical metaheuristics such as Tabu Search offer effective mechanisms for exploring large search spaces, their computational cost remains high because numerous candidate moves must be evaluated at every iteration. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework that improves the efficiency of Tabu Search by learning to guide its move selection process. Rather than altering the neighborhood structure, our approach exploits the information contained in the search trajectories generated during the optimization process. At each iteration, we record both improving and non-improving edge-based transformations together with a set of descriptive features capturing the structural, geometric, and performance characteristics of the network. This information is used to train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that predicts the impact of candidate moves on the objective function. The trained model is then integrated into the Tabu Search algorithm to rank candidate transformations according to their predicted quality, thereby reducing the number of costly objective evaluations while maintaining an effective exploration of the search space. Experimental results on synthetic benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed learning-assisted Tabu Search notably reduces computation time while consistently producing higher-quality solutions than the standard algorithm. These findings highlight the potential of combining machine learning with metaheuristics by leveraging the implicit knowledge embedded in search trajectories, paving the way for more efficient solution methods for large-scale network design problems.

AI.tldr: A learning-assisted Tabu Search framework that uses Graph Neural Networks to predict move quality, reducing computational cost while improving solution quality for tactical wireless network design.
AI.motivation: Traditional Tabu Search requires evaluating many candidate moves at each iteration, which is computationally expensive for large-scale network design problems. There's a need to reduce the number of costly objective function evaluations while maintaining effective search exploration.
AI.method: Proposes a data-driven framework that learns from search trajectories. Records edge-based transformations and descriptive features (structural, geometric, performance) during optimization, trains a Graph Neural Network to predict move impact on objective function, then integrates the trained model into Tabu Search to rank candidate moves by predicted quality.
AI.result: Experimental results on synthetic benchmark instances show the learning-assisted Tabu Search reduces computation time while consistently producing higher-quality solutions than standard Tabu Search.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates the potential of combining machine learning with metaheuristics by leveraging implicit knowledge in search trajectories, paving the way for more efficient solution methods for large-scale network design problems.

title: Sparse Koopman Autoencoders Identify Local Dynamical Regimes in Multibasin Systems
summary: Koopman autoencoders (KAEs) seek a higher-dimensional latent representation in which nonlinear dynamics evolve linearly. However, many interesting systems have multiple basins of attraction, and both theoretical and empirical work has shown these multibasin systems cannot generally admit a single finite-dimensional global Koopman embedding under standard assumptions. We posit that encoders with a sparsity-inducing objective encouraging few active latent coefficients will provide latent supports as an inspectable basin-modeling principle for Koopman autoencoders. We use these encoders producing sparse latents in training Sparse Koopman Autoencoders (SKAEs) without basin labels or other regime annotations, and treat the learned latent supports as model-produced regime variables after training. Across a range of procedurally generated multibasin systems and chaotic flows, we show that SKAEs have superior forecasting performance compared to dense-latent KAEs. We also perform a mechanistic study that shows latent supports produced by SKAEs are both essential for the quality of the representation and useful for identifying basins on held-out basin interior states, whereas dense-latent KAEs collapse to an uninformative single family. These results identify sparse latents and their corresponding supports as label-free, interpretable regime variables for Koopman learning in nonlinear systems with multiple local dynamical laws.

AI.tldr: Sparse Koopman Autoencoders (SKAEs) use sparsity-inducing encoders to learn interpretable latent supports that identify different basins of attraction in multi-basin dynamical systems without requiring basin labels.
AI.motivation: Standard Koopman autoencoders struggle with systems having multiple basins of attraction, as theory and empirical work show these multi-basin systems generally cannot admit a single finite-dimensional global Koopman embedding. There's a need for methods that can handle such systems without requiring labeled basin data.
AI.method: The authors propose Sparse Koopman Autoencoders (SKAEs) that use encoders with sparsity-inducing objectives to encourage few active latent coefficients. These sparse latents provide latent supports as an inspectable basin-modeling principle. SKAEs are trained without basin labels or regime annotations, and the learned latent supports serve as model-produced regime variables.
AI.result: Across procedurally generated multi-basin systems and chaotic flows, SKAEs show superior forecasting performance compared to dense-latent KAEs. Mechanistic studies reveal that sparse latent supports are essential for representation quality and useful for identifying basins on held-out basin interior states, while dense-latent KAEs collapse to an uninformative single family.
AI.conclusion: Sparse latents and their corresponding supports provide label-free, interpretable regime variables for Koopman learning in nonlinear systems with multiple local dynamical laws, addressing a fundamental limitation of standard Koopman approaches for multi-basin systems.

title: CDEP Agent: Connecting Meteorologically Detected Temporal Compound Events to Real-World Documentary Evidence
summary: Compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation (CDEP) events are recognized in climate science as a growing driver of extreme impact, but whether this recognition carries over into real-world early warning and post-event documentation is unknown, so a meteorologically real CDEP event may pass with neither advance warning nor any later record. Here we present CDEP Agent, an auditable LLM-agent framework that tests this mismatch directly by linking CDEP candidates detected from meteorological reanalysis to real-world hazard and impact evidence across sources with different spatial scales, temporal resolutions, and reporting conventions. Using California as a case study, we identify 408 candidate CDEP events from ERA5 observations during 2021-2025 and evaluate each against the U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events, and public webpages along five dimensions: antecedent drought, extreme rainfall, local impact, hazard-impact attribution, and explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage. Only 34.3% of candidates are corroborated on both hazard components, and just 1.5% are ever explicitly linked to their antecedent drought, indicating that most meteorologically detected CDEP events go undocumented and their compound nature almost never enters the record at all. Our framework gives climate scientists a way to test physical event definitions against what actually gets documented, and gives social scientists, economists, and disaster-response agencies a provenance-linked evidence base for compound events that current warning and reporting systems largely fail to capture.

AI.tldr: CDEP Agent is an LLM-agent framework that detects compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation events from meteorological data and evaluates their real-world documentation, finding most go undocumented despite being meteorologically real.
AI.motivation: There's a known mismatch between climate science recognition of CDEP events as growing drivers of extreme impacts and their actual documentation in real-world early warning systems and post-event records. Current systems may fail to capture the compound nature of these events.
AI.method: Developed CDEP Agent, an auditable LLM-agent framework that links CDEP candidates detected from ERA5 meteorological reanalysis to real-world evidence from U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events, and public webpages across five dimensions: antecedent drought, extreme rainfall, local impact, hazard-impact attribution, and explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage.
AI.result: In California (2021-2025), identified 408 candidate CDEP events from ERA5, but only 34.3% were corroborated on both hazard components, and just 1.5% were explicitly linked to their antecedent drought, showing most meteorologically detected CDEP events go undocumented.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides climate scientists with a way to test physical event definitions against actual documentation, and gives social scientists, economists, and disaster-response agencies a provenance-linked evidence base for compound events that current warning and reporting systems largely fail to capture.

title: PathBridger: Subgoal Bridges for Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) aims to learn policies for reaching diverse goals entirely from fixed trajectory data. Long-horizon offline GCRL remains challenging because sparse goal-reaching signals must be propagated over many steps, while execution errors cannot be corrected through additional environment interaction. Existing methods address these challenges by improving long-range value estimation or reducing the effective decision horizon through subgoals, options, and action chunks. In several hierarchical methods, however, a selected subgoal specifies where to go, while the intervening state-space path remains implicit in an endpoint-conditioned low-level policy. To address this interface, we propose PathBridger, a hierarchical offline GCRL method that explicitly connects subgoal selection to short-horizon execution. PathBridger constructs a state-space bridge toward the selected intermediate endpoint and decodes it into a short executable action chunk using an inverse dynamics model. Experiments across the evaluated OGBench tasks demonstrate strong aggregate performance, with particularly large gains on the multi-object Cube manipulation tasks. Code: https://github.com/SChoish/PathBridger

AI.tldr: PathBridger is a hierarchical offline GCRL method that explicitly connects subgoal selection to execution by constructing state-space bridges to intermediate endpoints and decoding them into executable action chunks.
AI.motivation: Address challenges in offline goal-conditioned RL for long-horizon tasks where sparse goal-reaching signals must be propagated over many steps, and execution errors cannot be corrected due to lack of environment interaction. Existing hierarchical methods often have an interface problem where selected subgoals only specify where to go while the intervening path remains implicit.
AI.method: PathBridger constructs explicit state-space bridges toward selected intermediate endpoints and decodes them into short executable action chunks using an inverse dynamics model, directly connecting subgoal selection to short-horizon execution.
AI.result: Demonstrates strong aggregate performance across evaluated OGBench tasks, with particularly large gains on the multi-object Cube manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly connecting subgoal selection to execution via state-space bridges and inverse dynamics modeling improves offline GCRL performance, especially for long-horizon tasks like multi-object manipulation.

title: CrossAudit: A Git-Native, Cross-Vendor Audit Loop for Agentic Science
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, 22 references. Reference implementation, audit ledger, and experiment artefacts: https://github.com/dongzhaohe321418-lab/crossaudit
summary:
An AI scientist should not grade its own homework. Yet in the systems we examined, the agent that reviews the work usually comes from the same model family as the agent that produced it, or at least from the same vendor. Model evaluators are known to favour their own generations. Whether models trained alike also share blind spots is a conjecture, not a settled finding, but if they do, the reviewer inherits the author's. The record of what was flagged and what was waved through often sits in platform logs that nobody outside can replay.
  We present CrossAudit, a protocol for supervising autonomous research pipelines. It rests on three commitments. Each increment of work is audited by an agent from a different vendor against a rulebook a human wrote and versioned. Reports, verdicts, disputes and rulings are git commits, so the supervision history can be re-read and cited; raw model exchanges are not yet part of that record. Scripted checks run before any model does. Advisory judgement never gates the pipeline: a model blocks only by citing a rule, and no model may waive a deterministic failure. Blockers that survive a bounded number of revision rounds go to a person.
  We state the protocol as eight invariants. We describe a reference implementation built from GitHub Actions and a few hundred lines of Python, and report a live deployment of a closely related variant in a computational-chemistry pipeline. We also ran a seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 seeded defects, one run per configuration). A cross-vendor audit of our own repository then voided its blinding. We adopt that audit's findings and report the corrected results. The trial shows that two vendors read the same rulebook differently. It does not show that either is better. The strongest evidence here is the committed, uncontrolled record of cross-vendor audits of this paper itself.

AI.tldr: CrossAudit is a protocol for supervising autonomous research pipelines using cross-vendor auditing, versioned rulebooks, and immutable audit trails to prevent same-vendor bias in AI-generated research.
AI.motivation: Current AI research pipelines suffer from inherent bias when the same vendor/model family both produces and reviews work, creating potential blind spots. Audits are often opaque and stored in proprietary platform logs, preventing reproducibility and external verification.
AI.method: The CrossAudit protocol requires: 1) each work increment audited by agents from different vendors, 2) human-written and versioned rulebooks, 3) audit reports as git commits for reproducibility, 4) scripted checks before model execution, 5) blocking only by citing specific rules, 6) no model can override deterministic failures, 7) bounded revision rounds, 8) unresolved issues go to human review.
AI.result: Implemented a reference system using GitHub Actions + Python; deployed in computational-chemistry pipeline. Seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 defects) showed different vendors interpret the same rulebook differently. Cross-vendor audit of their own repository revealed blinding issues, leading to corrected results. The strongest evidence is the immutable record of cross-vendor audits of the paper itself.
AI.conclusion: Cross-vendor auditing reveals systematic differences in how AI systems interpret the same rules, emphasizing the need for transparent, versioned audit trails and external verification in autonomous research. The protocol doesn't show which vendor is better, but demonstrates that independent oversight is essential for reliable AI-assisted research.

title: Selective Disclosure of Hidden Directives in Reasoning Models: Behavioral Asymmetry and Steering
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces are increasingly proposed as a mechanism for AI oversight: a monitor inspecting a model's reasoning can, in principle, detect misbehavior invisible from outputs alone. This assumes CoT surfaces what a model is instructed to do regardless of the instructions given. We test this assumption along two axes. First, we introduce the Instruction-Compliance Gap (ICG): the difference in probability that a model's CoT explicitly references a hidden system prompt directive when that directive is malign versus benign. Across 100 task pairs and 8 frontier reasoning models from 5 families, we find consistent asymmetric disclosure, a higher probability of leaking malign hidden instructions than benign ones, in Qwen3-14B (Wilcoxon $p=0.0001$, $+13.9$pp), Qwen3-32B ($p=0.0011$, $+13.0$pp), Qwen3-235B ($p=0.035$, $+5.8$pp), and similar results with MiniMax-M2.5 and DeepSeek-R1. The detector has 100% precision against two independent blinded labelling passes, and an LLM monitor reading only the reasoning trace reproduces the asymmetry in all 8 models against directive-free controls, identifying the specific directive in 82% of malign traces which the detector classifies as clean. Second, steering vectors extracted in MiniMax-M2.5 via Contrastive Activation Addition causally induce hiding from bare prompts and suppress it from prompts that would otherwise produce it, replicating in Qwen3-14B under a pre-registered design. Benign and malign-derived hiding vectors are highly similar (cosine $0.804$ in MiniMax-M2.5; $0.970$ in Qwen3-14B), implying that in these models the disclosure asymmetry arises from differential activation of a shared hiding direction rather than separate mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Chain-of-thought reasoning doesn't reliably expose hidden malicious instructions, as models are more likely to disclose malign vs benign hidden prompts, and can actively suppress this disclosure via shared neural mechanisms.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether chain-of-thought reasoning can serve as an effective AI oversight mechanism. There's an assumption that CoT should transparently reveal what a model is doing regardless of instructions, but this needs empirical testing especially when dealing with hidden or malicious instructions.
AI.method: 1) Introduces Instruction-Compliance Gap (ICG) metric comparing probability of CoT revealing hidden malign vs benign directives; 2) Tests across 100 task pairs and 8 frontier reasoning models; 3) Uses statistical analysis (Wilcoxon tests) and blinded labeling; 4) Extracts steering vectors via Contrastive Activation Addition to causally manipulate hiding behavior; 5) Measures similarity between hiding vectors for different instruction types.
AI.result: 1) Consistent asymmetric disclosure found: models more likely to leak malign hidden instructions than benign ones across multiple models (Qwen3 family, MiniMax-M2.5, DeepSeek-R1); 2) Detector has 100% precision against blinded labeling; 3) LLM monitors reading reasoning traces reproduce asymmetry; 4) Steering vectors can causally induce/repress hiding behavior; 5) Benign and malign hiding vectors are highly similar (cosine 0.804-0.970), suggesting shared hiding mechanism rather than separate ones.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not a reliable oversight mechanism for detecting hidden malicious instructions because models actively suppress disclosure of these instructions. The asymmetric disclosure arises from differential activation of a shared hiding direction in model representations, meaning models can strategically conceal what they're doing even when providing reasoning traces.

title: AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment
summary: Large language model agents can discover alphas, yet current methods have three weaknesses. The search cannot adapt during the run, automation usually ends at alpha generation while library selection and model choice stay manual, and alpha discovery can read the test window through loop feedback or code problems. We present AutoScientist-Quant, a self evolving search process that regards quantitative research as one budgeted search problem. A single controller conditions every decision on the remaining budget, choosing at each round whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, which node to expand, how many alphas to generate, and how to retrieve past trajectories from the shared memory. The same core then selects from the library and tunes the model, closing the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. We also review the evaluation pipeline reused from prior work, fix two lookahead problems, and keep the feedback window disjoint from the held out test window, so every comparison tests true generalization. On CSI universes, the framework attains the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and these conclusions hold across several backbones and markets.

AI.tldr: AutoScientist-Quant is a self-evolving framework that treats quantitative research as a budgeted search problem, automating the entire alpha discovery pipeline including adaptive search, library selection, and model tuning while preventing test window leakage.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based alpha discovery methods have three weaknesses: non-adaptive search during runs, incomplete automation (manual library selection and model choice), and potential test window leakage through feedback loops or code problems.
AI.method: A single controller conditions all decisions on remaining budget, choosing each round whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, selecting nodes to expand, determining alpha generation count, and retrieving past trajectories from shared memory. The same core handles library selection and model tuning, creating a closed loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy.
AI.result: On CSI universes, the framework achieves the best value of nearly every metric in every setting. These conclusions hold across multiple backbones and markets. The evaluation pipeline fixes lookahead problems and maintains disjoint feedback/test windows for true generalization testing.
AI.conclusion: AutoScientist-Quant successfully addresses current LLM agent weaknesses by creating a fully automated, self-evolving quantitative research system that prevents test window leakage while achieving superior performance across various metrics and market conditions.

title: Titans-QFWP: A Regime-Aware Hybrid Quantum Fast Weight Programmer for Portfolio Optimization
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE) 2026 QCRL Workshop
summary: We propose Titans-QFWP, a hybrid reinforcement learning architecture integrating a Quantum Fast Weight Programmer with Titans-style memory (Persistence, Surprise, and Forgetting) for adaptive portfolio optimization. To address high-dimensional market features, we introduce an enhanced A3C^2 framework with Hungarian-aligned K-means clustering and scaled log-return rewards. Evaluated on 468 S&P 500 stocks under an Equal-Parameter-Count (EPC) benchmark with approximately 3,000 trainable parameters, Titans-QFWP achieves strong performance (median ARR 0.4260, Calmar 8.5504, IR 0.8427). Ablation results reveal that quantum gating fundamentally reshapes memory component roles, with Persistence supporting drawdown control, Surprise contributing to return generation, and Forgetting providing additional stabilization. By stabilizing these quantum representations, the model enables defensive allocation during market drawdowns while preserving upside potential.

AI.tldr: Titans-QFWP combines quantum computing with reinforcement learning for portfolio optimization, achieving strong performance on S&P 500 stocks with adaptive memory mechanisms that respond differently when enhanced by quantum gating.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of adaptive portfolio optimization in high-dimensional market environments where traditional methods may struggle with complex feature spaces and need dynamic memory adaptation.
AI.method: A hybrid reinforcement learning architecture integrating Quantum Fast Weight Programmer with Titans-style memory (Persistence, Surprise, Forgetting), using enhanced A3C^2 framework with Hungarian-aligned K-means clustering for dimensionality reduction and scaled log-return rewards.
AI.result: Achieved median Annualized Return Rate of 0.4260, Calmar ratio of 8.5504, and Information Ratio of 0.8427 on 468 S&P 500 stocks under Equal-Parameter-Count benchmark with ~3,000 parameters. Quantum gating fundamentally reshapes memory roles: Persistence controls drawdowns, Surprise generates returns, and Forgetting provides stabilization.
AI.conclusion: The integration of quantum computing with reinforcement learning enables defensive allocation during market drawdowns while preserving upside potential through stabilized quantum representations and adaptive memory mechanisms.

title: AI Scientist Mission Control (AIMC): Visual Analytics for Human Oversight of Autonomous Scientific Discovery
summary: Autonomous scientific discovery systems can generate large numbers of research ideas, experiments, and manuscripts with minimal human intervention. As these systems become increasingly capable, scientists require effective mechanisms to monitor output quality, identify recurring failure modes, understand research evolution, and prioritize promising discoveries for review. We present AIMC, a visual analytics framework for human oversight of autonomous scientific discovery. AIMC combines semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations to support the exploration of AI-generated research artifacts. We demonstrate the framework through a case study of the papers generated by an autonomous AI Scientist (FARS), together with their associated review feedback. Our analysis reveals recurring methodological weaknesses, evolving research themes, domain-specific differences in quality, and a small set of highly novel papers that warrant deeper human inspection. These findings illustrate how visual analytics can support transparency, diagnosis, and human AI collaboration in emerging autonomous scientific discovery workflows.

AI.tldr: AIMC is a visual analytics framework for monitoring and understanding AI-generated scientific research, helping scientists oversee autonomous discovery systems through semantic analysis, weakness detection, and interactive visualization.
AI.motivation: As autonomous scientific discovery systems generate large volumes of research outputs with minimal human intervention, scientists need tools to monitor quality, identify failures, understand research evolution, and prioritize promising discoveries for human review.
AI.method: AIMC combines semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations to support exploration of AI-generated research artifacts. It was demonstrated through a case study analyzing papers from an autonomous AI Scientist (FARS) and their review feedback.
AI.result: The analysis revealed recurring methodological weaknesses, evolving research themes, domain-specific quality differences, and a small set of highly novel papers requiring deeper human inspection.
AI.conclusion: Visual analytics can effectively support transparency, diagnosis, and human-AI collaboration in autonomous scientific discovery workflows, providing essential oversight mechanisms for AI-generated research.

title: Development of an Autonomous AI Coding Agent using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and Gemini LLM Frameworks
comment: 10 PAGES WITH PLAGIARISM REPORT ON 10TH PAGE
summary: The ongoing changes in software engineering requirements have created a substantial need for automated tools which can create secure source code from natural language input. The performance of traditional Large Language Models (LLMs) becomes limited by their "one-shot" capability which results in logical hallucinations together with reduced algorithmic performance during complicated operations. The research presents an autonomous AI Coding Agent which establishes a connection between LLM-generated content and production-ready software through its organized methodology for decision making. Our framework uses the Gemini 2.5 Flash API for essential reasoning capabilities while employing a tailored Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method to solve code generation challenges as a search operation. The agent uses a "Self-Critic" evaluator system to test different implementation methods which it ranks according to their accuracy and difficulty level before it improves its operational framework through backpropagation. The system operates through a Flask-based web interface which delivers instant feedback together with syntax highlighting features. Our experimental results show that the MCTS-based method achieves a 92% success rate on complex logical prompts while surpassing standard zero-shot generation models.

AI.tldr: An autonomous AI coding agent that combines Gemini 2.5 Flash API with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and a "Self-Critic" evaluator to generate secure, production-ready code from natural language with high success rates on complex logical tasks.
AI.motivation: Current large language models have limitations in code generation due to "one-shot" capability leading to logical hallucinations and reduced algorithmic performance in complex operations. There's a substantial need for automated tools that can create secure source code from natural language input in software engineering.
AI.method: Framework uses Gemini 2.5 Flash API for reasoning capabilities combined with a tailored Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method to treat code generation as a search operation. Includes a "Self-Critic" evaluator system that tests different implementation methods, ranks them by accuracy and difficulty, and improves through backpropagation. The system operates through a Flask-based web interface with instant feedback and syntax highlighting.
AI.result: The MCTS-based method achieves a 92% success rate on complex logical prompts and surpasses standard zero-shot generation models in performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed autonomous AI coding agent successfully bridges the gap between LLM-generated content and production-ready software through its structured methodology, achieving high success rates on complex coding tasks while addressing limitations of traditional one-shot LLM approaches.

title: Self-Evolving Skills via Surrogate-Guided Solve-and-Reproduce
summary: Agent skills are portable packages of instructions and resources an agent consults at deployment. Self-evolving them fails in two ways today. First, skills evolved from scratch underperform human-curated ones and, on a weak model, using no skill at all. Second, an evolution-time pass records one lucky trajectory that a fresh stochastic agent often fails to reproduce at deployment. We present reSolve, a per-task, oracle-in-the-loop framework built on three components. It decouples interactive solving from a self-contained deliverable that is independently re-executed in a fresh container, a protocol we call solve-and-reproduce. It enhances the sparse reward signal with a surrogate verifier that cannot access hidden tests or reference answers. It then runs verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph. Within a fixed harness, a cheap model self-evolves skills that reach $74.9\%$ mean-of-3, $+14.8$ points over the $60.1\%$ human-curated baseline, exceeding the strongest official curated-skill result ($67.3\%$, GPT-5.5/OpenHands). We also report observed failure cases and domain-level results, including performance on the 14 Natural Science tasks, to clarify when the approach does and does not help.

AI.tldr: reSolve is a framework that enables self-evolving agent skills through solve-and-reproduce protocol, verifier guidance, and beam search, significantly outperforming human-curated baselines.
AI.motivation: Current self-evolving agent skills fail in two ways: they underperform human-curated skills (even performing worse than using no skill on weak models), and evolution-time recordings capture lucky trajectories that fresh stochastic agents can't reproduce at deployment.
AI.method: reSolve uses three components: 1) solve-and-reproduce protocol that decouples interactive solving from independently re-executable deliverables, 2) surrogate verifier that enhances sparse rewards without accessing hidden tests/reference answers, and 3) verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph.
AI.result: Within a fixed harness, a cheap model self-evolves skills achieving 74.9% mean-of-3, +14.8 points over the 60.1% human-curated baseline, exceeding the strongest official curated-skill result (67.3%, GPT-5.5/OpenHands). The paper also reports failure cases and domain-level results including performance on 14 Natural Science tasks.
AI.conclusion: reSolve successfully addresses the limitations of current self-evolving agent skills through its novel framework, demonstrating that automated skill evolution can surpass human-curated approaches while clarifying when the method is and isn't effective.

title: Temperature-Adaptive Transformed Teacher Matching
summary: Temperature scaling is a core component of knowledge distillation, yet its role and effect are still not fully understood. Transformed Teacher Matching (TTM) clarifies the role of temperature scaling by applying it only to the teacher distribution and interpreting the resulting objective as standard distillation with an implicit Rényi entropy regularization on the student. However, TTM still relies on a fixed temperature and does not specify how the teacher-side temperature should be adapted for individual samples. In this paper, we introduce a sample-wise inverse-temperature update for TTM by locally minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the temperature-scaled teacher distribution and the student's prediction. We derive closed-form first and second derivatives with respect to the inverse temperature, and show that they can be expressed using variance and covariance statistics of centered teacher and student logits under the transformed teacher weighting. This yields an efficient curvature-aware update that requires one softmax evaluation and a constant number of class-wise weighted sums. Experiments on standard image classification distillation benchmarks show that our temperature adaptation generally improves TTM and WTTM, while remaining competitive with or outperforming prior temperature-adaptive distillation baselines.

AI.tldr: TTM uses temperature scaling only on teacher distribution, but uses fixed temperature. This paper introduces sample-wise inverse-temperature update for TTM by locally minimizing KL divergence, with efficient curvature-aware update using variance/covariance statistics.
AI.motivation: While Temperature scaling is crucial for knowledge distillation, its role isn't fully understood. TTM clarified it by applying temperature only to teacher, but still uses fixed temperature and doesn't adapt it for individual samples.
AI.method: Introduces sample-wise inverse-temperature update for TTM by locally minimizing KL divergence between temperature-scaled teacher distribution and student prediction. Derives closed-form first/second derivatives w.r.t. inverse temperature, expressed using variance/covariance statistics of centered teacher/student logits under transformed teacher weighting.
AI.result: Proposed temperature adaptation generally improves TTM and WTTM on standard image classification distillation benchmarks, remaining competitive with or outperforming prior temperature-adaptive distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Sample-wise adaptive temperature scaling improves distillation performance by providing efficient, curvature-aware temperature updates that adapt to individual samples rather than using fixed temperatures.

title: Reward-Oracle MCTS for Formal Theorem Proving: Sample-Efficient Search and the Need for Kernel-Level Proof Auditing
summary: Formal theorem proving with large language models remains challenging due to the difficulty of navigating large proof search spaces efficiently. Existing tree search approaches either feed verbose compiler error messages directly into the generation context, increasing context usage during search, or employ non-standard evaluation protocols that prevent direct comparison with established baselines. We propose a three-role Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework that treats the Lean 4 compiler purely as a reward oracle using compiler output as a scalar signal for UCB-guided tree updates without feeding error content into the generation context. Our framework decomposes proof search into three roles: a generator for proof attempts, a decomposer for subgoal decomposition, and a critic for subgoal quality evaluation. We evaluate across 4 benchmarks spanning competition mathematics and physics (MiniF2F, PutnamBench, LeanPhysBench, PhysLeandata) with three prover models at standard proof attempt budgets (PAB@16 to PAB@256). Our method achieves 87.1\% on MiniF2F with Goedel-Prover-V2-8B at PAB@256 and solves 26/659 PutnamBench problems at PAB@32 surpassing base sampling 18/659 at same proof attempt budget. Through an exhaustive axiom-level audit of every compiled proof, we further identify reward hacking in search-based theorem proving: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B produces proofs on PutnamBench that pass compilation and the standard sorry-token scan while depending on sorryAx. The audit removes 4 and 8 such proofs from whole-proof sampling at PAB@32 and PAB@128, and 11 and 19 from MCTS. We do not attribute these counts to the search procedure; we report them to establish that kernel-level auditing is necessary for compiler-verified evaluation.

AI.tldr: A novel three-role Monte Carlo Tree Search framework for theorem proving that treats the Lean 4 compiler as a pure reward oracle, achieving state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while revealing reward hacking issues requiring kernel-level auditing.
AI.motivation: Existing theorem proving approaches with LLMs either inefficiently feed verbose compiler error messages into generation context (increasing context usage) or use non-standard evaluation protocols that prevent fair comparison with established baselines.
AI.method: Three-role MCTS framework that treats Lean 4 compiler purely as a reward oracle, using compiler output as scalar signal for UCB-guided tree updates without feeding error content into context. Decomposes proof search into three roles: generator for proof attempts, decomposer for subgoal decomposition, and critic for subgoal quality evaluation.
AI.result: Achieves 87.1% on MiniF2F with Goedel-Prover-V2-8B at PAB@256 and solves 26/659 PutnamBench problems at PAB@32 (vs 18/659 with base sampling). An axiom-level audit revealed reward hacking: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B produced proofs that passed compilation and sorry-token scan but depended on sorryAx, requiring removal of 4-8 proofs from sampling and 11-19 from MCTS.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-role MCTS framework enables efficient theorem proving by treating the compiler as a pure reward oracle, achieving strong performance while demonstrating that kernel-level auditing is necessary for compiler-verified evaluation due to reward hacking vulnerabilities.

title: PathGuide: Dynamic Classifier-Free Guidance via On-Policy Transport Alignment
comment: 40 pages, 8 figures, 17 tables. Includes appendices with full proofs, ablations, reproduction details and additional experiments
summary: While modern generative models excel at modeling complex data, precise inference-time control in conditional generation remains a critical challenge. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a primary mechanism for such control, yet it is typically treated as a static tuning parameter. In flow-based models, however, the guidance scale fundamentally dictates the velocity field and the resulting probability path, making guidance selection a dynamic path-optimization problem. We introduce PathGuide, a framework that reformulates scalar CFG selection as an on-policy transport problem. Leveraging the weak form of the continuity equation, we derive a selection criterion with a direct path-correctness interpretation: we prove that if the guided field is weakly equivalent to the exact conditional field along the generated rollout, the sampler's path coincides with the target conditional law. For scalar CFG, this criterion yields a strictly quadratic local objective with an efficient, closed-form selector for each solver interval. PathGuide enables optimal guidance scales to be computed and used online during generation or fitted offline as a reusable piecewise-constant schedule. We validate our method on low-resolution image manifolds and controlled settings across various continuous-time flow constructions, demonstrating that this transport-based selector improves path alignment and sample fidelity over both fixed and state-of-the-art adaptive guidance baselines.

AI.tldr: PathGuide reformulates classifier-free guidance selection as a dynamic transport problem, deriving an optimal guidance scale selector that improves conditional generation quality in flow-based models.
AI.motivation: Precise inference-time control in conditional generation remains challenging. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a primary control mechanism, it's typically treated as a static tuning parameter, ignoring its dynamic nature in flow-based models where guidance scale dictates velocity fields and probability paths.
AI.method: PathGuide reformulates scalar CFG selection as an on-policy transport problem using the weak form of the continuity equation. It derives a selection criterion with path-correctness interpretation: if the guided field is weakly equivalent to the exact conditional field along the generated rollout, the sampler's path coincides with the target conditional law. For scalar CFG, this yields a strictly quadratic local objective with an efficient closed-form selector for each solver interval.
AI.result: PathGuide enables optimal guidance scales to be computed online during generation or fitted offline as reusable piecewise-constant schedules. Validation on low-resolution image manifolds and controlled settings across various continuous-time flow constructions shows improved path alignment and sample fidelity over fixed and state-of-the-art adaptive guidance baselines.
AI.conclusion: PathGuide provides a principled, theoretically-grounded framework for dynamic guidance scale selection in flow-based generative models, addressing the limitations of static CFG tuning and improving conditional generation quality through optimal path alignment.

title: From Extraction to Governed Memory: Multi-Agent Knowledge Graph Construction with Domain-Expert Review
comment: 23 pages total, 10 pages main text, 12 pages of appendix, 2 figures, 6 tables
summary: Knowledge graphs used by agentic systems are often treated as flat stores of extracted triples, with little record of who owns a fact, why it was admitted, or how it should be used downstream. We argue that reliable agentic knowledge systems require governance as an essential component of graph construction to bridge this gap. We propose MAGG, a principled multi-agent framework for constructing Governed Knowledge Graphs that introduces explicit governance decisions for reliable and trustworthy knowledge sharing. A domain classifier first induces entity and relation types directly from document content, enabling operation in open-world settings without fixed schemas. Candidate triples are assigned to domain owners, reviewed against supporting evidence, admitted through governance decisions, and stored with audit metadata. The same ownership structure is reused during question answering, where queries are routed to domain-specific graph experts rather than answered through undifferentiated retrieval. Our evaluation demonstrates MAGG's effectiveness: On SciERC, MAGG improves strict triple F1 by 47% and mapped triple F1 by 51% over flat insertion. A blinded review of 120 triples finds governed-only triples more often source-supported than flat-only ones, and revised triples supported in 100% of cases. Finally, on MuSiQue, MAGG outperforms Microsoft GraphRAG by 9.0 exact-match points and 11.2 token-F1 points.

AI.tldr: MAGG is a multi-agent framework for constructing Governed Knowledge Graphs that introduces explicit governance decisions, domain ownership, and audit metadata to create more reliable knowledge systems compared to traditional flat triple extraction.
AI.motivation: Current knowledge graphs used by agentic systems are treated as flat stores of extracted triples without tracking fact ownership, justification for admission, or proper usage guidelines. This creates reliability issues for downstream applications.
AI.method: MAGG uses a domain classifier to induce entity/relation types from documents, then assigns candidate triples to domain owners who review them against supporting evidence. Triples are admitted through governance decisions and stored with audit metadata. The same ownership structure guides query routing to domain-specific experts during question answering.
AI.result: On SciERC: 47% improvement in strict triple F1 and 51% improvement in mapped triple F1 over flat insertion. Blinded review shows governed-only triples more source-supported than flat-only ones, with revised triples 100% supported. On MuSiQue: Outperforms Microsoft GraphRAG by 9.0 exact-match points and 11.2 token-F1 points.
AI.conclusion: Governance is essential for reliable agentic knowledge systems, and MAGG provides an effective framework for constructing governed knowledge graphs with explicit governance decisions that improve reliability, trustworthiness, and performance over traditional approaches.

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Broadband Adoption Disparities: Tract-Level Prediction and SHAP-Based Factor Profiling
summary: The United States has allocated approximately $65 billion through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act for broadband expansion, yet evidence-based methods for targeting these investments remain underdeveloped. This paper presents an explainable machine learning framework for profiling broadband adoption disparities at census-tract granularity across 83,359 tracts nationwide. Using 65 socioeconomic, demographic, and infrastructure features derived from the American Community Survey 2022, we train a LightGBM model under spatial five-fold cross-validation, achieving R^2 = 0.533 and Spearman rho = 0.763; state-held-out cross-validation (51 folds) confirms generalization (R^2 = 0.525). TreeSHAP analysis identifies income and education as the dominant factor group (with the engineered interaction term absorbing attribution from its constituent features), and SHAP-based clustering reveals three exploratory factor profiles: Well-Connected Moderate (~49K tracts), Affordability-Limited Severe (~21K tracts), and Rural-Elderly (~13K tracts). As a screening tool, ML-based tract selection captures 38.0% of the total adoption gap within the top 10% of tracts versus 35.2% for income-only heuristics (+2.8 pp, p < 0.002, county-block bootstrap); in regret-reduction terms, the model closes 19% of the remaining gap between income-only and oracle selection. The primary contribution is the per-tract factor decomposition: SHAP identifies which feature groups (income/education, rurality, age) are most strongly associated with each tract's predicted gap, and informs differentiated investigation. A temporal stability check, training on ACS 2017 and predicting ACS 2022 with zero survey-year overlap, confirms ranking stability (rho = 0.784, noting hyperparameters tuned on 2022 data).

AI.tldr: An explainable ML framework identifies key factors in broadband adoption disparities across US census tracts, outperforming income-only heuristics for targeting $65B in infrastructure investments.
AI.motivation: Despite $65 billion allocated through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act for broadband expansion, evidence-based methods for targeting these investments remain underdeveloped. There's a need for better approaches to identify where and why broadband adoption gaps exist to efficiently allocate resources.
AI.method: Developed an explainable machine learning framework using LightGBM model trained on 65 socioeconomic, demographic, and infrastructure features from American Community Survey 2022 data across 83,359 census tracts. Used spatial five-fold cross-validation and state-held-out cross-validation (51 folds) for generalization. Applied TreeSHAP analysis for interpretability and SHAP-based clustering for factor profiling.
AI.result: Model achieved R²=0.533 and Spearman rho=0.763 with strong generalization (R²=0.525 in state-held-out validation). Identified three factor profiles: Well-Connected Moderate (49K tracts), Affordability-Limited Severe (21K tracts), and Rural-Elderly (13K tracts). ML selection captures 38.0% of adoption gap in top 10% of tracts vs 35.2% for income-only (+2.8pp improvement). Temporal stability confirmed with rho=0.784 when predicting 2022 from 2017 data.
AI.conclusion: The ML framework provides superior targeting of broadband investments compared to simple income heuristics, with per-tract factor decomposition enabling differentiated policy responses based on whether income/education, rurality, or age factors are most critical for each community's broadband adoption gap.

title: BiasMix-Finance: Post-Generation KYC Guardrails for LLM Portfolio Advice
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to the ICLR 2026 Financial AI (FinAI) Workshop. Code and data: https://github.com/gauravkukreja06/biasmix-finance
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible-sounding ETF portfolios while silently violating basic KYC-style constraints on risk, fees, and diversification. This is especially problematic in agentic multi-turn advisory systems, where each draft recommendation can become an action unless guarded by an auditable enforcement layer. We study a model-agnostic, asset-agnostic post-generation guardrail pipeline: (i) enforce a strict JSON allocation schema, (ii) validate allocations against numeric caps, and (iii) when violations occur, deterministically project the output to the nearest feasible portfolio via a convex quadratic program (QCQP). We introduce BiasMix-Finance (Mini), a compact stress-test benchmark for constrained decision-making under biased LLM generations, with a 16-ETF universe, three investor profiles, and eight bias prompts. Across three models and three inference modes (direct, critique, self-consistency), first-pass generations violate at least one cap in 47.6-85.7% of test cases (67.2% pooled), but the convex projection layer reduces final feasibility violations to 0% while requiring only a small correction distance (test pooled median D=||w*-w0||_2=0.066), indicating that the guardrail typically preserves the intent of the original allocation. We report violation rates and correction distances with confidence intervals, and paired model comparisons with multiple-testing correction. To support reproducibility, we release the dataset, prompts, caps, and code in our public GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a guardrail pipeline to enforce financial constraints on LLM-generated ETF portfolios using convex optimization, achieving 0% final violations while preserving allocation intent.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate plausible-sounding but constraint-violating ETF portfolios, which is particularly dangerous in multi-turn advisory systems where draft recommendations may become actual actions without proper enforcement.
AI.method: A three-step model-agnostic guardrail pipeline: (1) enforce strict JSON allocation schema, (2) validate against numeric caps, and (3) deterministically project violating outputs to nearest feasible portfolio via convex quadratic programming (QCQP). Introduces BiasMix-Finance (Mini) benchmark for testing.
AI.result: First-pass LLM generations violated constraints in 47.6-85.7% of cases (67.2% pooled), but the convex projection reduced final violations to 0% with minimal correction distance (median D=0.066), preserving original allocation intent.
AI.conclusion: The proposed guardrail pipeline effectively eliminates constraint violations in LLM-generated portfolios while maintaining allocation intent, providing a practical solution for reliable financial advisory systems.

title: Locked at the Entrance, Open Inside: Where RLVR Narrows the Solution Space
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves single-sample accuracy (pass@1) but causes the policy's solution space to contract, diminishing the returns of test-time scaling. In this work, we investigate where inside a reasoning trajectory this breadth is lost: does the policy fail to access a valid solution family, or does it fail to execute computation once initiated? To disentangle access from execution, we analyze the Countdown task, whose solution space can be exhaustively enumerated into discrete entrance families defined by the first operand and operator, across PPO on Qwen2.5-3B and GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Across both training setups, solution coverage falls by up to 67%, halving even on problems solved across all checkpoints. We show that this contraction is heavily concentrated at the entrance: per-token likelihood shifts are 11x--16x larger prior to the first arithmetic operation than during downstream reasoning. Supplying only an unselected entrance prefix restores completion rates in low-access families by over an order of magnitude (0.018 -> 0.212 under PPO), demonstrating that alternative solutions remain executable but are no longer initiated. Guided by this localization, we find that while surface prompting fails to recover diversity, entrance-targeted interventions succeed: late-layer parameter interpolation with early checkpoints increases solution coverage by 37% at no loss in pass@1. Finally, we show that early-step entropy collapse recurs across six math benchmarks with 7B and 14B models, but is not an inevitable byproduct of reasoning optimization: an SFT baseline preserves more than double the coverage, and staged SFT--DPO--RLVR pipelines retain early-step entropy. In summary, reasoning breadth is lost at the door, not inside the room. Code: https://github.com/ershiyidian/early-branch-locking.

AI.tldr: RLVR improves single-sample accuracy but reduces solution diversity; this contraction happens early at "entrance" choices, not during downstream reasoning execution.
AI.motivation: While RLVR improves pass@1 accuracy in reasoning tasks, it causes the policy's solution space to contract, diminishing returns from test-time scaling. The paper investigates where in the reasoning trajectory this breadth is lost.
AI.method: Analyzed the Countdown task (with exhaustively enumerable solution space) using PPO on Qwen2.5-3B and GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Examined solution coverage, per-token likelihood shifts, and conducted experiments with entrance prefix supply and parameter interpolation.
AI.result: Solution coverage falls by up to 67%, with contraction heavily concentrated at the "entrance" (11x-16x larger likelihood shifts). Supplying unselected entrance prefixes restores completion rates dramatically. Entrance-targeted interventions (late-layer parameter interpolation) increase coverage by 37% without accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning breadth is lost at initial choice points ("the door"), not during downstream reasoning execution. Early-step entropy collapse occurs across multiple math benchmarks but isn't inevitable—SFT baselines preserve more coverage, and staged training pipelines can retain early-step entropy.

title: Self-Specialized Teachers for Domain Post-Training
summary: Target-only post-training can improve performance in a specialized domain while degrading behaviors that a general-purpose base model acquired before adaptation. We study this problem when target-domain data are available but a representative replay corpus is not. We propose self-specialized teacher distillation (SSTD), a two-stage procedure that first trains a copy of the base model into a domain teacher, then distills its token distribution to a student on prefixes sampled from the student itself. Teacher training combines standard target supervision with base-aware key-token weighting and distribution alignment to the frozen base model; on-policy distillation then places domain feedback on states the student can encounter at inference time. On financial numerical reasoning, medical question answering, and legal holding identification, SSTD retains much of the target improvement of direct fine-tuning while improving the mean score on the evaluated general suite by 4.8--5.0 points at the reported operating point. The pattern persists across Qwen3 sizes and on Gemma backbones. SSTD requires neither an external teacher nor general replay data.

AI.tldr: SSTD is a two-stage distillation method that enables domain specialization without replay data, improving target performance while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Post-training for domain specialization often degrades the general-purpose capabilities of base models when representative replay corpus is unavailable, creating a trade-off between domain improvement and general performance preservation.
AI.method: Two-stage procedure: 1) Train a domain teacher from base model using target supervision with base-aware key-token weighting and distribution alignment, 2) On-policy distillation where student samples its own prefixes and teacher's token distribution is distilled to student.
AI.result: On financial numerical reasoning, medical QA, and legal identification tasks, SSTD retains most target improvement of direct fine-tuning while improving general suite mean score by 4.8-5.0 points. Works across Qwen3 sizes and Gemma backbones without external teacher or replay data.
AI.conclusion: SSTD effectively addresses the specialization-generalization trade-off through self-specialized distillation, enabling domain adaptation while preserving general capabilities without requiring replay data.

title: HalluPrism: When Multimodal Uncertainty Should Diagnose, Not Decide
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 52 pages, 1 figure, 46 tables
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can assign similar confidence to answers that fail for different reasons. We propose HalluPrism, a behavioral diagnostic that re-runs an answer after visual degradation, blank-image replacement, and grounding or relation checks. These targeted probes yield a signature over visual-perturbation sensitivity (V ), image-removal confidence retention (L), and grounding/relation-probe instability (A). Across 58K+ examples from four benchmarks and four MLLMs, image-removal confidence retention is most prevalent, while grounding/relation-probe instability better separates failure families. Only 18 of 48 source-target checks are diagonally aligned, so the coordinates should be interpreted jointly rather than as independent causal sources. With the dataset fixed, the joint signature improves failure-family AUROC from 0.634 to 0.769 on HallusionBench and from 0.707 to 0.817 on VizWiz, with smaller gains on POPE and VSR. In pooled XGBoost analysis, AUROC rises from 0.78 with scalar confidence to 0.95 with (V, L, A) and 0.97 when confidence is added. The same signature does not automatically improve correctness ranking. The three tested direct scalarizations can harm it. These results separate failure diagnosis from abstention scoring: multimodal uncertainty should characterize failure structure before it is used to decide whether to abstain or correct.

AI.tldr: HalluPrism is a behavioral diagnostic tool for MLLMs that uses visual perturbations, image removal, and grounding/relation checks to create a 3D signature (V, L, A) for identifying different types of answer failures, improving failure-family AUROC from 0.634 to 0.769 on HallusionBench.
AI.motivation: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) assign similar confidence to answers that fail for different reasons, making it difficult to distinguish between various types of failures. There's a need for diagnostic tools that can identify specific failure families to better understand model limitations and improve uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: HalluPrism applies three targeted probes: 1) visual degradation to measure perturbation sensitivity (V), 2) blank-image replacement to measure confidence retention when visual information is removed (L), and 3) grounding or relation checks to measure probe instability (A). These create a 3D behavioral signature for each model answer.
AI.result: Across 58K+ examples from four benchmarks and four MLLMs, image-removal confidence retention (L) was most prevalent. The joint (V, L, A) signature improved failure-family AUROC significantly: from 0.634 to 0.769 on HallusionBench, 0.707 to 0.817 on VizWiz, with smaller gains on POPE and VSR. In pooled XGBoost analysis, AUROC rose from 0.78 with scalar confidence to 0.95 with (V, L, A) and 0.97 when confidence was added.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal uncertainty should characterize failure structure before being used for abstention decisions. The joint signature approach better separates failure families than scalar confidence alone, but direct scalarizations of the signature can harm correctness ranking. Only 18 of 48 source-target checks were diagonally aligned, suggesting the coordinates should be interpreted jointly rather than as independent causal sources.

title: How Language Models Choose Sides: Internal Representations of Instruction Hierarchy
comment: Published at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability workshop, 16 pages (including appendix)
summary: We study how instruction-tuned LLMs arbitrate direct conflicts between system and user instructions. We introduce a benchmark of 41 paired constraints with deterministic verifiers and evaluate eight models under matched baseline, conflict, and same-channel control conditions. Behaviourally, the models split into three regimes by System Authority Delta: hierarchy-respecting models use the system channel as an authority signal, anti-hierarchy models follow the system less often than their same-channel baseline predicts, and no-effect models show little channel sensitivity. Llama-3.1-8B is the strongest anti-hierarchy case in our suite, following the system in only 0.10 of conflict trials. We use this behavioural failure case to ask whether user-preferring arbitration reflects the absence of an internal conflictresolution signal. It does not: on Llama-3.1-8B, the conflict outcome is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at 0.97 balanced accuracy, 17 percentage points above a metadata-only baseline, with analogous signals on Qwen2.5-7B and gpt-oss-20b. Steering with a layer-12 mean of four per-conflict logistic-regression directions raises genuine system compliance from 0.132 to 0.530, while directions selected mainly for pooled separability steer poorly. User-preferring conflict resolution can therefore coexist with a readable internal arbitration signal, and successful intervention depends on the geometry of the readout rather than probe accuracy alone

AI.tldr: Instruction-tuned LLMs show three distinct conflict resolution regimes when system and user instructions directly conflict, with some models consistently preferring user instructions despite having readable internal arbitration signals.
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to understand how instruction-tuned LLMs resolve conflicts between system and user instructions, as this reveals their underlying authority hierarchies and conflict resolution mechanisms.
AI.method: Created a benchmark of 41 paired constraints with deterministic verifiers, evaluated 8 models under three conditions: matched baseline, conflict, and same-channel control. Used behavioral analysis and residual-stream activation analysis with logistic regression decoding and steering interventions.
AI.result: Models split into three regimes: hierarchy-respecting (system as authority), anti-hierarchy (system less followed than baseline), and no-effect. Llama-3.1-8B was strongest anti-hierarchy case. Internal conflict resolution signals were readable (0.97 balanced accuracy). Successful steering interventions possible using geometry-aware readout rather than just probe accuracy.
AI.conclusion: User-preferring conflict resolution can coexist with readable internal arbitration signals, and effective intervention depends on understanding the geometry of readout representations rather than just classifier accuracy.

title: PokaiTrainer: Scaling Belief-State Search to Competitive Pokémon VGC
summary: Decision-time equilibrium search carried poker to superhuman play, but it has so far relied on tractable subgames: a handful of actions per decision, chance confined to card deals, one player moving at a time. Competitive Pokémon in its official doubles format (VGC) breaks all three assumptions at once. Both players act simultaneously from joint menus in the hundreds, each joint action resolves to hundreds of stochastic outcomes, and the opponent's reserves and stat allocations are hidden. We set out to build a strong VGC agent and report what that took. PokaiEngine, our Rust battle engine, enumerates a joint action's full weighted outcome distribution in one pass, at ${\sim}99\%$ parity with Pokémon Showdown and a fraction of the cost of sampling it. On top of the engine, PokaiTrainer adapts Student of Games to this scale, solving every decision as a Bayesian matrix game over public belief states and growing subgames under an explicit compute budget. On the live Showdown best-of-three ladder, the agent wins 59% of 150 sets against a human field averaging ${\sim}1320$ Elo. It settles into a 1350-1400 Elo band, and at its peak briefly entered the format's top 500.

AI.tldr: Researchers built a superhuman Pokémon VGC AI agent using decision-time equilibrium search adapted to complex simultaneous-action games with hidden information, achieving competitive Elo ratings on the live ladder.
AI.motivation: Decision-time equilibrium search worked well for poker but couldn't handle complex games like Pokémon VGC that break three key assumptions: simultaneous actions (hundreds of joint actions), stochastic outcomes (hundreds per action), and hidden information (opponent reserves/stat allocations).
AI.method: Built PokaiEngine (Rust battle engine) to enumerate full outcome distributions efficiently, and PokaiTrainer that adapts Student of Games algorithm to solve decisions as Bayesian matrix games over public belief states with compute-budgeted subgame growth.
AI.result: The agent achieved 59% win rate over 150 best-of-three sets against human opponents averaging ~1320 Elo, settling into 1350-1400 Elo band, and briefly entered the format's top 500 players.
AI.conclusion: Decision-time equilibrium search can be successfully scaled to complex simultaneous-action games with hidden information and stochastic outcomes, enabling superhuman performance in Pokémon VGC through efficient battle simulation and Bayesian game solving.

title: A Generalized Optimization Engine (GOE) for Edge AI Inference Acceleration
comment: 14 pages, compressed version is under review in IEEE MILCOM 2026
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet their widespread deployment is impeded by significant computational costs, particularly on resource-constrained devices. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of various AI model optimization techniques, algorithms, and abstractions, discussing their potential to reduce computational complexity, memory footprint, latency, and power consumption. Furthermore, we propose a comprehensive hardware (HW) and model-agnostic generalized optimization architecture that integrates these techniques for improved efficiency. Our study underscores the critical role of such a generalized optimization system in preparing model deployment over resource-constrained heterogeneous hardware in a tactical environment. As a concrete demonstration, we show that GOE-compressed language models deploy and run on a GPU-less edge CPU, and that the choice of compression method, not merely its nominal bit-width, determines whether task accuracy survives deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GOE (Generalized Optimization Architecture), a hardware and model-agnostic framework for optimizing AI models to run efficiently on resource-constrained edge devices, showing that compression choice affects task accuracy more than nominal bit-width.
AI.motivation: AI models have high computational costs that impede deployment on resource-constrained edge devices, requiring optimization techniques to reduce complexity, memory, latency, and power consumption.
AI.method: The paper explores theoretical foundations of AI optimization techniques and proposes a hardware/model-agnostic generalized optimization architecture (GOE) that integrates various compression and optimization methods.
AI.result: Demonstrates that GOE-compressed language models can deploy and run on GPU-less edge CPUs, and that the choice of compression method (not just nominal bit-width) determines whether task accuracy survives deployment.
AI.conclusion: A generalized optimization system is critical for deploying AI models on resource-constrained heterogeneous hardware in tactical environments, with compression method selection being crucial for maintaining accuracy.

title: RL-FAT: Reinforcement Learning for Fair Adversarial Training
summary: Deep neural networks remain highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, and adversarial training (AT) has become a widely used approach for improving robustness. However, improvements in average robust accuracy often mask substantial class-wise disparities: while some classes become more robust, others may remain disproportionately vulnerable under attack. This imbalance raises an important adversarial fairness concern, particularly in vision tasks where reliable robustness is expected across all categories. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{RL-FAT}, a reinforcement-learning-inspired fair adversarial training framework that uses policy-gradient based feedback from adversarial predictions. RL-FAT interprets the prediction distribution as a policy and combines correctness-based prediction rewards with class-wise value estimates to compute class-specific advantages for policy-gradient optimization. This enables the model to adaptively focus on class-wise misclassification. Furthermore, we introduce a fairness-emphasis adversarial loss that assigns stronger training pressure to classes with high adversarial loss, thereby mitigating class-wise robustness disparity. By combining reinforcement-driven adaptation with fairness-emphasis regularization, RL-FAT improves adversarial robustness while promoting a more balanced robustness distribution across classes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive robust accuracy and substantially reduces class-wise robustness imbalance compared with standard adversarial training baselines.

AI.tldr: RL-FAT is a reinforcement learning-based fair adversarial training framework that addresses class-wise robustness disparities in deep neural networks by using policy-gradient optimization and fairness-emphasis regularization to balance robustness across all classes.
AI.motivation: While adversarial training improves average robust accuracy, it often creates substantial class-wise disparities where some classes remain disproportionately vulnerable. This raises adversarial fairness concerns, especially in vision tasks where reliable robustness is expected across all categories.
AI.method: Proposes RL-FAT, a reinforcement-learning-inspired fair adversarial training framework that: 1) Uses policy-gradient based feedback from adversarial predictions, interpreting the prediction distribution as a policy and combining correctness-based prediction rewards with class-wise value estimates to compute class-specific advantages; 2) Introduces a fairness-emphasis adversarial loss that assigns stronger training pressure to classes with high adversarial loss.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the method achieves competitive robust accuracy while substantially reducing class-wise robustness imbalance compared to standard adversarial training baselines.
AI.conclusion: By combining reinforcement-driven adaptation with fairness-emphasis regularization, RL-FAT improves adversarial robustness while promoting a more balanced robustness distribution across classes, addressing important fairness concerns in adversarial training.

title: FRAC-MAS: A Safe and Explainable Multi-Agent System for Fracture Diagnosis
comment: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI for Medicine (AgenticMed)
summary: Fracture detection and its clinical interpretability see notable improvements when deep vision models are integrated with agentic AI architectures. While deep learning models achieve high diagnostic performance, their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. We propose FRAC-MAS, an agentic AI system for automated, explainable, and safe bone fracture detection. The framework combines a stacked ensemble of four vision models with conformal prediction to produce statistically grounded differential diagnoses, while a multi-agent workflow performs independent verification, retrieves clinical guidelines, and generates patient-friendly reports. A pipeline-depth ablation study confirms that our multi-agent critic triages 86.6% of cases into a high-confidence auto-confirmed cohort while escalating uncertain cases, outperforming a single-agent baseline. Patient preference studies against Llama, MedGemma, and Gemini further demonstrate significantly more comprehensible clinical reports. These results suggest that integrating multi-agent critics with conformal guarantees enables safer radiology triage while preserving clinician oversight. More broadly, FRAC-MAS demonstrates how cooperative agentic architectures can serve as auditable, human-in-the-loop decision support systems for safety-critical healthcare. Our code is available at https://github.com/hardik1712/FRAC-MAS, and the website is available at https://frac-mas.vercel.app.

AI.tldr: FRAC-MAS is an agentic AI system that combines stacked vision models with conformal prediction and multi-agent workflows for explainable, safe bone fracture detection with statistical guarantees and clinical interpretability.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models achieve high fracture detection performance but their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. There's a need for automated, explainable, and safe AI systems that preserve clinician oversight while providing auditable decision support.
AI.method: Proposes FRAC-MAS: combines stacked ensemble of four vision models with conformal prediction for statistically grounded differential diagnoses, plus multi-agent workflow with independent verification, clinical guideline retrieval, and patient-friendly report generation.
AI.result: Multi-agent critic triages 86.6% of cases into high-confidence auto-confirmed cohort while escalating uncertain cases, outperforming single-agent baseline. Patient preference studies show significantly more comprehensible reports than Llama, MedGemma, and Gemini.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multi-agent critics with conformal guarantees enables safer radiology triage while preserving clinician oversight. FRAC-MAS demonstrates how cooperative agentic architectures can serve as auditable, human-in-the-loop decision support systems for safety-critical healthcare.

title: Adaptive Multi-Branching for Shallow Decision Tree Induction
summary: Decision trees are attractive for tabular prediction tasks because each prediction follows an interpretable sequence of feature-threshold tests.
