In this paper, control performance guarantee is first established by deriving tracking error bound for the in-network control architecture, while accounting for computational delays. The derived tracking error bound allows for diverse communication and computation strategies under a specific condition, including time-/event-triggered mechanisms. Additionally, the trade-off between communication and computation performances is shown for a given desired control performance. Furthermore, to enhance the efficiency in both communication and computation, an efficient control framework with an asynchronous event-triggered mechanism in both control and online learning is devised under the existence of computational delay. The proposed event-triggered strategy is proven to achieve the same control performance as time-triggered scenario while excluding Zeno behavior. Finally, we derive an explicit expression of the proposed event-trigger condition for exponentially stabilizable systems, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations.

AI.tldr: Online learning-based control with remote computation faces computational delays; paper establishes performance guarantees, shows trade-offs between communication/computation, and proposes efficient event-triggered framework that achieves same performance as time-triggered while avoiding Zeno behavior.
AI.motivation: Online learning-based control is promising for uncertain systems but faces challenges: resource-intensive learning algorithms introduce significant computational delays, especially on systems with limited local computational resources. There's a need to mitigate these delays while maintaining control performance.
AI.method: Uses an in-network online learning-based control structure with remote computation nodes. Establishes control performance guarantees by deriving tracking error bounds accounting for computational delays. Shows trade-off between communication and computation performances. Devises an efficient control framework with asynchronous event-triggered mechanisms in both control and online learning. Proves the event-triggered strategy achieves same performance as time-triggered scenario while excluding Zeno behavior.
AI.result: Derived tracking error bounds that accommodate diverse communication/computation strategies (time-/event-triggered). Showed explicit trade-off between communication and computation for desired control performance. Developed event-triggered framework with proven performance matching time-triggered case without Zeno behavior. Derived explicit expression for event-trigger condition for exponentially stabilizable systems and demonstrated effectiveness through simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed in-network control architecture with event-triggered mechanisms effectively addresses computational delay challenges in online learning-based control, maintaining performance guarantees while improving communication/computation efficiency. The framework provides practical solutions for resource-constrained control systems.

title: Agent2UCB: Agentic System for Generative Engine Optimization
summary: Large language model driven search engines such as Google AI Overviews and Perplexity have created new opportunities for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) the practice of refining content to increase its likelihood of being cited or summarized by generative systems. We demonstrate Agent2UCB, an agentic GEO system that autonomously improves content visibility through customized, feedback-driven optimization. For each content item, the system evaluates nine GEO strategies, identifies the most effective method, and accelerates selection using a bandit-based Agent2UCB policy that integrates LLM priors with online reward signals. To monitor side effects, the system also provides a lightweight, text-only SEO readiness evaluation covering readability, topical coverage, and EEAT-style credibility. Experiments on GEO-Bench show consistent visibility gains while preserving SEO quality. The demo allows users to choose the websites of interest, observe the optimization workflow, and compare GEO/SEO outcomes across methods.

AI.tldr: Agent2UCB is an autonomous system for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) that uses LLM agents and bandit algorithms to optimize content for generative search engines while maintaining SEO quality.
AI.motivation: The rise of LLM-driven search engines (like Google AI Overviews and Perplexity) has created new opportunities for content optimization beyond traditional SEO, requiring automated systems to improve content visibility in generative search results.
AI.method: The system evaluates nine GEO strategies per content item, uses an Agent2UCB bandit policy that combines LLM priors with online reward signals to accelerate strategy selection, and includes a lightweight SEO evaluation for monitoring side effects on readability, topical coverage, and credibility.
AI.result: Experiments on GEO-Bench show consistent visibility gains in generative search while preserving SEO quality, demonstrating effective optimization for both GEO and SEO objectives.
AI.conclusion: Agent2UCB provides an effective autonomous system for GEO that balances generative engine optimization with traditional SEO concerns, offering practical tools for content visibility in the era of generative search.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: LLM-powered Long-term Chaotic Time Series Forecasting under Short-term Observations
summary: Chaotic time series forecasting is a challenging task due to its sensitivity to initial conditions and long-term unpredictability. Traditional methods typically rely on sufficient temporal trajectories to learn long-term dynamics, which limits their applicability when only short-term observations are available. While recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown great potential for time series forecasting, their temporal representations are not explicitly tailored to the phase-space structure and nonlinear evolution of chaotic systems. To address these issues, we propose PAC-LLM, a phase-space-aware adaptive fusion framework for long-term chaotic time series forecasting powered by LLMs. PAC-LLM leverages learned phase-space features and textual information to fully enable LLM's time series forecasting capacity. In particular, we design an auxiliary feature module and a gated weighting mechanism for multivariate coupling information fusion and selection. Extensive experiments on representative chaotic systems demonstrate that our method outperforms existing fine-tuned and zero-shot baselines in both short-term and long-term predictions. Our ablation study further confirms the effectiveness of each key component in PAC-LLM.

AI.tldr: PAC-LLM is a phase-space-aware adaptive fusion framework that uses LLMs for chaotic time series forecasting, outperforming existing methods by combining learned phase-space features with textual information.
AI.motivation: Traditional methods for chaotic time series forecasting require sufficient temporal trajectories to learn long-term dynamics, limiting their use when only short-term observations are available. While LLMs show potential for time series forecasting, their temporal representations aren't specifically designed for the phase-space structure and nonlinear evolution of chaotic systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes PAC-LLM, a phase-space-aware adaptive fusion framework that leverages learned phase-space features and textual information to enhance LLMs' forecasting capabilities. It includes an auxiliary feature module and a gated weighting mechanism for multivariate coupling information fusion and selection.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on representative chaotic systems show that PAC-LLM outperforms existing fine-tuned and zero-shot baselines in both short-term and long-term predictions. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each key component in the framework.
AI.conclusion: PAC-LLM successfully addresses the limitations of traditional methods and existing LLM approaches by incorporating phase-space awareness, making it an effective solution for chaotic time series forecasting with limited observational data.

title: Revolutionizing Turn-by-Turn Navigation with Cloud-Edge Deep Learning
comment: This paper has accepted by IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
summary: Turn-by-turn (TBT) navigation systems are integral to modern driving experiences, providing real-time audio instructions to guide drivers safely to destinations. However, existing audio instruction policy often relies on rule-based approaches that struggle to balance informational content with cognitive load, potentially leading to driver confusion or missed turns in complex environments. To overcome these difficulties, we first model the generation of navigation instructions as a multi-task learning problem by decomposing the audio content into combinations of modular elements. Then, we propose a novel deep learning framework that leverages the powerful spatiotemporal information processing capabilities of Transformers and the strong multi-task learning abilities of Mixture of Experts (MoE) to generate real-time, context-aware audio instructions for TBT driving navigation. A cloud-edge collaborative architecture is implemented to handle the computational demands of the model, ensuring scalability and real-time performance for practical applications. Experimental results in the real world demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the yaw rate (the proportion of vehicles deviating from navigation routes) compared to traditional methods, delivering clearer and more effective audio instructions. This is the first large-scale application of deep learning in driving audio navigation, marking a substantial advancement in intelligent transportation and driving assistance technologies.

AI.tldr: A novel deep learning framework using Transformers and Mixture of Experts generates real-time audio navigation instructions through cloud-edge collaboration, significantly reducing vehicle deviation rates compared to traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based audio navigation systems struggle to balance information content with cognitive load, often causing driver confusion or missed turns in complex environments, highlighting the need for smarter, context-aware instruction generation.
AI.method: Models navigation instruction generation as multi-task learning by decomposing audio content into modular elements; uses Transformer spatiotemporal processing and MoE multi-task capabilities within a cloud-edge collaborative architecture for real-time performance.
AI.result: Experimental results show significant reduction in yaw rate (vehicles deviating from navigation routes) compared to traditional methods, delivering clearer and more effective audio instructions in real-world applications.
AI.conclusion: This represents the first large-scale deep learning application in driving audio navigation, marking a substantial advancement in intelligent transportation and driving assistance technologies.

title: On the Resilience of Text-to-Video Diffusion Models to Hardware Faults
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Workshop on From Frames to Stories (F2S)
summary: We present the first systematic study of the resilience of text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models under random hardware-level faults. While T2V models are widely used for automated video generation due to their ability to produce high-quality, temporally coherent, and realistic videos, their iterative denoising process and spatiotemporal dependencies introduce unique failure modes. We perform an extensive fault-injection study covering both computational and memory faults across three T2V models and a representative benchmark. Our results show that (1) a single fault can degrade overall performance by up to 3.7\%, with semantic correctness more affected than perceptual quality; (2) memory faults are more damaging than computational faults, high-order exponent bits are particularly vulnerable, and the widely-used bfloat16 is more susceptible than alternative formats; and (3) 7-28\% of faults cause visible artifacts, including semantic changes such as added objects, suggesting that single faults are sufficient to alter output semantics. Our findings reveal reliability risks in deployed T2V systems and motivate further research on improving fault resilience. Code: \href{https://github.com/ztcoalson/T2V-Resilience}{https://github.com/ztcoalson/T2V-Resilience}.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of text-to-video (T2V) diffusion model resilience under random hardware faults, revealing significant reliability risks including up to 3.7% performance degradation and 7-28% of faults causing visible artifacts or semantic changes.
AI.motivation: T2V models are widely used for automated video generation but their iterative denoising process and spatiotemporal dependencies create unique failure modes. There's a need to understand the resilience of these systems to hardware faults, as single faults can potentially alter output semantics, posing reliability risks in deployed systems.
AI.method: Comprehensive fault-injection study covering both computational and memory faults across three T2V models and a representative benchmark. The study systematically injects random hardware-level faults to evaluate their impact on model performance and output quality.
AI.result: (1) Single faults degrade overall performance up to 3.7%, with semantic correctness more affected than perceptual quality; (2) Memory faults are more damaging than computational faults, high-order exponent bits are particularly vulnerable, and bfloat16 format is more susceptible than alternatives; (3) 7-28% of faults cause visible artifacts including semantic changes like added objects.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals significant reliability risks in deployed T2V systems, showing that single hardware faults are sufficient to alter output semantics. These findings motivate further research on improving fault resilience in text-to-video diffusion models.

title: Nested Convex-Body Chasing for Online Optimization with Evolving Feasible Sets
summary:
We study online optimization with nested shrinking feasible regions in two settings: convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets (CONES) and adversarial constrained online convex optimization (COCO). Our algorithms separate loss control from geometric movement: constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests preserve regret guarantees, while a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser limits movement.
  For CONES with a $G$-Lipschitz, $μ$-strongly convex objective on a diameter-$D$ domain, we chase intersections of the current feasible set with adaptive objective sublevel sets. Using the Euclidean chasing ratio $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)})$, we obtain nonpositive regret at every prefix and movement $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)\,GD\log(eT)/μ})$. The bound adapts to the increase in the constrained optimum value. In dimension two, with all other parameters fixed, every randomized algorithm with terminal expected regret $O(T^β)$, $β<1$, suffers $Ω(\sqrt{\log T})$ expected movement on some deterministic nested sequence, proving optimal horizon dependence. Under linear growth away from the constrained minimizer set, Steiner-point tracking yields movement independent of $T$.
  For general convex COCO, one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets gives regret $O(G_fD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$ and cumulative constraint violation $O(G_gD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$. For strongly convex losses, both are $O(d\log(1+d)\log(eT))$ when other parameters are fixed. These reductions replace the $O(d^{d/2})$ projection-path factor in prior analyses by the polynomial dimension dependence of Euclidean nested convex-body chasing.

AI.tldr: The paper presents new algorithms for online convex optimization with nested shrinking constraints (CONES) and adversarial constrained optimization (COCO), achieving improved movement and regret bounds using convex-body chasing techniques.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address online optimization problems with evolving constraints where feasible regions shrink over time, which occurs in applications with gradually revealed information or increasingly strict requirements. Prior analyses had poor dimension dependence (O(d^{d/2})), so the goal is to develop algorithms with better dimension scaling.
AI.method: The method separates loss control from geometric movement: using constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests to preserve regret guarantees while employing a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser to limit movement. For CONES, they chase intersections of current feasible sets with adaptive objective sublevel sets. For COCO, they use one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets.
AI.result: For CONES with strongly convex objectives: nonpositive regret at every prefix and movement O(√[d log(1+d) GD log(eT)/μ]). For general convex COCO: regret O(G_fD√[d log(1+d)T]) and cumulative constraint violation O(G_gD√[d log(1+d)T]). For strongly convex losses: both bounds reduce to O(d log(1+d) log(eT)). These improve the O(d^{d/2}) projection-path factor in prior work to polynomial dimension dependence.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that separating geometric movement control from loss optimization enables significantly better dimension dependence in online constrained optimization problems with shrinking feasible regions, achieving near-optimal horizon dependence and polynomial instead of exponential dimension dependence.

title: Adaptive Doubly Robust Off-Policy Evaluation for Ranking Policies under Diverse User Behavior
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at CONSEQUENCES 2026 and selected for oral presentation
summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) of ranking policies is challenging be- cause selecting and ordering multiple items from a candidate set makes the number of possible rankings grow combinatorially with the number of candidates and the ranking length. Consequently, Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS), whose importance weight is the full-ranking probability ratio under the evaluation and logging policies, can have excessive variance. Independent IPS (IIPS) and Reward Interaction IPS (RIPS) reduce variance by imposing fixed assumptions on how users browse rankings, but may introduce bias when those assumptions mismatch actual behavior. Adaptive Inverse Propensity Scoring (AIPS) addresses this trade-off by adap- tively marginalizing importance weights over the actions that affect each position-wise reward. It attains minimum variance within a class of unbiased IPS-based estimators when the true user be- havior model is observed. However, its estimation accuracy may still degrade for longer rankings, and AIPS does not use a reward model for residual correction. We propose Adaptive Doubly Robust (ADR), which combines adaptive importance weighting with re- ward regression through a control-variate correction. We establish its unbiasedness when the true user behavior model is observed and characterize a sufficient condition under which it reduces vari- ance relative to AIPS. Across synthetic experiments with 10,000 simulations per condition, ADR improves mean squared error over AIPS and conventional ranking OPE estimators across a range of logged-data sizes and ranking lengths.

AI.tldr: ADR (Adaptive Doubly Robust) combines adaptive importance weighting with reward regression for off-policy evaluation in ranking, reducing variance while maintaining unbiasedness compared to existing IPS-based methods.
AI.motivation: Off-policy evaluation of ranking policies is challenging due to combinatorial explosion of possible rankings, leading to excessive variance in Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS). Existing variance reduction methods (IIPS, RIPS, AIPS) either make fixed browsing assumptions that may introduce bias or don't use reward models for residual correction, and their accuracy degrades for longer rankings.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Doubly Robust (ADR) which combines: 1) Adaptive importance weighting (similar to AIPS) that marginalizes importance weights over actions affecting each position-wise reward, and 2) Reward regression through control-variate correction for residual error reduction.
AI.result: ADR maintains unbiasedness when true user behavior model is observed. It provides a sufficient condition under which it reduces variance relative to AIPS. In synthetic experiments with 10,000 simulations per condition, ADR improves mean squared error over AIPS and conventional ranking OPE estimators across various logged-data sizes and ranking lengths.
AI.conclusion: ADR effectively addresses the variance-bias trade-off in ranking OPE by combining adaptive importance weighting with doubly robust estimation, providing better performance than existing methods, especially for longer rankings and limited logged data.

title: HANIA: Planner-Guided Multimodal Graph Evidence Selection for Grounded Question Answering
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at Graph-enhanced LLMs for trustwOrthy Web data management (GLOW), ISWC 2026 Workshops, Bari, Italy
summary: Multimodal question answering remains sensitive to noisy, incomplete, and weakly grounded evidence. Long unstructured contexts can introduce redundancy and encourage unsupported generation, while flat retrieval may overlook relations needed for multi-step reasoning. We present HANIA, a planner-guided multimodal graph framework for evidence-grounded question answering. HANIA processes the supplied image and text using a frozen vision-language model to extract concise question-relevant visual evidence with explicit abstention. It then constructs an input-grounded multimodal graph and applies a two-group finite-state planner to coordinate descriptive and relational evidence. Coverage-aware pruning retains a compact evidence set based on relevance, graph confidence, concept coverage, and modality diversity. The selected passages, visual statements, and graph triples are provided to a frozen instruction-tuned decoder. We evaluate HANIA on ScienceQA using answer accuracy, evidence-filtering quality, evidence-budget sensitivity, and efficiency. The results show that structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval can support competitive multimodal question answering without target-dataset fine-tuning or iterative retrieval. The code is available at https://github.com/Zafar-southeast/HANIA.

AI.tldr: HANIA is a planner-guided multimodal graph framework for evidence-grounded QA that uses structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval without requiring target-dataset fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Multimodal QA is sensitive to noisy, incomplete, and weakly grounded evidence. Long unstructured contexts cause redundancy and unsupported generation, while flat retrieval overlooks relations needed for multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: HANIA uses a frozen VLM to extract concise visual evidence with explicit abstention, constructs a multimodal graph, applies a two-group finite-state planner for descriptive/relational evidence coordination, and performs coverage-aware pruning based on relevance, graph confidence, concept coverage, and modality diversity. Final evidence is passed to a frozen instruction-tuned decoder.
AI.result: Evaluation on ScienceQA shows HANIA achieves competitive multimodal QA performance without target-dataset fine-tuning or iterative retrieval, with good evidence-filtering quality, evidence-budget sensitivity, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval can effectively support competitive multimodal question answering without requiring costly fine-tuning or complex retrieval iterations.

title: Wide Learning: Learning to Reach Evidence
summary: Machine learning is usually evaluated after an evidence interface has been fixed. A dataset, sensor suite, query language, action set, or experimental protocol determines which observations can be obtained, and learning is judged by what it extracts from them. We study a complementary capability. A learner's state can determine which evidence-generating experiments it can reliably realise under bounded resources, even when primitive affordances remain fixed. We call this learner-relative experiment family its effective epistemic reach, and use Wide Learning for task-relevant learning-induced changes in that family.We formalise effective reach relative to learner state, deployment budget, reliability threshold, and evaluation distribution. In a controlled construction, two hidden worlds have exactly the same public observation law. An informative diagnostic exists in a fixed five-primitive substrate. Before calibration, one address attempt realises it with probability at most $2^{-10} = 1/1024$, below a pre-specified 0.95 threshold; after calibration, held-out realisation is 1. Public-channel total variation is 0, whereas the realised diagnostic has total variation 1, and sealed binary risk moves from approximately 1/2 to 0. The construction establishes that learning can change effective epistemic reach even when primitive affordances and deployment resources are held fixed. It opens a complementary evaluation question for learning systems: not only what they infer from available evidence, but what informative evidence experience teaches them to bring within reach.

AI.tldr: Learning systems can change which experiments they can reliably perform, not just what they learn from available evidence.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML evaluation focuses on what learners extract from fixed evidence interfaces (datasets, sensors, etc.), but ignores how learning can change which evidence-generating experiments learners can reliably perform.
AI.method: Formalizes "effective epistemic reach" relative to learner state, deployment budget, reliability threshold, and evaluation distribution. Uses a controlled construction with two hidden worlds having identical public observation laws, where a diagnostic exists in a fixed primitive substrate.
AI.result: Before calibration, diagnostic realization probability is ≤ 2⁻¹⁰ (< 0.95 threshold); after calibration, held-out realization probability is 1. Public-channel total variation is 0, while diagnostic total variation is 1, and sealed binary risk moves from ~½ to 0.
AI.conclusion: Learning can change effective epistemic reach even with fixed primitive affordances and deployment resources, establishing a complementary evaluation question: not just what systems infer from available evidence, but what informative evidence they learn to bring within reach.

title: EviAnchor: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Regional Visual Evidence Compensation
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) frequently generate content unsupported by visual inputs. Preliminary experiments show that visual evidence is primarily incorporated into answer-side representations in early-to-middle decoder layers, while its direct influence progressively weakens in later layers. This attenuation suggests that visual evidence acquired earlier may be insufficiently utilized during subsequent generation. Based on this observation, we propose EviAnchor, a training-free and single-branch inference framework that preserves and reactivates visual evidence throughout generation. EviAnchor introduces Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots to progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially structured representations. It then strengthens the current decision state's access to these visual anchors through decision-conditioned evidence routing, mitigating excessive dependence on textual context. Finally, the model resumes its native Transformer computation to integrate the retrieved visual evidence with question semantics and generation history. Experiments across POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in visual grounding.

AI.tldr: EviAnchor is a training-free, single-branch inference framework that preserves and reactivates visual evidence throughout generation in large vision-language models to improve visual grounding.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models often generate content unsupported by visual inputs, as visual evidence is primarily incorporated in early-to-middle decoder layers but its influence weakens in later layers, suggesting insufficient utilization of acquired visual evidence during subsequent generation.
AI.method: EviAnchor introduces Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots to progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially structured representations, then strengthens the current decision state's access to these visual anchors through decision-conditioned evidence routing, mitigating excessive dependence on textual context. The model then resumes native Transformer computation.
AI.result: Experiments across POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in visual grounding.
AI.conclusion: EviAnchor effectively addresses the visual evidence attenuation problem in LVLMs by preserving and reactivating visual evidence throughout generation, leading to better visual grounding without requiring additional training.

title: Unsupervised Multi-Scale Gromov-Wasserstein Hypergraph Alignment
summary: We study unsupervised hypergraph alignment, where the goal is to infer node correspondences between two hypergraphs using only structural information, without node features, labels, seed matches, or side information. Direct higher-order formulations can represent hyperedge interactions faithfully, but they can be computationally demanding and cumbersome for non-uniform hypergraphs. Graph-reduction approaches introduce a different challenge: clique expansions keep the alignment problem on the original node set but collapse all hyperedge evidence into one pairwise graph, whereas bipartite expansions preserve incidence structure but enlarge the problem from nodes to nodes plus hyperedges. We introduce FALCON (Filtration-based hypergrAph aLignment via Cross-scale Optimal traNsport), an unsupervised optimal-transport framework for hypergraph alignment. Instead of representing each hypergraph by a single collapsed clique graph, FALCON constructs a filtration-induced sequence of clique-based co-occurrence dissimilarity matrices and jointly aligns all levels through one shared multi-scale Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) objective. The shared transport plan enforces a globally consistent node correspondence across filtration levels while avoiding the auxiliary hyperedge nodes introduced by bipartite expansion. Experiments on perturbation benchmarks derived from real-world hypergraphs show that FALCON is robust to structural noise and in almost all cases outperforms strong graph- and hypergraph-alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: FALCON is an unsupervised hypergraph alignment framework using multi-scale Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport on filtration-induced clique graphs, avoiding both graph reduction limitations and hyperedge node expansion.
AI.motivation: Existing hypergraph alignment methods face trade-offs: direct higher-order formulations are computationally demanding, graph-reduction approaches either collapse hyperedge evidence (clique expansions) or enlarge the problem with hyperedge nodes (bipartite expansions). There's a need for an efficient method that preserves hypergraph structure while maintaining computational feasibility.
AI.method: FALCON constructs a filtration-induced sequence of clique-based co-occurrence dissimilarity matrices from each hypergraph (instead of single collapsed graph), then jointly aligns all levels using a shared multi-scale Gromov-Wasserstein objective. This enforces globally consistent node correspondence across filtration levels without introducing auxiliary hyperedge nodes.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world hypergraph perturbation benchmarks show FALCON is robust to structural noise and outperforms strong graph- and hypergraph-alignment baselines in almost all cases.
AI.conclusion: FALCON provides an effective unsupervised hypergraph alignment framework that balances structural fidelity with computational efficiency by leveraging multi-scale optimal transport on filtration-induced representations, addressing limitations of both direct higher-order methods and graph-reduction approaches.

title: SafeAtlas-VL: Beyond Binary Multimodal Safety with Large-Scale Data and Guard Models
summary: Multimodal safety moderation requires distinguishing risks arising from visual content, user intent, and assistant behavior. Existing safeguards, however, are typically trained for a single judgment target and reduce safety assessment to a binary decision. Consequently, risk becomes difficult to compare across a multimodal interaction, and ambiguous cases are obscured. We introduce SafeAtlas-VL, a dataset of 1.5M training instances that places image-, request-, and response-level judgments on a five-level ordered scale. We curate a broad collection of safety-relevant data from both real-world and synthetic sources and apply a disagreement-aware annotation procedure. The resulting dataset spans 15 harm categories and 55 fine-grained subcategories, covering a broad range of multimodal safety scenarios. We also construct SafeAtlas-Bench, a held-out set of 5,000 instances for evaluating five-level predictions and continuous risk scores. Upon this dataset, we train the SafeAtlas Guard series of models via target-conditioned tuning for multimodal safety detection. Our models not only perform five-way classification of safety levels but also map safety to continuous scores through a soft cumulative ordinal head. Experimental results demonstrate that guard models trained on our dataset exhibit strong generalization: even without using the training sets of other benchmarks, they achieve competitive performance on the corresponding test sets. Notably, our 8B model attains the overall best performance, outperforming the previous SOTA by approximately 4% in F1 score. Code, data, and models are released to support further research. Warning: this paper contains example data that may be offensive, harmful, graphic, or disturbing.

AI.tldr: SafeAtlas introduces a multimodal safety moderation framework with ordered risk scales, a large training dataset, and models that generalize well across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal safety moderation systems are limited to binary judgments and single targets, making it difficult to compare risks across multimodal interactions and handle ambiguous cases effectively.
AI.method: Created SafeAtlas-VL dataset with 1.5M instances using five-level ordered scales for image, request, and response judgments. Employed disagreement-aware annotation across 15 harm categories and 55 subcategories. Developed target-conditioned tuning for SafeAtlas Guard models with a soft cumulative ordinal head for continuous risk scoring.
AI.result: Models achieve competitive performance on benchmark test sets even without using their training data. The 8B model outperforms previous SOTA by ~4% F1 score. Dataset covers broad multimodal safety scenarios with improved generalization capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The ordered scale approach and comprehensive dataset enable more nuanced multimodal safety assessment with strong generalization, advancing beyond binary classification systems. Code, data, and models are released to support further research.

title: LLMODE: Aligning ODEs with LLMs via Gated Token Injection for Irregular Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for spatio-temporal forecasting, but existing approaches often rely on regularly sampled token sequences and struggle with irregular observations because of temporal asynchrony, representation-space misalignment, and limited context windows. We propose LLMODE, a token-efficient framework for irregular spatio-temporal forecasting with a frozen LLM backbone. LLMODE first uses a graph-aware ODE encoder to reconstruct irregular graph observations as a continuous-time latent trajectory. A Fixed-Budget Perceiver Resampler then compresses this variable-length trajectory into a fixed number of dynamic memory tokens. In parallel, compact statistical descriptors are encoded and resampled into context memory tokens. A dual-source gated cross-attention module injects both memories into the frozen LLM, enabling controlled utilization of external spatio-temporal evidence. Experiments on three real-world urban datasets and two physical-dynamics benchmarks show competitive overall performance, with clearer advantages under sparse or dynamically complex irregular sampling. Additional evaluations on unseen urban regions further demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization without adaptation.

AI.tldr: LLMODE: A token-efficient framework using frozen LLMs for irregular spatio-temporal forecasting, solving irregular observation challenges through continuous-time encoding, memory token compression, and dual-source attention injection.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM approaches for spatio-temporal forecasting struggle with irregular observations due to temporal asynchrony, representation-space misalignment, and limited context windows, motivating the need for a more efficient and effective method.
AI.method: Proposes LLMODE framework with: 1) Graph-aware ODE encoder to reconstruct irregular graph observations as continuous-time latent trajectory; 2) Fixed-Budget Perceiver Resampler compresses trajectory into fixed dynamic memory tokens; 3) Compact statistical descriptors encoded into context memory tokens; 4) Dual-source gated cross-attention injects both memories into frozen LLM backbone.
AI.result: Competitive overall performance on three real-world urban datasets and two physical-dynamics benchmarks, with clearer advantages under sparse or dynamically complex irregular sampling, and strong zero-shot generalization on unseen urban regions without adaptation.
AI.conclusion: LLMODE demonstrates an effective token-efficient framework for irregular spatio-temporal forecasting using frozen LLMs, overcoming limitations of existing approaches while maintaining competitive performance and showing strong generalization capabilities.

title: Clustering as Approximation by Constrained Projectors: Theory and Guarantees
summary: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework showing that a broad family of clustering methods, including k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel k-means, kernel FCM, and spectral clustering, can all be expressed as structured low-rank projectors acting on a signal-derived matrix. By formulating each method as an instance of min over B in C of ||M - M P_B||_F^2, with different constraint sets C, we establish a common optimization template that clarifies the algebraic links among hard, fuzzy, kernel-induced, and orthonormal projections. Within this framework, we derive non-trivial theoretical results, including geodesic convexity properties on the projection manifold, perturbation bounds quantifying stability to matrix noise, and exact recovery guarantees under ideal block-model conditions. The analysis further explains when different clustering families collapse to the same optimal subspace and how deviations arise under small inter-cluster leakage. Overall, the work provides a coherent, theory-first foundation for understanding clustering through structured projectors.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that many clustering methods (k-means, spectral clustering, etc.) can all be expressed as structured low-rank projectors on a signal matrix, providing a unified theoretical framework.
AI.motivation: To establish a coherent theoretical foundation that unifies diverse clustering methods (hard, fuzzy, kernel, spectral) under a common algebraic framework, clarifying their relationships and shared mathematical structure.
AI.method: Formulates clustering methods as min over B in C of ||M - M P_B||_F^2 where C represents different constraint sets, creating a unified optimization template. Uses structured low-rank projectors acting on a signal-derived matrix M.
AI.result: Derives non-trivial theoretical results: geodesic convexity properties on projection manifold, perturbation bounds for stability under matrix noise, exact recovery guarantees under ideal block-model conditions, explains when different clustering families collapse to the same optimal subspace, and characterizes deviations under small inter-cluster leakage.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a coherent, theory-first foundation for understanding clustering through structured projectors, establishing algebraic links among hard, fuzzy, kernel-induced, and orthonormal projections, offering a unified perspective on clustering methodology.

title: Reward-guided Fine-Tuning of One-Step Generative Models via Wasserstein Gradient Flow
summary: To mitigate the time complexity of generative models, one-step generative models have recently emerged through direct mapping from noise to data in a single forward pass. However, the reward-guided fine-tuning method of one-step generative models remains largely unexplored. To address this, we consider one-step generators from an optimal transport view, investigating Wasserstein Gradient Flow (WGF) for modeling smooth and controlled distributional evolution in probability space. We then propose a novel reward-guided fine-tuning of a one-step generative model via WGF. We derive a practical training method that requires no reward gradients, thereby handling both non-differentiable and differentiable rewards. Moreover, our method provides smooth and stable reward-guided distributional updates while mitigating reward hacking and mode collapse. Experiments on 2D synthetic data, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet 256$\times$256 with diverse rewards, including JPEG (in)compressibility, class probability, Black-and-White and CLIP alignment, show that our method achieves better reward alignment compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes a novel reward-guided fine-tuning method for one-step generative models using Wasserstein Gradient Flow, enabling smooth distributional updates without requiring reward gradients.
AI.motivation: One-step generative models offer faster inference but lack exploration of reward-guided fine-tuning methods. Existing approaches for reward optimization in generative models haven't been effectively adapted to one-step architectures.
AI.method: Views one-step generators through optimal transport theory and applies Wasserstein Gradient Flow for smooth distributional evolution. Derives a practical training method that doesn't need reward gradients, handling both non-differentiable and differentiable rewards while preventing reward hacking and mode collapse.
AI.result: The method achieves better reward alignment than baselines across various tasks: 2D synthetic data, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet 256x256 with diverse rewards including JPEG compressibility, class probability, Black-and-White, and CLIP alignment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed WGF-based reward-guided fine-tuning provides an effective, stable approach for optimizing one-step generative models with diverse rewards, addressing key limitations of existing methods while maintaining training stability.

title: Emergent Misalignment Is Not Magical
summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on narrowly harmful datasets can lead to misalignment broadly, a phenomenon known as emergent misalignment (EM). EM poses a challenge for AI safety and our understanding of LLMs. Prior work often frames EM as an unexpected behavior, and explains it by appealing to general misalignment directions or anthropomorphizing it as acquiring an evil persona. However, the mechanisms behind these framings remain obscure. In this work, we show that EM is a predictable and data-dependent generalization phenomenon. By examining the base model's representation of EM training data and evaluation prompts, we find that evilness after EM training is highly predictable from representational distance: the closer an evaluation prompt is to training data centroid, the more evilness it elicits from EM models after training (with an average Spearman correlation of -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings). Building upon this analysis, we further demystify EM by showing that (1) its effectiveness changes significantly based on training data format; (2) there is not a general misalignment direction that transfers across different EM models; (3) the effect of EM is fundamentally different from persona changes. Furthermore, we extend the EM generalization metric from a scalar distance to a dataset-specific generalization direction, which robustly predicts EM models' evilness under semantics-preserving prompt perturbations including appending random tokens and paraphrasing, where other methods do not reliably generalize.

AI.tldr: EM (emergent misalignment) in LLMs is not about acquiring evil personas but rather a predictable data-dependent generalization phenomenon where model "evilness" correlates with representational distance from training data centroid.
AI.motivation: Emergent misalignment poses a challenge for AI safety and understanding of LLMs. Prior explanations frame it as unexpected behavior, appealing to general misalignment directions or anthropomorphizing as evil personas, but these mechanisms remain obscure. The authors aim to demystify EM by showing it's actually a predictable generalization phenomenon.
AI.method: Examine base model's representation of EM training data and evaluation prompts, finding that evilness correlates with representational distance. Extend EM generalization metric from scalar distance to dataset-specific generalization direction, and test under semantics-preserving prompt perturbations.
AI.result: Evilness after EM training is highly predictable from representational distance (average Spearman correlation of -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings). EM's effectiveness changes based on training data format, no general misalignment direction transfers across EM models, and EM effect differs from persona changes. Extended generalization direction robustly predicts evilness under prompt perturbations.
AI.conclusion: EM is a predictable, data-dependent generalization phenomenon rather than acquisition of evil personas or general misalignment directions. This demystification provides more concrete understanding of misalignment mechanisms for AI safety.

title: A Target-Centric Survey of Quantization-Aware Training
summary: The rapid development of LLMs incurs prohibitive memory footprints and intensive computational demands. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) techniques have emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges by explicitly simulating quantization effects during model training, yielding low-bit models that achieve accuracy comparable to their full-precision counterparts. In this work, we provide a target-centric survey of QAT, aimed at clarifying both its theoretical foundations and its evolving implementation landscape. We systematically review existing QAT methods through a target-centric taxonomy and synthesize cross-target differences in error characteristics, numerical formats, and strategy transferability. We further summarize QAT evaluation paradigms and discuss challenges in optimization and deployment, outlining potential directions for future research.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) methods for LLMs, covering theoretical foundations, implementation landscape, taxonomy, and future directions.
AI.motivation: The rapid development of Large Language Models incurs prohibitive memory footprints and intensive computational demands, creating a need for efficient solutions like quantization.
AI.method: The paper provides a target-centric survey of QAT, using a systematic taxonomy to review existing methods, analyze error characteristics, numerical formats, and strategy transferability across different targets.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes cross-target differences in QAT approaches, summarizes evaluation paradigms, and discusses optimization and deployment challenges for low-bit models.
AI.conclusion: QAT techniques enable efficient low-bit models with accuracy comparable to full-precision counterparts, and future research should address optimization challenges and deployment issues in this evolving field.

title: Beyond Correctness: Validity-Oriented Evaluation of Biomedical LLM Judges
summary: We propose a scalable, validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when high-quality human judgments are scarce. First, we augment existing human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations that produce auditable preference pairs. Second, we evaluate judges beyond aggregate correctness using three deployment-relevant dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with the requested output format. We use this pipeline to assess Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four regimes: (1) base, using the instruct model as is; (2) SFT, distillation-based supervised fine-tuning only; (3) RL, GRPO-based reinforcement learning only; and (4) SFT$\rightarrow$RL, SFT followed by RL. The base and single-stage regimes struggle on structured medical discrimination such as PICO extraction and clinical calculations, whereas SFT$\rightarrow$RL performs best across correctness, compliance, and robustness; gains concentrate on decomposable tasks (PICO, MedCalc), at times matching or outperforming frontier models.

AI.tldr: A validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when human judgments are scarce, using metric-grounded mutations to create preference pairs and assessing models across correctness, robustness, and compliance dimensions.
AI.motivation: There's a need to evaluate biomedical LLM judges when high-quality human judgments are scarce, requiring scalable methods that go beyond aggregate correctness metrics to assess deployment-relevant dimensions.
AI.method: Proposed pipeline has two main components: (1) augmenting existing human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations to produce auditable preference pairs, and (2) evaluating judges across three dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with requested output format. Applied this pipeline to assess Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four training regimes.
AI.result: SFT→RL (supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning) performs best across correctness, compliance, and robustness dimensions. Gains are concentrated on decomposable tasks like PICO extraction and clinical calculations, with this approach sometimes matching or outperforming frontier models. Base and single-stage regimes struggle with structured medical discrimination tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline provides a scalable, validity-oriented approach for evaluating biomedical LLM judges, demonstrating that sequential training (SFT followed by RL) yields superior performance on medical discrimination tasks compared to base or single-stage approaches, particularly for structured decomposable tasks.

title: Creation begins with understanding: LLMs as strategy designers for privacy-preserving tabular data synthesis
summary: Sharing tabular data in high-stakes domains is constrained by privacy regulations. Synthetic data offer a promising alternative, but deep generative models are costly to train and difficult to audit, while LLM-based methods often serialize records as text, obscuring tabular structure and exposing sensitive data. We introduce Tabular Synthesis Strategy Designer (TabSSD), which uses an LLM to design synthesis procedures rather than directly generate records. TabSSD provides the LLM with tree-derived summaries of variable dependence rather than raw records, which produces Python programs for local execution and evaluation. Across twelve datasets, TabSSD strikes a favourable balance among statistical fidelity, predictive utility, and empirical privacy risk, achieving the best average rank across six metrics among ten methods. Moreover, it substantially reduces local computation and token consumption relative to the compared methods. By enabling human-guided refinement and eliminating user-side model tuning, TabSSD lowers the expertise and infrastructure barriers to transparent tabular data synthesis.

AI.tldr: TabSSD uses LLMs to design synthesis procedures instead of generating records directly, achieving strong privacy-utility tradeoffs for tabular data synthesis with reduced computational costs.
AI.motivation: Sharing tabular data in regulated domains faces privacy constraints. Existing synthetic data methods have issues: deep generative models are costly to train and audit, while LLM-based methods serialize records as text, losing tabular structure and potentially exposing sensitive data.
AI.method: TabSSD uses an LLM to design synthesis procedures rather than directly generate records. It provides the LLM with tree-derived summaries of variable dependence instead of raw records, producing Python programs for local execution and evaluation.
AI.result: Across twelve datasets, TabSSD achieves the best average rank across six metrics (statistical fidelity, predictive utility, empirical privacy risk) among ten methods. It substantially reduces local computation and token consumption compared to other methods.
AI.conclusion: TabSSD lowers expertise and infrastructure barriers to transparent tabular data synthesis by enabling human-guided refinement and eliminating user-side model tuning, offering a practical solution for privacy-preserving data sharing.

title: APIFlow-Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Survive Long, Dependent API Workflows
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Under review at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Evaluation of Interactive Agents (IAEval). Harness, frozen task bank, and 44,362 execution transcripts: https://github.com/postmanlabs/APIFlow-Bench
summary: Tool-using agents are commonly evaluated by a single bit: whether an end-to-end workflow completed. This metric fails to distinguish failures that matter in production, such as expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution followed by incorrect final delivery. We introduce APIFlow-Bench, a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes performance into seven engineering capabilities and requires agents to produce answers supported by the actual call path. We generate synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask; each subtask is admitted only after a zero-LLM self-test triad verifies its grader and an oracle establishes solvability, and an adversarial audit identified and fixed six grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive: a state check traces a mock-minted canary through the API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, and a typed answer card is verified field by field. We release all answer keys and 44,362 unredacted execution transcripts. Across 19 frontier and open-weight models under one neutral scaffold, we find: (1) longer dependency chains degrade success, from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains and 61% when including the 8% of chain trials that a model-consensus screen flags as passed by no model; (2) reliability separates models more than best-case capability, with best-of-five spanning seven points but all-five-of-five reliability spanning 44 points; (3) the independent-error account of compounding failure does not fit the data: pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and on the clean slice 77% of failing runs reached the correct final state and failed only at delivery.

AI.tldr: APIFlow-Bench is a detailed benchmark for evaluating tool-using AI agents on long-horizon REST-API workflows, focusing on auditable execution paths and distinguishing various failure types beyond simple pass/fail metrics.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of tool-using agents uses simplistic pass/fail metrics that don't distinguish important failure types in production (like expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution with incorrect delivery). There's a need for more granular, auditable benchmarks that decompose performance into specific engineering capabilities.
AI.method: The benchmark generates synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask, with rigorous validation. Each subtask undergoes zero-LLM self-test triad verification of its grader, oracle establishment for solvability, and adversarial auditing to fix grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive, using state checks that trace mock-minted canaries through API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, with typed answer cards verified field by field.
AI.result: Results from 19 frontier and open-weight models show: (1) Longer dependency chains degrade success rates from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains and 61% when including flagged trials. (2) Reliability separates models more than best-case capability, with best-of-five spanning 7 points but all-five-of-five reliability spanning 44 points. (3) The independent-error compounding failure model doesn't fit the data - actual pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and 77% of failing runs reached correct final state but failed at delivery.
AI.conclusion: APIFlow-Bench provides a comprehensive, auditable evaluation framework that reveals important distinctions in agent performance, highlighting that current simplistic metrics mask significant engineering capability differences and that compound failure models need refinement to account for real-world execution patterns.

title: Last Step Matters: Early Uncertainty Cannot Predict Failure in Long-Horizon Agents
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Early failure prediction is important for long-horizon agents, as it enables timely intervention and can reduce inference and tool-use costs. Uncertainty quantification, such as verbal confidence and perplexity, offers a promising approach to detecting agent failures; however, it has not been explored whether these signals retain their discriminative power during the intermediate stages of long-horizon execution. We evaluate mainstream uncertainty signals on deep-research tasks and find that verbal confidence reliably distinguishes failures at trajectory completion, achieving a mean AUROC of 0.85, whereas all evaluated signals offer limited predictive value earlier in execution, with none exceeding a mean AUROC of 0.60 at 50% trajectory progress. We identify an underlying mechanism explaining this gap: path switching, where agents frequently abandon their current search direction in-trajectory, breaking the link between early signal and final outcome. These findings challenge the assumption that intermediate uncertainty can reliably guide early intervention. They also motivate a practical recommendation for agent harnesses in deep-research settings: use final-step confidence to decide whether to restart, an approach that our experiments find more effective than in-trajectory intervention.

AI.tldr: Early uncertainty signals are ineffective for predicting agent failures during intermediate stages of long-horizon tasks, but final-step confidence works well for deciding when to restart.
AI.motivation: Early failure prediction is important for long-horizon agents to enable timely intervention and reduce computational costs. The paper investigates whether uncertainty quantification signals remain effective during intermediate execution stages.
AI.method: The researchers evaluate mainstream uncertainty signals (verbal confidence and perplexity) on deep-research tasks. They analyze the discriminative power of these signals at different trajectory progress points (completion, 50% progress) and identify path switching as a key mechanism.
AI.result: Verbal confidence reliably distinguishes failures at trajectory completion (mean AUROC 0.85), but all signals offer limited predictive value earlier in execution (none exceeding mean AUROC 0.60 at 50% progress). The gap is explained by "path switching" where agents abandon current search directions mid-trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate uncertainty cannot reliably guide early intervention for long-horizon agents. The practical recommendation is to use final-step confidence to decide whether to restart, which is more effective than in-trajectory intervention.

title: More Perspectives, Stronger Signals: Multi-Perspective Enhancement and Progressive Fusion for Multimodal Entity Representation Learning
summary: Learning effective multimodal entity representations is fundamental for reasoning tasks such as multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC). However, existing methods often suffer from semantic over-smoothing within modalities and ineffective noise filtration across modalities, particularly under sparse or ambiguous conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrismF, a unified framework that synergizes multi-perspective enhancement with progressive fusion to extract stronger signals from diverse inputs. PrismF enhances fine-grained intra-modal semantics through a multi-perspective mechanism that decomposes each modality into complementary views and constrains them with a decoupling loss to reduce representation collapse. Furthermore, it improves cross-modal integration through a progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates inter-modal interactions, enabling the model to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noisy or unreliable ones. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that PrismF achieves the strongest overall performance, including relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on KVC16K. Our code can be found at https://github.com/HubuKG/PrismF.

AI.tldr: PrismF is a multimodal knowledge graph completion framework that uses multi-perspective enhancement and progressive fusion to improve entity representations by reducing semantic over-smoothing and better filtering noise across modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for multimodal entity representations suffer from semantic over-smoothing within modalities and ineffective noise filtration across modalities, especially under sparse or ambiguous conditions, which limits their effectiveness in tasks like multimodal knowledge graph completion.
AI.method: Proposed PrismF framework with two key components: 1) Multi-perspective enhancement that decomposes each modality into complementary views with a decoupling loss to prevent representation collapse, and 2) Progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates inter-modal interactions to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noise.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show PrismF achieves strongest overall performance, including relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on KVC16K dataset.
AI.conclusion: PrismF effectively addresses limitations of existing multimodal representation learning by synergizing multi-perspective enhancement with progressive fusion, resulting in superior performance for multimodal knowledge graph completion tasks.

title: Higher-Dimensional Rotary Position Embedding
summary: Transformers rely on position embedding mechanisms in long context modeling in most cases. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) embeds positional information with independent 2D rotations, forming relative position terms in self-attention. However, its pairwise, block-based, and decoupled structure limits deep mixing and robustness across channels. We propose HD-RoPE, which extends RoPE from independent 2D rotations to higher-dimensional rotations and introduces a Paley-I orthogonal basis to obtain balanced, isotropic, and dense phase mixing within each rotation subspace. This significantly enhances channel coupling and rotational degrees of freedom while maintaining orthogonal stability and the relative position closure property. Furthermore, HD-RoPE is easily optimized for engineering efficiency without introducing additional trainable parameters. We have conducted extensive evaluation results demonstrating that HD-RoPE achieves significant performance improvements over standard RoPE across various popular benchmarks and in both long and short contexts.

AI.tldr: HD-RoPE is a novel position embedding method that extends Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) from 2D rotations to higher-dimensional rotations, improving channel coupling and robustness for better long-context modeling in Transformers.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE has limitations: its pairwise, block-based, and decoupled structure restricts deep mixing and robustness across channels in position embeddings for Transformers.
AI.method: Extends RoPE from independent 2D rotations to higher-dimensional rotations using Paley-I orthogonal basis to create balanced, isotropic, and dense phase mixing within rotation subspaces.
AI.result: Significant performance improvements over standard RoPE across various popular benchmarks in both long and short contexts, with enhanced channel coupling and rotational degrees of freedom while maintaining orthogonal stability.
AI.conclusion: HD-RoPE provides a superior alternative to RoPE that improves channel coupling and robustness without adding trainable parameters, making it efficient for both long and short context modeling in Transformers.

title: JudgePanel: A Compact Judge with Panel Deliberation via Adaptive Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation. However, single-model judges are limited by their inherent model biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that mitigate this through diverse deliberation are prohibitively expensive at inference time. To this end, we propose \textbf{\modelname}, which equips a compact \underline{Judge} model with multi-agent \underline{Panel} deliberation capability. Specifically, we first train on panel deliberation traces from an ensemble of strong evaluators, capturing structured patterns of discussion, disagreement, and resolution. To further improve judgment quality beyond SFT, we introduce \textit{AdaReward}, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as different objectives saturate at different rates during RL training. For practical deployment, we further design a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains with few hundred labeled samples. As a result, (i) \textit{Novel}: the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost; (ii) \textit{Effective \& Reliable}: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and rapidly specializes to new domains with few hundred samples.

AI.tldr: JudgePanel is a compact judge model with multi-agent panel deliberation capability that achieves superior evaluation performance at single-model inference cost, using adaptive multi-reward RL and lightweight domain adaptation.
AI.motivation: Single-model LLM judges suffer from inherent biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that use diverse deliberation are too computationally expensive at inference time. There's a need for a scalable solution that combines the benefits of multi-agent deliberation with the efficiency of single-model inference.
AI.method: 1) Train on panel deliberation traces from an ensemble of strong evaluators to capture discussion patterns; 2) Introduce AdaReward, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as objectives saturate at different rates; 3) Design a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains with few hundred samples.
AI.result: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and can rapidly specialize to new domains with few hundred samples.
AI.conclusion: JudgePanel successfully provides the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost, offering an effective and reliable solution to the limitations of current LLM-as-a-Judge approaches.

title: GraM-Diff: A Unified Graph-Mamba Diffusion Framework for EEG-Based Alzheimer's Disease Data Generation and Diagnosis
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a promising, non-invasive, and cost-effective modality for Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection, but deep learning methods are limited by small and imbalanced clinical datasets. Generative augmentation offers a solution, yet existing approaches rely on inefficient class-specific models or fail to capture complex spatial and temporal brain dynamics. To address this, we propose GraM-Diff, a unified classifier-guided Graph-Mamba diffusion framework for EEG synthesis. It embeds Graph Convolutional Networks within a diffusion U-Net to model inter-electrode connectivity and Bidirectional Mamba state-space blocks for linear-complexity long-range temporal modeling. Latent-space classifier guidance lets a single model generate both healthy and pathological EEG within a shared representation, avoiding fragmented per-cohort pipelines. Across four EEG-based AD benchmarks, synthetic augmentation improves classification, yields superior Context-FID and correlation scores over strong generative baselines, and enhances robustness in data-scarce settings.

AI.tldr: GraM-Diff: A unified Graph-Mamba diffusion framework for EEG synthesis that improves Alzheimer's disease detection through better generative augmentation of clinical EEG data.
AI.motivation: EEG is promising for Alzheimer's disease detection but deep learning suffers from small, imbalanced clinical datasets. Existing generative augmentation methods are inefficient (requiring class-specific models) or fail to capture complex brain spatial-temporal dynamics.
AI.method: GraM-Diff: A classifier-guided Graph-Mamba diffusion framework that combines Graph Convolutional Networks within diffusion U-Net for spatial connectivity modeling and Bidirectional Mamba state-space blocks for efficient long-range temporal modeling. Uses latent-space classifier guidance to generate both healthy and pathological EEG with a single model.
AI.result: Synthetic augmentation improves Alzheimer's disease classification across four EEG-based benchmarks, achieves superior Context-FID and correlation scores compared to strong generative baselines, and enhances robustness in data-scarce settings.
AI.conclusion: GraM-Diff provides an effective unified solution for EEG synthesis that overcomes limitations of small clinical datasets and fragmented generative approaches, significantly improving Alzheimer's disease detection performance.

title: An Explainable Coherence Score for Detecting Temporal Inconsistencies in Political News
summary: Temporal inconsistencies, such as mandates attributed outside their real interval, events presented as past before they occurred, or inverted causal sequences, are a form of political disinformation that evades style-based fake news detectors: a well-written article with a single wrong date carries no lexical signal of falsehood. This paper introduces the Temporal Coherence Score (TCS), a continuous, intrinsically interpretable metric that quantifies the temporal coherence of a news article, computed by a four-stage pipeline: extraction of temporal facts, construction of a temporal knowledge graph, hierarchical verification against internal consistency rules and external reference sources, and score aggregation with automatically generated explanations. Verification combines eight internal checkers derived from Allen's interval algebra with a five-level external hierarchy ranging from a locally stored reference knowledge base of 1{,}256 curated political facts to live Wikidata SPARQL queries. On a benchmark of 100 political news articles with injected temporal errors, the system reaches a precision of 0.909 at the selected operating threshold, with a single residual false positive, a profile deliberately tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking assistance, where false alarms are costlier than missed detections. Unlike lexical baselines that output only a binary label, every flagged article is accompanied by the inconsistency type, the entities involved, and the reference source that contradicts the claim.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Temporal Coherence Score (TCS) system that detects temporal inconsistencies in news articles by extracting temporal facts, constructing knowledge graphs, verifying against internal rules and external sources, and generating explanations - achieving 90.9% precision on political news with injected errors.
AI.motivation: Temporal inconsistencies in news (wrong dates, inverted sequences) are a form of political disinformation that evades traditional style-based fake news detectors since well-written articles with single wrong dates carry no lexical signals of falsehood.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: 1) Extract temporal facts from articles, 2) Construct temporal knowledge graphs, 3) Hierarchical verification using 8 internal checkers based on Allen's interval algebra and 5-level external hierarchy from local curated knowledge base (1,256 political facts) to live Wikidata queries, 4) Score aggregation with automatic explanations.
AI.result: Achieves 0.909 precision at selected operating threshold on benchmark of 100 political news articles with injected temporal errors, with single residual false positive. System is tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking where false alarms are costlier than missed detections.
AI.conclusion: TCS provides continuous, interpretable metric for temporal coherence that outperforms binary lexical baselines by providing inconsistency types, involved entities, and contradictory reference sources for every flagged article, making it suitable for fact-checking assistance.

title: ECA-BLS: An Efficient Complex-Augmented Broad Learning System
summary: Broad Learning System (BLS) is an efficient alternative to deep architectures due to its fast training, analytical learning, and strong generalization under limited data. However, existing BLS variants are confined to real-valued representations, restricting their ability to capture nonlinear interactions and second-order statistical dependencies inherent in real-world data. Notably, no prior BLS model fully exploits the complete second-order statistics that naturally emerge when data are embedded in the complex domain. To address this limitation, this paper introduces the first complex augmented Broad Learning System (CA-BLS), which transforms real-valued inputs into phase-encoded complex representations and adopts widely linear modeling to jointly leverage covariance and pseudo-covariance information via complex conjugate augmentation. This enables effective modeling of latent nonlinearities, coherence structures, and second-order dependencies inaccessible to conventional BLS formulations. To mitigate the additional computational cost of complex augmentation, an Efficient Complex Augmented BLS (ECA-BLS) is further developed, reformulating CA-BLS entirely in the real domain while preserving its exact decision function, achieving up to 75\% fewer multiplications and over 60\% fewer additions. A rigorous theoretical analysis proves the mathematical equivalence between CA-BLS and ECA-BLS, ensuring zero theoretical loss. Extensive experiments on 26 benchmark datasets from the UCI and KEEL repositories demonstrate that ECA-BLS consistently outperforms classical BLS and recent state-of-the-art randomized neural networks in accuracy, average rank, and statistical significance, establishing augmented second-order modeling as a critical and previously missing dimension of BLS research.

AI.tldr: CA-BLS introduces complex-valued augmentation to Broad Learning Systems for capturing second-order statistics, with an efficient real-domain equivalent that reduces computational cost while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Existing BLS variants are limited to real-valued representations, preventing them from capturing nonlinear interactions and second-order statistical dependencies that naturally emerge in complex-domain embeddings. No prior BLS model fully exploits complete second-order statistics available in complex representations.
AI.method: 1) CA-BLS transforms real inputs into phase-encoded complex representations using widely linear modeling with complex conjugate augmentation to jointly leverage covariance and pseudo-covariance. 2) ECA-BLS reformulates CA-BLS entirely in real domain while preserving exact decision function, reducing computations by up to 75% multiplications and 60% additions.
AI.result: ECA-BLS consistently outperforms classical BLS and recent state-of-the-art randomized neural networks across 26 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL repositories in accuracy, average rank, and statistical significance. Theoretical analysis proves mathematical equivalence between CA-BLS and ECA-BLS with zero theoretical loss.
AI.conclusion: Augmented second-order modeling via complex representations addresses a critical missing dimension in BLS research, enabling effective capture of latent nonlinearities, coherence structures, and second-order dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency through real-domain reformulation.

title: How Identity and Opinion Shape Political Sycophancy in LLMs
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes increasingly important. However, many existing benchmarks for assessing political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and do not fully capture how a model's stance may adapt to user-provided context during interaction. We introduce a framework that disentangles two distinct triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes, we evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. We uncover a dissociation: a model's susceptibility to explicit opinions does not necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues, and vice versa. When both signals are present, their effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. Additionally, system-level personas primarily shift a model's baseline stance while having limited effect on the stance shift caused by user opinion or identity. Ultimately, our results suggest that LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in the model's behaviors.
