AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit political sycophancy in two distinct ways - opinion alignment and identity stereotyping, with these effects being sub-additive rather than simply cumulative, showing that political stance in LLMs is interactively vulnerable rather than fixed.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes important, but existing benchmarks using closed-ended questions don't capture how model stances adapt to user context during interaction.
AI.method: Introduced a framework that disentangles two triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Used 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes to evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs.
AI.result: Found dissociation: a model's susceptibility to explicit opinions doesn't necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues. When both signals are present, effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. System-level personas primarily shift baseline stance but have limited effect on stance shift caused by user opinion or identity.
AI.conclusion: LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in model behaviors.

title: PruneShift: A Framework for Evaluating Decision Reliability in Structured Pruning
summary: Structured pruning uses surrogate objectives because direct task evaluation over every feasible mask is too expensive. Most evaluations report average surrogate error or rank correlation on broadly sampled masks. These summaries do not directly test the mask chosen by the surrogate. We introduce PruneShift, an evaluation framework that separates broad predictive fidelity, fidelity near selector outputs, and the quality of the selected pruning decision. We first prove that Spearman and Kendall agreement can approach one while normalized selection regret remains maximal. We then derive sufficient conditions based on uniform error, selector suboptimality, decision margin, density ratio, and comparison mass. The analysis also yields a finite pool certificate with an explicit excess cost bound. Four studies test different links in this argument. External TextbookQA confirmation is heterogeneous: 7 of 20 simultaneous intervals favor the surrogate-selected mask, 6 favor its fixed comparator, and 7 cross zero. On a fixed Natural Questions pool, strict improvement holds in one of four settings. A controlled QQP experiment supports the proposed coverage mechanism in all 16 prespecified endpoints, although the sufficient bounds are conservative. Finally, a restricted OSSCAR reconstruction study on OPT-125M shows better local than broad fidelity in 68 of 75 primary endpoints. Independent fixed-mask confirmation is inconclusive in 24 of 25 endpoints and favors the comparator in one. These results show why predictive fit, decision reliability, and pruning method quality require separate evidence.

AI.tldr: PruneShift evaluation framework reveals that common pruning surrogate metrics (like Spearman/Kendall correlation) can be misleading, and shows why we need separate evaluation of predictive fit, decision reliability, and pruning method quality.
AI.motivation: Current structured pruning methods use surrogate objectives because evaluating every feasible pruning mask directly is too expensive. Most evaluations only report average surrogate error or rank correlation on broadly sampled masks, which doesn't directly test the actual mask chosen by the surrogate method.
AI.method: Introduces PruneShift evaluation framework that separates three aspects: broad predictive fidelity, fidelity near selector outputs, and quality of selected pruning decisions. Derives mathematical conditions based on uniform error, selector suboptimality, decision margin, density ratio, and comparison mass, including a finite pool certificate with explicit excess cost bound.
AI.result: Four experimental studies: 1) TextbookQA shows heterogeneous results with mixed support for surrogate vs comparator masks; 2) Natural Questions shows strict improvement in only 1 of 4 settings; 3) QQP controlled experiment supports coverage mechanism in all 16 endpoints; 4) OSSCAR reconstruction on OPT-125M shows better local than broad fidelity in most cases.
AI.conclusion: Predictive fit, decision reliability, and pruning method quality require separate evidence - current aggregated metrics like correlation can be misleading even when approaching perfect agreement, as selection regret can remain maximal.

title: Benevolent Bias in Multi-Turn Human-Agent Dialogue
summary: Bias in human-agent interaction can manifest not only through hostile language but also as benevolent bias, whereby unequal treatment hides behind a warm, positive tone. To make it detectable, we operationalise benevolent bias along two dimensions, tone and treatment, yielding three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. Building on these definitions, we construct BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues spanning user and agent demographics, roles, and generators, to support controlled evaluation. We then test two detector families on it: off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted large language model (LLM) judges. Our results reveal a detection gap: off-the-shelf detectors reliably flag overt bias yet largely miss benevolent bias, while LLM judges catch more under more explicit detection criteria but increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias, and demographic context amplifies the false alarms. These findings suggest that fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must look beyond surface cues to whether the agent's treatment is disparate.

AI.tldr: Researchers identify a "benevolent bias" problem where AI agents show unequal treatment through warm language, create a dataset to detect it, and find current detection methods either miss it or falsely flag neutral support.
AI.motivation: The paper identifies that bias in human-agent interaction isn't limited to hostile language, but can also manifest as "benevolent bias" where unequal treatment is hidden behind positive, warm tones. This subtle form of bias is difficult to detect with current methods, requiring new approaches to identify when AI agents treat users differently despite appearing supportive.
AI.method: Researchers operationalize benevolent bias along two dimensions (tone and treatment) creating three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. They build BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues with controlled variables. They test two detector families: off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted LLM judges with explicit detection criteria.
AI.result: Off-the-shelf detectors reliably flag overt bias but largely miss benevolent bias. LLM judges catch more benevolent bias with explicit criteria but increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias. Demographic context amplifies false alarms. There's a detection gap where current methods either under-detect or over-detect depending on approach.
AI.conclusion: Fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must look beyond surface linguistic cues to whether the agent's treatment is actually disparate. The findings reveal limitations in current bias detection methods and highlight the need for more nuanced approaches that distinguish between tone and substantive treatment differences.

title: Structure Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mixture of Experts
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has so far rarely been applied to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and existing MoE designs leave the alignment between experts and the structure of the data to emerge on its own. We propose an architecture search framework that makes this alignment an explicit search variable: the assignment of data clusters to experts is optimised jointly with the per-expert architectures. We cast the joint problem as a cluster-aware likelihood maximisation, show that it coincides with the incomplete-data maximum likelihood of a latent-variable mixture, and solve it by a generalised Expectation-Maximisation procedure whose otherwise intractable expert-quality term is supplied by an adaptively refined surrogate. We prove that the iterates converge whenever the surrogate errors are summable, and that at every limit point no candidate the search produces improves the true objective. On a heterogeneous image-classification mixture the method recovers the underlying domain partition on 95% of clusters without ever observing domain labels, and on that benchmark and a four-domain time-series forecasting one alike it outperforms the MoE and NAS baselines that likewise use no label information.

AI.tldr: Proposes a neural architecture search framework for Mixture-of-Experts models that jointly optimizes expert assignment and per-expert architectures through cluster-aware likelihood maximization.
AI.motivation: Current NAS methods are rarely applied to MoE models, and existing MoE designs don't explicitly align experts with data structure - this alignment emerges passively rather than being optimized.
AI.method: Formulates joint optimization as cluster-aware likelihood maximization, treats it as incomplete-data maximum likelihood of latent-variable mixture, solves via generalized Expectation-Maximization with adaptively refined surrogate for intractable expert-quality term.
AI.result: Method recovers underlying domain partition on 95% of clusters without domain labels on heterogeneous image-classification, outperforms both MoE and NAS baselines on image classification and time-series forecasting benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully aligns experts with data structure through joint optimization, achieving better performance than existing methods while discovering meaningful domain partitions without label supervision.

title: Hyper-Fold: Exploring the Expressive Limit of Sequence-Geometry Learning for Proteins via Hypergraph Modeling
summary: Protein structure modeling rests on a single computational primitive: the interaction between what a residue is (sequence content) and where it sits (three-dimensional geometry). What is the expressive limit of this layer class? We show that the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products--the sufficient statistic of all second-order interactions--is the expressive ceiling, while the additive message passing of mainstream geometric GNNs is provably blind to content-geometry binding. We then introduce Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone approaching this ceiling at message-passing cost: each radius neighborhood is organized into a sequence hyperedge and a contact hyperedge, modulated by an edge-conditioned matrix-valued operator factorized into K learned basis operators with geometry-generated coefficients. Across enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection, Hyper-Fold and its hierarchical variant Hyper-Fold-Deep achieve the best results among protein-specific structure encoders; Hyper-Fold-Pocket, an anchored set-prediction head, surpasses UniSite-3D on UniSite-DS and two zero-shot benchmarks with no sequence language model features, 68x fewer parameters, and 4.8x lower latency--suggesting that a sufficiently expressive 3D backbone recovers information that fusion architectures previously borrowed from evolution-scale pretraining.

AI.tldr: Hyper-Fold introduces a novel protein structure modeling approach using rank-K separable convolutional backbones that capture content-geometry interactions more expressively than standard geometric GNNs, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple protein tasks.
AI.motivation: Current geometric GNNs use additive message passing that is provably blind to content-geometry binding interactions, while the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products represents the expressive ceiling for protein structure modeling.
AI.method: Hyper-Fold organizes each radius neighborhood into sequence hyperedge and contact hyperedge, modulated by an edge-conditioned matrix-valued operator factorized into K learned basis operators with geometry-generated coefficients, enabling rank-K separable convolutional backbone at message-passing cost.
AI.result: Hyper-Fold achieves best results among protein-specific structure encoders for enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection. Hyper-Fold-Pocket surpasses UniSite-3D with 68x fewer parameters, 4.8x lower latency, and no sequence language model features.
AI.conclusion: A sufficiently expressive 3D backbone recovers information that fusion architectures previously borrowed from evolution-scale pretraining, demonstrating that better geometric modeling can reduce reliance on sequence language models for protein structure analysis.

title: Designing for the Next Click: Bandits for Real-Time Page Layout
comment: Accepted to The Web Conference 2026 (short paper track), but later withdrawn due to internal prioritization. Subsequently accepted to the Online & Adaptive Recommender Systems Workshop (held in conjunction with the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems, RecSys 2026)
summary: E-commerce platforms increasingly personalize user experiences through machine learning, yet page layout decisions remain dominated by static rules and manual curation. We present a scalable bandit-based system that optimizes product page layouts in real time while preserving human control over design intent. A contextual bandit model dynamically selects the most effective layout for each session using user, item, and category-level features. The system leverages a LinUCB-based policy to balance exploration and exploitation as it learns from live user interactions. The architecture is designed for seamless integration into large-scale web serving stacks, supporting low-latency inference and continuous model updates. The system was first tested on entry product pages. In online A/B deployments on a major retail platform, our approach achieved positive lifts in session-level performance metrics over a strong heuristic baseline. Our results demonstrate that contextual bandits can effectively optimize visual and structural aspects of product discovery for user engagement, providing a scalable path toward learning-to-design the web.

AI.tldr: A contextual bandit system for real-time product page layout optimization that balances ML-driven personalization with human design control, achieving positive engagement lifts in A/B tests.
AI.motivation: E-commerce platforms currently rely on static rules and manual curation for page layout decisions, despite advances in ML personalization. There's a need for dynamic, data-driven layout optimization that maintains human design oversight while improving user engagement.
AI.method: A contextual bandit system using LinUCB-based policy with user, item, and category-level features to dynamically select optimal layouts. Designed for low-latency web serving integration with continuous model updates, tested first on entry product pages.
AI.result: In online A/B deployments on a major retail platform, the system achieved positive lifts in session-level performance metrics compared to a strong heuristic baseline, demonstrating effectiveness for user engagement optimization.
AI.conclusion: Contextual bandits provide an effective approach for optimizing visual and structural aspects of product discovery, offering a scalable path toward "learning-to-design" web interfaces while preserving human control over design intent.

title: Imag-Eval: a language-grounded framework for interpretable Text-to-Image instruction following evaluation
comment: Accepted to the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have recently achieved impressive visual fidelity, yet their evaluation remains constrained by benchmarks that are often difficult to interpret and insufficiently diagnostic. Existing skill-based evaluations tend to overlook critical failure modes that strongly impact usability but fall outside standard taxonomies, such as global incoherence arising from missing parts or physically implausible configurations (e.g., floating objects). In addition, prompt difficulty is typically controlled along a single dimension; either prompt length or the number of elements to generate. To address these limitations, we introduce Imag-Eval, a controlled benchmark designed to assess how T2I models ground compositional natural-language instructions into visual outputs. Unlike prior work that conflates surface linguistic complexity with compositional difficulty, Imag-Eval explicitly seeks to disentangles these factors by independently varying both the number of instances and the combination of constraints (rules), while avoiding error propagation. This design enables fine-grained and interpretable analysis of where cross-modal instruction following fails. Our benchmark comprises 1,140 prompts and 8,842 combined rules, and we evaluate it on several state-of-the-art models. Complementing this analysis with an additional study of over 2,000 prompts from a concurrent benchmark, our results suggest that, for structured skills, compositional difficulty is primarily governed by the number of grounded rules and their binding to instances,, rather than by prompt length alone.

AI.tldr: Imag-Eval is a controlled benchmark for evaluating text-to-image models' ability to follow compositional natural-language instructions, designed to disentangle linguistic complexity from compositional difficulty by varying instances and constraints independently.
AI.motivation: Current T2I model evaluations are limited - they overlook critical failure modes like global incoherence and physically implausible configurations, and they typically control prompt difficulty along only a single dimension (either length or number of elements). Existing benchmarks are difficult to interpret and insufficiently diagnostic for real-world usability.
AI.method: Imag-Eval explicitly disentangles linguistic complexity from compositional difficulty by independently varying both the number of instances and the combination of constraints (rules), avoiding error propagation. The benchmark comprises 1,140 prompts and 8,842 combined rules, evaluated on state-of-the-art models. Complementary analysis includes over 2,000 prompts from a concurrent benchmark.
AI.result: The results suggest that for structured skills, compositional difficulty is primarily governed by the number of grounded rules and their binding to instances, rather than by prompt length alone. This provides fine-grained and interpretable analysis of where cross-modal instruction following fails.
AI.conclusion: Imag-Eval addresses key limitations in current T2I evaluation by providing a controlled benchmark that enables more diagnostic and interpretable assessment of compositional instruction following, revealing that rule complexity and instance binding are more critical factors than simple prompt length in determining model performance.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Replay Memory for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Uncertainty estimation provides promising capabilities for reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Notably, estimating uncertainty can reduce the training time and enable agents to obtain greater rewards over time by exploiting information related to whether an action would facilitate exploration of portions of an environment that are well-known versus those that are relatively unknown. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of the experience replay buffer commonly used in RL that we call uncertainty-driven replay memory (UDRM), which entails an update scheme for internally stored memories based on uncertainty estimates obtained by an RL model during training. In contrast to existing forms of RL, which typically use temporal difference error or the distribution of transitions to update the replay memory buffer and train RL controllers, our scheme biases the memory buffer to store more uncertain transitions that will improve an RL agent's generalization throughout training. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed uncertainty-aware replay buffer enables an RL agent to obtain higher rewards during training compared to other existing uncertainty-aware RL frameworks.

AI.tldr: UDRM (Uncertainty-Driven Replay Memory) is a novel replay buffer formulation that uses uncertainty estimates to bias memory storage toward uncertain transitions, improving RL agent generalization and reward performance.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods typically use temporal difference error or transition distributions for replay buffer updates, but these approaches don't explicitly exploit uncertainty information to improve agent generalization and training efficiency.
AI.method: Proposed UDRM (Uncertainty-Driven Replay Memory) with update scheme that biases memory buffer to store more uncertain transitions based on uncertainty estimates obtained by the RL model during training.
AI.result: Experimental results show UDRM enables RL agents to obtain higher rewards during training compared to other existing uncertainty-aware RL frameworks.
AI.conclusion: UDRM effectively leverages uncertainty estimation to improve RL training by prioritizing uncertain transitions in replay memory, leading to better generalization and reward performance than existing approaches.

title: Computational Depth Measurement in Thermographic Video: Overcoming Spatial Overfitting via Spatio-Temporal Decoupling
summary: Accurate through-thickness measurement of subsurface delamination depth in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) is important for structural assessment because defect location determines affected load-bearing layers. Optical pulsed thermography (OPT) provides a two-dimensional thermal video rather than volumetric measurements, so depth must be inferred from temporal heat-diffusion responses. A challenge is spatial dataset bias: when calibration defects follow regular grids, regression models may memorize their geometry instead of learning physical relationship between thermal decay and depth. This work introduces a spatio-temporal decoupling architecture that separates spatial defect localization from temporal depth measurement. Defect regions are first localized using segmentation methods, after which thermal responses are spatially averaged and converted into sixteen physics-informed temporal, energy, statistical, and geometric features. These features expose the one-dimensional heat-conduction relationship while withholding pixel coordinates from the depth model. Four regression models are evaluated using specimen-level cross-validation: Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Advanced Multi-Layer Perceptron (Adv-MLP), and XGBoost. Unregularized trees and over-parameterized Adv-MLP exhibit calibration collapse under geometric shifts, with errors exceeding 0.5 mm. In contrast, regularized XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains cross-specimen calibration, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.056 mm and root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.085 mm. Predicted depths are merged with masks to generate Delaunay-triangulated three-dimensional defect models in three to five seconds per specimen. Results show that mathematical regularization and spatio-temporal decoupling reduce spatial memorization in thermal-video depth regression.

AI.tldr: Spatio-temporal decoupling architecture separates defect localization from depth measurement to prevent spatial memorization in optical pulsed thermography for CFRP delamination depth assessment, achieving sub-millimeter accuracy with regularized XGBoost.
AI.motivation: Accurate through-thickness measurement of subsurface delamination depth in CFRP is crucial for structural assessment. Optical pulsed thermography provides 2D thermal videos, requiring depth inference from temporal responses. Spatial dataset bias occurs when calibration defects follow regular grids, causing regression models to memorize geometry rather than learn the physical heat-diffusion relationship.
AI.method: Proposes a spatio-temporal decoupling architecture: first localize defect regions using segmentation methods, then spatially average thermal responses and extract 16 physics-informed features (temporal, energy, statistical, geometric). These features expose 1D heat-conduction relationship while withholding pixel coordinates. Evaluates four regression models with specimen-level cross-validation: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Advanced Multi-Layer Perceptron, and XGBoost with L1/L2 regularization.
AI.result: Unregularized trees and over-parameterized Adv-MLP show calibration collapse under geometric shifts (errors > 0.5 mm). Regularized XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains cross-specimen calibration, achieving MAE of 0.056 mm and RMSE of 0.085 mm. Delaunay-triangulated 3D defect models generated in 3-5 seconds per specimen.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical regularization and spatio-temporal decoupling effectively reduce spatial memorization in thermal-video depth regression for CFRP subsurface delamination measurement, enabling accurate volumetric assessment from 2D thermal data while preventing model overfitting to geometric patterns.

title: Partially Linear Autoencoders for Manifold Learning and Dimensionality Reduction
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Preprint also available on HAL: https://hal.science/hal-05646575
summary: Autoencoders are widely used for nonlinear dimensionality reduction and manifold learning. While most common implementations rely on both nonlinear encoders and decoders, we investigate the specific role of the encoder and the extent to which it can be constrained to be linear without reducing accuracy. We conduct a comparative study on four autoencoder architectures: standard fully nonlinear autoencoders (AE), linear-encoder autoencoders (Lenc-AE), linear-decoder autoencoders (Ldec-AE), and fully linear autoencoders (LAE), evaluated on synthetic manifolds, computational mechanics data sets, and real-world image data sets including MNIST. We demonstrate that imposing a linear encoder preserves most of the representational capacity of the autoencoder, provided the decoder remains nonlinear. In particular, Lenc-AE consistently outperforms both Ldec-AE and LAE, and achieves reconstruction quality comparable to fully nonlinear AE, while offering advantages in terms of parsimony and interpretability of the latent representation. These results suggest that the nonlinear decoder is the critical component for manifold learning, rather than the encoder. A geometric interpretation of this finding is developed, which identifies the precise conditions under which a linear encoder is sufficient, and the specific manifold configurations that expose its limitations.

AI.tldr: Linear-encoder autoencoders (with nonlinear decoders) achieve performance comparable to fully nonlinear autoencoders, suggesting nonlinear decoders are the critical component for manifold learning, not encoders.
AI.motivation: To investigate the specific roles of encoder and decoder components in autoencoders, particularly whether linear encoders can be constrained without reducing accuracy for nonlinear dimensionality reduction and manifold learning tasks.
AI.method: Comparative study of four autoencoder architectures: standard nonlinear AE, linear-encoder AE (Lenc-AE), linear-decoder AE (Ldec-AE), and fully linear AE (LAE). Evaluated on synthetic manifolds, computational mechanics datasets, and real-world image data (MNIST).
AI.result: Lenc-AE consistently outperforms both Ldec-AE and LAE, and achieves reconstruction quality comparable to fully nonlinear AE. Linear encoders preserve most representational capacity when decoders remain nonlinear.
AI.conclusion: The nonlinear decoder is the critical component for manifold learning, not the encoder. Linear encoders offer advantages in parsimony and interpretability of latent representations while maintaining performance.

title: Towards an Expressivity-Normalized Energy-Demand Comparison of ANNs and SNNs
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are often regarded as energy-efficient alternatives to artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet their advantage depends critically on both network architecture and data properties. We develop an analytical framework to compare fully-connected ReLU ANNs and integrate-and-fire SNNs for time-series data with respect to their theoretical energy efficiency at matched expressive capacity. By relating an inference-energy model to theoretical bounds on representational expressivity, we derive an expressivity-normalized efficiency ratio and explicit thresholds in network width, spike sparsity, and ANN depth scaling. Our analysis characterizes the regimes in which event-driven computation offsets the temporal overhead of SNNs, providing capacity-aware principles for designing energy-efficient temporal networks. It shows that ANNs exceed SNNs in expressivity-normalized efficiency only in specific regimes.

AI.tldr: An analytical framework comparing energy efficiency of spiking vs. artificial neural networks for time-series data, showing SNNs are more efficient in many regimes when considering matched expressive capacity.
AI.motivation: While SNNs are often claimed to be more energy-efficient than ANNs, their advantage depends on architecture and data properties, and there's a need for systematic analysis comparing them under matched expressive capacity for time-series tasks.
AI.method: Developed an analytical framework to compare fully-connected ReLU ANNs and integrate-and-fire SNNs for time-series data, using inference-energy models and theoretical bounds on representational expressivity to derive expressivity-normalized efficiency ratios and thresholds.
AI.result: Derived explicit thresholds in network width, spike sparsity, and ANN depth scaling, characterizing regimes where event-driven computation offsets SNN temporal overhead, showing ANNs exceed SNNs in expressivity-normalized efficiency only in specific regimes.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides capacity-aware principles for designing energy-efficient temporal networks, demonstrating that SNNs can be more efficient than ANNs in many practical scenarios when properly accounting for expressivity and temporal dynamics.

title: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge
summary: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by Large Language Models (LLMs). While often plausible, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted and augmented by LLMs from informal culinary sources. Developed as part of FKG.in, a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic framework for validating LLM-augmented recipe data, thereby strengthening the foundations of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

AI.tldr: A semi-automated workflow to validate LLM-generated recipe data that combines formal grammars, vocabulary checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformers, and retrieval verification to address hallucinations and inaccuracies in culinary content.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly generating recipe content online, but these outputs often contain hallucinated ingredients, incorrect quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction.
AI.method: A multi-stage pipeline combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification to identify and address structural inconsistencies, semantic incoherence, and deviations from source texts.
AI.result: Developed as part of FKG.in (knowledge graph of Indian food), the workflow provides a practical framework for validating LLM-augmented recipe data, applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains beyond just Indian recipes.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides an auditable, application-agnostic framework for validating LLM-generated recipe data, strengthening the foundations of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

title: Structural Hierarchy and Geometry in Molecular Representation Learning
summary: Molecular self-supervised learning uses chemical structures to guide which molecular embeddings should be similar. We study whether explicitly encoding a molecule's Bemis-Murcko scaffold and using it to supervise the molecular embedding changes what the model learns. We further test whether this effect depends on the embedding geometry by comparing Euclidean and Lorentz contrastive objectives. Across two augmentation strengths, scaffold-supervised models consistently organize molecules according to both identical and structurally related scaffolds. The resulting embeddings also improve molecular property prediction on several tasks, while the exact gains depend on the predicted property. The effect of scaffold supervision on molecular organization is stronger under Lorentz objectives, but neither geometry provides a consistent overall advantage. These results show that explicitly teaching the relation between a molecule and its structural core can reliably shape the organization of molecular embedding space, while the extent of usefulness of this organization remains task dependent.

AI.tldr: Scaffold supervision improves molecular organization in embeddings, enhancing property prediction in some tasks, with Lorentz geometry showing stronger effects but no consistent overall advantage.
AI.motivation: To study whether explicitly encoding a molecule's Bemis-Murcko scaffold and using it to supervise molecular embeddings changes what models learn, and whether this effect depends on embedding geometry (Euclidean vs Lorentz).
AI.method: Used molecular self-supervised learning with explicit scaffold encoding as supervision. Compared Euclidean and Lorentz contrastive objectives across two augmentation strengths. Evaluated how scaffold-supervised models organize molecules and tested on molecular property prediction tasks.
AI.result: Scaffold-supervised models consistently organize molecules according to both identical and structurally related scaffolds. Embeddings improve molecular property prediction on several tasks, with gains depending on the predicted property. Lorentz objectives show stronger effects of scaffold supervision on molecular organization, but neither geometry provides consistent overall advantage.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly teaching the relation between a molecule and its structural core reliably shapes molecular embedding space organization, but the usefulness of this organization remains task-dependent, with no consistent advantage of one geometry over the other.

title: Sensitivity-Constrained Neural Operators for Data-Efficient Forward and Inverse Modeling of Partial Differential Equation Systems
summary: Neural operators provide fast surrogates for partial differential equation (PDE) solvers, but their reliability can degrade for high-dimensional spatial inputs and inverse or repeated inference. State-only training constrains solution values but not the learned input--output response. We study sensitivity-constrained neural operators (SC-NOs), which augment standard training with sampled solver-derived Jacobian supervision. Selected sensitivities from differentiable solvers or discrete adjoints are matched during training, allowing response information to be amortized across minibatches without imposing the full Jacobian at every update. We evaluate SC-NO on advection--diffusion and RANS--Spalart--Allmaras benchmarks, input-dimensionality scaling tests, long-horizon autoregressive rollout, and a shallow-water Tohoku tsunami source-inversion case. Sensitivity supervision improves forward prediction and yields larger gains in gradient-based inverse reconstruction of distributed fields. Scaling experiments show an improved accuracy--cost tradeoff for high-dimensional gridded inputs, while ablations indicate that state values and Jacobian information provide complementary supervision. In the tsunami case, SC-FNO reconstructs gridded seafloor deformation from sparse early gauge observations and forecasts subsequent wave propagation in a near-real-time proof-of-concept workflow. These results support sampled sensitivity supervision as a practical way to improve neural PDE surrogates when forward accuracy, inverse stability, robustness, and computational cost must be considered together.

AI.tldr: Sensitivity-constrained neural operators (SC-NOs) improve PDE surrogate reliability by adding sampled solver-derived Jacobian supervision to standard state-only training, enhancing forward accuracy and inverse stability for high-dimensional problems.
AI.motivation: Neural operators for PDE solving face reliability issues with high-dimensional spatial inputs and inverse/repeated inference. State-only training constrains solution values but not the learned input-output response, limiting performance for complex tasks.
AI.method: SC-NOs augment standard training with sampled solver-derived Jacobian supervision. Selected sensitivities from differentiable solvers or discrete adjoints are matched during training, allowing response information to be amortized across minibatches without imposing the full Jacobian at every update.
AI.result: Sensitivity supervision improves forward prediction and yields larger gains in gradient-based inverse reconstruction of distributed fields. Scaling experiments show improved accuracy-cost tradeoff for high-dimensional gridded inputs. In a tsunami case, SC-FNO successfully reconstructs gridded seafloor deformation from sparse gauge observations and forecasts wave propagation.
AI.conclusion: Sampled sensitivity supervision is a practical way to improve neural PDE surrogates when forward accuracy, inverse stability, robustness, and computational cost must be considered together. State values and Jacobian information provide complementary supervision.

title: Dynamic Important Example Mining for Reinforcement Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is increasingly used to strengthen the reasoning abilities of large models, yet its effectiveness is bound by how training data are selected and used. Most data-centric RFT methods rely on static or heuristic sample selection, implicitly assuming a sample's value is fixed over training. This overlooks the non-stationary dynamics of policy learning and can lead to suboptimal updates. We propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), a principled and fully automated framework that makes data utilization adaptive throughout RFT. DIEM integrates two components into each optimization step: (i) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement; and (ii) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving the update's gradient magnitude to stabilize optimization. Across several reasoning benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines. The code will be released via https://github.com/hrtan/DIEM.

AI.tldr: DIEM is an adaptive data selection framework for reinforcement fine-tuning that dynamically estimates sample importance through gradient alignment and reweights batches to maximize policy improvement while maintaining stable optimization.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement fine-tuning methods use static or heuristic data selection, assuming sample value is fixed throughout training. This ignores the non-stationary nature of policy learning and leads to suboptimal updates, creating a need for adaptive data utilization methods.
AI.method: DIEM integrates two components per optimization step: (1) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement, and (2) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving gradient magnitude for stable optimization.
AI.result: DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines across several reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance in adaptive data utilization for reinforcement fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic Important Example Mining provides a principled, fully automated framework for adaptive data selection in reinforcement fine-tuning that addresses the non-stationary nature of policy learning and improves upon traditional static approaches.

title: Joint Spatiotemporal Spectral Neural Operators for Learning PDEs on Irregular Domains
summary: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) on irregular and geometry-dependent domains remains a central challenge in scientific machine learning. While spectral methods provide strong inductive biases for modeling global interactions, they are typically limited to regular domains, and existing neural approaches often require domain warping, interpolation, or costly geometric embeddings. We introduce the \textbf{Graph Spectral Neural Operator (GSNO)}, a neural operator that combines spatial graph spectral decompositions with temporal Fourier transforms through a unified space--time spectral kernel. This formulation enables globally coherent operator learning on non-Cartesian discretizations without domain warping or autoregressive rollouts. By replacing learned geometric embeddings with a graph Laplacian spectral basis, GSNO provides geometry-aware spectral learning with low parameter complexity. Across steady and unsteady PDE benchmarks on irregular and geometry-dependent domains, GSNO achieves strong accuracy with reduced runtime and parameter counts, while demonstrating robust zero-shot generalization across mesh resolutions and geometry families.

AI.tldr: GSNO is a neural operator that combines graph spectral decompositions with temporal Fourier transforms for solving PDEs on irregular domains without requiring domain warping or autoregressive rollouts.
AI.motivation: Current neural approaches for learning PDE solution operators on irregular domains often require domain warping, interpolation, or costly geometric embeddings, while spectral methods are limited to regular domains. There's a need for efficient, geometry-aware operator learning on non-Cartesian discretizations.
AI.method: The Graph Spectral Neural Operator (GSNO) combines spatial graph spectral decompositions (using graph Laplacian spectral basis) with temporal Fourier transforms through a unified space-time spectral kernel. This replaces learned geometric embeddings with graph-based spectral analysis, enabling global coherent operator learning without domain warping.
AI.result: GSNO achieves strong accuracy on steady and unsteady PDE benchmarks on irregular domains with reduced runtime and parameter counts compared to existing methods. It demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization across mesh resolutions and geometry families.
AI.conclusion: GSNO provides an effective approach for geometry-aware spectral learning on irregular domains with low parameter complexity, eliminating the need for domain warping or costly geometric embeddings while maintaining accuracy and generalization capabilities.

title: RACER: Reinforced Agent Collaboration for Explainable Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
comment: 15 pages, 1 figures, This paper has been accepted by ICONIP 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffer from hallucination and struggle with complex reasoning tasks requiring multi-hop domain knowledge. While integrating Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provides a structured and verifiable information source, current KG-enhanced LLM paradigms usually rely on single-agent path extraction and fixed prompting, lacking adaptability and facing huge search spaces. To address these challenges, we propose RACER, a Reinforced Agent Collaboration framework for Explainable Reasoning on knowledge graphs. RACER employs a semantic-aware action pruning and teacher-guided reinforcement learning mechanism to efficiently extract high-quality reasoning pathways from large-scale KGs. Furthermore, to mitigate single-path generation pitfalls, we introduce a cross-task accumulated shared memory graph paired with an attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement module. Finally, RACER orchestrates these components through a four-role multi-agent collaboration system (GraphAgent, TemplateAgent, AnswerAgent, and CriticAgent) to dynamically refine prompts and evaluate answers. Extensive experiments on CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA datasets demonstrate that RACER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines with an average improvement of 5\%, offering robust and highly interpretable reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: RACER is a multi-agent KG-LLM framework using reinforcement learning and semantic pruning for explainable reasoning, achieving 5% improvement over SOTA baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucination and struggle with complex reasoning requiring multi-hop domain knowledge. Current KG-enhanced LLM approaches lack adaptability due to single-agent path extraction and fixed prompting, facing huge search spaces in large-scale KGs.
AI.method: Proposes RACER: a Reinforced Agent Collaboration framework with semantic-aware action pruning, teacher-guided reinforcement learning for efficient pathway extraction, cross-task accumulated shared memory graph, attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement, and a four-role multi-agent system (GraphAgent, TemplateAgent, AnswerAgent, CriticAgent) for dynamic prompt refinement and answer evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA datasets show RACER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines with an average improvement of 5%, demonstrating robust and highly interpretable reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: RACER addresses limitations of current KG-LLM integration through multi-agent collaboration and reinforcement learning, providing effective, adaptable, and explainable reasoning while handling large search spaces in knowledge graphs.

title: INTERVenE: Temporal-Abstraction-Interval Based Transformers for Short-Horizon Medical Event Prediction
summary: Electronic Health Record (EHR) prediction models in the intensive care unit must learn from sparse and irregular measurements while preserving the clinical meaning of time and supporting transparent decision-making. We present INTERVenE, a family of Transformer architectures whose input is an interval-based, knowledge-based temporal abstraction (KBTA), a token stream of named clinical concepts (states, trends, events, contexts) drawn from a curated medical ontology, rather than an unnamed bin index or a raw measurement triplet. This naming layer is what we ask KBTA to do: it makes the model's per-token attributions resolve to clinical concepts by construction. INTERVenE offers two complementary variants: an auto-regressive decoder that generates future abstraction trajectories with a per-step risk readout (localizing \emph{when} and \emph{after which events} risk rises), and a bidirectional encoder for single-pass joint risk and time-to-event prediction. Evaluated on 57,078 MIMIC-IV admissions against GRU-D, STraTS, and KarmaLego, INTERVenE-Enc reaches a support-weighted AUPRC$_w$ of 0.672, improving by 0.041 over the strongest neural baseline with non-overlapping 95\% bootstrap CIs, while also taking the best AUROC$_w$ (0.901) and length-of-stay MAE (44.4\,h). INTERVenE-Ar (AUROC$_w$ $0.854$, AUPRC$_w$ $0.587$ under the same evaluation contract - a strictly harder generative readout) provides a complementary token-level risk trajectory. An input-representation ablation confirms the lift transfers across structured discretizations, positioning KBTA-based intervals as the interpretable substrate that makes per-token attributions resolve to meaningful clinical concepts within the deployed model.

AI.tldr: INTERVenE is a Transformer-based EHR prediction model that uses knowledge-based temporal abstractions (KBTA) to create interpretable clinical concept tokens, offering both auto-regressive trajectory generation and bidirectional risk prediction for ICU patients.
AI.motivation: ICU EHR prediction models need to handle sparse, irregular measurements while preserving clinical meaning of time and supporting transparent decision-making. Existing approaches using unnamed bin indices or raw measurement triplets lack interpretability.
AI.method: INTERVenE uses Transformer architectures with KBTA input - interval-based token streams of named clinical concepts (states, trends, events, contexts) from a curated medical ontology. Two variants: auto-regressive decoder for future abstraction trajectories with per-step risk readout, and bidirectional encoder for joint risk and time-to-event prediction.
AI.result: On 57,078 MIMIC-IV admissions, INTERVenE-Enc achieves AUPRC_w of 0.672 (improving 0.041 over strongest neural baseline), AUROC_w of 0.901, and length-of-stay MAE of 44.4h. INTERVenE-Ar achieves AUROC_w 0.854 and AUPRC_w 0.587 under generative readout. KBTA-based intervals enable interpretable per-token attributions.
AI.conclusion: KBTA provides an interpretable substrate for EHR prediction models by resolving per-token attributions to meaningful clinical concepts, enabling both accurate prediction and transparent decision-making in ICU settings.

title: EpaCache: Error-Propagation-Aware Caching for Accelerating Diffusion-Based Visual Generation
comment: This is a preview version of EpaCache, which is still under review
summary: Diffusion-based visual generative models deliver strong image and video synthesis quality but incur high inference costs because sequential samplers repeatedly evaluate large networks. Caching-based methods reduce inference latency by reusing intermediate computations across adjacent timesteps. However, existing cache controllers rely primarily on local temporal variation and overlook the trajectory-level consequences of cache reuse. We introduce Error-Propagation-Aware Cache (EpaCache), a training-free caching policy that adaptively allocates the reuse budget on timesteps with lower downstream impact. Experiments on image and video synthesis models demonstrate that EpaCache consistently improves the latency--fidelity trade-off over existing caching methods. On FLUX.1-dev, EpaCache outperforms the prior state-of-the-art caching method in both latency and fidelity, reducing inference time from $11.7$ s to $11.3$ s while improving PSNR from $21.4$ to $22.8$. On HunyuanVideo, EpaCache achieves a $2.63\times$ speedup over uncached inference and improves SSIM from $0.891$ to $0.905$ over the prior state-of-the-art method at matched latency.

AI.tldr: EpaCache is a training-free caching policy for diffusion models that reduces inference latency by adaptively reusing computations based on downstream error propagation, improving both speed and fidelity compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models have high inference costs due to repeated network evaluations during sequential sampling. Existing caching methods focus on local temporal variations but ignore the trajectory-level consequences of cache reuse decisions.
AI.method: EpaCache (Error-Propagation-Aware Cache) is a training-free caching policy that dynamically allocates the computational reuse budget to timesteps with lower downstream impact, considering how cache decisions propagate errors through the sampling trajectory.
AI.result: On FLUX.1-dev, EpaCache reduced inference time from 11.7s to 11.3s while improving PSNR from 21.4 to 22.8. On HunyuanVideo, it achieved 2.63× speedup over uncached inference and improved SSIM from 0.891 to 0.905 over SOTA methods at matched latency.
AI.conclusion: EpaCache provides an effective, training-free approach to improving the latency-fidelity trade-off in diffusion-based visual generative models by considering error propagation in cache decisions, outperforming existing caching methods across both image and video synthesis tasks.

title: Diffusion-Based Inverse Design of Dielectric Resonator Metasurfaces for Shaping Smart Electromagnetic Environments
summary: Future wireless systems are expected to transform the surrounding space from a passive propagation medium into a smart electromagnetic environment, where engineered surfaces control wave propagation, support wireless sensing, and create programmable electromagnetic fingerprints. A key challenge in realizing this vision is the inverse design of metasurfaces for tailored electromagnetic propagation. While forward analysis evaluates the response of a known geometry, the inverse task starts from a prescribed scattering signature and seeks a physically realizable structure that produces it. This inverse task is inherently nonlinear and often high-dimensional, while candidate solutions may be non-unique and provide no direct indication of practical realizability. Here, we introduce a conditional diffusion framework for inverse design of dielectric resonator metasurfaces from target angular scattering patterns. Trained on T-matrix simulated geometry-response pairs, the model learns a conditional distribution of geometries instead of a deterministic mapping, enabling multiple candidate designs for the ill-posed inverse problem. The best generated metasurface achieves a mean percentage error of 1.39%, outperforming CMA-ES optimization (4.1% after 10 h) while requiring only about one minute for after-training inference. The model also produces lower error distributions than deterministic neural baselines for out-of-distribution spectra, highlighting the potential of diffusion models for efficient metasurface design.

AI.tldr: A diffusion model framework for inverse design of metasurfaces achieves high accuracy (1.39% error) in generating physical structures from target scattering patterns, outperforming traditional optimization methods by orders of magnitude in speed.
AI.motivation: Future wireless systems need smart electromagnetic environments where engineered surfaces control wave propagation, but inverse design of metasurfaces for tailored electromagnetic responses is challenging due to nonlinearity, high dimensionality, non-uniqueness, and practical realizability concerns.
AI.method: Introduces a conditional diffusion framework trained on T-matrix simulated geometry-response pairs to learn a conditional distribution of geometries rather than a deterministic mapping, enabling multiple candidate designs for the ill-posed inverse problem.
AI.result: The best generated metasurface achieves 1.39% mean percentage error, outperforming CMA-ES optimization (4.1% after 10 hours) while requiring only about one minute for inference. The model also produces lower error distributions than deterministic neural baselines for out-of-distribution spectra.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models offer promising potential for efficient metasurface design by enabling multiple physically realizable candidate structures from target scattering patterns, significantly accelerating the inverse design process compared to traditional optimization methods.

title: Understanding Deep Learning via Entropy Space Theory
summary: Deep learning is often criticized for its theoretical research lagging behind practice. To make deep learning easier to understand, the entropy space theory is first introduced here. The entropy space can cover all the possibilities of any deep learning model by topological structure. It is independent of network parameters. Through the designed fundamental operations and norm, entropy space is proven to be a normed space within the formal axiomatic framework. Based on the theory, a unified coordinate system is proposed. It can coordinatize every state of a model and rank them by compression of the maximal value of information entropy. The theory offers a novel priori framework for mathematical fundamentals of deep learning.

AI.tldr: A novel entropy space theory is introduced as a topological framework to make deep learning more mathematically understandable, providing a unified coordinate system independent of network parameters.
AI.motivation: Deep learning suffers from a gap between theoretical research and practical applications, making it difficult to understand mathematically. The paper aims to provide a more comprehensible theoretical foundation for deep learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce an entropy space theory with topological structure that covers all possible deep learning models. They design fundamental operations and a norm to prove entropy space is a normed space within a formal axiomatic framework, and propose a unified coordinate system.
AI.result: The entropy space theory provides a topological framework independent of network parameters that can coordinatize every state of a model and rank them by compression of the maximal value of information entropy.
AI.conclusion: The entropy space theory offers a novel priori framework for mathematical fundamentals of deep learning, addressing the theoretical research lag in the field and providing a more understandable foundation.

title: On the Recoverability of Private Information Unlearning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize sensitive information, raising serious privacy concerns. Machine unlearning offers a potential solution to remove such information, but it remains unclear whether existing methods truly erase it or merely hide it within the model. A key challenge is quantifying the persistence of sensitive data under a unified evaluation framework. To address this, we construct a synthetic dataset containing fake private information and propose a white-box auditing framework to systematically assess whether claimed-forgotten information is genuinely removed. Using this framework, we evaluate five existing unlearning methods and find that a simple "inverse greedy" decoding -- selecting the least likely token at each step -- can recover supposedly forgotten private information. Our results reveal that current unlearning approaches often fail to fully eliminate sensitive information, highlighting the need for more reliable methods to ensure privacy in deployed LLMs.

AI.tldr: Current LLM unlearning methods often fail to truly erase sensitive information, as a simple inverse greedy decoding can recover supposedly forgotten private data, revealing privacy vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Large language models can memorize sensitive information, raising privacy concerns. While machine unlearning promises to remove such information, there's uncertainty about whether existing methods genuinely erase data or merely hide it within models. A key challenge is quantifying the persistence of sensitive data under a unified evaluation framework.
AI.method: Constructed a synthetic dataset containing fake private information and proposed a white-box auditing framework to systematically assess whether claimed-forgotten information is genuinely removed. Using this framework, evaluated five existing unlearning methods and tested recovery using an "inverse greedy" decoding approach that selects the least likely token at each step.
AI.result: The inverse greedy decoding method successfully recovered supposedly forgotten private information from models that had undergone unlearning. The evaluation revealed that current unlearning approaches often fail to fully eliminate sensitive information.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM unlearning methods are insufficient for ensuring privacy, as sensitive information remains recoverable. The findings highlight the need for more reliable and verifiable unlearning methods to ensure privacy in deployed LLMs.

title: MMPCBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models on Proactive Critique of Flawed Inputs
summary: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) evolve into sophisticated interactive assistants, their reliability depends not only on following instructions but also on validating them. We define Proactive Critique as the model's autonomous ability to identify, analyze and fix faulty user inputs without extra prompts. However, evaluations mainly test models under ideal circumstances or simple refusal behaviors, largely ignoring active error processing. To fill this gap, we propose MMPCBench, a comprehensive framework for evaluating MLLMs' proactive critique competence. It features a fine-grained taxonomy of 4 primary error types spanning 12 subcategories, ranging from cross-modal contradictions to missing visual premises. We adopt a hierarchical evaluation protocol to measure models' error detection, diagnosis and resolution performance, and apply alignment-aware metrics to assess the coherence between internal reasoning and final responses. Tests on 14 mainstream MLLMs show obvious weaknesses in proactive critique, especially in dealing with subtle visual anomalies. Notably, we identify a pervasive "consistency gap": reasoning models can often correctly identify and analyze errors during internal reasoning yet suppress these valid insights in final outputs to prioritize response compliance. The code and data is available at https://github.com/ALIENS32/MMPCBench.

AI.tldr: A framework called MMPCBench is proposed to evaluate multimodal LLMs' ability to autonomously identify, analyze, and fix faulty user inputs without extra prompts, revealing significant weaknesses in proactive critique capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current MLLM evaluations mainly test models under ideal circumstances or simple refusal behaviors, largely ignoring their active error processing capabilities. There's a need to assess models' autonomous ability to validate and fix faulty user inputs.
AI.method: Proposes MMPCBench - a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring fine-grained taxonomy of 4 primary error types across 12 subcategories (cross-modal contradictions, missing visual premises, etc.). Uses hierarchical evaluation protocol to measure error detection, diagnosis, and resolution, with alignment-aware metrics to assess coherence between internal reasoning and final responses.
AI.result: Tests on 14 mainstream MLLMs show obvious weaknesses in proactive critique, especially in dealing with subtle visual anomalies. Identifies a pervasive "consistency gap": models can often correctly identify and analyze errors during internal reasoning yet suppress these valid insights in final outputs to prioritize response compliance.
AI.conclusion: MLLMs have significant deficiencies in proactive critique capabilities, revealing a troubling tendency to prioritize compliance over correctness. The "consistency gap" highlights that models know what's wrong but choose not to express it, posing reliability concerns for real-world applications.

title: Robust Broad Learning System with Wave Loss for Classification under Data Uncertainty
summary: Broad Learning System (BLS) offers an efficient alternative to deep architectures by enabling fast learning through randomized feature mapping and closed-form solutions. However, its reliance on squared error loss makes it highly sensitive to noise, outliers, and corrupted labels, limiting its reliability in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose Wave-BLS, a robust broad learning framework that integrates the wave loss function, which is asymmetric, bounded, and smooth, enabling controlled penalization of large errors. The proposed formulation replaces the standard least-squares objective with a wave-loss-based optimization problem, solved efficiently using a Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG)-based scheme without requiring matrix inversion, thereby improving scalability. Extensive experiments on 30 UCI benchmark datasets demonstrate that Wave-BLS consistently outperforms classical BLS and several robust variants. Statistical validation using Friedman and Nemenyi post-hoc tests confirms the significance of the observed improvements. Furthermore, robustness evaluations under controlled noise and outlier injection reveal that Wave-BLS exhibits substantially slower performance degradation compared to BLS, even in challenging contamination settings. These results establish Wave-BLS as a stable and robust alternative to existing broad learning models for learning under data uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Wave-BLS: A robust broad learning framework using asymmetric wave loss function to handle noise and outliers, outperforming classical BLS with better scalability and stability.
AI.motivation: Classical Broad Learning System (BLS) is sensitive to noise, outliers, and corrupted labels due to its reliance on squared error loss, limiting its reliability in real-world scenarios with data uncertainty.
AI.method: Proposes Wave-BLS that integrates an asymmetric, bounded, and smooth wave loss function to replace the standard least-squares objective. Uses Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG) optimization scheme without matrix inversion for improved scalability.
AI.result: Wave-BLS consistently outperforms classical BLS and robust variants on 30 UCI benchmark datasets. Shows substantially slower performance degradation under controlled noise and outlier injection. Statistical validation confirms significance of improvements.
AI.conclusion: Wave-BLS establishes a stable and robust alternative to existing broad learning models for learning under data uncertainty, offering improved noise resistance and scalability.

title: Accelerating Unified Multimodal Models with Core-Expansion Routing and Unified Computation Scheduling
summary: Unified multimodal models jointly support understanding and generation, but incur substantial redundant computation across tokens, layers, and generation timesteps. Through token-importance probing, we identify an asymmetric core-expansion structure: understanding exhibits a stable importance component, while generation largely shares this component but requires progress-dependent corrections. We therefore propose CE-Router, which uses a task-shared core scorer and progress-conditioned generation expansions, optimized through generation decomposition and cross-task core alignment. At inference, CE-Router compacts token computation and supplies a learned routing signal to Unified Computation Scheduling, which coordinates layer skipping, FFN pruning, diffusion-head cache reuse, and denoising-step early exit. Experiments on two representative UMM architectures demonstrate consistent quality--efficiency improvements across both tasks, retaining 98.03\% of dense understanding performance with a 1.93$\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.

AI.tldr: CE-Router optimizes unified multimodal models by identifying asymmetric core-expansion structure and implementing token computation compaction with learned routing for efficient understanding and generation.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models incur substantial redundant computation across tokens, layers, and generation timesteps, motivating the need for more efficient inference without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Through token-importance probing, identifies asymmetric core-expansion structure, then proposes CE-Router with task-shared core scorer and progress-conditioned generation expansions. Uses generation decomposition and cross-task core alignment for optimization. At inference, implements Unified Computation Scheduling with layer skipping, FFN pruning, diffusion-head cache reuse, and denoising-step early exit.
AI.result: Experiments on two representative UMM architectures demonstrate consistent quality-efficiency improvements, retaining 98.03% of dense understanding performance with 1.93× end-to-end inference speedup.
AI.conclusion: The CE-Router approach successfully identifies and exploits the asymmetric structure of unified multimodal models to achieve significant computational efficiency gains while maintaining high task performance.

title: The Intervention Gap in Latent World Models
summary: Planning-time intervention fidelity is a distinct, measurable property of a learned world model: whether the model's own open-loop transitions move task variables the way matched environment interventions do. In the settings we test, it is neither revealed by reward fit nor ensured by task-anchored training. Across released TD-MPC2 checkpoint sizes, episode return falls as an operator-error diagnostic on task observables grows, while reward-prediction error stays small and nearly flat, and a self-supervised world model trained without task signal preserves the same operator substantially better than a task-anchored model on the shared task. A capture-gated matched-intervention audit then localizes what fails. On Cheetah, three LeWorldModel checkpoints capture the current task query and support decodable real intervention effects; however, their imagined five-step effects are worse than predicting no effect and worse than an environment-endpoint oracle. The failure is task-direction rotation with excess gain, not feature collapse. This severe pattern is conditional: five PreJEPA seeds retain an oracle-relative deficit without it, Finger Spin experiments extend the deficit beyond locomotion with heterogeneous severity across seeds, and shared-bank effect geometry is both candidate- and support-dependent. We also test practice-side questions. In DreamerV3 the posterior distribution, not its sample, carries the current query; ensemble disagreement ranks error only near training support; and a frozen support-aware score degrades held-out error ranking in both tested transfer directions while native disagreement remains informative in both. We conclude that intervention fidelity must be audited directly, capture-first, on the model's native interface.

AI.tldr: Planning-time intervention fidelity is a measurable property of world models that differs from reward fit; audit reveals models often fail to imagine intervention effects accurately, with task-direction rotation being a key failure pattern.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to show that intervention fidelity (how well a world model's imagined transitions match real environment interventions) is distinct from reward fit and not ensured by task-anchored training, requiring direct auditing.
AI.method: Proposes a capture-gated matched-intervention audit that measures how well learned world models capture intervention effects by comparing open-loop transitions to actual environment interventions, testing across various checkpoint sizes and model architectures.
AI.result: Found that intervention fidelity declines with checkpoint size while reward prediction stays flat; task-anchored models show worse intervention fidelity than self-supervised models; identified specific failure patterns like task-direction rotation with excess gain.
AI.conclusion: Intervention fidelity must be directly audited on models' native interfaces using capture-first methods, as it's not captured by reward metrics and reveals critical failure patterns in world models that affect their planning utility.

title: Predicting Future Organ Dysfunction in ICU Patients Using Temporal Convolutional Networks on MIMIC-IV Data
summary: Predicting future organ dysfunction in Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine learning approaches have largely treated the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score as an input to binary mortality prediction rather than as a continuous clinical outcome in its own right. We investigate the extent to which a Temporal Convolutional Net work (TCN) can predict next-day SOFA scores from multivariate ICU time-series data extracted from MIMIC-IV, characterise the relative contribution of each organ system to total SOFA variance and deterioration, and identify distinct trajectory patterns across ICU stays. A residual TCN trained on three-day sliding windows achieved a five-fold cross-validation R2 of 0.740 +- 0.013 and MAE of 1.431 +- 0.022, outperforming a naive persistence baseline on RMSE and R2. SHAP interpretability analysis revealed that the model functions primarily as a severity-anchoring mechanism rather than a true sequence model, with predictions dominated almost entirely by the most recent observation day. Cardiovascular dysfunction emerged as the strongest discriminator of both cross-sectional severity and acute deterioration, and unsupervised trajectory clustering identified two clinically meaningful phenotypes, an improving group (58.9%) and a persistently severe group (41.1%), differentiated by cardiovascular, hepatic, coagulation, and renal involvement. We conclude that TCNs can extract meaningful predictive signal from ICU physiological data, but that short input windows and complete-case selection bias currently limit their clinical utility, motivating future work on longer input horizons, alternative missing-data strategies, and external validation.

AI.tldr: TCN model predicts next-day SOFA scores from ICU time-series data, achieving good performance but limited by short input windows and functioning more as severity anchoring than sequence modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing ML approaches treat SOFA scores only as inputs for mortality prediction rather than as continuous clinical outcomes. Need better prediction of future organ dysfunction in ICU patients for early intervention.
AI.method: Used Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with residual connections trained on three-day sliding windows of multivariate ICU time-series data from MIMIC-IV. Compared against persistence baseline and used SHAP for interpretability analysis. Performed unsupervised trajectory clustering.
AI.result: TCN achieved R² of 0.740 ± 0.013 and MAE of 1.431 ± 0.022, outperforming baseline. Model functions as severity anchoring rather than true sequence model. Cardiovascular dysfunction was strongest predictor. Identified two phenotypes: improving (58.9%) and persistently severe (41.1%) groups.
AI.conclusion: TCNs can extract meaningful predictive signal from ICU data, but current limitations (short input windows, complete-case selection bias) restrict clinical utility. Future work needed on longer input horizons, alternative missing-data strategies, and external validation.

title: Error Detection for PET/CT Radiology Reports: Domain-Specific vs Large Language Models
summary: Errors in radiology reports can adversely affect patient treatment, yet automated report quality assurance remains challenging because errors are often subtle and require domain expertise to detect. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently been proposed for radiology report verification, their ability to detect clinically meaningful errors beyond chest X-ray datasets remains under-explored. To this end, we present the first systematic evaluation of language models for PET/CT report error detection, comparing compact domain-specific models with SOTA open-weight LLMs. We collected 30,633 oncology FDG PET/CT reports from 23 radiologists over 10 years. We trained domain-specific BERT models to detect clinically motivated synthetic reporting errors and evaluated alongside zero-/few-shot Qwen3-32B, Gemma-3-27B and Llama-3.3-70B on a held-out benchmark of 11,500 reports. A 15M-parameter model achieved 94.4% balanced accuracy with a 5.8% false-positive rate, compared with 84.0% for the strongest prompted LLM. Task-specific adaptation of Llama-3.3-70B closed this performance gap (94.4%) but retained substantially greater computational requirements. Our results suggest that domain-specific training matters more than model scale for PET/CT report error detection, supporting compact models as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to automated radiology report quality assurance.

AI.tldr: Compact domain-specific BERT models outperform large language models for PET/CT report error detection, achieving 94.4% accuracy with 15M parameters versus 84.0% for the best prompted LLM.
AI.motivation: Errors in radiology reports can adversely affect patient treatment, but automated quality assurance is challenging due to subtle errors requiring domain expertise. While LLMs have been proposed for chest X-ray report verification, their effectiveness for PET/CT report error detection remains unexplored.
AI.method: Collected 30,633 oncology FDG PET/CT reports from 23 radiologists over 10 years. Trained domain-specific BERT models to detect clinically motivated synthetic reporting errors. Evaluated alongside zero-/few-shot Qwen3-32B, Gemma-3-27B, and Llama-3.3-70B on a held-out benchmark of 11,500 reports.
AI.result: A 15M-parameter domain-specific BERT model achieved 94.4% balanced accuracy with 5.8% false-positive rate, significantly outperforming the strongest prompted LLM (84.0%). Task-specific adaptation of Llama-3.3-70B matched the performance (94.4%) but required substantially greater computational resources.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific training matters more than model scale for PET/CT report error detection. Compact domain-specific models provide an accurate and computationally efficient approach to automated radiology report quality assurance.

title: Formal Concept Analysis with Three Types of Negation
summary: Classic Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) primarily focuses on the positive relationships between objects and attributes and does not have mechanisms for handling negation.To overcome this limitation, we introduce three types of negation concepts (contradictory negation, opposite negation, intermediary negation) into FCA.Based on the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI with these three types negation, we define formal context, Galois connection operators, formal concept and concept lattice with three types of negation,this leads to the proposal of a FCACOI: Formal Concept Analysis with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation.For the reasoning in FCACOI, this paper focuses on attribute implication reasoning. Based on the logic LCOI+PLCOI and its semantics, we introduce the notion of ICOI-entailment as the semantic implication for attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI.
