Through ICOI-entailment, a connection is established between attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI and inference in the logic LCOI+PLCOI, it indicate that formally proven inference rules (theorems) in LCOI+PLCOI are valid in the attribute implication reasoning of FCACOI, LCOI+PLCOI provides a logical foundation for attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI. To illustrate the capability of attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI, we discuss its application in a concrete example. Moreover, we explore attribute reduction of the formal context in FCACOI, propose two research frameworks for attribute reduction from different perspectives, and compare their characteristics.We believe that, based on richer logic and semantics, FCACOI elevates FCA from a theory that describes affirmations to one that can describe affirmations and its contradiction(either this or that), opposition(extreme negation) and intermediary (transitional states between oppositions).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Formal Concept Analysis with three types of negation (contradictory, opposite, intermediary) called FCACOI, extending classical FCA to handle negation in attribute implication reasoning and formal concept lattices.
AI.motivation: Classic Formal Concept Analysis focuses only on positive relationships between objects and attributes and lacks mechanisms for handling negation. This limitation prevents FCA from describing contradictory, opposite, and intermediary relationships.
AI.method: The paper introduces three types of negation concepts (contradictory, opposite, intermediary) into FCA based on the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI. It defines formal context, Galois connection operators, formal concept, and concept lattice with these three negation types. For reasoning, it focuses on attribute implication reasoning using ICOI-entailment as semantic implication.
AI.result: The paper establishes FCACOI as a formal extension of FCA with negation handling. It connects attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI to inference in logic LCOI+PLCOI, showing that formally proven inference rules in LCOI+PLCOI are valid in FCACOI. The approach is illustrated with concrete examples, and attribute reduction frameworks are proposed.
AI.conclusion: FCACOI elevates FCA from a theory describing only affirmations to one that can describe affirmations, contradictions, oppositions, and intermediary states. It provides richer logic and semantics for handling negation in formal concept analysis, with LCOI+PLCOI serving as the logical foundation for attribute implication reasoning.

title: Multiclass Linear Perceptrons with Multiplicative Margins
summary: This paper introduces a family of multiclass linear Perceptron classifiers with a multiplicative margin mechanism (MMPerc), as an alternative to standard margin-free and additive margin Perceptrons. The multiplicative formulation enforces classification confidence by requiring the true class score to exceed that of competing classes by a specified fraction of itself, rather than by a fixed additive threshold. This avoids dependence on score magnitudes arising from varied norms of data and class weight vectors. We propose several architectural and algorithmic variants of MMPerc, derive associated loss functions and mistake bounds for both linearly separable and non-separable data, and analyze key design considerations, including bias, margin threshold selection, and training modes. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that MMPerc classifiers typically outperform the standard Perceptron, as well as classic baselines such as Support Vector Machines and Ridge classifiers. Owing to their simplicity, minimalistic design, and computational efficiency, MMPerc classifiers are promising candidates for conventional machine learning tasks, linear evaluation of Deep Neural Networks, integration with Hyperdimensional Computing / Vector Symbolic Architecture representations, and deployment in resource-constrained applications.

AI.tldr: A novel family of multiclass linear Perceptron classifiers with multiplicative margin mechanism (MMPerc) outperforms standard Perceptrons and baselines, offering classification confidence through relative rather than fixed thresholds.
AI.motivation: Standard Perceptrons lack margins, while additive margin Perceptrons depend on score magnitudes affected by data and weight vector norms. There's a need for margin mechanisms that avoid this dependence and provide better classification confidence.
AI.method: Introduces MMPerc classifiers that enforce classification confidence by requiring the true class score to exceed competing class scores by a specified fraction of itself (multiplicative margin) rather than by a fixed additive threshold. Proposes several architectural variants, derives associated loss functions and mistake bounds for both separable and non-separable data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets show MMPerc classifiers typically outperform standard Perceptrons, Support Vector Machines, and Ridge classifiers. They offer simplicity, minimalistic design, and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: MMPerc classifiers are promising candidates for conventional machine learning tasks, linear evaluation of Deep Neural Networks, integration with Hyperdimensional Computing/Vector Symbolic Architecture representations, and deployment in resource-constrained applications due to their effectiveness and efficiency.

title: BIRD-History: A Benchmark for History-Driven Text-to-SQL with Fine-Grained Knowledge Annotations
comment: Accepted at Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP, 2026
summary: While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based text-to-SQL systems achieve impressive performance on standard benchmarks, they struggle when user queries implicitly rely on domain-specific knowledge, such as business logic, data conventions, and analytical practices, that is neither captured by the schema nor explicitly stated in the natural language question. Historical SQL query logs offer a valuable source of such knowledge, yet existing benchmarks do not adequately support evaluation of history-driven approaches. To address this gap, we introduce BIRD-History, a benchmark consisting of 1,393 tasks across 11 databases, designed to evaluate text-to-SQL systems' ability to ground underspecified natural language questions using historical SQL scripts. Each task is annotated with ground-truth labels specifying which historical queries contain relevant knowledge and which SQL clauses encode it, enabling systematic evaluation of both retrieval effectiveness and knowledge utilization. Alongside the benchmark, we propose a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts, then retrieves and reranks relevant fragments for query generation. The retriever integrates seamlessly into existing few-shot text-to-SQL pipelines without requiring prompt modifications. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across four text-to-SQL systems, highlighting the value of leveraging historical query logs for handling underspecified queries. Dataset and code are open-sourced on https://github.com/zjuidg/BIRD-History.

AI.tldr: BIRD-History is a new benchmark for evaluating text-to-SQL systems' ability to use historical SQL query logs to handle underspecified questions that require domain knowledge.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based text-to-SQL systems struggle with user queries that implicitly rely on domain-specific knowledge not captured in database schemas or explicitly stated in questions. While historical SQL query logs contain valuable domain knowledge, existing benchmarks don't adequately support evaluation of history-driven approaches.
AI.method: Created BIRD-History benchmark with 1,393 tasks across 11 databases, each annotated with ground-truth labels specifying which historical queries contain relevant knowledge and which SQL clauses encode it. Also proposed a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts and retrieves/reranks relevant fragments for query generation without requiring prompt modifications.
AI.result: The benchmark enables systematic evaluation of retrieval effectiveness and knowledge utilization. Experiments show consistent improvements across four text-to-SQL systems when using the proposed retriever, demonstrating the value of leveraging historical query logs for handling underspecified queries.
AI.conclusion: Historical SQL query logs are a valuable resource for addressing underspecified queries in text-to-SQL systems, and the BIRD-History benchmark provides a systematic way to evaluate and improve such history-driven approaches, with the open-sourced dataset and code facilitating further research.

title: Forget or Fine-tune? A Comparative Study of Machine Unlearning Strategies for Noisy Label Correction
summary: Noisy labels remain a critical challenge for training deep neural networks, since memorizing incorrect labels degrades generalization. Once noisy samples are identified after training, the standard solution is to retrain the model from scratch on the cleaned dataset, which is increasingly expensive as datasets and models grow. Machine Unlearning (MU) has recently emerged as a computationally efficient alternative, but the relative effectiveness of different MU strategies for noisy-label correction remains poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comparative empirical study of five MU methods (NegGrad, Fine-Tuning (FT), Random Labeling (RL), SalUn, and MUNBa) across symmetric, asymmetric, instance-dependent, and open-set noise on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and the real-world noisy dataset Food-101N. Our central finding is that the appropriate unlearning strategy is conditioned on the noise structure. Simple FT is a strong baseline across most closed-set scenarios; RL and SalUn are the most consistently robust methods and, under instance-dependent noise, approach retraining accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost; MUNBa shows advantages mainly under extreme symmetric noise. Under open-set noise, in contrast, we show that retraining on the cleaned subset degrades accuracy relative to the noisy baseline, so approximating the retrained model is not an adequate objective in this regime. On Food-101N, all MU methods remain competitive and achieve accuracies close to retraining despite reducing runtime by an order of magnitude. These findings provide practical guidelines for selecting MU strategies for post-training noisy-label correction.

AI.tldr: Comparative study shows machine unlearning methods can efficiently correct noisy labels, with optimal strategy depending on noise type - simple fine-tuning works for most closed-set noise, while Random Labeling and SalUn excel with instance-dependent noise, achieving near-retraining accuracy at much lower cost.
AI.motivation: Noisy labels degrade deep neural network generalization, and traditional retraining from scratch on cleaned data becomes computationally expensive with large datasets and models. Machine unlearning offers an efficient alternative, but there's limited understanding of which unlearning strategies work best for different types of noisy labels.
AI.method: Comparative empirical study of five machine unlearning methods (NegGrad, Fine-Tuning, Random Labeling, SalUn, and MUNBa) across different noise types (symmetric, asymmetric, instance-dependent, open-set) on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and real-world Food-101N dataset.
AI.result: Optimal unlearning strategy depends on noise structure: Fine-Tuning is strong baseline for closed-set noise; Random Labeling and SalUn are most consistently robust, approaching retraining accuracy with instance-dependent noise at fraction of cost; MUNBa works best with extreme symmetric noise. Open-set noise revealed retraining degrades accuracy, making approximation inadequate. All MU methods remain competitive on Food-101N with order of magnitude runtime reduction.
AI.conclusion: Machine unlearning provides practical, computationally efficient solutions for noisy-label correction, with selection guidelines based on noise type. The study offers evidence-based recommendations for choosing appropriate unlearning strategies in different noisy label scenarios.

title: Extending TotalSegmentator: Predicting Patient and Acquisition Characteristics from CT and MR Images
summary:
Background: Patient details and acquisition metadata are important for clinical decisions, image quality control, and automated research pipelines, but may be missing or unreliable in imaging archives.
  Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fast open-source model that predicts patient and acquisition characteristics directly from CT and MR images.
  Materials and Methods: Separate 3D ResNet-10 ensembles for CT and MR were trained on 57,291 and 43,200 clinical examinations acquired from 2011 to 2025. Both predicted weight, height, age, sex, contrast presence, vertebral coverage, and image noise. The CT model additionally predicted scanner manufacturer, tube voltage, tube current, convolution kernel, and post-injection time; the MR model predicted sequence class. Performance was evaluated on internal CT (n=501) and MR (n=636) test sets and an external CT dataset (n=54).
  Results: Internal CT MAEs were 3.90 kg, 3.68 cm, and 4.42 years for weight, height, and age, with sex F1=0.990; corresponding MR results were 4.34 kg, 4.62 cm, 7.13 years, and F1=0.970. The CNN outperformed a segmentation-derived XGBoost baseline for all four core targets in both modalities (adjusted P<=.042). F1 scores were 0.963 for CT contrast, 0.953 for MR sequence, and 0.823 for MR contrast. External CT MAEs were 4.45 kg, 4.05 cm, and 5.17 years, with sex F1=0.971. CPU inference required 20 seconds for CT and 12 seconds for MR.
  Conclusion: One 3D multitask model per modality can rapidly recover patient and acquisition characteristics from heterogeneous CT and MR examinations. Models are available in TotalSegmentator: https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator

AI.tldr: A fast open-source 3D multitask model was developed to predict patient characteristics and acquisition parameters directly from CT and MR images using ResNet-10 ensembles trained on large clinical datasets.
AI.motivation: Patient details and acquisition metadata are crucial for clinical decisions, quality control, and research pipelines but often missing or unreliable in imaging archives, creating a need for automated prediction from images themselves.
AI.method: Separate 3D ResNet-10 ensembles were trained for CT (57,291 exams) and MR (43,200 exams) from 2011-2025 clinical data. Models predicted weight, height, age, sex, contrast presence, vertebral coverage, noise, plus modality-specific parameters like scanner manufacturer, tube settings for CT, and sequence class for MR.
AI.result: Models achieved accurate predictions: CT internal test - 3.90 kg, 3.68 cm, 4.42 years MAE for weight, height, age; sex F1=0.990. MR internal test - 4.34 kg, 4.62 cm, 7.13 years MAE; sex F1=0.970. Outperformed segmentation-based XGBoost baseline (P≤.042). Fast inference (20s CT, 12s MR on CPU).
AI.conclusion: A single 3D multitask model per modality can rapidly and accurately recover patient and acquisition characteristics from diverse CT and MR examinations, with models available in the open-source TotalSegmentator repository.

title: When 3D Gaussian Splatting Recovers Real Surfaces
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 30 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; includes supplementary material
summary: When does 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) recover the true scene surface rather than just overfitting view-dependent appearance? We answer this by developing a mathematical framework based on a first-hit rendering abstraction that cleanly isolates geometry from appearance. We prove that geometric misalignment forcefully converts spatial textures into high-frequency angular signals via parallax. This establishes a strict identifiability window: if angular capacity is bounded, surface-consistent solutions are mathematically preferred; if unrestricted, the same images can be perfectly explained by an incorrect, opaque billboard geometry. Experiments on synthetic stress tests confirm this prediction, showing billboard failures emerge precisely at high angular capacities. Conversely, in the real-world datasets we evaluate under standard capture protocols, reconstructions remain surface-consistent even at high SH degrees, which is consistent with the prediction that rich spatial texture can push billboard solutions outside the tested angular-capacity range.

AI.tldr: 3D Gaussian Splatting only recovers true scene geometry when angular capacity (view-dependent representation) is bounded; unlimited angular capacity can lead to incorrect billboard solutions that overfit appearance.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand when 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) recovers actual scene surfaces rather than just overfitting view-dependent appearance effects, addressing a fundamental ambiguity in neural scene representations.
AI.method: The authors develop a mathematical framework using a "first-hit rendering abstraction" that separates geometry from appearance. They prove that geometric misalignment converts spatial textures into high-frequency angular signals via parallax, establishing identifiability conditions based on angular capacity constraints.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows: (1) With bounded angular capacity, surface-consistent solutions are mathematically preferred; (2) With unrestricted angular capacity, the same images can be perfectly explained by incorrect opaque billboard geometry. Synthetic experiments confirm billboard failures emerge at high angular capacities, while real-world datasets under standard capture protocols remain surface-consistent even with high SH degrees.
AI.conclusion: The identifiability of true scene geometry in 3D Gaussian Splatting depends critically on bounding angular capacity; rich spatial texture in real-world scenes helps keep solutions surface-consistent even with higher view-dependent representation capacity.

title: Cross-Relational Preference Learning for Better LLM Instruction Following
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) still exhibit limited capability in following complex instructions. While existing approaches often rely on preference learning to enhance this ability, they typically overlook the relationships between the permissible response spaces of different instructions, which restricts a model to align with subtle and diverse constraint variations. To address this, we propose Cross-Relational Preference Learning (CRPL), a novel framework for constructing preference data that explicitly models inter-instruction relationships through two key techniques: Cross-Relationship Perturbation and Cross-Region Pair Sampling. This enables the generation of more diverse preference data that captures a wide spectrum of constraint variations. Additionally, we introduce an atomic constraint-based verification mechanism to rigorously assess response satisfaction, ensuring high-quality preference pair construction. Extensive experiments across multiple preference learning methods (e.g., DPO, KTO), LLM backbones and four instruction-following benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves substantial improvements over prior baselines and exhibits strong generalization.

AI.tldr: CRPL framework improves LLM instruction-following by modeling relationships between instruction response spaces, generating diverse preference data, and using constraint verification for high-quality training.
AI.motivation: Large Language Models still have limited capability in following complex instructions. Existing preference learning approaches overlook relationships between permissible response spaces of different instructions, restricting models from aligning with subtle and diverse constraint variations.
AI.method: Proposes Cross-Relational Preference Learning (CRPL) framework that explicitly models inter-instruction relationships through Cross-Relationship Perturbation and Cross-Region Pair Sampling. Also introduces atomic constraint-based verification mechanism to assess response satisfaction and ensure high-quality preference pair construction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple preference learning methods (DPO, KTO), LLM backbones, and four instruction-following benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over prior baselines and strong generalization.
AI.conclusion: CRPL effectively enhances LLMs' instruction-following capability by addressing the limitation of ignoring inter-instruction relationships in existing preference learning approaches, leading to better alignment with diverse constraint variations.

title: How do World Models and Policies Compose in LLM Agents? A Joint Spectral and Behavioral Account
summary: How do LLM agents come to both understand environments they act in and master tasks set within them? Through controlled experiments combining world-model training (next-state prediction) and policy training (reward maximization), we investigate this question. We dissect the resulting models through their additive parameter updates. Geometrically, we find effective world-model updates are low-rank and share an input-feature subspace with policy updates while writing to nearly orthogonal output directions, whether trained separately or sequentially. However, we find that, in projection interventions, the sequential update induces more robustness than separate policy RL when removing the world model's leading input directions, suggesting that it has learned alternative input pathways. Behaviorally, we find the sequentially trained agent explores a wider range of states and actions. Based on this, we ask: does policy training preserve world knowledge as well as it could? We probe this with training-free merging built on the geometrically motivated input basis plus an online world-model loss during policy RL, and show both improve over the untreated baseline. Our findings suggest world knowledge and task-directed ability can be learned in geometrically complementary forms, and that future post-training pipelines should consider how best to engineer the interface between them.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how LLM agents learn both world models and task policies, finding they develop complementary geometric structures, and proposes methods to better preserve world knowledge during policy training.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how LLM agents simultaneously develop understanding of environments (world modeling) and master tasks (policy learning), and whether these two capabilities can be learned in complementary ways that preserve world knowledge during policy optimization.
AI.method: Researchers conducted controlled experiments combining world-model training (next-state prediction) and policy training (reward maximization), analyzing parameter updates geometrically. They used projection interventions to test robustness, behavioral analysis to examine exploration patterns, and developed training-free merging techniques based on geometric insights plus an online world-model loss during policy RL.
AI.result: World-model updates are low-rank and share input-feature subspace with policy updates while writing to nearly orthogonal output directions. Sequentially trained agents are more robust, explore more widely, and the proposed geometric merging methods improve world-knowledge preservation over baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: World knowledge and task-directed ability can be learned in geometrically complementary forms, suggesting future post-training pipelines should carefully engineer the interface between world models and policy learning to better preserve both capabilities.

title: APPSolver: Adaptive Patch Partitioning for Point-Wise Ship Flow Prediction on Unstructured Meshes
summary: Large non-uniform point sets make direct attention-based surrogate modeling costly for ship hydrodynamics. We introduce APPSolver, a point-wise flow-prediction framework built around Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP), a deterministic quadtree representation for fixed two-dimensional horizontal slices extracted from ship CFD simulations. APP assigns finer patches near the hull and coarser patches farther away, downsamples patch contents, and recovers predictions to the full reference point set. Under a corrected protocol that constructs natural $(t,t+1)$ pairs before splitting, reuses training-set normalization statistics, and reports three model seeds, learned tokenizers are more accurate than APP-Transformer, and a persistence baseline has lower one-step MAE on all three ShipBench hulls. The supported benefit of APP is therefore computational rather than universal predictive superiority: on a representative DTC input, APP-Transformer requires 1.815 GFLOPs and 1.309 ms per model forward, while a matched ablation shows that adaptive partitioning reduces MAE by 16.4-24.9\% relative to a uniform partition augmented with learned slicing. Condition encoders provide setting-dependent gains in leave-one-hull-out evaluation, but the current absolute next-state objective does not establish accurate long-horizon dynamics. These results characterize APP as a compact spatial representation with an explicit accuracy--efficiency trade-off. Code is available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/APPSolver .

AI.tldr: APPSolver is a point-wise flow prediction framework using Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP) for ship hydrodynamics that balances computational efficiency with accuracy through quadtree-based spatial representation.
AI.motivation: Large non-uniform point sets in ship CFD simulations make direct attention-based surrogate modeling computationally expensive, creating a need for more efficient spatial representations that maintain accuracy while reducing computational cost.
AI.method: Uses Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP) - a deterministic quadtree representation for 2D horizontal slices from ship simulations that assigns finer patches near the hull and coarser ones farther away, downsamples patch contents, then recovers predictions to full reference points. Also implements corrected protocol with natural (t,t+1) pair construction, reused training statistics, and three model seeds.
AI.result: APP-Transformer requires 1.815 GFLOPs and 1.309 ms per forward pass, with adaptive partitioning reducing MAE by 16.4-24.9% compared to uniform partitioning. However, learned tokenizers outperformed APP-Transformer in accuracy, and a persistence baseline had lower one-step MAE across all three ShipBench hulls.
AI.conclusion: APP provides computational benefits rather than universal predictive superiority, offering a compact spatial representation with explicit accuracy-efficiency trade-off for ship hydrodynamics simulations. Current objective doesn't establish accurate long-horizon dynamics, but condition encoders show setting-dependent improvements in cross-hull evaluation.

title: Selection, Representation, and Execution in Sparse Fourier Neural Operators
summary: Sparse representations are often expected to make models smaller and also reduce inference cost. For Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), these objectives are not equivalent or do not always align: removing parts of the learned operator can leave the underlying transforms and dense computations unchanged, while changing the grid on which the model is evaluated can introduce overhead of its own. We therefore distinguish sparsity in the representation, in the stored parameters, in the theoretical operation count, and in measured runtime, and present an empirical study of several routes toward sparse FNOs that tests each transition between them separately. Coarsening the execution grid reduces the theoretical cost without reducing measured latency, and adding a correction term recovers accuracy at the cost of making the model slower. Even an 83\% parameter reduction remains slower than the dense baseline under ordinary execution. These results motivate a stricter definition of useful sparsity: the deployed operator must preserve solution accuracy and map its reduced support to a genuinely cheaper execution path.

AI.tldr: Sparsity in Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) doesn't necessarily reduce inference cost or runtime - various sparsity definitions (representation, parameters, theoretical cost, runtime) can diverge, with many approaches actually slowing models down despite parameter reduction.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the misconception that sparsity in FNOs automatically leads to smaller models and reduced inference costs. In reality, these objectives often don't align - removing parts of learned operators may not affect underlying computations, while grid changes introduce their own overhead.
AI.method: The authors distinguish four types of sparsity: in representation, stored parameters, theoretical operation count, and measured runtime. They conduct an empirical study testing transitions between these sparsity types using several approaches for sparse FNOs, including grid coarsening and correction terms.
AI.result: Grid coarsening reduces theoretical cost but not measured latency. Adding correction terms recovers accuracy but makes models slower. Even 83% parameter reduction remains slower than dense baselines under ordinary execution. Most sparsity approaches fail to translate theoretical gains to actual runtime improvements.
AI.conclusion: The study motivates a stricter definition of useful sparsity: deployed operators must preserve solution accuracy AND map reduced support to genuinely cheaper execution paths, not just reduce theoretical costs or parameter counts. Practical sparsity requires end-to-end efficiency improvements.

title: Plant-Inspired AI: Plants as Inspiration for Novel Problem Formulations, and Two Case Studies
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has long been inspired by studies of biological intelligence. Reinforcement learning, for instance, drew inspiration from studies involving animal learning and is now a powerful paradigm for solving many real-world problems. Recently, plant biologists have uncovered a wide range of complex behaviors in plants that enable them to flexibly adapt to variable environments. Here, we argue that such behavior can motivate new AI frameworks encompassing a range of problems overlooked by existing problem-solving frameworks such as supervised learning, tree search, and constraint satisfaction. We illustrate this idea with two examples of intelligent problem-solving in plants: (1) leaf mimicry in Boquila trifoliolata, a vine capable of altering its leaves' morphology to resemble those of multiple host trees simultaneously; and (2) coordinated root-shoot growth, wherein plants allocate resources across organ systems exploring distinct environments. While leaf mimicry is highly specific to Boquila, coordination of root-shoot growth is shared across most plants. For both examples, we capture underlying computational principles and identify problems fitting these frameworks that are currently unaddressed by AI. Finally, we outline preliminary task formulations and discuss how these formulations may be applied to non-plant problems.

AI.tldr: AI can learn new problem-solving frameworks from plant intelligence, particularly leaf mimicry adaptation and root-shoot coordination, to address problems overlooked by current AI paradigms.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by recent discoveries in plant biology showing complex adaptive behaviors in plants that could inspire new AI frameworks. Existing AI paradigms like supervised learning, tree search, and constraint satisfaction overlook certain types of problems that plant intelligence addresses.
AI.method: The authors analyze two specific examples of intelligent problem-solving in plants: (1) leaf mimicry in Boquila trifoliolata, and (2) coordinated root-shoot growth. For each example, they capture the underlying computational principles and develop preliminary task formulations that could be applied to non-plant problems.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that plant intelligence offers computational principles for adaptive morphology (leaf mimicry) and distributed resource allocation across heterogeneous environments (root-shoot coordination). These principles can address AI problems currently unaddressed by existing frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Plant intelligence provides valuable inspiration for developing new AI frameworks that can solve a broader range of adaptive, distributed, and resource allocation problems, potentially leading to advances in AI applications beyond biological systems.

title: Tracing Generated Samples to Training-Data Clusters in Flow-Matching Models
summary:
Understanding which training samples influence a generated image is an important problem in generative modeling. In flow matching, training samples influence the generated image through the velocity field along the generation trajectory. Removing samples to examine their counterfactual influence changes the velocity field, and the resulting effect on the final image depends on how the change propagates through the trajectory. Consequently, local changes in the velocity field do not necessarily predict the final counterfactual effect.
  This work investigates attribution in flow-matching models through a hybrid analytical--learned approach, and uses it to derive trajectory-based attribution scores at the cluster level. We evaluate these attribution scores using independently retrained leave-one-cluster-out (LOO) models, and compare with several attribution baselines using two different flow-matching latent spaces. Our experiments show that semantic similarity constitutes a strong baseline, while the closed-form trajectory-based attribution is competitive in some metrics without requiring counterfactual retraining or model gradients.
  Our results show that attribution in flow matching depends not only on semantic similarity to training samples, but also on the latent representation, trajectory dynamics, and how influence is propagated to the final output.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates attribution methods in flow-matching generative models to understand how training samples influence generated images, proposing a hybrid analytical-learned approach for trajectory-based attribution at the cluster level.
AI.motivation: Understanding which training samples influence generated images is important in generative modeling, but in flow matching, removing samples to examine counterfactual influence changes the velocity field in complex ways, and local changes don't necessarily predict final effects on generated images.
AI.method: The authors use a hybrid analytical-learned approach to derive trajectory-based attribution scores at the cluster level, evaluating them using independently retrained leave-one-cluster-out (LOO) models, and comparing with several attribution baselines using two different flow-matching latent spaces.
AI.result: Semantic similarity constitutes a strong baseline, while the closed-form trajectory-based attribution is competitive in some metrics without requiring counterfactual retraining or model gradients. Attribution in flow matching depends on semantic similarity, latent representation, trajectory dynamics, and influence propagation to the final output.
AI.conclusion: Attribution in flow-matching models is complex and depends on multiple factors beyond just semantic similarity, including trajectory dynamics and influence propagation mechanisms, and trajectory-based methods can provide competitive attribution without costly retraining.

title: LiteSearch-VL: Small Multimodal Search Agents via Trajectory Distillation and Synthetic Step-DPO
summary: Multimodal search agents answer visual questions by interleaving image understanding, web retrieval, tool use, and evidence synthesis. Strong systems exist, but in two expensive regimes: proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 and Gemini, or large open vision-language backbones trained with substantial agentic data and reinforcement learning. We ask a different question: when released agent trajectories are distilled into much smaller backbones under a single-node budget, what is actually transferred? We study this with LiteSearch-VL, a low-compute recipe for Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B that uses only released OpenSearch-VL trajectories, parameter-efficient LoRA adapters, and synthetic step-level preferences: DPO on GPT-5-generated hard negatives targeting five local failure modes (premature answer, wrong tool, weak query, repeated query, ignored image). Across 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts on SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini, the dominant effect is behavioral rather than a uniform accuracy lift: full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning transfers the agent contract, taking the 2B model from almost never emitting a usable answer (1,237/1,240 no_answer rollouts) to 28.4% macro Pass@1, matching or slightly exceeding the off-the-shelf 4B base (25.6%). Synthetic preference learning and compact tool distillation act as refinements rather than phase transitions (best 4B configuration: 30.8% macro Pass@1). Finally, a controlled VDR step-budget ablation shows that extra search turns convert abstentions into wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers, identifying answer verification, not search depth, as the next bottleneck for small multimodal agents.

AI.tldr: Small vision-language models (2B/4B parameters) can learn multimodal agent behaviors through supervised fine-tuning on released agent trajectories, achieving similar performance to larger base models, with preference learning providing incremental improvements rather than dramatic gains.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal search agents are expensive, requiring either proprietary frontier models (GPT-5, Gemini) or large open vision-language backbones with extensive agentic data and reinforcement learning. The authors investigate whether smaller models can effectively learn agent behaviors through distillation from released agent trajectories under single-node budget constraints.
AI.method: Proposed LiteSearch-VL: a low-compute recipe using Qwen3-VL-2B/4B models trained with released OpenSearch-VL trajectories, parameter-efficient LoRA adapters, and synthetic step-level preferences (DPO) targeting five failure modes (premature answer, wrong tool, weak query, repeated query, ignored image). Evaluated across 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts on multiple benchmarks.
AI.result: Behavioral transfer rather than uniform accuracy lift: full-trajectory SFT enables 2B model to achieve 28.4% macro Pass@1 (vs. near zero initially), matching/slightly exceeding off-the-shelf 4B base (25.6%). Synthetic preference learning acts as refinement (best 4B: 30.8% macro Pass@1). Additional search turns convert abstentions to wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers.
AI.conclusion: Small multimodal models can learn agent contracts through trajectory distillation, but face limitations: refinement techniques provide incremental gains, and answer verification (not search depth) is the key bottleneck for improving small multimodal agents' performance.

title: A Lightweight Phenology-Aware YOLOv5 Framework for Tomato Growth Stage Detection in Resource-Constrained Bhutanese Greenhouse Environments
summary: Accurate detection of tomato growth stages is essential for stage-specific greenhouse management and precision agriculture. In Bhutan, greenhouse cultivation is affected by altitude variability, large diurnal temperature fluctuations, diffuse illumination, limited automation, and a scarcity of locally annotated datasets, limiting the applicability of conventional deep learning models. This work proposes Pheno-Lite + Efficient Channel Attention (ECA), a lightweight, phenology-aware object detection architecture derived from Ultralytics YOLOv5 for tomato growth stage recognition. A balanced dataset of 2,464 annotated images was constructed from locally collected greenhouse images in Bhutan and publicly available tomato images, with augmentation designed to simulate local greenhouse conditions. The dataset includes vegetative (820), flowering (824), fruiting (820), and background (26) samples. The proposed architecture introduces two customized backbone modules: C3 PhenoLite, which enhances spatial and texture feature extraction using depthwise residual refinement, and C3 ECA, which strengthens inter-channel feature interactions through efficient channel attention. The proposed model achieves 90.6% precision, 88.8% recall, and 92.6% mAP@50, with 4.0 million parameters and 10.9 GFLOPs at 640 x 640 resolution. These results demonstrate its potential for real-time and climate-resilient greenhouse deployment in Bhutan.

AI.tldr: A lightweight object detection model called Pheno-Lite + ECA is proposed for tomato growth stage recognition in Bhutan's challenging greenhouse conditions, achieving high accuracy with reduced computational requirements.
AI.motivation: Accurate tomato growth stage detection is crucial for stage-specific greenhouse management in Bhutan, but conventional deep learning models face limitations due to altitude variability, large temperature fluctuations, diffuse illumination, limited automation, and scarcity of locally annotated datasets.
AI.method: The paper proposes Pheno-Lite + ECA, a lightweight architecture based on YOLOv5 with two customized backbone modules: C3 PhenoLite for enhanced spatial/texture feature extraction using depthwise residual refinement, and C3 ECA for strengthened inter-channel feature interactions through efficient channel attention. A balanced dataset of 2,464 annotated images (vegetative, flowering, fruiting, background) was created from local Bhutan greenhouse images and public sources with augmentation simulating local conditions.
AI.result: The proposed model achieves 90.6% precision, 88.8% recall, and 92.6% mAP@50 with only 4.0 million parameters and 10.9 GFLOPs at 640 x 640 resolution, demonstrating high accuracy with low computational requirements.
AI.conclusion: The Pheno-Lite + ECA architecture demonstrates potential for real-time and climate-resilient greenhouse deployment in Bhutan, offering an effective solution for tomato growth stage recognition under challenging local conditions with limited computational resources.

title: TRACER: Per-Tool Context Retention for LLM Agents via Consequence-Attributed Reinforcement Learning
summary: Enterprise data agents answer business queries by chaining many tool calls over multiple reasoning steps, routinely accumulating hundreds of thousands of context tokens per session. Existing compression strategies typically allocate retention budgets without accounting for the downstream consequences of removing individual tool outputs. Aggressive compression may therefore trigger costly tool re-invocations that offset the initial savings. We call this the compression--consequence gap. To close it, we propose TRACER, which formulates compression as a sequential per-tool decision problem. A lightweight REINFORCE policy assigns query-conditioned retention ratios using only information available at each compression event. Its consequence-aware objective jointly accounts for task success, total token consumption, and post-compression tool re-invocations. To improve credit assignment, TRACER uses a learned outcome model to compare the predicted consequences of the selected retention ratio with those of fully retaining each tool output. On held-out production queries across three compressor backends, TRACER reduces total token consumption by 29--46% relative to keeping all context while maintaining comparable or higher task success. Compared with a tool-type-conditional static policy, TRACER provides an additional 15--18% of token savings. Interventional rollouts show that the learned per-tool credit scores correlate with measured single-tool consequences. The learned policy also yields positive savings when transferred across agent backbones and compressor architectures, and reduces token consumption by 18--25% on five held-out LOCA-bench environments. These results demonstrate the value of consequence-aware, per-tool context retention for improving the efficiency of long-horizon language agents.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a consequence-aware compression method for enterprise data agents that reduces token consumption by 29-46% while maintaining task success, by treating compression as a sequential decision problem with learned retention policies.
AI.motivation: Enterprise data agents accumulate hundreds of thousands of context tokens per session during tool chaining. Existing compression strategies don't account for downstream consequences of removing tool outputs, leading to aggressive compression that triggers costly tool re-invocations, creating a "compression-consequence gap."
AI.method: TRACER formulates compression as a sequential per-tool decision problem using a lightweight REINFORCE policy. It assigns query-conditioned retention ratios using information available at each compression event, with a consequence-aware objective that jointly considers task success, total token consumption, and post-compression tool re-invocations. It uses a learned outcome model for credit assignment by comparing predicted consequences of selected retention ratios with fully retaining each tool output.
AI.result: On held-out production queries across three compressor backends, TRACER reduces total token consumption by 29-46% relative to keeping all context while maintaining comparable or higher task success. It provides 15-18% additional token savings over tool-type-conditional static policies. Learned policies transfer well across agent backbones and compressor architectures, reducing token consumption by 18-25% on five held-out LOCA-bench environments.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the value of consequence-aware, per-tool context retention for improving the efficiency of long-horizon language agents, effectively closing the compression-consequence gap by optimizing retention decisions based on downstream consequences.

title: SMOTE-VAR: An Uncertainty-Aware Oversampling Method for Predicting Depression Remission in University Students
summary: University students experience disproportionately high rates of common mental health conditions, such as depression, which can impair learning, social functioning, and overall well-being. Although lifestyle interventions such as mindfulness and physical activity can reduce the symptoms, many do not achieve symptomatic remission. Developing new approaches to identify students with poor outcomes could enable earlier and more targeted intervention. Machine learning (ML) methods have increasingly been used to predict remission in depressive patients. However, these ML models often suffer from class imbalance, where there may be an unequal proportion of people in the remitted group relative to the non-remitted group. This imbalance can reduce model accuracy and bias predictions. To address this, studies commonly employ the popular oversampling strategy SMOTE. However, SMOTE has a notable limitation: it may generate invalid synthetic minority samples. In a clinical context, these false positives can lead to incorrect risk stratification, potentially delaying necessary escalated care for patients unlikely to remit. In this paper, we introduce a novel and effective oversampling method that addresses this shortcoming. Our approach leverages the variance function of a Gaussian process to estimate the uncertainty of generated minority samples to reduce false positives. We validate our method on a depression dataset collected from university students and demonstrate that it is better than existing oversampling approaches in predicting remission (i.e., treatment outcome). By improving the reliable identification of non-responders, our method provides a robust computational tool to help clinicians rapidly pivot to adjunctive therapies, thereby personalizing and optimizing mental health care pathways.

AI.tldr: A novel Gaussian process-based oversampling method for predicting depression remission in university students that reduces false positives compared to traditional SMOTE approaches.
AI.motivation: University students have high depression rates, and while lifestyle interventions help, many don't achieve remission. Current machine learning models for predicting remission suffer from class imbalance issues, and popular SMOTE oversampling creates invalid synthetic minority samples that can lead to false positives and delayed care.
AI.method: The paper introduces a novel oversampling method that uses the variance function of a Gaussian process to estimate uncertainty of generated minority samples, reducing false positives by validating synthetic samples before inclusion.
AI.result: The method was validated on a depression dataset from university students and demonstrated superior performance over existing oversampling approaches in predicting depression remission (treatment outcome).
AI.conclusion: The proposed method improves reliable identification of non-responders to depression treatment, providing a robust computational tool to help clinicians pivot to adjunctive therapies more rapidly, thereby personalizing and optimizing mental health care pathways for students.

title: Reviving our data foundations is the most disruptive step to data maturity
summary: The most disruptive step that enterprises of small-medium size and maturity can take to make the most of the latest technological advances in AI is to step back from the hype and focus on establishing or reviving a good knowledge foundation layer. It is a hard message to present to the executive team; therefore, it needs to be backed by evidence, and its implementation needs to be of minimal impact on the existing processes. In this vision statement, we discuss how we need to rethink what evidence speaks to the decision-makers and propose a low-impact data strategy that adapts to the existing and ever-changing data flows and processes across the company. We firmly believe that knowledge graph techniques will increasingly become non-negotiable in the data strategy of an AI-powered enterprise, provided that we approach their design in a modular, dynamic and cross-functional way.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that small-medium enterprises should focus on building a solid knowledge foundation layer rather than chasing AI hype, proposing a low-impact data strategy using knowledge graphs in a modular, dynamic, and cross-functional way.
AI.motivation: Enterprises, especially small-medium sized and less mature ones, face pressure to adopt AI but risk making poor decisions due to hype. They need practical, evidence-based approaches that minimize disruption to existing processes while leveraging AI advances.
AI.method: The authors propose rethinking what evidence should be presented to decision-makers and introducing a low-impact data strategy that adapts to existing data flows and processes. They advocate for knowledge graph techniques implemented in a modular, dynamic, and cross-functional design approach.
AI.result: The paper presents a vision for how knowledge graph techniques can become essential in enterprise data strategies for AI implementation, provided they are designed to be minimally disruptive and adaptable to current organizational structures.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graph techniques will increasingly become non-negotiable for AI-powered enterprises, but only if implemented with a focus on minimal impact, modularity, dynamism, and cross-functional integration - representing a practical approach to AI adoption over hype-driven strategies.

title: Graph4BiLO: Graph Neural Network Approximation for Bilevel Mixed-Integer Linear Optimization
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Bilevel mixed-integer linear optimization problems model hierarchical decision processes in which a leader anticipates the optimal response of a follower. Although expressive, these problems are computationally challenging because lower-level optimality is embedded in the leader's feasible region. Value-function reformulations replace the nested follower optimization with a constraint involving the follower's optimal value, but evaluating this value function exactly can itself be expensive. This paper introduces Graph4BiLO, a graph neural network (GNN) approach for learning bilevel value functions from variable--constraint graph representations. In contrast to fixed-length multilayer perceptron (MLP) representations, the GNN uses shared message-passing parameters and can therefore be applied across multiple problem sizes with a single trained model. The learned ReLU network is encoded exactly as mixed-integer linear constraints and embedded in an approximate single-level formulation. A repair step subsequently re-solves the follower problem for the selected leader decision to recover a bilevel-feasible follower response. We evaluate Graph4BiLO on knapsack interdiction instances with 20--100 items against the exact MibS solver and the learning-based Neur2BiLO method. Graph4BiLO obtains objective values comparable to Neur2BiLO across all tested sizes while avoiding size-specific neural networks. An additional out-of-distribution experiment demonstrates zero-shot transfer from 20-item training instances to previously unseen 40- and 60-item instances. However, embedding message passing at every graph node substantially increases the resulting mixed-integer formulation size and solve time. These results identify a central tradeoff between size-generalizable graph representations and the computational cost of embedding GNNs within optimization models.

AI.tldr: Graph4BiLO uses graph neural networks to learn bilevel optimization value functions that work across different problem sizes, avoiding the need for size-specific models while maintaining comparable performance to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Bilevel mixed-integer linear optimization problems are computationally challenging because lower-level optimality constraints are embedded in the leader's feasible region. Value-function reformulations are expensive to evaluate exactly, and existing learning approaches require size-specific models.
AI.method: Uses graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn bilevel value functions from variable-constraint graph representations. The GNN uses shared message-passing parameters allowing application across multiple problem sizes. The learned ReLU network is encoded exactly as mixed-integer linear constraints and embedded in an approximate single-level formulation, followed by a repair step to recover bilevel-feasible solutions.
AI.result: Graph4BiLO achieves objective values comparable to Neur2BiLO across knapsack interdiction instances with 20-100 items while avoiding size-specific neural networks. Shows zero-shot transfer from 20-item training to unseen 40- and 60-item instances. However, embedding message passing increases mixed-integer formulation size and solve time.
AI.conclusion: The method demonstrates a tradeoff between size-generalizable graph representations and computational cost of embedding GNNs in optimization models, offering a promising approach for bilevel optimization across varying problem sizes.

title: FORESIGHT-9: Prospective and Process-Aware Evaluation of Adaptive Trading Agents
summary: Retrospective backtests provide a limited test of adaptive trading agents: they cannot rule out historical contamination, expose sensitivity to a single realized market path, or reveal internal degeneration during long-horizon adaptation. We introduce FORESIGHT-9, a prospective and process-aware benchmark built from nine auditable counterfactual stress worldlines branching from a common July 2026 information boundary. Each worldline specifies staged macro-financial events and joint multi-asset anchors; a deterministic generator realizes the trajectories, while observations are disclosed according to in-world time. A common contract standardizes observations and execution while preserving each agent's native adaptation loop. We evaluate two adaptive trading-agent frameworks with two foundation-model backbones across 36 long-horizon runs. Agent rankings vary substantially across worldlines and backbones, and a fixed equal-weight policy outperforms 31 of 36 runs. Process telemetry exposes failures that terminal returns conceal: in one high-return run, the live factor library collapsed while executed holdings converged to the equal-weight fallback, even though decision records continued to report an active factor ensemble. FORESIGHT-9 therefore evaluates not only portfolio outcomes, but whether adaptive agent state and execution remain coherent across alternative futures. We release the worldlines, trajectories, audit traces, and regeneration scripts.

AI.tldr: FORESIGHT-9 is a prospective benchmarking framework for evaluating adaptive trading agents using nine counterfactual future worldlines starting from July 2026, addressing limitations of retrospective backtests by testing agents' internal coherence and performance across alternative market scenarios.
AI.motivation: Traditional retrospective backtests have significant limitations: they cannot rule out historical contamination, only expose sensitivity to a single realized market path, and fail to reveal internal agent degeneration during long-horizon adaptation. There's a need for more robust evaluation of adaptive trading agents that goes beyond historical path dependency.
AI.method: The authors create FORESIGHT-9, a prospective benchmark with nine auditable counterfactual stress worldlines branching from a common July 2026 information boundary. Each worldline specifies staged macro-financial events and joint multi-asset anchors, with deterministic trajectory generation. Observations are disclosed according to in-world time, and a common contract standardizes observations/execution while preserving each agent's native adaptation loop. The method includes process telemetry to monitor agent internal state.
AI.result: Evaluation of two adaptive trading-agent frameworks with two foundation-model backbones across 36 long-horizon runs showed: agent rankings varied substantially across worldlines and backbones; a fixed equal-weight policy outperformed 31 of 36 runs. Process telemetry revealed critical failures: in one high-return run, the live factor library collapsed while executed holdings converged to equal-weight fallback, though decision records continued to report an active factor ensemble.
AI.conclusion: FORESIGHT-9 successfully addresses retrospective backtest limitations by evaluating not only portfolio outcomes but also whether adaptive agent state and execution remain coherent across alternative futures. The framework exposes internal degradation that terminal returns conceal, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of trading agents. The authors release the worldlines, trajectories, audit traces, and regeneration scripts to support further research.

title: Supraglacial Lake Fate Is Knowable Long Before the Season Ends
summary: A supraglacial lake on the Greenland Ice Sheet ends its melt season in one of four ways: it drains rapidly through a hydrofracture, drains slowly across the surface, refreezes in place, or is buried by late-season snowfall. Which one occurs decides whether the meltwater reaches the ice bed. Satellite classifiers recover the outcome accurately but only after the season closes, and how much of a season each outcome actually requires has never been measured. We measure it directly: holding the representation and the classifier fixed, we truncate the input at $14$ cutoffs from 1 May to 31 December, retrain at each, and record the earliest cutoff at which each outcome's per-class $F_1$ reaches a fixed target. The outcomes resolve in a consistent order, two of them months early: rapid drainage by 15 July and slow drainage by 1 August, $92$ and $75$ days ahead of the earliest date a full-season pipeline can be computed at all, with buried and refreeze following at $44$ and $30$ days. Five further learners, from a majority-class floor and $54$ summary statistics to a trigger-based early classifier, leave the ordering intact: every learner that produces a per-class trajectory reproduces it despite end-of-season accuracies differing by up to $18$ percentage points, and it survives leave-one-basin-out evaluation, though not the substitution of machine labels for expert ones in an unseen season. Every feature we compute at day $t$ reads only days up to $t$, at a cost of at most $1.3$ percentage points. A monitoring system should therefore not have one release date: rapid drainage can be flagged on 15 July, three months before a full-season pipeline can be computed at all.

AI.tldr: Supraglacial lakes on Greenland Ice Sheet resolve their fate in a predictable sequence, with rapid drainage detectable by July 15 (92 days before full-season analysis), enabling earlier monitoring alerts.
AI.motivation: Current satellite classifiers only identify supraglacial lake outcomes after the melt season ends, creating a lag in understanding when meltwater reaches the ice bed. There's a need to determine how early in the season each outcome can be reliably predicted to enable timely monitoring.
AI.method: Using a fixed classifier, researchers truncated input data at 14 time cutoffs from May 1 to December 31, retraining at each cutoff to find the earliest date when each outcome's F1 score reaches a target threshold. Tested with five additional learners and cross-validation approaches.
AI.result: Outcomes resolve in consistent order: rapid drainage by July 15, slow drainage by August 1 (92 and 75 days before full-season analysis), with burial and refreeze following 44 and 30 days before season end. Order remains stable across different learners despite accuracy variations.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring systems should have staggered release dates rather than single end-of-season reporting, enabling early detection of rapid drainage events months before traditional analysis. Daily-computed features maintain accuracy while enabling real-time monitoring.

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
summary: Code generation increasingly relies on large transformer models, whose capability advances with scale. Yet such a scale is costly, creating demand for small models, especially where data is limited. Recursive models address this by reusing a single block to add depth rather than stacking independent layers. Such models are typically evaluated by teacher-forced fit (next-token loss on ground-truth prefixes) or task accuracy, at a single checkpoint, whereas code is produced by free-running generation, where the model extends its own output. Whether a teacher-forced advantage survives free-running generation, and whether it holds across training, remains open. To study both, we compare a ~28M-parameter autoregressive Tiny Recursive Model (TRM-AR) on natural-language-to-Python code generation against parameter-matched and depth-matched controls, tracking fit and generation across 40 epochs and three seeds. The fit ranking between the recursive model and the depth-matched control reverses twice. Selecting each checkpoint by validation loss and examining the trajectory yields a consistent comparison. At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates, and generalizes better than the parameter-matched control while recovering approximately 45% of the validation-loss gap and 57% of the generation-quality gap between the two controls, at roughly 175 times the per-step cost of the parameter-matched control. However, at equal effective depth, the larger transformer fits and generates better at its validation optimum, suggesting TRM-AR's advantage lies in resistance to overfitting, not greater capability. These findings suggest that recursive code generation models should be evaluated jointly on fit and generation across the training trajectory rather than at a single checkpoint.

AI.tldr: Recursive models for code generation show teacher-forced advantages that don't always translate to better free-running generation. At equal parameters, they outperform controls but recover only part of the performance gap with larger transformers.
AI.motivation: Large transformer models for code generation are costly, creating demand for smaller models especially in data-limited settings. Recursive models reuse a single block to add depth, but existing evaluations focus on teacher-forced fit or task accuracy at single checkpoints, not free-running generation across training.
AI.method: Compared a ~28M-parameter autoregressive Tiny Recursive Model (TRM-AR) on natural-language-to-Python code generation against parameter-matched and depth-matched controls. Tracked both teacher-forced fit and free-running generation across 40 epochs and three seeds, using validation loss for checkpoint selection.
AI.result: At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates, and generalizes better than parameter-matched control, recovering ~45% of validation-loss gap and ~57% of generation-quality gap between controls, but at ~175x per-step cost. At equal effective depth, larger transformer performs better at validation optimum, suggesting TRM-AR's advantage lies in overfitting resistance rather than greater capability.
AI.conclusion: Recursive code generation models should be evaluated jointly on fit and generation across the entire training trajectory rather than at single checkpoints, as teacher-forced advantages may not translate to free-running generation.

title: TPR-Attention for Combinatorial Generalization
summary: Systematic generalization remains a significant challenge in deep learning. In particular, combinatorial generalization - generalizing to new configurations of known factors of variation - is effortless for humans but difficult for standard neural architectures that rely on statistical correlations rather than explicit structural representations. We introduce a new architectural component that embeds structured inductive bias into deep learning: an attention mechanism operating over tensor-product representations (TPRs). Through controlled experiments on compositional tasks, we show that this TPR-attention mechanism outperforms existing architectural components in combinatorial generalization. These results highlight the value of integrating explicit compositional structure into neural attention and point toward a promising path for models capable of systematic generalization.

AI.tldr: A novel attention mechanism using tensor-product representations improves combinatorial generalization in deep learning by embedding structured inductive biases.
AI.motivation: Systematic generalization, especially combinatorial generalization (generalizing to new configurations of known factors), is a major challenge in deep learning. Humans excel at this, but standard neural networks rely on statistical correlations rather than explicit structural representations.
AI.method: Introduces a new architectural component: an attention mechanism operating over tensor-product representations (TPRs). This embeds structured inductive bias into deep learning through explicit compositional structure.
AI.result: Controlled experiments on compositional tasks show that the TPR-attention mechanism outperforms existing architectural components in combinatorial generalization.
AI.conclusion: Integrating explicit compositional structure into neural attention is valuable and points toward a promising path for developing models capable of systematic generalization.

title: EvoGenUI-Bench: Evaluating LLMs as Multi-Turn Generative UI Assistants
summary: Large language models can generate interactive web interfaces, but reliable generative UI requires maintaining an executable artifact as user requests evolve. We introduce EvoGenUI-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn interface maintenance comprising 150 five-turn tasks and 750 turns across three scenarios: information presentation, executable interaction, and tool-grounded external state. We execute generated artifacts in a browser and evaluate them using screenshots, source and DOM evidence, actor traces, and runtime logs. Beyond turn-level and episode-level success, we measure cross-turn retention with Adjacent Pass Retention. Across eight models, even the strongest achieves 74.9% Turn Pass while completing only 37.3% of five-turn episodes; APR further falls to 52.4% on tool-grounded tasks. Diagnostic analysis shows that presentation failures center on information architecture, interaction failures on derived-state propagation and affordance binding, and tool-grounded failures additionally involve external-state grounding and requirement decomposition. These results reframe generative UI evaluation from judging isolated outputs to testing whether interface behavior, derived state, external state, and assistant claims remain synchronized as the artifact evolves.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvoGenUI-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating how well large language models can maintain evolving web interfaces over multiple turns, revealing significant challenges in cross-turn consistency and state synchronization.
AI.motivation: While large language models can generate interactive web interfaces, there's a need to assess how well these models can maintain executable artifacts as user requests evolve over multiple turns, moving beyond single-turn evaluation to test continuous interface maintenance.
AI.method: The authors create EvoGenUI-Bench with 150 five-turn tasks (750 turns total) across three scenarios: information presentation, executable interaction, and tool-grounded external state. They evaluate generated artifacts in a browser using screenshots, source/DOM evidence, actor traces, and runtime logs, measuring both turn-level success and cross-turn retention with Adjacent Pass Retention (APR).
AI.result: Across eight models, even the strongest achieves only 74.9% Turn Pass while completing just 37.3% of five-turn episodes. APR drops to 52.4% on tool-grounded tasks. Analysis shows presentation failures center on information architecture, interaction failures on derived-state propagation and affordance binding, and tool-grounded failures involve external-state grounding and requirement decomposition.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight that generative UI evaluation needs to shift from judging isolated outputs to testing whether interface behavior, derived state, external state, and assistant claims remain synchronized as the artifact evolves over multiple turns, revealing significant maintenance challenges for current models.

title: Converse and Collision-Based Achievability for Node Localization with Hybrid Distance-Spectral Graph Positional Encodings
summary: Graph positional encodings are widely used in graph neural networks and graph Transformers, yet it remains unclear when the code itself can identify nodes. We study a hybrid distance-spectral encoding that combines anchor-distance profiles with quantized low-frequency Laplacian-energy coordinates. Treating the encoding as an observation map yields a simplex-refined converse, an exact collision factorization \(κ_H=κ_Dκ_{S|D}\), and the collision information \(I_H=-\logκ_D-\logκ_{S|D}\). On random regular graphs, the criterion is made explicit through a bounded-correlation Gaussian-wave surrogate; for actual Laplacian-energy coordinates, we give the distance-conditioned spectral collision condition sufficient for conditional actual-coordinate achievability. Experiments show that \(I_H/\log n\) calibrates localization success, and PE-only structural task probes on Universal Dependencies trees show that hybrid encodings better recover syntactic-tree geometry than distance-only or spectral-only baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes graph positional encodings that combine anchor-distance profiles with quantized Laplacian-energy coordinates, developing a theoretical framework for when nodes can be identified and showing experimentally that hybrid encodings outperform distance-only or spectral-only baselines on syntactic tree tasks.
AI.motivation: There's a lack of clear understanding about when graph positional encodings can actually identify nodes, despite their widespread use in graph neural networks and graph Transformers. The authors aim to provide theoretical insights into node identifiability conditions for hybrid encodings that combine distance and spectral information.
AI.method: The paper proposes a hybrid distance-spectral encoding combining anchor-distance profiles with quantized low-frequency Laplacian-energy coordinates. It develops theoretical analysis treating the encoding as an observation map, deriving a collision factorization (κ_H = κ_D κ_{S|D}) and collision information. On random regular graphs, analysis uses a bounded-correlation Gaussian-wave surrogate model. The paper also provides distance-conditioned spectral collision conditions for conditional achievability with actual coordinates.
AI.result: Experiments show that the normalized collision information (I_H/log n) calibrates localization success. On Universal Dependencies trees, PE-only structural task probes demonstrate that hybrid encodings better recover syntactic-tree geometry compared to distance-only or spectral-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid distance-spectral encodings provide better node identifiability than either approach alone, with theoretical foundations explaining when nodes can be distinguished and practical improvements demonstrated on real-world syntactic parsing tasks.

title: Toward Latent Language Model Skills Steering and Optimization: An Empirical Study
summary: Skills, as a useful abstraction for the procedural capabilities of large language models (LLMs), capture how models perform structured, multi-step reasoning and program execution. Existing approaches typically treat skills as explicit, surface-level constructs specified through prompts or programs, leaving open the question of how such procedural capabilities are represented inside the model and whether they can be manipulated as structured objects in latent space. In this empirical study, we investigate whether procedural LLM skills can be represented as directions in activation space and whether vector-space operations over these directions can express skill-level behaviors. We find that procedural skills admit a vector-space representation: individual skill directions can be activated to shift model behavior; independently extracted directions can compose to form higher-level skills. Contrastive directions yield context-conditioned algorithmic personalization and optimization trajectories over skill directions evolve non-monotonically, with intermediate states often surpassing fully optimized solutions. These results support a representation-level view of procedural LLM skills: they admit a latent vector-space organization that allows direct manipulation through internal interventions.

AI.tldr: LLM skills can be represented as directions in activation space, enabling vector-space operations to manipulate procedural capabilities directly within the model's latent representations.
AI.motivation: Current approaches treat LLM skills as explicit, surface-level constructs via prompts or programs, leaving unanswered how procedural capabilities are internally represented and whether they can be manipulated as structured objects in latent space.
AI.method: Empirical investigation examining whether procedural LLM skills can be represented as directions in activation space, and testing vector-space operations over these directions to express skill-level behaviors.
AI.result: Procedural skills admit vector-space representation: skill directions can be activated to shift model behavior; independently extracted directions can compose to form higher-level skills; contrastive directions enable context-conditioned algorithmic personalization; optimization trajectories over skill directions evolve non-monotonically with intermediate states often surpassing fully optimized solutions.
AI.conclusion: LLM skills have a latent vector-space organization that allows direct manipulation through internal interventions, supporting a representation-level view of procedural capabilities.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Symbolic Equation Solving
summary: We present a reinforcement-learning agent that solves symbolic equations step by step, covering both nonlinear closed equations (radicals, exponentials, trigonometric) and a controlled class of restricted-open families requiring a change of variables (CoV) such as completing the square. We cast algebra as an MDP with a dynamic action space and a tree-structured policy (TreeMLP). The main policy learns from reward alone with no supervised solution traces; the CoV substitution comes from a supervised generator interchangeable with a CAS call. On closed equations the agent matches the prior best on CommonCore (0.93 greedy vs. ConPoLe's 0.925) under a single policy. On four hand-designed restricted-open families (quadratic, cubic, quartic, exponential) it reaches 0.79 beam / 0.67 greedy, exceeding the strongest non-learned search (A-star, 0.64). Learned CoV timing has content only on the exponential family, the one requiring a nested CoV, where a natural rule solves none of the held-out equations while the policy solves 75% from reward alone. At 10x scale a sharp seed-level bimodality emerges; a UCB learning-progress curriculum shows a non-significant positive trend toward mitigating it. We do not claim general open-equation solving: every open-equation result is confined to these four controlled families.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning agent solves symbolic equations step-by-step, handling nonlinear closed equations and restricted-open families requiring change of variables, using a tree-structured policy trained primarily from reward signals.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop an AI system that can solve symbolic equations autonomously, particularly addressing both closed-form equations and certain restricted-open equation families that require changes of variables, going beyond traditional computer algebra systems by learning solution strategies.
AI.method: The method frames algebra solving as a Markov Decision Process with dynamic action space using a tree-structured MLP (TreeMLP). The main policy learns from reward signals without supervised solution traces. Change of variable substitutions come from a supervised generator that can be interchangeable with computer algebra system calls. They use beam search and explore learning progress curriculum strategies.
AI.result: On closed equations, the agent matches prior best performance (0.93 greedy vs ConPoLe's 0.925). On four restricted-open equation families (quadratic, cubic, quartic, exponential), it achieves 0.79 beam/0.67 greedy, exceeding non-learned A-star search (0.64). The learned change of variable timing shows content only on exponential family requiring nested CoV, solving 75% of held-out equations vs 0% for natural rules. At larger scale, seed-level bimodality emerges, with UCB learning-progress curriculum showing non-significant positive trend for mitigation.
