We introduce an evidence-gated trust-promotion model that keeps generated data provisional until a deterministic monitor verifies it against the source document. The monitor admits a candidate for a specified downstream use only when the source contains a unique supporting quotation, the relevant fields occur within the same laboratory row, and the required provenance is preserved. The generator cannot approve its own output, missing or ambiguous evidence causes refusal, and refused candidates remain available for human review rather than being silently discarded. We implement the model in Medical DataCloud, a personal health-record application, and evaluate it through automated tests and a replay of saved extraction outputs. All 22 conformance and mutation tests pass. The replay covers nine historical laboratory PDF reports containing 102 manually labelled rows. The reports produce 97 numeric candidates: schema validation accepts all 97, an earlier packet-level evidence check accepts 94, and the hardened quotation- and row-level policy admits 72 while retaining 25 for review. The study evaluates system integrity rather than clinical correctness or clinical safety. The results demonstrate the technical feasibility of an enforceable boundary that prevents generated claims from authorizing their own reuse in a longitudinal health record.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed an evidence-gated trust-promotion model that prevents LLMs from inserting unsupported medical data into longitudinal health records by requiring deterministic verification against source documents before approval.
AI.motivation: Large language models can generate plausible but unsupported medical data from documents, creating integrity risks in longitudinal health records where unverified data could influence future summaries, trends, and preventive-care computations.
AI.method: Introduces an evidence-gated trust-promotion model where generated data remains provisional until verified by a deterministic monitor against source documents. The monitor only admits candidates when: (1) source contains unique supporting quotation, (2) relevant fields occur within same laboratory row, and (3) required provenance is preserved. Generator cannot approve its own output, and missing evidence leads to refusal with candidates available for human review.
AI.result: Implemented in Medical DataCloud application. All 22 conformance and mutation tests passed. Replay of 9 historical lab PDFs (102 manually labeled rows) produced 97 numeric candidates: schema validation accepted all 97, packet-level evidence check accepted 94, and hardened quotation-and-row-level policy admitted 72 while retaining 25 for review.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates technical feasibility of an enforceable boundary that prevents generated claims from authorizing their own reuse in longitudinal health records, addressing system integrity (though not clinical correctness or safety).

title: Beyond Churn: Predicting Financial Fragmentation in Retail Banking with Temporal Machine Learning
summary: Retail banking attrition is usually represented as a terminal binary event, even though client relationships often weaken earlier through partial movements of deposits, investments, and recurring activity to external financial institutions. This paper defines that preceding state as financial fragmentation and presents an end-to-end temporal machine-learning system for predicting it before complete disengagement. Using anonymized multi-source data from a large retail bank, the framework predicts whether a valid external transfer or investment event will occur within 90 days. The study uses 595,220 client-month observations, with 346 engineered features combining monthly client profiles, balances, product relationships, prior flow-of-funds behavior, macroeconomic conditions, and competitor activity. A four-stage XGBoost cascade estimates (1) whether an external outflow will occur within 90 days, (2) the expected amount, (3) the originating product, and (4) the destination financial institution. The primary classifier achieved a test precision-recall area under the curve of 0.823. At the validation-selected threshold, it produced 86.4% precision, 75.1% recall, and an F1 score of 0.803. Ranking test observations in descending Stage 1 fragmentation score, the top 1% of clients yielded 95.3% precision, while the top 5% captured 78.7% of observed outflow cases. The amount model placed 94.9% of predictions within an adjacent amount bucket. Destination prediction reached a macro-F1 of 0.81 across 27 classes; source-product prediction achieved a weighted F1 of 0.92. By moving the analytical focus from terminal churn to earlier fund migration, the proposed approach provides a practical foundation for proactive, explainable, and economically informed client-retention decision support.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end ML system predicts financial fragmentation (early fund migration) in retail banking using a four-stage XGBoost cascade to forecast external outflows, amounts, sources, and destinations with high precision.
AI.motivation: Traditional retail banking attrition analysis focuses on terminal binary churn events, but client relationships often weaken earlier through partial fund movements to external institutions, which is undetected by current approaches.
AI.method: Developed a four-stage XGBoost cascade system using 595,220 client-month observations with 346 engineered features (client profiles, balances, product relationships, flow-of-funds behavior, macroeconomic conditions, competitor activity). The system predicts: (1) whether external outflow occurs within 90 days, (2) expected amount, (3) originating product, and (4) destination financial institution.
AI.result: Primary classifier achieved test precision-recall AUC of 0.823, with 86.4% precision, 75.1% recall, and F1 score of 0.803. Top 1% of high-risk clients yielded 95.3% precision. Amount predictions were 94.9% within adjacent buckets. Destination prediction reached macro-F1 of 0.81 across 27 classes; source-product prediction achieved weighted F1 of 0.92.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from terminal churn to early financial fragmentation enables proactive, explainable client-retention decision support, providing a practical foundation for economically informed interventions before complete disengagement.

title: EDGE: Engine for Deterministic Graph Evaluation through Conversation Simulation from Graph Structured DSL Configuration
summary: As agentic systems evolve into complex multi agent orchestration workflows, there is a growing and critical need for systematic frameworks that measures an agent's behavioral consistency and determinism. In this paper, we introduce a formal evaluation methodology that is grounded in AgentGraph, a planner powered by a domain specific language that represents agent reasoning through a dynamically adjustable directed graph. We leverage this structural formalism and utilize graph traversal algorithms that exhaustively enumerate conversational paths, forming a comprehensive evaluation set that captures the agent's complete behavioral space. We then systematically replay these reproducible trajectories to compare observed outputs and state transitions against the intended DSL specification. To quantify reliability, we define novel metrics that measure response and trajectory determinism, structural adherence and semantic consistency across both exact replays and their linguistic variants. Our system's results demonstrate that agents configured using frameworks like AgentGraph and LangGraph with explicitly structured node transitions show superior determinism over agents that are not configured with controlled transitions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a formal evaluation methodology for measuring agent behavioral consistency and determinism using AgentGraph, a planner with domain-specific language to represent agent reasoning through dynamically adjustable directed graphs.
AI.motivation: As agentic systems evolve into complex multi-agent orchestration workflows, there is a growing critical need for systematic frameworks to measure an agent's behavioral consistency and determinism.
AI.method: The methodology leverages AgentGraph's structural formalism and uses graph traversal algorithms to exhaustively enumerate conversational paths, creating a comprehensive evaluation set capturing the agent's complete behavioral space. It systematically replays reproducible trajectories to compare observed outputs and state transitions against intended DSL specifications.
AI.result: The system defines novel metrics measuring response and trajectory determinism, structural adherence, and semantic consistency across exact replays and linguistic variants. Results show that agents configured using frameworks like AgentGraph and LangGraph with explicitly structured node transitions demonstrate superior determinism over agents without controlled transitions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formal evaluation methodology provides a systematic way to measure agent behavioral consistency, showing that explicitly structured agent frameworks yield better determinism and reliability compared to uncontrolled approaches.

title: Mode Connectivity Beyond Classifiers: Evidence from Generative and Contrastive Models
summary: The loss landscape of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) exhibits highly complex and non-convex properties. Recent studies have revealed the phenomenon of mode connectivity, demonstrating that independently trained network modes can be connected via a continuous low-loss path. However, existing mode connectivity research is predominantly confined to classifier-based models, leaving it an open question whether similar geometric properties exist in modern complex models. In this paper, we extend the boundaries of mode connectivity to generative and contrastive domains (specifically DDPM and NanoCLIP). Addressing the unique architecture of DDPM and CLIP, we propose an architecture-aware connection building algorithm. Extensive empirical results demonstrate for the first time that we successfully discover mode connectivity between independently trained DDPM and NanoCLIP modes. Our work provides a novel perspective for understanding the geometric properties of the loss landscapes in modern generative and contrastive models.

AI.tldr: First demonstration of mode connectivity in generative (DDPM) and contrastive (NanoCLIP) models using architecture-aware connection algorithm.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to extend mode connectivity research beyond classifier-based models to determine if similar geometric properties exist in modern complex models like generative and contrastive models.
AI.method: The authors propose an architecture-aware connection building algorithm specifically designed for the unique architectures of DDPM and CLIP models to discover mode connectivity.
AI.result: Extensive empirical results demonstrate for the first time that mode connectivity can be successfully discovered between independently trained DDPM and NanoCLIP modes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that mode connectivity is a general geometric property that extends beyond classifiers to modern generative and contrastive models, providing a novel perspective for understanding their loss landscapes.

title: An Open-Source, Event-Driven Pipeline for Cryptocurrency Market Data: Ingestion, Forecasting, and On-Chain Fraud Detection
summary: Cryptocurrency markets generate high-frequency, multi-source data that is expensive to work with unless a team already has commercial-grade streaming and warehousing infrastructure in place. This paper describes a fully open-source pipeline that reproduces the behavior of a cloud-native, event-driven system -- file arrival triggering a message, a message triggering compute -- entirely on commodity hardware, using Apache Kafka and a filesystem-watching poller in place of managed cloud triggers. The pipeline partitions historical Gemini exchange data into hourly and minutely files, ingests them asynchronously through two independently grouped Kafka consumers (one for audit logging, one for Spark-triggered ETL), and lands cleaned output in a PostgreSQL warehouse with historical and aggregated schemas plus asset-specific data marts. We use the resulting Bitcoin data mart to compare a seasonal ARIMA model against a single-layer LSTM network for price forecasting, and separately apply Random Forest and Gradient Boosting classifiers, with additional engineered features, to the public Ethereum fraud detection benchmark introduced by Farrugia et al. We report the architecture, the modeling methodology, and the resulting metrics, and we are explicit about the limitations of comparing forecasts issued at different horizons and of evaluating fraud detection on a static, already-labeled dataset.

AI.tldr: An open-source pipeline for processing cryptocurrency market data using Apache Kafka and Spark on commodity hardware, applied to Bitcoin price forecasting and Ethereum fraud detection.
AI.motivation: Cryptocurrency markets generate expensive high-frequency data requiring commercial-grade infrastructure. The paper aims to provide a fully open-source alternative that runs on commodity hardware without relying on managed cloud services.
AI.method: Builds an event-driven pipeline using Apache Kafka and filesystem-watching pollers to simulate cloud-native triggers. Partitions Gemini exchange data into hourly/minutely files, uses asynchronous Kafka consumers for audit logging and Spark ETL, and loads cleaned data into PostgreSQL with historical/aggregated schemas and asset-specific data marts.
AI.result: Applied the pipeline to create Bitcoin and Ethereum data marts: compared seasonal ARIMA vs LSTM for Bitcoin price forecasting, and Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting for Ethereum fraud detection on the Farrugia benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Presents a reproducible open-source architecture for cryptocurrency data processing, but acknowledges limitations in comparing different forecasting horizons and evaluating fraud detection on static labeled datasets.

title: Beat-Synchronous Tokenization for ECG Transformers
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Machine Learning for Signal Processing (MLSP 2026)
summary: Transformer-based electrocardiogram (ECG) models commonly tokenize waveforms into fixed temporal patches. Though convenient, fixed patching can split heartbeat structures across token boundaries. We study beat-synchronous tokenization as a physiologically grounded alternative, comparing fixed patches with three beat-aligned strategies: resampled beats, adaptive pooled beats, and resampled beats augmented with R--R interval information. Experiments span two settings: 10-second 12-lead diagnostic classification on PTB-XL after MIMIC-IV-ECG masked pretraining, and 60-second single-lead rhythm classification on Icentia11k after patient-level contrastive pretraining. On PTB-XL, resampled beat tokens achieve the highest mean macro Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC; 0.8945) and nearly match the best fixed-patch macro Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC; 0.7414), reducing average sequence length from 100 to 11.2 tokens. On Icentia11k, beat-synchronous tokenizers obtain comparable AUPRC to fixed patching with better stability across runs. These results suggest morphology-preserving beat tokenization is a compact, competitive alternative to fixed temporal patching.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based ECG models using beat-synchronous tokenization (resampling beats to fixed lengths) outperforms fixed patching by preserving heartbeat morphology while dramatically reducing sequence length from 100 to 11.2 tokens.
AI.motivation: Fixed temporal patching in Transformer-based ECG models can split heartbeat structures across token boundaries, disrupting physiological patterns. The authors propose beat-synchronous tokenization as a physiologically grounded alternative that preserves complete heartbeat morphology.
AI.method: Three beat-aligned tokenization strategies: 1) resampled beats (to fixed length), 2) adaptive pooled beats, and 3) resampled beats augmented with R-R interval information. Experiments compared these with fixed patching on two settings: PTB-XL (10-second 12-lead diagnostic classification after MIMIC-IV-ECG pretraining) and Icentia11k (60-second single-lead rhythm classification after contrastive pretraining).
AI.result: On PTB-XL, resampled beat tokens achieved highest mean macro AUROC (0.8945) and nearly matched best fixed-patch AUPRC (0.7414) while reducing sequence length from 100 to 11.2 tokens. On Icentia11k, beat-synchronous tokenizers achieved comparable AUPRC to fixed patching with better stability across runs.
AI.conclusion: Morphology-preserving beat tokenization is a compact and competitive alternative to fixed temporal patching for ECG analysis with Transformers, offering physiological grounding, shorter sequences, and comparable or better performance.

title: AutoCRAT: Within-trajectory Joint Control of Stochasticity and Compute for LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance, which depends critically on inference-time decisions. Yet these decisions are commonly handled by static, one-size-fits-all policies, limiting adaptation to diverse tasks and reasoning stages. Recent adaptive methods partially address this limitation, but they primarily adapt either decoding stochasticity (how the model explores) or reasoning compute (how long the model reasons) in isolation, leaving their interaction within a single reasoning trajectory unmodeled. To address this challenge, we shift toward a within-trajectory joint control view, and instantiate it in AutoCRAT, a decoder-side controller for frozen backbones. Using only signals available during decoding, AutoCRAT jointly adjusts sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget during generation. AutoCRAT operates over a discrete action space and updates control decisions only at semantic boundaries, improving stability while remaining responsive to the evolving reasoning process. Comprehensive evaluation across 6 benchmarks demonstrates that AutoCRAT (I) uses 13.8-52.7% fewer inference tokens on average than recommended static configurations, (II) surpasses recommended static and adaptive baselines by 1.5-4.5% in relative accuracy, and (III) enjoys strong cross-backbone transferability.

AI.tldr: AutoCRAT is a decoder-side controller that jointly adapts sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget during LLM inference, reducing token usage by 13.8-52.7% while improving accuracy by 1.5-4.5% over static baselines.
AI.motivation: Current LLM inference uses static, one-size-fits-all policies that don't adapt to diverse tasks or reasoning stages. While recent adaptive methods address either decoding stochasticity or reasoning compute separately, they fail to model their interaction within a single reasoning trajectory, limiting adaptive control.
AI.method: AutoCRAT implements a within-trajectory joint control approach that adjusts both sampling stochasticity (exploration) and reasoning budget (compute) during generation. It operates over a discrete action space and updates control decisions only at semantic boundaries, using only signals available during decoding to maintain stability while responding to the evolving reasoning process.
AI.result: Evaluation across 6 benchmarks shows AutoCRAT reduces inference tokens by 13.8-52.7% compared to recommended static configurations, improves relative accuracy by 1.5-4.5% over both static and adaptive baselines, and demonstrates strong cross-backbone transferability.
AI.conclusion: AutoCRAT successfully addresses the limitation of existing adaptive methods by jointly controlling sampling stochasticity and reasoning budget within trajectories, achieving both efficiency and accuracy improvements while maintaining transferability across different backbone models.

title: Convergence rates for the RMSprop optimizer with full control of the hyperparameters
summary:
Popular adaptive stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems include the RMSprop, the Adam, and the AdamW optimizers, where the adaptivity parts in Adam and AdamW basically just coincide with RMSprop. Such adaptive methods involve several hyperparameters including the regularization parameter $ε$ (which ensures that one does not divide by 0 and is often chosen to be very close to zero such as $10^{-8}$ in PyTorch by default) and the second moment decay parameter $β$ (which is often chosen to be very close to $1$ such as 0.99 (RMSprop) and 0.999 (Adam and AdamW) in PyTorch by default). Despite the high relevance of such methods, it remains an open research problem to provide error estimates for such methods with the error constants being not exploding but uniformly bounded with the respect to the hyperparameters, even in the situation of convex stochastic optimization problems.
  It is the key contribution of this work to essentially solve this problem for RMSprop. Specifically, we bound the expectation of the stopped evaluation of the objective function at the RMSprop process from above by the sum of an initialization term that decays exponentially in the training time, a stochastic approximation remainder of order $γ_n$, and a memory error of order $( 1 - β)^2$ with the error constants being uniformly controlled over all admissible choices of the step sizes, the second moment decay parameter $β$ and the regularization parameter $ε\in[0,1]$ (also covering $ε=0$). Our non-asymptotic error estimates hold not just for all sufficiently large n but hold for every gradient step $n=1,2,3,...$ with all error constants being explicitly specified. The key innovative new feature in the proof of our analysis are suitable inverse moment bounds for the second moment process in RMSprop.

AI.tldr: Provides first non-asymptotic error bounds for RMSprop with uniformly controlled constants over all hyperparameters, solving a long-standing open problem.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of adaptive SGD methods (RMSprop, Adam, AdamW), there are no error estimates with uniformly bounded error constants across hyperparameter choices, even for convex problems. The regularization parameter ε and second moment decay β are critical hyperparameters but current analyses fail to provide uniform error control.
AI.method: Develops novel mathematical analysis for RMSprop, introducing key innovative inverse moment bounds for the second moment process. The approach provides non-asymptotic error estimates valid for every gradient step (n=1,2,3,...) with explicitly specified constants.
AI.result: Proves error bounds for RMSprop expectation: error ≤ (initialization term exponentially decaying) + (stochastic approximation term O(γ_n)) + (memory error term O((1-β)²)). These bounds hold uniformly over all admissible step sizes, β∈(0,1), and ε∈[0,1] (including ε=0).
AI.conclusion: First work to essentially solve the open problem of providing non-exploding, uniformly bounded error estimates for RMSprop across all hyperparameter choices. The novel inverse moment bounds technique enables rigorous analysis of adaptive methods and opens doors for better understanding of Adam/AdamW.

title: Automatic Conversion of NICE Guidelines to an Executable Computational Model Using Large Language Models
comment: 18 pages. Published in Learning Health Systems (2026)
summary: Introduction: NICE guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for clinical care but remain largely in unstructured natural language. Existing approaches to converting them into computable representations often focus on individual diseases, require substantial manual encoding, and do not scale. Large language models (LLMs) may enable much of this translation to be automated. Methods: We present an end-to-end approach that converts textual clinical guidelines into executable models capable of generating explainable, patient-specific recommendations. A stepwise LLM-based transformation with in-context examples produces human-inspectable intermediate artifacts. We apply the approach to NICE pancreatic and lung cancer guidelines, use expert review to assess rule alignment, and evaluate the executable pancreatic cancer model on 20 patient vignettes. Results: Expert review showed strong alignment between the source guidelines and generated executable models. Most discrepancies were partial omissions rather than incorrect logic, while hallucinated or fundamentally incorrect rules were rare. On the patient vignettes, the executable model achieved an F1 score of 82.5%. Conclusion: LLMs can transform natural-language NICE guidelines into interpretable, executable models that preserve guideline structure, support transparent inspection and modification, and generate patient-specific recommendations. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of scalable automated generation of computable clinical guidelines.

AI.tldr: LLM-based automated conversion of unstructured clinical guidelines into executable models for patient-specific recommendations, achieving 82.5% F1 score on pancreatic cancer cases.
AI.motivation: NICE clinical guidelines are evidence-based but unstructured, making them difficult to use computationally. Existing approaches are manual, disease-specific, and don't scale. LLMs offer potential for automated translation to computable forms.
AI.method: End-to-end approach using stepwise LLM transformation with in-context examples to convert textual guidelines into executable models with human-inspectable intermediate artifacts. Applied to NICE pancreatic and lung cancer guidelines, with expert review for rule alignment and evaluation on 20 patient vignettes.
AI.result: Expert review showed strong alignment between source guidelines and generated models, with most discrepancies being partial omissions rather than incorrect logic. On pancreatic cancer vignettes, the executable model achieved 82.5% F1 score. Hallucinated or fundamentally incorrect rules were rare.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively transform natural-language clinical guidelines into interpretable, executable models that preserve structure, support inspection/modification, and generate patient-specific recommendations, demonstrating feasibility of scalable automated guideline generation.

title: RSLM: Training-Free Vector Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
summary:
By introducing RSLM (Rotated Scaled Lloyd-Max), a family of training-free vector quantization codecs compressing embeddings to 1--4 bits per dimension, we reduce memory cost and memory bandwidth of a typical large-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search system, while reducing its complexity and keeping or improving recall across multiple benchmark datasets. State-of-the-art systems filter candidates using coarse partitions, approximately score them to narrow the set, and then rescore the best with higher precision representations (often >=8 bits per dimension). Our relativized codecs can bring this down to 2--4 bits per dimension.
  We use the properties of the ANN system to encode residual vectors instead of full vectors, both for the approximate scoring phase and the rescoring phase. Since Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is very sensitive to vector norms, we correct the $L_2$ norms of quantized vectors. Our major innovation is that we correct the $L_2$ norm of the final reconstructed vector rather than just the residual. Our rescaling replaces more complicated schemes, such as Anisotropic loss. The residualization scheme gives us a more favorable quality vs size trade-off than generic quantization methods.
  Our high-performance implementation leverages a block-wise cascaded Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform (FWHT) with linear-like complexity, AVX SIMD-optimized codebooks, and a steganographic encoding of scaling factors for perfect cache-line alignment.

AI.tldr: RSLM introduces rotated scaled Lloyd-Max quantization for embedding compression, reducing ANN systems to 2-4 bits per dimension while maintaining or improving recall.
AI.motivation: Reduce memory cost and bandwidth in large-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor search systems while maintaining or improving recall performance. Current systems use coarse partitions with high-precision representations (≥8 bits per dimension) for scoring.
AI.method: 1) RSLM quantization compressing embeddings to 1-4 bits per dimension. 2) Encode residual vectors instead of full vectors for both approximate scoring and rescoring phases. 3) Correct L2 norms of quantized vectors for MIPS sensitivity. 4) Implement with block-wise cascaded Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform, AVX SIMD-optimized codebooks, and steganographic encoding of scaling factors.
AI.result: Achieves more favorable quality vs size trade-off than generic quantization methods. Reduces memory requirements while maintaining or improving recall across multiple benchmark datasets. Enables compression down to 2-4 bits per dimension for scoring phases.
AI.conclusion: RSLM provides an effective training-free vector quantization approach that significantly reduces ANN system complexity, memory cost, and bandwidth while preserving or enhancing search accuracy through innovative residual encoding and norm correction techniques.

title: Interpreting and Steering for Safe and Correct Code Generation
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate source code containing vulnerabilities, yet little work studies the internal mechanisms that distinguish safe from vulnerable generation in them. In this work, we systematically perform a mechanistic interpretation of LLMs, aiming at both understanding how code safety-vs-vulnerability is represented or driven by components in an LM and turning the insights into actionable steering strategies to encourage safer code generation. To this end, we introduce CodeSec-Pairs, a dataset of 9,342 Python safe-and-vulnerable contrastive code pairs, sampled from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Utilizing the dataset, we explore approaches to localize layers and attention heads that relate to code safety, and further experiment with different steering strategies for inference-time vulnerability reduction. In particular, we propose DuoSteer, a double-steering approach that simultaneously applies safety and code-correctness steering to attention heads. In experiments over five vulnerability types, DuoSteer leads to an average of -26.9% vulnerability rate reduction and +7.5% functional correctness improvement, which outperforms not only other steering variants but also prompting and supervised fine-tuning baselines. The advantage also replicates on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with another 2,500 contrastive pairs sampled from that model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CodeSec-Pairs dataset and DuoSteer method for reducing vulnerability rates in LLM-generated code through mechanistic interpretation and steering techniques.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently generate vulnerable code, but little is known about the internal mechanisms that distinguish safe from vulnerable code generation. There's a need to understand how code safety is represented in LMs and turn these insights into practical steering strategies.
AI.method:
1. Create CodeSec-Pairs dataset of 9,342 Python safe-vulnerable contrastive code pairs from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
2. Use mechanistic interpretation to localize layers and attention heads related to code safety.
3. Develop DuoSteer - a double-steering approach that simultaneously applies safety and code-correctness steering to attention heads during inference.
AI.result: DuoSteer achieves -26.9% average vulnerability rate reduction and +7.5% functional correctness improvement across five vulnerability types. It outperforms other steering variants, prompting, and supervised fine-tuning baselines. Results replicate on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with 2,500 additional pairs.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretation can effectively identify safety-related components in LLMs, and the proposed DuoSteer method provides an effective inference-time steering strategy for reducing vulnerabilities while improving code correctness.

title: DASC: Decay-Aware State Compression for Hybrid Linear-Attention Serving
summary: Hybrid linear-attention architectures have recently scaled to large open-weight models, offering quality competitive with full attention while substantially reducing key/value (KV) cache growth. However, their in-place recurrent-state updates complicate cache management: prefix reuse requires state checkpoints alongside full-attention KV, while storing state checkpoints in full increases memory pressure, leading to more evictions and repeated prefill. By analyzing the decay structure of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), we find that different heads and channels retain prefix information over markedly different timescales, which we term \emph{retention horizons}. This variation suggests substantial compression potential in persistent state checkpoints. Building on this observation, we introduce \emph{Decay-Aware State Compression} (DASC), which derives retention horizons from model weights, selects long-horizon state units, and packs them into a ragged state checkpoint layout. To integrate efficiently with tensor-parallel inference engines, DASC furtherly balances compressed state checkpoints across TP ranks. On reuse, DASC either zero-fills omitted units or refreshes them from a bounded suffix with additional compute cost. Across retrieval and end-to-end reasoning benchmarks on Kimi-Linear, conservative DASC configurations remain close to full caching while compressing KDA recurrent state checkpoints by $2.63\times$. Under fixed state checkpoint memory budgets, the resulting capacity gains reduce mean Time to First Token (TTFT) by 42.6\% and improve input throughput by 68.4\%. At larger compression ratio, suffix refresh recovers much of the accuracy lost to more aggressive omission, at the cost of additional replay computation. Qwen with GDN exhibits a similar quality--efficiency trend, showing that DASC extends from channel-wise KDA to head-wise GDN.

AI.tldr: DASC (Decay-Aware State Compression) is a compression technique for hybrid linear-attention models that identifies varying retention horizons across heads/channels, compresses state checkpoints by selecting long-horizon units, and balances them across TP ranks for efficient inference.
AI.motivation: Hybrid linear-attention models have recurrent state updates that complicate cache management. Storing full state checkpoints alongside full-attention KV caches increases memory pressure, causing more evictions and repeated prefill computations. There's substantial compression potential in persistent state checkpoints due to varying retention horizons across different heads and channels.
AI.method: Analyzed decay structure of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) to identify retention horizons. Developed DASC which: 1) derives retention horizons from model weights, 2) selects long-horizon state units, 3) packs them into ragged state checkpoint layouts, 4) balances compressed checkpoints across TP ranks, and 5) uses zero-filling or suffix refresh for omitted units during reuse.
AI.result: Compressed KDA recurrent state checkpoints by 2.63× while maintaining close to full caching performance. Under fixed state checkpoint memory budgets: reduced mean TTFT by 42.6% and improved input throughput by 68.4%. At higher compression, suffix refresh recovers most accuracy loss at additional compute cost. Method extends from channel-wise KDA to head-wise GDN.
AI.conclusion: DASC effectively compresses recurrent state checkpoints in hybrid linear-attention models by leveraging retention horizon analysis, enabling significant memory savings and performance improvements while maintaining model quality.

title: Beyond Uncertainty: Multi-Solver Disagreement Rewards for Self-Evolving Reasoning Curricula
comment: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26), November 07--11, 2026, Rome, Italy
summary: Self-evolving reasoning frameworks train a Challenger to generate questions exposing a Solver's weaknesses, creating adaptive curricula without human data. However, existing approaches use a single solver's sampling uncertainty as the Challenger's reward. This creates a fundamental bottleneck: as the solver grows confident on the Challenger's question distribution, all sampled answers converge identically, collapsing the reward to zero and starving the Challenger of learning signal. Critically, this single-model reward cannot distinguish genuinely easy questions from those that merely align with one solver's learned biases. We propose a multi-solver disagreement reward using a heterogeneous ensemble varying in model capacity and sampling temperature. A normalized Shannon entropy over the ensemble's per-question plurality answers explicitly rewards questions where solvers produce conflicting solutions---capturing difficulty as inter-model divergence rather than intra-model sampling variance. This richer gradient enables the Challenger to discover questions targeting true capability boundaries, producing a curriculum that forces downstream Solvers to develop robust reasoning strategies generalizing across problem types. Our approach is a drop-in reward function replacement requiring no framework modifications or additional data. Experiments with Qwen3-4B show that Solvers trained on disagreement-Challenger questions achieve +1.34 points average improvement on competition-math benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC, Olympiad), suggesting that multi-solver disagreement provides a complementary and scalable signal for curriculum generation in self-play reasoning systems.

AI.tldr: Using multi-solver disagreement as reward for Challenger training enables better curriculum generation in self-evolving reasoning systems, leading to improved solver performance on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving reasoning frameworks use single solver's sampling uncertainty as Challenger reward, which collapses to zero as solver becomes confident, and cannot distinguish genuinely easy questions from those aligning with one solver's biases.
AI.method: Propose multi-solver disagreement reward using heterogeneous ensemble varying in model capacity and sampling temperature. Use normalized Shannon entropy over ensemble's per-question plurality answers to reward questions where solvers produce conflicting solutions.
AI.result: Solvers trained on disagreement-Challenger questions achieve +1.34 points average improvement on competition-math benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC, Olympiad). The approach is a drop-in reward function replacement requiring no framework modifications.
AI.conclusion: Multi-solver disagreement provides a complementary and scalable signal for curriculum generation in self-play reasoning systems, enabling Challenger to discover questions targeting true capability boundaries and forcing solvers to develop robust reasoning strategies.

title: Uncertainty of Vision Medical Foundation Models
summary: Accurate uncertainty estimation is essential for machine learning systems de- ployed in high-stakes domains such as medicine. Traditional approaches primarily rely on probability outputs from trained models (point predictions), which provide no formal guarantees on prediction coverage and often require additional calibra- tion techniques to improve reliability. In contrast, conformal prediction (region prediction) offers a principled alternative by generating prediction sets with finite- sample validity guarantees, ensuring that the ground truth is contained within the set at a specified confidence level. In this study, we explore the impact of pre-training approach, dataset scale and domain on both point and region-level uncertainty quantification, by studying domain-specific vision medical foundation models vs. general domain vision foundation models. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across foundation models trained on retinal, histopathological, and Chest X-Rays data, applying various calibration techniques. Our results demonstrate that (1) pre-training on higher-quality domain-specific datasets along with self-supervised learning leads to better-calibrated point predictions than general domain pre-training, (2) stan- dard re-calibration methods alone cannot fully mitigate uncertainty discrepancies across models trained on different data sources, (3) domain-specific foundation model can lead to more efficient conformal prediction. These findings highlight the importance of careful model selection and the inte- gration of both point and region prediction to enhance the reliability and trust- worthiness of medical AI systems. Our work underscores the need for a holistic approach to uncertainty quantification in recent development of medical vision foundation model, ensuring robust and interpretable AI-driven decision-making.

AI.tldr: Domain-specific medical vision foundation models with self-supervised pre-training produce better calibrated predictions and more efficient conformal prediction sets than general domain models, though standard calibration methods can't fully bridge uncertainty gaps across data sources.
AI.motivation: Accurate uncertainty estimation is critical for medical AI systems, where traditional probability outputs lack formal guarantees and require calibration. Conformal prediction offers principled uncertainty quantification with finite-sample validity, but the impact of pre-training approaches, dataset scale, and domain on uncertainty quantification remains unexplored for medical vision foundation models.
AI.method: Comprehensive evaluation across foundation models trained on retinal, histopathological, and Chest X-Ray data, comparing domain-specific medical vision models vs. general domain vision models. Applied various calibration techniques to both point predictions (probability outputs) and region predictions (conformal prediction sets).
AI.result: (1) Pre-training on high-quality domain-specific datasets with self-supervised learning yields better calibrated point predictions than general domain pre-training. (2) Standard re-calibration methods cannot fully mitigate uncertainty discrepancies across models from different data sources. (3) Domain-specific foundation models lead to more efficient conformal prediction sets.
AI.conclusion: Careful model selection and integration of both point and region prediction is essential for reliable medical AI. Domain-specific foundation models with self-supervised pre-training offer superior uncertainty quantification, highlighting the need for holistic approaches in medical vision foundation model development.

title: Balance of Benchmarks: Semantic Density Reweighting for Benchmark Multiplicity and Task-Conditioned Evaluation
summary: Language models are commonly compared by averaging scores across a benchmark list with equal weight. Such lists grow through publication outside an explicit measurement design, so equal weighting turns the density of published benchmarks into an implicit capability weight: densely benchmarked regions count repeatedly. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB), which embeds benchmark descriptions and assigns each benchmark an inverse-density semantic weight. Nearby entries share aggregate influence at a disclosed density scale. After equating heterogeneous scores onto a common latent scale, a residual field uses the same geometry to condition model rankings on a task query. The two components serve distinct empirical roles. On a snapshot of 586 models and 14 benchmarks, BoB predicts which models are unusually strong on a held-out task beyond their general ability, reaching a profile correlation of 0.462 compared with 0.049 under equal weighting. It also limits the influence of densely repeated benchmarks on the aggregate. After adding four copies of each benchmark in turn, the resulting rankings retain a Kendall tau of 0.995, compared with 0.936 under equal weighting. The residual field therefore provides task-conditioned prediction, and inverse-density weighting provides robustness to benchmark multiplicity. Together, they turn benchmark-list composition from an incidental property of evaluation suites into an explicit, controllable part of measurement design, providing a principled foundation for task-aware and multiplicity-robust model evaluation.

AI.tldr: BoB introduces inverse-density weighting to reduce influence of densely benchmarked tasks and a residual field for task-conditioned model evaluation, improving prediction of task-specific strengths and robustness to benchmark replication.
AI.motivation: Current benchmark evaluation methods equally weight all benchmarks, making densely benchmarked regions count repeatedly and turning benchmark publication density into an implicit capability weight without explicit measurement design.
AI.method: BoB embeds benchmark descriptions and assigns inverse-density semantic weights to each benchmark. Nearby entries share aggregate influence at a disclosed density scale. After equating scores to a common scale, a residual field uses the same geometry to condition model rankings on task queries.
AI.result: On 586 models and 14 benchmarks, BoB predicts which models are unusually strong on held-out tasks beyond general ability (profile correlation 0.462 vs 0.049 under equal weighting). After adding benchmark copies, rankings retain Kendall tau of 0.995 vs 0.936 under equal weighting.
AI.conclusion: BoB turns benchmark-list composition from an incidental property into an explicit, controllable part of measurement design, providing principled foundation for task-aware and multiplicity-robust model evaluation.

title: Foundation Models Meet Agriculture: Challenges Beyond Pretraining
summary: Global food security and sustainable climate action increasingly rely on robust, scalable agricultural monitoring. Earth observation foundation models have emerged as powerful, label-efficient tools across general remote sensing domains, yet early attempts to deploy them for agricultural applications have yielded surprisingly poor results. We hypothesize that this performance gap stems from the extreme heterogeneity of agricultural landscapes and the inherent inability of current earth observation foundation models to adapt to task-specific nuances. In this work, we systematically evaluate two critical bottlenecks hindering the deployment of foundation models in agricultural tasks, benchmarking two earth observation foundation models, a foundation model designed for tabular data, and conventional supervised baselines across seven real-world agricultural datasets spanning yield prediction, phenology estimation, and crop classification. First, we identify a pretraining-deployment modality gap: agricultural downstream tasks frequently require diverse, non-imagery data modalities that earth observation foundation models are architecturally unequipped to ingest, while a foundation model built for tabular data handles this heterogeneity more naturally. Second, we formalize the agricultural task space across five structural axes to demonstrate why current models fail to generalize reliably, resulting in highly unstable model rankings across evaluation settings. By characterizing these structural and modal gaps, our insights highlight the friction between general-purpose architectures and specialized agricultural downstream data, providing a strategic roadmap for developing the next generation of domain-aware foundation models.

AI.tldr: Current earth observation foundation models perform poorly on agricultural tasks due to architectural limitations in handling diverse data modalities and inability to generalize across heterogeneous agricultural landscapes, revealing critical gaps between general-purpose models and specialized agricultural data needs.
AI.motivation: Global food security and sustainable climate action require robust agricultural monitoring. While earth observation foundation models show promise in general remote sensing, they perform surprisingly poorly on agricultural applications, creating a performance gap that needs investigation.
AI.method: Systematically evaluated two critical bottlenecks by benchmarking two earth observation foundation models, one tabular data foundation model, and conventional supervised baselines across seven real-world agricultural datasets spanning yield prediction, phenology estimation, and crop classification. Formalized the agricultural task space across five structural axes.
AI.result: Identified two main bottlenecks: 1) pretraining-deployment modality gap where agricultural tasks require diverse non-imagery data that earth observation models can't handle architecturally, while tabular foundation models handle heterogeneity better, and 2) models fail to generalize reliably across agricultural tasks, resulting in highly unstable model rankings across evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: The research highlights friction between general-purpose architectures and specialized agricultural data, providing a strategic roadmap for developing next-generation domain-aware foundation models that can better handle agricultural heterogeneity and diverse data modalities.

title: Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
summary: Recent AI systems promise autonomous scientific discovery, claiming to discover algorithms and produce research papers, yet understanding whether they exhibit creativity, the capacity to produce solutions that are both novel and useful, remains an open question. We present a framework for evaluating multi-turn LLM research agents' creativity using ML engineering tasks as a testbed, through three dimensions: P-Creativity (psychological novelty: novel relative to the agent's own prior solutions within a run), H-Creativity (historical novelty: novel relative to the corpus of human solutions), and Usefulness (task performance). Evaluating two agent frameworks, AIDE and AIRA-Dojo, on 10 Kaggle-style machine learning tasks from MLE-Bench, we develop an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline and verify its strong correlation with human creativity judgments, providing a reliable automated metric for P-Creativity evaluation at scale. Applying this pipeline to agent trajectories, we find: (1) all agents exhibit declining P-Creativity as they transition from exploration to exploitation; (2) LLMs exhibit greater H-Creativity than medal-winning humans, yet achieve lower performance. Our findings reveal that current agents can explore novel regions of the solution space but lack the capacity to convert this novelty into improved task performance.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the creativity of AI research agents in scientific discovery tasks, measuring both novelty (relative to AI's own solutions and human solutions) and usefulness (task performance), finding that AI can explore novel solutions but struggles to convert that novelty into better performance.
AI.motivation: Recent AI systems claim to achieve autonomous scientific discovery, but there's an open question about whether they exhibit true creativity (producing solutions that are both novel and useful). The paper aims to systematically evaluate the creativity of multi-turn LLM research agents using ML engineering tasks as a testbed.
AI.method: Developed a framework evaluating creativity through three dimensions: P-Creativity (novelty relative to agent's own prior solutions), H-Creativity (novelty relative to human solutions), and Usefulness (task performance). Evaluated two agent frameworks (AIDE and AIRA-Dojo) on 10 Kaggle-style ML tasks from MLE-Bench, using an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline validated against human creativity judgments.
AI.result: (1) All agents show declining P-Creativity as they shift from exploration to exploitation; (2) LLMs exhibit greater H-Creativity than medal-winning humans but achieve lower performance. The LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline showed strong correlation with human judgments for P-Creativity evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Current AI research agents can explore novel regions of the solution space but lack the capacity to convert this novelty into improved task performance, highlighting a gap between exploratory creativity and practical usefulness in scientific discovery systems.

title: TopGQ: Fast GNN Post-Training Quantization Leveraging Topology Information
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC 2026)
summary: Existing GNN quantization methods suffer from considerable quantization overhead, which severely limits their practical usage in real-world scenarios. To this end, we present TopGQ, an accurate post-training GNN quantization framework, alleviating redundant quantization overhead. We propose dual-axis scale absorption, which enables activation quantization along both the outer and inner dimensions by merging one into the adjacency matrix. On top of that, we introduce TopPIN, a proxy for nodes' local structure, and use it to group nodes with similar topology during quantization. Experimental results show that TopGQ reduces quantization time by an order of magnitude while preserving accuracy.

AI.tldr: TopGQ is a post-training GNN quantization framework that reduces quantization overhead by dual-axis scale absorption and topological proxy-based node grouping
AI.motivation: Existing GNN quantization methods suffer from considerable quantization overhead that severely limits their practical usage in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Proposes dual-axis scale absorption that enables activation quantization along both outer and inner dimensions by merging one into the adjacency matrix, and introduces TopPIN (topology proxy for nodes' local structure) to group nodes with similar topology during quantization.
AI.result: Experimental results show that TopGQ reduces quantization time by an order of magnitude while preserving accuracy.
AI.conclusion: TopGQ is an effective post-training GNN quantization framework that significantly reduces quantization overhead while maintaining accuracy through innovative scale absorption and topology-aware node grouping techniques.

title: Spec2Twin-Chain: Orchestrating Bi-Level Optimization with LLMs for Blockchain Digital Twin Construction
summary: Building a blockchain digital twin largely requires translating domain knowledge and specific system descriptions into a simulator architecture, calibrating its parameters against behavioral evidence, and validating the constructed twin. These steps are commonly performed through application-specific modeling efforts that can be difficult to reuse across systems and downstream decision problems. We consider automating this process through Spec2Twin-Chain, a framework that formulates blockchain digital-twin construction as a bi-level optimization problem. At the upper level, a large language model proposes and revises structurally admissible architectures using system specifications, behavioral evidence, and feedback from evaluated designs. At the lower level, a simulation-based optimizer calibrates the architecture-conditioned parameters under explicit objectives and guardrail constraints. The two levels iterate. The evaluated candidates at lower levels are retained in a global archive and used to guide subsequent proposals at upper levels. We conduct controlled experiments involving twin calibration, feedback-driven recovery, stress analysis, downstream policy optimization, and policy updating. The results demonstrate that the framework can construct behaviorally accurate twins, improve initial designs through iterative feedback, and reuse calibrated twins to support downstream decisions.

AI.tldr: Spec2Twin-Chain automates blockchain digital twin construction using LLM-guided architecture design and simulation-based parameter calibration in a bi-level optimization framework.
AI.motivation: Current blockchain digital twin construction requires manual, application-specific modeling that is difficult to reuse across systems and downstream decision problems, creating barriers to automated digital twin development.
AI.method: Bi-level optimization where an LLM proposes/revises structurally admissible architectures (upper level) based on system specifications and feedback, while a simulation-based optimizer calibrates parameters (lower level) under objectives and constraints.
AI.result: The framework successfully constructs behaviorally accurate twins, improves designs through iterative feedback, and reuses calibrated twins to support downstream decisions in experiments involving calibration, recovery, stress analysis, and policy optimization.
AI.conclusion: Spec2Twin-Chain provides an automated framework that overcomes reuse barriers in blockchain digital twin construction and effectively supports various decision-making applications.

title: Locally-Guided Actor-Critic: Training a Goal-conditioned Actor with a Subgoal-aware Critic
summary: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning struggles with long horizons when rewards are sparse. While a planner can provide subgoals to guide a low-level policy, its use at test time may introduce practical subgoal management difficulties. An alternative paradigm utilizes a high-level planner to assist learning, while the policy remains conditioned only on the final goal, enabling planner-free deployment. Among these methods, Reinforcement Learning with Imagined Subgoals (RIS) introduces a regularization term that encourages the policy to take the same actions for the final goal as it does for an intermediate goal. This regularization, however, may lead to goal-chaining issues when intermediate goals are low-dimensional. Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) translates plans into an additional reward while ensuring that the optimal policy remains unchanged. Yet, it can generate deceptive rewards in terminal states. We study these failure cases and first propose an alternative reward shaping method (RS) that removes these deceptive rewards at the expense of theoretical guarantees of PBRS. Similar to this RS variant, we then propose another method named Locally-Guided Actor Critic (LG-AC) that rewards the agent for reaching intermediate goals. Unlike RS, where intermediate rewards are implicit in the shaping signal, we explicitly condition a value estimator on the full sequence of intermediate goals but represent the value function as a sum of subgoal-conditioned value functions, enabling dense hindsight relabeling. We evaluate all these methods in tasks with challenging goal-chaining requirements and empirically highlight specific cases in which either action regularization or reward shaping yield low performance, while LG-AC achieves the best overall performance across tasks.

AI.tldr: LG-AC combines explicit subgoal-conditioned value functions with dense hindsight relabeling to outperform action regularization and reward shaping methods in tasks requiring goal-chaining with sparse rewards.
AI.motivation: Goal-conditioned RL struggles with long horizons and sparse rewards. Existing methods like RIS (action regularization) and PBRS (reward shaping) have limitations: RIS suffers from goal-chaining issues with low-dimensional intermediate goals, while PBRS can generate deceptive rewards in terminal states.
AI.method: The paper proposes two approaches: 1) A reward shaping (RS) variant that removes deceptive rewards from PBRS but loses theoretical guarantees. 2) Locally-Guided Actor Critic (LG-AC) which explicitly conditions a value estimator on full sequences of intermediate goals, representing the value function as a sum of subgoal-conditioned value functions to enable dense hindsight relabeling.
AI.result: LG-AC achieves the best overall performance across tasks with challenging goal-chaining requirements, outperforming both action regularization (RIS) and reward shaping (RS) methods in cases where either approach alone yields low performance.
AI.conclusion: LG-AC effectively addresses goal-chaining problems in sparse-reward, long-horizon tasks by combining explicit subgoal conditioning with dense hindsight relabeling, demonstrating superior empirical performance over existing action regularization and reward shaping approaches.

title: Mitigating Over-Optimization in PRM-Guided Search in Mathematical Reasoning by Optimizing the Guide
summary: Process reward models (PRMs) provide dense step-level guidance for search-based reasoning, enabling inference-time compute to be allocated toward promising partial solutions. However, recent evidence suggests that PRM-guided search can over-optimize imperfect process rewards, pruning viable trajectories while expanding spurious ones. In this work, we theoretically show that directly leveraging PRM score is vulnerable to verifier noise through an extreme-value effect: non-viable prefixes become more likely to receive spuriously high scores as reasoning depth increase. Therefore, we formulate the PRM-guided search as a robust optimization problem over plausible reward perturbations, termed maximin PRM-guided search, leading to a training-free robust process supervision method that preserves promising alternatives when step-level scores are noisy. Maximin PRM-guided search mitigates this failure mode by reducing sensitivity to over-optimized PRM outliers. Without fine-tuning or online adaptation, maximin search consistently improves the PRM-guided search by 17-35\% on average, outperforming outcome- and step-level baselines in 14 out of 16 settings. Our source code is available at https://github.com/tjoo512/maximin-search.

AI.tldr: Maximin PRM-guided search addresses the over-optimization problem in process reward models by formulating search as a robust optimization problem that reduces sensitivity to noisy step-level scores.
AI.motivation: PRM-guided search can over-optimize imperfect process rewards, pruning viable trajectories while expanding spurious ones due to verifier noise and extreme-value effects in deeper reasoning steps.
AI.method: Formulate PRM-guided search as a robust optimization problem over plausible reward perturbations, creating training-free maximin PRM-guided search that preserves promising alternatives when step-level scores are noisy.
AI.result: Maximin search consistently improves PRM-guided search by 17-35% on average, outperforming outcome- and step-level baselines in 14 out of 16 settings without fine-tuning or online adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The maximin PRM-guided search effectively mitigates the failure mode of over-optimization to PRM outliers through robust optimization, providing a training-free solution for noisy process supervision.

title: No Equivariant Architecture Covers All Equivariant Attention
summary: We give a complete characterization of equivariant multi-head self-attention (MHSA): if an MHSA layer is equivariant to a symmetry group $G$, then $G$ can only act by permuting head-clusters, with QK and OV matrices satisfying an equivariance constraint tied to the group action. As a consequence, we prove that any fixed MHSA architecture that achieves exact equivariance by polynomially parameterizing unconstrained MHSA parameters inevitably leads to expressivity loss within the class of equivariant maps: the equivariance locus of unconstrained MHSA forms a union of extremely many Zariski-irreducible components in a reduced parameter space, and any single architecture covers at most one. For $G=D_4$ acting on $C$ copies of the regular representation as the token feature space, we show that there are $Ω(C^{64})$ components for eight attention heads.

AI.tldr: Complete characterization of equivariant multi-head self-attention shows that achieving exact equivariance requires constrained QK and OV matrices, leading to significant expressivity loss in fixed architectures due to Zariski-irreducible components.
AI.motivation: Understanding the limitations of achieving exact equivariance in multi-head self-attention layers while preserving expressive power, particularly when constrained by symmetry groups in transformer architectures.
AI.method: Mathematical characterization of equivariant MHSA layers, analyzing constraints on QK and OV matrices under group actions, and studying the geometric structure of the equivariance locus in parameter space using algebraic geometry concepts like Zariski-irreducible components.
AI.result: Complete characterization shows equivariant MHSA only allows group actions by permuting head-clusters with specific constraints on QK and OV matrices. Proof that polynomial parameterization for exact equivariance leads to expressivity loss, with equivariance locus forming many Zariski-irreducible components (Ω(C^64) for D_4 group with 8 heads).
AI.conclusion: Exact equivariance in fixed MHSA architectures imposes strict constraints that severely limit expressive power, as the space of equivariant maps decomposes into numerous irreducible components that cannot be covered by single polynomial parameterizations, highlighting fundamental trade-offs between symmetry and expressivity in transformer design.

title: Game-Agnostic Value Functions through Automatic JSON Feature Extraction
comment: 4 pages, to be published in Conference on Games (CoG) 2026
summary: JSON Bag-of-Tokens (JSON-Bag) is a recently proposed method to generically represent game trajectories by tokenizing their JSON descriptions. We introduce JSON-Bag VF, a game-agnostic approach to training value functions for game-playing agents using JSON-Bag prototypes. We show that this approach can be enhanced with Random Forest-based feature selection and a method to select game-stage-specific features. We evaluate JSON-Bag VF with One-step-look-ahead (JSON-Bag OSLA) on six tabletop games over different combinations of prototype-tokenization and feature selections. JSON-Bag OSLA outperforms baseline OSLA agents in most games. Our analysis also shows that feature selection significantly improves JSON-Bag VF and that feature selection is the most important factor in JSON-Bag VF performance, over prototype-tokenization.

AI.tldr: JSON-Bag VF trains game-agnostic value functions using JSON tokenization, enhanced with Random Forest feature selection, outperforming baseline agents in most tabletop games.
AI.motivation: There's a need for game-agnostic approaches to train value functions for game-playing agents that can work across different games without game-specific engineering. JSON-Bag provides a generic representation method for game trajectories, but its application to value function training needs improvement and systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The paper introduces JSON-Bag VF, which uses JSON-Bag prototypes (JSON tokenization of game trajectories) to train value functions. The method is enhanced with two key techniques: 1) Random Forest-based feature selection to identify important features, and 2) game-stage-specific feature selection to adapt features to different phases of gameplay. They evaluate this with One-step-look-ahead (OSLA) agents across six tabletop games.
AI.result: JSON-Bag OSLA outperforms baseline OSLA agents in most of the six tabletop games tested. Analysis shows that feature selection significantly improves JSON-Bag VF performance, and more importantly, feature selection is identified as the most important factor in performance, even more critical than the choice of prototype-tokenization method itself.
AI.conclusion: JSON-Bag VF with appropriate feature selection provides an effective game-agnostic approach for training value functions. The success of feature selection suggests that carefully selecting relevant features from JSON-Bag representations is more important than the specifics of how the JSON is tokenized, offering practical guidance for implementing such systems.

title: Confounding Masquerading as Improvement: A Systematic Evaluation of Offline Reinforcement Learning for Stroke Antithrombotic Treatment in a 129,000-Patient Registry
comment: 37 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at Machine Learning for Healthcare (MLHC) 2026; to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), vol. 340
summary:
Recent offline reinforcement learning (RL) studies report policies that outperform physician decisions on clinical outcomes. We conduct a systematic, partially crossed evaluation of five offline RL algorithm families and 14 reward designs in 44,894 post-2018 acute ischemic stroke patients from a nationwide registry (N = 129,033).
  Standard Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) yields an apparent policy-improvement estimate of +0.0069; adding an Early Neurological Deterioration penalty increases it to +0.0101. We identify reward-embedded confounding, in which a proxy terminal reward encodes baseline severity and prognosis as well as treatment efficacy. A 2 x 2 factorial analysis finds that terminal reward confounding accounts for 218.6% of the observed signal change, so its removal overshoots the null.
  After DML-inspired GBM reward residualization, the FQE estimate attenuates to +0.0033 (p = 0.132), and full deconfounding yields +0.0025 (p = 0.291). FQE-based diagnostics, T-learner analyses, and direct recurrence analyses converge away from a clinically meaningful aggregate improvement. A 1-year mRS factorial analysis replicates the attenuation. We provide an empirically motivated six-step evaluation checklist. NIHSS-stratified heterogeneity is hypothesis-generating for prospective trial design; hospital-level disagreement does not persist after full reward deconfounding.

AI.tldr: Offline RL algorithms initially appear to outperform physician decisions in stroke treatment, but reward design confounders account for most of the observed improvement signal; after proper deconfounding, the benefit becomes statistically insignificant.
AI.motivation: Recent offline RL studies claim policies that outperform physicians on clinical outcomes, but these claims may be inflated due to reward design issues like reward-embedded confounding where proxy rewards encode baseline patient characteristics rather than treatment effects.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of 5 offline RL algorithm families and 14 reward designs in 44,894 acute ischemic stroke patients from a nationwide registry. Used Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE), factorial analyses to isolate confounding, DML-inspired GBM reward residualization, T-learner analyses, and recurrence analyses.
AI.result: Initial FQE showed +0.0069 policy improvement; adding neurological deterioration penalty increased to +0.0101. However, terminal reward confounding accounted for 218.6% of signal change. After deconfounding, FQE estimate attenuated to +0.0033 (p=0.132) and full deconfounding to +0.0025 (p=0.291). No clinically meaningful aggregate improvement was found across multiple validation methods.
AI.conclusion: Apparent offline RL superiority over physicians in stroke treatment largely results from reward design artifacts rather than true treatment effects. Researchers should address reward-embedded confounding using proper deconfounding methods and follow a six-step evaluation checklist for more reliable offline RL clinical evaluations.

title: VERA: Authority-Preserving Edge Revocation for Federated AI-Agent Workflows
summary: Modern agent frameworks compose planners, tool agents, remote services, and shared specialists into runtime delegation graphs, but their revocation APIs still resemble token or subtree invalidation. When one delegation is withdrawn, the runtime must know which agents lose authority while independently authorized agents keep working. We study this authority consistency problem and introduce VERA (Verifiable Edge Revocation for Agents), a verifier-checkable revocation contract and API emitted by agent-runtime adapters as signed evidence. Under disjunctive authority, revoking edge e invalidates exactly T_intent(e,G) = reach(G) \ reach(G \ {e}), the agents whose every authorizing root path used e. Used as a contract, this target exposes two runtime failures: tree cascades over-revoke shared agents, while deployer-scoped cascades under-revoke cross-domain descendants. In a LangGraph framework-replt cells repeated 20 times yield 500compiled-framework traces and 2,000 valid signed delegation decisions; 13/25 cells contain runtime multi-parsharing and 8/25 contain cross-deployer shies 500/500 target proofs, preserves all320 alternate-parent shared-agent cases that tree cascade revokes, and rejects unauthorized signers and omission attacks. Baseline replay over 1,9that holder/node and tree-style targetscannot express this behavior. We further validate schema portability on A2A, AutoGen, and CrewAI artifacts: nine traces, including five executable Cregned delegation events that pass schema and signature checks.

AI.tldr: VERA introduces verifiable edge revocation for agent frameworks with disjunctive authority, ensuring precise revocation targets while preventing over-revocation of shared agents and under-revocation of cross-domain descendants.
AI.motivation: Modern agent frameworks use complex delegation graphs but have inadequate revocation APIs (token or subtree invalidation). When one delegation is withdrawn, the system needs to know exactly which agents lose authority while keeping independently authorized agents working. This creates an authority consistency problem.
AI.method: Introduces VERA (Verifiable Edge Revocation for Agents): a verifier-checkable revocation contract and API emitted by agent-runtime adapters as signed evidence. Uses disjunctive authority model where revoking edge e invalidates exactly T_intent(e,G) = reach(G) \ reach(G \ {e}) - agents whose every authorizing root path used edge e.
AI.result: Evaluation on LangGraph framework: 20 repetitions yield 500 compiled-framework traces and 2,000 valid signed delegation decisions. VERA produced 500/500 target proofs, preserved 320 alternate-parent shared-agent cases that tree cascade would over-revoke, and rejected unauthorized signers/omission attacks. Baseline methods couldn't express this behavior. Schema validation on A2A, AutoGen, and CrewAI artifacts showed portability with 9 traces and 5 executable delegation events passing checks.
AI.conclusion: VERA provides precise, verifiable edge revocation for agent frameworks that avoids the two main runtime failures: over-revocation of shared agents (tree cascades) and under-revocation of cross-domain descendants (deployer-scoped cascades). The approach enables verifiable authority consistency in complex delegation graphs.

title: PRIME: Mitigating Subgroup Optimization Competition in Shared CTR Top Networks with Plug-in Residual Input-Conditioned Mixture of Expert
summary:
Click-through rate (CTR) models vary in feature-interaction design, yet their top networks usually remain a single multilayer perceptron shared by all examples. Heterogeneous user, item, and context subgroups therefore update the same parameters; weakly aligned learning signals make the aggregate gradient a compromise among competing directions. We study the competition on Avazu with 4 models and 4 semantic fields. Across all architectures, semantic subgroups show lower Top-NN gradient cosine similarity than random groups matched by sample size and label ratio, with reductions of 0.23-0.37.
  This competition motivates input-conditioned experts, but directly replacing an established Dense mapping changes its initial function, sharing pattern, and capacity, obscuring the source of gains. We introduce PRIME (Plug-in Residual Input-conditioned Mixture of Experts), a Dense-anchored mixture of low-rank residual experts. PRIME anchors the original prediction and uses zero-residual initialization to match the Dense baseline exactly at training onset. Input-dependent routing weights low-rank experts for example-specific logit corrections; multi-bag aggregation and EMA load biases stabilize conditional estimation.
  We evaluate PRIME on held-out Avazu and Criteo test sets across 13 CTR architectures and five paired seeds. Median paired AUC gains are +0.0022 and +0.0066, with LogLoss reductions of 0.0011 and 0.0081, respectively. On FiBiNET and DCNv2, PRIME outperforms APG in all ten seed-level AUC comparisons while using fewer parameters and lower inference latency on both backbones. These results show that function-preserving conditional residuals add input-dependent capacity while preserving the Dense path and its optimization stability. Code is available at https://github.com/YH-learning/PRIME.

AI.tldr: PRIME (Plug-in Residual Input-conditioned Mixture of Experts) improves CTR models by adding input-dependent experts while preserving original dense network functions via zero-residual initialization.
AI.motivation: Traditional CTR models use shared MLP parameters for all examples, causing gradient competition among heterogeneous user/item/context subgroups, which reduces optimization efficiency and model performance.
AI.method: PRIME anchors the original dense prediction and adds low-rank residual experts with input-dependent routing. It uses zero-residual initialization to match baseline exactly at training start, multi-bag aggregation, and EMA load biases for stability.
AI.result: On Avazu and Criteo datasets across 13 CTR architectures, PRIME achieves median AUC gains of +0.0022 and +0.0066, with LogLoss reductions of 0.0011 and 0.0081. It outperforms APG in all comparisons while using fewer parameters and lower latency.
AI.conclusion: Function-preserving conditional residuals add input-dependent capacity while maintaining the optimization stability of the original dense path, providing consistent improvements across various CTR architectures.

title: A.X K2 Technical Report
summary: We introduce A.X K2, a 688B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model trained from scratch as a high-performance foundation for \emph{agentic} applications. Trained on approximately 8.5T tokens---fewer than its predecessor, A.X K1---on a smaller but higher-quality mixture with substantially expanded agentic and software-engineering data, it nonetheless improves over A.X K1 across the board, by over 30 percentage points on some benchmarks, reflecting large gains in token efficiency. To support long contexts efficiently, we introduce Sparse Gated Attention (SGA), which combines sparse attention with gated attention, and adopt Gated Norm (GN) to stabilize large-scale training. SGA is trained natively at 128K through a \emph{sparse} indexer warmup that optimizes the indexer against its own sparse top-$k$ selection rather than the dense attention distribution, making adaptation markedly cheaper: each query reads only 2,048 positions, yet long-context quality is unchanged and A.X K2 scores 94.6 on RULER out to 256K. The outlier suppression of GN in turn keeps 4-bit NVFP4 serving within one point of FP8 accuracy. A simple yet effective Think-Fusion recipe further lets users switch between thinking and non-thinking modes within a single unified model. Extensive evaluations show that A.X K2 performs competitively against strong open-weight baselines, matching or exceeding them on math and Korean-language benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A.X K2 is a 688B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model trained for agentic applications with improved token efficiency, long-context support via Sparse Gated Attention, and competitive performance across various benchmarks.
