AI.motivation: To create a high-performance foundation model specifically for agentic applications (AI agents/assistants) that improves upon previous models (A.X K1) while being more efficient and supporting longer contexts.
AI.method: 1) Trained 688B MoE model on 8.5T tokens with improved data quality; 2) Introduced Sparse Gated Attention for efficient long-context handling (128K native) with sparse indexer warmup; 3) Used Gated Norm for training stability; 4) Implemented Think-Fusion for switching between thinking/non-thinking modes.
AI.result: A.X K2 outperforms A.X K1 by over 30 percentage points on some benchmarks, achieves 94.6 on RULER at 256K context, maintains 4-bit quantization within 1% of FP8 accuracy, and performs competitively against open-weight baselines in math and Korean benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A.X K2 successfully advances agentic language modeling through improved efficiency (better token efficiency), novel architectures (SGA, GN), and practical features (Think-Fusion), establishing a strong foundation for agentic applications.

title: Self-Supervised Pretext Tasks for Infant Cry Analysis: A Controlled Comparison and a Cautionary Result on Donateacry
summary: We compare six self-supervised pretext tasks for infant cry analysis under a fixed budget, meaning the same compact encoder of 1.17M parameters, the same 115 hours of license-verified public pretraining audio, and the same evaluation protocol for every candidate. On cry detection the reconstructive objectives dominate, and a linear probe over a masked-spectrogram encoder reaches 0.988 AUC with subject-wise splits even though the encoder never observed a cry during pretraining. On cry-reason classification over donateacry, the de facto public benchmark for cry reasons, every encoder performs at chance (0.38 to 0.54 macro AUC over 5 classes), and neither domain adaptation on 1.8 hours of real cries nor end-to-end fine-tuning moves the result. Since a frozen HuBERT-base with 80 times more parameters shows the same pattern, the bottleneck must sit in the labels and not in model capacity. We then reproduce the 90\%+ accuracies of the donateacry literature on our own system by changing nothing but the evaluation protocol: clip-wise splits raise accuracy to 85.2% (barely above the 83.8% majority-class baseline), and applying augmentation before splitting raises it to 97.9%, matching the reported state of the art, from the same model that measures 0.49 macro AUC under subject-wise splits. Under leakage-free splits, a twentyfold augmentation of the labeled set (vocoder speaker perturbation and noise mixing, 21 hours) leaves cross-subject AUC unchanged: for this task the effective sample size is the number of infants. We release code, seeds and per-clip license manifests.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that current self-supervised methods for infant cry analysis work well for cry detection but fail at cry-reason classification due to data leakage in evaluation protocols, not model limitations.
AI.motivation: To rigorously evaluate self-supervised pretext tasks for infant cry analysis under controlled conditions with fixed compute/data budgets, and to identify why cry-reason classification benchmarks show misleadingly high performance.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of 6 self-supervised pretext tasks using: 1) fixed 1.17M parameter encoder, 2) 115 hours of license-verified pretraining audio, 3) same evaluation protocol for all. Tested on cry detection and cry-reason classification using subject-wise splits to prevent data leakage.
AI.result: 1) Cry detection: reconstructive objectives work best (0.988 AUC with masked-spectrogram encoder). 2) Cry-reason classification: all encoders perform at chance (0.38-0.54 AUC) with proper subject-wise splits. 3) Data leakage (clip-wise splits, augmentation before splitting) artificially boosts reported SOTA results to 97.9% vs actual 0.49 AUC. 4) Neither domain adaptation (1.8h real cries) nor fine-tuning nor 21h augmentation improves cross-subject performance.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck in cry-reason classification is not model capacity but evaluation protocols and dataset limitations; the effective sample size is the number of infants, not audio clips. Proper subject-wise splits reveal true model performance, challenging existing benchmarks in the field.

title: FaVOR: LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Factor Mining via Empirical Validation
summary: Traditional finance relies on experts to hand-craft factors through a principled process grounded in economic rationale. Recent LLM-based multi-agent systems have automated this process, scaling factor mining far beyond manual effort. However, these automated approaches optimize directly for returns and rarely check whether a generated factor still expresses the economic hypothesis that motivated it. We identify this inconsistency between mathematical form and economic meaning as a structural failure mode of return-oriented automation. The resulting factors blur the line between real signals and spurious correlations and break down across regime shifts. We propose FaVOR (Factor Validation through Observable Reasoning), an agentic framework that restructures factor mining around hypothesis-level evidence rather than return outcomes. In place of the standard hypothesis-to-formula leap, FaVOR enforces a three-stage consistency loop tying mathematical form to economic rationale throughout. (1) Decomposition splits a broad economic hypothesis into independent observable conditions. (2) Validation checks whether each factor reflects its intended condition. (3) Integration merges them into a composite whose structure remains interpretable. On the CSI 500 and S&P 500 in 2025, FaVOR outperforms existing baselines while remaining effective across regimes. FaVOR shows that hypothesis-grounded factor discovery produces signals that are interpretable by construction, regime-robust, and economically faithful. The code is available at https://github.com/damilab/FaVOR.

AI.tldr: FaVOR is an agentic framework that ensures factor mining maintains economic hypothesis consistency by validating observable conditions, making factors interpretable and regime-robust.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based automated factor mining systems optimize directly for returns without verifying if generated factors still express their motivating economic hypotheses, leading to factors that mix real signals with spurious correlations and fail during regime shifts.
AI.method: FaVOR restructures factor mining around hypothesis-level evidence with a three-stage consistency loop: (1) Decomposition - splits economic hypotheses into independent observable conditions, (2) Validation - checks if each factor reflects intended conditions, (3) Integration - merges conditions into an interpretable composite structure.
AI.result: On CSI 500 and S&P 500 datasets in 2025, FaVOR outperforms existing baselines while remaining effective across different market regimes.
AI.conclusion: Hypothesis-grounded factor discovery produces factors that are interpretable by construction, regime-robust, and economically faithful, addressing the structural failure mode of return-oriented automation in finance.

title: Learning Where Outcomes Change:Credit-Addressable Reasoning for Multimodal Geometry
summary: Multimodal geometry reasoning requires VLMs to extract precise visual relations and preserve them through multi-step deduction. Existing free-form traces obscure the decisions that determine the answer, and trajectory-level reinforcement learning distributes a single terminal signal across the entire response. We introduce credit-addressable reasoning, in which the semantic units exposed during inference also define where learning compares alternatives and assigns credit. We instantiate this principle with Code-CoT, which retains the diagram, represents visual relations as line-addressable executable code, and organizes reasoning into typed events, and CE-GRPO, which selects event boundaries using structural priors and type-normalized entropy, samples complete continuations from shared prefixes, and converts outcome differences into localized advantages. Across nine geometry benchmarks, CE-GRPO achieves an average accuracy of 76.04, outperforming Qwen3-VL-8B and trajectory-level GRPO by $8.09$ and 3.43 points, respectively. Its relative advantage increases with the number of intermediate events, demonstrating the value of representation--optimization co-design for long, dependency-heavy multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: Code-CoT and CE-GRPO: A credit-addressable reasoning framework for multimodal geometry tasks where reasoning units are exposed during inference to enable localized credit assignment, outperforming existing methods on nine geometry benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs for multimodal geometry reasoning have two key limitations: (1) free-form traces obscure the decisions that determine answers, making reasoning opaque, and (2) trajectory-level reinforcement learning distributes a single terminal signal across entire responses, preventing localized credit assignment. This makes it difficult to learn precise visual relations and preserve them through multi-step deduction.
AI.method: The paper introduces Code-CoT, which retains the diagram, represents visual relations as line-addressable executable code, and organizes reasoning into typed events. This is combined with CE-GRPO, which selects event boundaries using structural priors and type-normalized entropy, samples complete continuations from shared prefixes, and converts outcome differences into localized advantages. This enables "credit-addressable reasoning" where semantic units exposed during inference also define where learning compares alternatives and assigns credit.
AI.result: Across nine geometry benchmarks, CE-GRPO achieves an average accuracy of 76.04, outperforming Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.09 points and trajectory-level GRPO by 3.43 points. The relative advantage increases with the number of intermediate events, demonstrating effective representation-optimization co-design for long, dependency-heavy multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that exposing structural reasoning units during inference enables localized credit assignment, which is crucial for multimodal geometry tasks. The success of CE-GRPO shows the value of representation-optimization co-design for complex reasoning problems, particularly as reasoning chains become longer and more dependent on intermediate visual relations.

title: SPARK: Skeleton-Guided Reasoning Synthesis from Large-Scale Scientific Literature
summary: Scientific reasoning remains challenging for open-source models, largely due to the lack of high-quality scientific reasoning data. Existing datasets are often dominated by factual recall or formulaic problem solving, with limited emphasis on mechanism understanding, evidence-grounded reasoning, and hypothesis evaluation. To address this, we introduce SPARK (Scientific Paper Abstracted Reasoning sKeleton), a paper-oriented synthesis framework built on Sci-Base, a large-scale corpus of research papers spanning 10 scientific disciplines. Instead of directly converting papers into question-answer pairs, SPARK treats the claim-evidence-derivation structure of a paper as the fundamental unit of reasoning synthesis. Specifically, SPARK (1) distills each paper into a compact reasoning skeleton capturing its central claims and supporting evidence, enabling self-contained question generation, and (2) synthesizes reasoning tasks from four scientific perspectives: mechanistic reasoning, hypothesis falsification, quantitative derivation, and boundary calibration. A final consistency verification stage further removes unsupported or contradictory outputs. Using this framework, we construct Spark-234K, a scientific reasoning dataset with substantially higher difficulty and diversity than existing resources. Experiments show that Spark-234K consistently outperforms existing scientific reasoning datasets while achieving stronger performance with significantly fewer training samples.

AI.tldr: SPARK is a paper-oriented synthesis framework that creates scientific reasoning datasets by distilling research papers into reasoning skeletons and generating challenging questions from four scientific perspectives, resulting in Spark-234K dataset that outperforms existing resources.
AI.motivation: Scientific reasoning remains challenging for open-source models due to lack of high-quality reasoning data. Existing datasets focus too much on factual recall or formulaic problem solving, lacking emphasis on mechanism understanding, evidence-grounded reasoning, and hypothesis evaluation.
AI.method: SPARK treats the claim-evidence-derivation structure of research papers as the fundamental unit. It (1) distills each paper into a compact reasoning skeleton capturing central claims and supporting evidence, and (2) synthesizes reasoning tasks from four scientific perspectives: mechanistic reasoning, hypothesis falsification, quantitative derivation, and boundary calibration, with a final consistency verification stage.
AI.result: Constructed Spark-234K dataset with substantially higher difficulty and diversity than existing resources. Experiments show Spark-234K consistently outperforms existing scientific reasoning datasets and achieves stronger performance with significantly fewer training samples.
AI.conclusion: The SPARK framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing scientific reasoning datasets by focusing on paper-oriented synthesis, creating high-quality reasoning data that better captures scientific reasoning processes, leading to more effective training for open-source models.

title: ToxLens: A Reproducible Graph-Learning Framework for Leakage-Aware, Uncertainty-Calibrated Molecular Toxicity Prediction
summary: Molecular toxicity prediction is increasingly used to prioritise compounds before experimental testing, but conventional benchmark performance can overstate practical utility when structurally related molecules occur across training and test folds. We introduce ToxLens, a reproducible multi-task graph-learning framework for 11 toxicity endpoints spanning Ames mutagenicity, acute oral toxicity, hERG inhibition, and Tox21 nuclear-receptor and stress-response assays. The workflow combines conservative chemical curation, sphere-exclusion filtering, a leakage-aware UMAP-HDBSCAN split, parallel graph and global-feature encoders joined by late concatenation, temperature-scaled Monte Carlo dropout with conformal-style prediction sets, applicability-domain analysis, and SHAP-guided toxicophore discovery with occlusion controls. On the leakage-controlled test fold, a five-seed soft-voting ensemble achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient score of 0.44, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve score of 0.83, and an area under the precision-recall curve score of 0.58. It exceeded four ECFP4-based shallow baselines on all 11 endpoints under the same split and validation-based threshold-selection protocol. Controlled ablations showed that the global pathway was important, whereas late concatenation outperformed the tested gated and feature-wise linear modulation fusion variants. Conformal-style prediction sets revealed substantial endpoint-specific variation in set efficiency, and discrimination and calibration improved with similarity to the training domain. Retraining on fixed published Tox21 Challenge and TDA folds produced competitive, but not uniformly state-of-the-art, performance. SHAP-guided occlusion and consensus subgraph mining yielded model-derived structural hypotheses, 44 of which contained at least one occurrence that passed the predefined counterfactual criteria.

AI.tldr: ToxLens: A multi-task graph-learning framework for molecular toxicity prediction with 11 endpoints, featuring conservative data curation, leakage-aware splits, ensemble modeling, conformal prediction, and toxicophore discovery.
AI.motivation: Current molecular toxicity prediction benchmarks can overestimate practical utility due to structural similarity between training and test data (data leakage). There's a need for more reliable, reproducible frameworks that properly handle chemical similarity and provide uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: 1) Conservative chemical curation and sphere-exclusion filtering to remove highly similar compounds; 2) Leakage-aware UMAP-HDBSCAN split to separate structurally related molecules; 3) Parallel graph and global-feature encoders with late concatenation; 4) Five-seed soft-voting ensemble with temperature-scaled Monte Carlo dropout; 5) Conformal-style prediction sets for uncertainty quantification; 6) SHAP-guided toxicophore discovery with occlusion controls for interpretability.
AI.result: On leakage-controlled test fold: MCC=0.44, AUROC=0.83, AUPRC=0.58. Outperformed four ECFP4-based baselines on all 11 toxicity endpoints. Global features proved important, late concatenation outperformed other fusion methods. Conformal prediction sets showed endpoint-specific variation in efficiency. Model-derived structural hypotheses generated 44 toxicophores meeting counterfactual criteria.
AI.conclusion: ToxLens provides a comprehensive, reproducible framework for molecular toxicity prediction that addresses data leakage issues, offers uncertainty quantification through conformal prediction, and enables interpretable toxicophore discovery. While not uniformly state-of-the-art on established benchmarks, it represents a more rigorous approach to practical toxicity prediction.

title: LaMoC: Loss-Aware Modular Compression for LLMs
summary: Modular compression has enabled considerable parameter reduction in LLMs while preserving strong language understanding and downstream task accuracy. However, existing joint modular compression methods primarily rely on activation statistics, leaving loss-sensitivity information and its module-level characterization underexplored. We investigate addressing this gap with LaMoC, a loss-aware modular compression methodology that blends activation and Empirical Fisher statistics through gradient-error alignment. LaMoC improves joint compression by selecting compression statistics that better align local module reconstruction error with the downstream loss. Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We characterize the Empirical Fisher as a module-level loss-aware proxy that can be blended with the activation statistics required for compression. (2) We reformulate joint modular compression as a two-tiered optimization problem that minimizes module reconstruction error while tuning the activation and gradient information blending rate. (3) We implement an empirically driven methodology with statistical validation to solve the resulting compression problem. We evaluate LaMoC across four model families spanning eight models. On the 4-8B models, LaMoC achieves an average 2.5% reduction in perplexity and a 1% relative improvement in task accuracy over state-of-the-art modular compression methods.

AI.tldr: LaMoC is a new loss-aware modular compression method for LLMs that combines activation statistics with Empirical Fisher statistics through gradient-error alignment to improve compression performance.
AI.motivation: Existing modular compression methods for LLMs primarily rely on activation statistics alone, ignoring loss-sensitivity information and its module-level characterization, creating a gap in joint compression optimization.
AI.method: LaMoC blends activation and Empirical Fisher statistics through gradient-error alignment, reformulates joint modular compression as a two-tiered optimization problem (minimizing module reconstruction error while tuning blending rates), and implements an empirically driven methodology with statistical validation.
AI.result: LaMoC achieves an average 2.5% reduction in perplexity and 1% relative improvement in task accuracy over state-of-the-art modular compression methods on 4-8B models across four model families.
AI.conclusion: Loss-aware modular compression through gradient-error alignment significantly improves compression performance by incorporating loss sensitivity information alongside activation statistics.

title: Measuring Memory and Generalization as Separable Geometric Channels: The Topo^2 Framework
summary: Deep networks trained on noisy labels simultaneously generalize on clean data and memorize flipped labels. These are usually conflated as pressures on one capacity. We present Topo^2, a measurement framework that makes them causally separable, measurable, and law-governed. Persistent-homology H1 structure of the representation space separates into a within-class manifold channel (a function of the training stopping point) and a cross-class channel (a monotone readout of memorized flipped samples). An intervention, the FM0 prescription (zero loss on flipped samples from epoch 0), reaches each setting's generalization ceiling while memorizing essentially nothing. Within the framework we establish a law set with graded evidence: (L2) FM0 separation prescription (9/9); (L1) the within-channel as a training-position function (mid-rise 6/6; convergence-back CIFAR 3/3, SVHN 2/3); (L3) a ring-construction identity (definitional, not a law); and TLS (memory-generalization topological layering): memory is causally additive, anchored (silencing clean collapses the representation), invertible (stripping memory restores near-ceiling generalization), and quantitatively billable (the memorization cost law, effective slope coefficient C ~ 0.38 at the reference capacity: CIFAR-10 0.3801 / SVHN 0.3806 / CIFAR-100 0.384 / VGG 0.3715, capacity-dependent in general and traced to clean-sample feature displacement). We also publish the framework's boundaries: a falsification ledger of nine dead ends, and an instrument-vindication section that excludes six families of global statistics as explanations of the within-channel. The framework turns "memorization" from an ill-defined capacity into a measurable, separable, invertible topological layer.

AI.tldr: Topo² is a topological measurement framework that separates and measures generalization and memorization in deep networks trained on noisy labels, establishing causal separation and quantitative laws with FM0 intervention achieving generalization ceiling without memorization.
AI.motivation: Deep networks trained on noisy labels simultaneously generalize on clean data and memorize flipped labels, but these effects are usually conflated as pressures on a single capacity. There's a need to separate these phenomena causally and make them measurable and law-governed rather than being ill-defined capacity issues.
AI.method: The Topo² framework uses persistent homology H1 structure of the representation space to separate into within-class manifold channels (training stopping point function) and cross-class channels (memorized flipped samples readout). The FM0 intervention prescribes zero loss on flipped samples from epoch 0. The framework establishes laws and includes boundaries documentation with falsification ledger of dead ends and instrument-vindication sections.
AI.result: FM0 separation prescription works perfectly (9/9 cases). Within-channel behaves as training-position function with strong evidence (mid-rise 6/6; convergence-back CIFAR 3/3, SVHN 2/3). Memory-generalization topological layering (TLS) shows memory is causally additive, anchored, invertible, and quantitatively billable with memorization cost coefficient C ~ 0.38 across datasets (CIFAR-10 0.3801, SVHN 0.3806, CIFAR-100 0.384, VGG 0.3715).
AI.conclusion: Topo² successfully turns "memorization" from an ill-defined capacity into a measurable, separable, and invertible topological layer. The framework provides causal separation of generalization and memorization, establishes quantitative laws, and demonstrates that generalization ceilings can be reached without memorization through the FM0 prescription.

title: Rethinking the Test-Time Prompt Tuning Objective from the Perspective of Calibration
summary: Test-time prompt tuning (TPT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm, refining prompts for each test sample via entropy minimization (EM) over multiple augmented views. However, we identify a limitation in the standard EM-based adaptation: it inherently drives the model toward overconfident predictions disregarding sample-specific uncertainty, leading to significant calibration degradation. To address these limitations, we propose a new objective that replaces the conventional EM loss by aligning the original-view prediction with a target distribution derived from augmented views via cross-entropy, while adversarially incorporating the entropy of the target distribution to capture sample-specific uncertainty. Furthermore, to better construct this target distribution, we apply confidence-aware temperature scaling to each augmented-view prediction according to its confidence, sharpening confident predictions while softening uncertain ones. This formulation allows the model to increase confidence only when the target distribution is reliable, while preserving uncertainty when it reflects ambiguous or conflicting augmented-view predictions. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art accuracy but also significantly improves model calibration.

AI.tldr: TPT calibrates test-time prompt tuning by replacing entropy minimization with a new objective that aligns original-view predictions with confidence-aware target distributions from augmented views, improving both accuracy and calibration.
AI.motivation: Standard test-time prompt tuning (TPT) uses entropy minimization over augmented views, but this approach drives models toward overconfident predictions and disregards sample-specific uncertainty, leading to poor calibration.
AI.method: Proposes a new objective replacing EM loss with: 1) cross-entropy between original-view predictions and target distributions from augmented views, 2) adversarial incorporation of target distribution entropy to capture uncertainty, and 3) confidence-aware temperature scaling on augmented-view predictions to sharpen confident predictions while softening uncertain ones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks show the approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving model calibration compared to standard TPT methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively addresses calibration degradation in test-time prompt tuning by properly handling sample-specific uncertainty through a new objective with confidence-aware target distribution construction.

title: When the Martingale Never Stops Firing: Anytime-Valid Gating on Real Forecast Streams
summary: Machine learning systems are increasingly corrected while they run, and the decision of when to intervene is increasingly delegated to statistical monitors. Anytime-valid inference promises evidence that can be acted on at any moment, exactly the guarantee this setting needs, and it is moving from theory into deployed monitoring. Conformal test martingales are the change-detection instrument, and Ville's inequality caps their false-alarm probability on exchangeable data. The guarantee is conditional. A deployment inherits it only if the stream it monitors behaves exchangeably. The premise is hardest to satisfy where these monitors are most useful, on dependent data and inside loops where the monitor modifies the learner whose scores it reads. It is also rarely measured. We measure it in a pre-specified case study, where such a monitor gates the online updates of a Kalman adapter correcting frozen time-series foundation models on five forecasting streams. On exchangeable synthetic streams, the same implementation fires in at most 1 of 60 runs. On the real streams, at alpha = 0.05, 135 of 135 clean-stream runs fired. The construction does not explain the firing; the failure comes from the deployed score stream itself. Repeated fires hold the gate's drift response active, and the gated filter amplifies the very transient it was designed to prevent. The component worth keeping makes no validity claim. Huber-style gating of the filter's own updates cuts isolated-spike degradation by an order of magnitude with no dataset specific tuning. Anytime-valid methods proposed for dependent data should therefore be accompanied by null-calibration controls and mechanism traces.

AI.tldr: Anytime-valid inference used for statistical monitoring fails in real deployments due to violation of exchangeability assumptions, causing monitoring systems to amplify problems rather than prevent them.
AI.motivation: Machine learning systems are increasingly corrected while running using statistical monitors, and anytime-valid inference promises the right guarantees for this setting. However, these guarantees rely on exchangeable data, which is rarely satisfied in practice where monitors operate on dependent data and in feedback loops.
AI.method: The authors conducted a pre-specified case study using conformal test martingales for change detection. They deployed a monitor that gates online updates of a Kalman adapter correcting frozen time-series foundation models on five forecasting streams. They tested on both exchangeable synthetic streams and real streams, measuring the firing rates.
AI.result: On exchangeable synthetic streams, the monitor fired in at most 1 of 60 runs (as expected). On real streams at alpha=0.05, it fired in 135 of 135 clean-stream runs - complete failure. The monitor's repeated firings kept the gate's drift response active, causing the gated filter to amplify the very transients it was designed to prevent. A simple Huber-style gating of the filter's own updates (with no validity claims) reduced isolated-spike degradation by an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Anytime-valid methods proposed for dependent data should be accompanied by null-calibration controls and mechanism traces. The theoretical guarantees of anytime-valid inference break down in practice when exchangeability assumptions are violated, and the failure comes from the deployed score streams themselves. Simpler approaches without validity claims may perform better in real deployments.

title: CoLa-ICD: A Knowledge-Enhanced Framework for Long-Tail Automated Medical Coding
summary: Automatic medical coding assigns ICD codes to clinical notes, but it remains challenging due to long documents, imbalanced label distributions, and diverse terms. These challenges are especially severe for rare codes, which have limited training instances and are easily confused with semantically similar labels. We introduce CoLa-ICD, a knowledge-enhanced framework for long-tail prediction. CoLa-ICD enriches ICD labels with external terms, models dependencies among related codes, and learns stronger alignment between label semantics and clinical evidence for long-tail prediction. Experiments show that CoLa-ICD improves long-tail prediction with larger gains in larger and sparser label spaces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in AUC, F1, and P@k. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/Cola-ICD.

AI.tldr: CoLa-ICD is a knowledge-enhanced framework that improves automatic medical coding by addressing long-tail prediction challenges through external term enrichment, code dependency modeling, and stronger label-evidence alignment.
AI.motivation: Automatic medical ICD coding faces challenges with long documents, imbalanced label distributions, and diverse terminology, especially for rare codes with limited training instances that are easily confused with semantically similar labels.
AI.method: CoLa-ICD enriches ICD labels with external terms, models dependencies among related codes, and learns stronger alignment between label semantics and clinical evidence specifically for long-tail prediction.
AI.result: Experiments show CoLa-ICD improves long-tail prediction with larger gains in larger and sparser label spaces, achieving state-of-the-art performance in AUC, F1, and P@k metrics.
AI.conclusion: CoLa-ICD is an effective knowledge-enhanced framework that addresses the critical long-tail prediction problem in automatic medical coding, with demonstrated performance improvements particularly in challenging scenarios with larger and sparser label spaces.

title: Tensor Methods for Language Models: From Token Representation to Training, Adaptation, Inference, Compression, and Interpretability
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are built from structured high-dimensional objects such as token representations, weights, adaptation updates, caches, and activations, whose multilinear structure is underexploited by the conventional matrix-centric view. Tensor decompositions and tensor networks provide a principled algebraic language for this structure, yet the literature often treats them as isolated compression mechanisms. This survey organizes tensor methods for LLMs through two complementary views: a seven-stage lifecycle taxonomy covering tokenization, embeddings, pre-training, adaptation, compression, inference, and interpretability, and a component view covering embeddings, attention, and feed-forward networks. We provide unified notation and theoretical foundations, analyze tensorization strategies for individual Transformer components, and compare methods at each lifecycle stage while making differences in evaluation protocols and model scales explicit. We further connect tensor methods to neighboring efficiency techniques and probabilistic tensor networks. Finally, we synthesize open challenges and introduce $ρ_{\rm gap}$, a metric for the compression-realization gap between theoretical memory reduction and measured system-level speedup. By treating tensorization as a common structural principle, the survey provides a structured entry point to tensorized language models and clarifies when parameter savings can plausibly translate into memory efficiency, computational efficiency, or interpretability. The GitHub page dedicated to this paper is accessible at \href{https://github.com/ma-tt-a/awesome-tensor-methods-for-llms}{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey organizing tensor methods for LLMs through lifecycle and component views, with unified notation, analysis of tensorization strategies, and introduction of a new metric for compression-realization gaps.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to LLMs use a matrix-centric view that underexploits the multilinear structure of token representations, weights, adaptations, caches, and activations. Tensor decompositions provide principled algebraic tools for this structure but are often treated as isolated compression mechanisms rather than a unified framework.
AI.method: Organizes tensor methods through two complementary views: 1) a seven-stage lifecycle taxonomy covering tokenization, embeddings, pre-training, adaptation, compression, inference, and interpretability, and 2) a component view covering embeddings, attention, and feed-forward networks. Provides unified notation and theoretical foundations, analyzes tensorization strategies, compares methods at each stage, and introduces ρ_gap metric for compression-realization gap analysis.
AI.result: The survey creates a structured entry point to tensorized language models, clarifies when parameter savings translate to memory/computational efficiency or interpretability, connects tensor methods to neighboring efficiency techniques and probabilistic tensor networks, and synthesizes open challenges with explicit comparison of evaluation protocols and model scales.
AI.conclusion: Treating tensorization as a common structural principle provides a unified framework for understanding and applying tensor methods to LLMs across their entire lifecycle, helping researchers and practitioners better leverage the multilinear structure inherent in LLM components while addressing the gap between theoretical compression and practical system-level efficiency.

title: LLM-Based Knowledge Graph Completion Combining Discrete Structural Coding with Similar Entity Information
comment: Accepted by ISWC 26 Posters and Demos Track
summary: Knowledge graph completion requires models to use both textual descriptions and relational structure. Existing LLM-based methods either encode KG structure as discrete tokens or refine a restricted set of candidate entities, and these two directions have largely been studied separately. We propose CoSC for LLM-based KGC, which combines discrete structural coding with similar entity information. Specifically, an LLM generates an initial candidate entity ranking from discrete structural codes, after which information from entities with structures similar to that of the query entity refines the ranking. Experiments on FB15k-237 show that CoSC outperforms existing baselines on MRR and Hits@10 while remaining competitive on Hits@1.

AI.tldr: CoSC combines discrete structural coding with similar entity information for LLM-based knowledge graph completion, improving performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based methods for knowledge graph completion either encode KG structure as discrete tokens or refine a restricted set of candidate entities, but these two approaches have been studied separately, creating a need for integration.
AI.method: CoSC combines discrete structural coding with similar entity information. First, an LLM generates an initial candidate entity ranking from discrete structural codes. Then, information from entities with structures similar to the query entity refines this ranking.
AI.result: Experiments on FB15k-237 show that CoSC outperforms existing baselines on MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) and Hits@10 metrics while remaining competitive on Hits@1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CoSC approach successfully integrates discrete structural coding with similar entity information, demonstrating improved performance in LLM-based knowledge graph completion tasks.

title: Trajectory-Initialized Neural Double Q-Routing for Large-Scale Overhead Hoist Transport Systems
summary: Large-scale industrial robot fleets share constrained physical infrastructure, making vehicle travel times dependent on safety separation, intersection access, downstream blocking, and station contention. We study this problem in overhead hoist transport (OHT) systems, a representative ceiling-mounted material-handling system used in semiconductor fabs. Static shortest-path routing cannot account for these time-varying traffic costs, whereas tabular Q-routing adapts online but learns each destination--node--action value independently, limiting information sharing across sparsely visited routing contexts and making startup behavior sensitive to inaccurate value estimates. We propose Neural Double Q-routing, which replaces destination-indexed tables with a shared state--action value network. The network is warm-started through return-to-go regression on mixed simulator-generated routing trajectories and then refined online using Double-Q updates, local congestion correction, and event-stratified structured replay. Across nine matched fleet-size--arrival-rate settings with 100, 150, and 200 OHTs, the proposed framework reduces mean completion time relative to tabular Double Q-routing by $0.8\%$--$8.8\%$. It achieves the lowest mean completion time among all compared methods in the six 150- and 200-OHT settings, whereas Dijkstra remains best in the three 100-OHT settings. Completed-task counts remain within $1\%$ of tabular Double Q-routing in eight of nine settings, and 95th-percentile completion time decreases in eight settings. In two matched startup scenarios, offline initialization increases the number of completed tasks by up to $23\%$ and reduces tail completion time by up to $15\%$.

AI.tldr: Neural Double Q-routing improves overhead hoist transport efficiency by replacing destination-indexed Q-tables with a shared neural network, enabling better information sharing and startup behavior, achieving up to 8.8% reduction in mean completion time compared to tabular methods.
AI.motivation: Industrial robot fleets like OHT systems in semiconductor fabs face time-varying traffic congestion from safety separation, intersection access, blocking, and station contention. Static routing can't adapt to traffic, while tabular Q-routing learns independently for each destination-node-action pair, limiting information sharing across contexts and making startup behavior sensitive to inaccurate value estimates.
AI.method: Proposes Neural Double Q-routing that replaces destination-indexed Q-tables with a shared state-action value network. The network is warm-started through return-to-go regression on mixed simulator-generated routing trajectories, then refined online using Double-Q updates, local congestion correction, and event-stratified structured replay.
AI.result: Across 9 fleet-size-arrival-rate settings (100-200 OHTs), the framework reduces mean completion time by 0.8%-8.8% relative to tabular Double Q-routing. Achieves lowest mean completion time in all 150- and 200-OHT settings, while Dijkstra remains best in 100-OHT settings. Completed-task counts within 1% of tabular Double Q-routing in 8 of 9 settings, with 95th-percentile completion time decreasing in 8 settings. Offline initialization improves completed tasks by up to 23% and reduces tail completion time by up to 15% in startup scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Neural Double Q-routing effectively addresses limitations of both static routing and tabular Q-learning for industrial robot fleets by leveraging shared neural network representation for better information sharing and initialization, leading to significant performance improvements in congested systems while maintaining comparable task completion rates.

title: Generating Workflow DAGs from Natural Language with Non-Reasoning LLMs
summary: This paper addresses the problem of translating natural-language routing rules written by business administrators into executable workflow graphs for enterprise contact centers. Each target is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of conditional actions with parallel branches, hit-first fallback chains, and per-branch Boolean predicates, encoded in the JSON dialect of a commercial routing platform. We show that neuro-symbolic decomposition enables lower-cost, non-reasoning large language models to generate complex workflow DAGs at production-relevant quality without expensive extended-reasoning models. Our central diagnostic is an emission-density bottleneck: on a 635-rule benchmark of manufactured synthetic data, models select the correct graph nodes with high accuracy but increasingly misconfigure attributes and Boolean grouping as the number of interdependent nodes emitted in one pass grows. We therefore move combinatorial graph construction from the model into a deterministic compiler driven by a compact intermediate representation, with a learned registry-selection front end that focuses generation on relevant vocabulary. Across four models, the full system reaches approximately 89% LLM-judge validity, approximately 90% exact-match condition accuracy, and 99-100% valid JSON while using roughly half the per-rule prompt tokens of a monolithic prompt. On GPT-5.3-chat, the method improves judge validity by 24 percentage points and achieves statistical equivalence to a reasoning model's out-of-the-box quality, although an approximately 8-point frontier gap remains. We also present a deployment path and transferable lessons for structured-generation applications.

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic decomposition enables cost-effective LLMs to translate natural language routing rules into executable workflow DAGs by separating combinatorial graph construction from learned generation.
AI.motivation: Business administrators write natural language routing rules for contact centers, but translating these into executable workflow graphs (complex DAGs with parallel branches, fallback chains, and Boolean predicates) is challenging. Current approaches using monolithic large language models face an emission-density bottleneck where models increasingly misconfigure attributes as they generate more interdependent nodes in one pass.
AI.method: The system uses neuro-symbolic decomposition: 1) a learned registry-selection front end that focuses generation on relevant vocabulary, and 2) a deterministic compiler that constructs combinatorial graphs from a compact intermediate representation. This separates the complex graph construction from the learned generation, allowing non-reasoning LLMs to produce correct outputs.
AI.result: On a 635-rule benchmark: 89% LLM-judge validity, 90% exact-match condition accuracy, 99-100% valid JSON, while using roughly half the per-rule prompt tokens of monolithic prompting. On GPT-5.3-chat, the method improves judge validity by 24 percentage points and achieves statistical equivalence to a reasoning model's quality, though an ~8-point gap remains.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic decomposition enables lower-cost, non-reasoning LLMs to generate complex workflow DAGs at production-relevant quality by addressing emission-density bottlenecks. The approach provides a deployment path with transferable lessons for structured-generation applications.

title: PAC: Progress-Augmented Advantage Curriculum for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning of LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is used to improve the reasoning abilities of LLMs, while training data span heterogeneous tasks. However, most RL post-training pipelines rely on fixed or manually designed task mixtures, even though task usefulness changes as training progresses. Online curriculum methods often define learnability by update magnitude, ignoring whether the update translates into reward gains, which can misallocate rollout budget toward tasks with large but ineffective updates. We propose PAC, a Progress-Augmented Advantage Curriculum for multi-task RL of LLMs that combines two task-level signals: advantage-derived learnability, which measures the magnitude of the policy update a task can induce, and recent reward gains, which show whether those updates have improved task performance. A Bayesian Thompson Sampling controller uses these signals to allocate rollouts across tasks during GRPO training. We evaluate PAC under two settings: a multi-level reasoning setting and a multi-domain reasoning setting. PAC improves sample efficiency and final performance: it reaches comparable validation scores with fewer rollout steps and achieves higher final averages than random sampling and advantage-based curriculum baselines in both settings. These results show that jointly tracking advantage signals and actual reward gains yields an effective online curriculum for LLM post-training.

AI.tldr: Proposed PAC curriculum combines advantage signals and reward gains to dynamically allocate training tasks, improving LLM RL sample efficiency and performance.
AI.motivation: Current RL post-training pipelines for LLMs rely on fixed or manually designed task mixtures, ignoring that task usefulness changes during training. Online curriculum methods often define learnability by update magnitude alone, which can misallocate rollout budget toward tasks with large but ineffective updates.
AI.method: Proposed PAC (Progress-Augmented Advantage Curriculum), which combines advantage-derived learnability (measuring policy update magnitude) and recent reward gains (tracking actual performance improvement). A Bayesian Thompson Sampling controller uses these signals to allocate rollouts across tasks during GRPO training.
AI.result: PAC improved sample efficiency and final performance: it reached comparable validation scores with fewer rollout steps and achieved higher final averages than random sampling and advantage-based curriculum baselines in both multi-level and multi-domain reasoning settings.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that jointly tracking advantage signals and actual reward gains yields an effective online curriculum for LLM post-training, as demonstrated by improved sample efficiency and final performance over baselines.

title: Q-Strata: Hierarchical Bit Allocation for Mixed-Precision Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
summary: Mixed-precision quantization (MPQ) assigns a different bitwidth to each linear layer of a large language model (LLM) to minimize the quantization-induced quality loss under a fixed budget, but Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models contain these layers in every expert of every MoE block, so the allocation space grows far larger than in a dense model. Existing methods either allocate within each block under a uniform per-block budget, or allocate across blocks through an additive proxy, and neither directly optimizes a model-level objective over the choices that couple the blocks. We propose Q-Strata, a bi-level allocator that ranks within-block assignments with a cheap proxy and allocates across blocks with a model-level objective evaluated on the assembled quantized model. Its inner stage caches a Pareto frontier of candidates per block over finely spaced budgets, leaving the outer stage to set one budget per block instead of a bitwidth for every linear layer. With the search reduced to one budget per block, the outer stage optimizes this model-level objective directly, capturing the inter-block coupling that additive proxies miss. On Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, and DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Q-Strata consistently achieves lower WikiText2 perplexity than uniform-bitwidth GPTQ and the state-of-the-art MoE MPQ methods MxMoE and GEMQ in the low-bit regime. The code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/Q-Strata/tree/main.

AI.tldr: Q-Strata is a bi-level mixed-precision quantization method for MoE LLMs that optimizes bitwidth allocation across blocks with a model-level objective, outperforming existing methods in low-bit regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing MPQ methods for MoE models either allocate within each block under uniform per-block budgets or use additive proxies that don't capture inter-block coupling, failing to directly optimize model-level objectives over the large allocation space of MoE models.
AI.method: Proposes Q-Strata, a bi-level allocator with inner stage that caches Pareto frontier candidates per block over finely spaced budgets, and outer stage that sets one budget per block and optimizes a model-level objective directly on the assembled quantized model.
AI.result: On Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, and DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Q-Strata consistently achieves lower WikiText2 perplexity than uniform-bitwidth GPTQ and state-of-the-art MoE MPQ methods MxMoE and GEMQ in low-bit regime.
AI.conclusion: Q-Strata effectively addresses the challenges of MPQ for MoE models by optimizing bitwidth allocation across blocks with direct model-level evaluation, capturing inter-block coupling missed by existing methods.

title: Ignorance or Incompetence? Constructing Knowledge-Gated, Verifiable Tasks for LLM Agents
summary: Professional agent tasks often depend on conventions that are absent from public corpora, yet benchmarks rarely control whether an agent has access to those conventions. We introduce a knowledge-gated task-construction protocol that separates a task instruction from a compact artefact containing private conventions, reference tables, and utility operators. Construction-time provenance, byte-identical task instructions across the provided- and withheld-artefact conditions, leak audits, and executable witnesses make dependence on the artefact explicit and testable. Across fifteen calibration tasks, one frontier agent configuration achieves a 68.0% pass rate with the artefact and 0% without it; on one task, a plausible but incorrect artefact also yields 0% across five trials. Deterministic solvers and rule corpora provide exact ground truth for structured tasks, while named criterion-level rubrics support outputs that cannot be checked by a single executable oracle. A configuration-relative calibration screen retains seven tasks satisfying our five-trial empirical knowledge-gating screen. These experiments validate the behavior of the construction protocol; they do not establish that the retained tasks improve post-training. We publicly release part of the task suite and supporting tooling at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/Knowledge-Gated-Task-Construction.

AI.tldr: A knowledge-gated task construction protocol separates task instructions from private conventions/artefacts, enabling explicit testing of agent dependence on specific knowledge through controlled access experiments.
AI.motivation: Professional agent tasks often rely on conventions not present in public datasets, but benchmarks rarely control whether agents have access to these private conventions. Current benchmarks fail to explicitly test knowledge dependence.
AI.method: Introduces a knowledge-gated task construction protocol that separates task instructions from compact artefacts containing private conventions, reference tables, and utility operators. Uses construction-time provenance, byte-identical instructions across conditions, leak audits, and executable witnesses to make artefact dependence explicit and testable.
AI.result: In experiments: one frontier agent configuration achieved 68.0% pass rate with artefact vs. 0% without it. On one task, a plausible but incorrect artefact also yielded 0% across five trials. The calibration screen retained seven tasks satisfying the five-trial empirical knowledge-gating criteria.
AI.conclusion: The protocol successfully validates knowledge dependence through controlled experiments, demonstrating that agents can fail without access to private conventions. The method provides a structured approach to creating knowledge-gated tasks, though further research is needed to determine if such tasks improve post-training outcomes.

title: Collapsibility of Performance Metrics in Clinical Predictive AI
summary:
Background: Population level assessments of predictive artificial intelligence (AI) can conceal performance disparities across subgroups. Fairness evaluations commonly rely on performance analyses across subgroups. However, some performance metrics are non-collapsible, meaning that the overall population performance value does not equal the weighted average of subgroup specific values.
  Objective: To examine the collapsibility properties of commonly reported performance metrics in predictive AI, with a focus on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, also known as c-statistic).
  Methods: We investigate the collapsibility of 15 performance metrics, either by expressing each metric as a linear combination of its stratum specific values or, where non-collapsible, by providing a counterexample inspired by Simpson's paradox as a formal disproof.
  Results: Five performance metrics (AUC, calibration intercept, calibration slope, expected calibration error, and Nagelkerke R^2) are shown to be non-collapsible, and ten (O:E ratio, logloss, Brier score, accuracy, F1-score, true positive rate, true negative rate, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and net benefit) are shown to be collapsible. The AUC is shown to be non-collapsible because it decomposes into within- and cross-group AUC terms when subpopulations coexist, such that its overall value may fall outside the range of subgroup specific AUCs.
  Conclusions: Non-collapsibility of performance metrics has important consequences for reporting, model appraisal, and fairness evaluation. It can generate spurious differences between subgroup and overall performance, which may mislead fairness evaluations. Explicitly acknowledging and reporting the collapsibility properties of performance metrics improves both the interpretability and transparency of fairness assessments.

AI.tldr: Five key predictive AI performance metrics (including AUC) are non-collapsible, meaning overall population performance may not equal weighted average of subgroup performance, which has important implications for fairness evaluations.
AI.motivation: Performance disparities across subgroups in predictive AI can be concealed by population-level assessments, and some performance metrics are non-collapsible, potentially misleading fairness evaluations.
AI.method: Investigated collapsibility of 15 performance metrics by expressing each as linear combinations of stratum-specific values or providing Simpson's paradox-inspired counterexamples for non-collapsible metrics.
AI.result: Five metrics (AUC, calibration intercept, calibration slope, expected calibration error, Nagelkerke R²) are non-collapsible, while ten others (including O:E ratio, Brier score, accuracy, F1-score, net benefit) are collapsible. AUC non-collapsibility arises from decomposition into within- and cross-group terms.
AI.conclusion: Non-collapsibility affects reporting, model appraisal, and fairness evaluation by generating spurious performance differences. Acknowledging and reporting collapsibility properties improves interpretability and transparency of fairness assessments.

title: Answer Probing-Guided Search for Diverse Solution Exploration of LLMs
summary: Generating multiple diverse and high-quality solutions is valuable for many applications, such as code-test generation and drug discovery. However, Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to converge on a single high-confidence solution during inference, limiting exploration of alternative valid solution paths. Existing test-time methods promote diversity through tree-like search and prune semantically similar branches using response-level semantic embeddings. However, we find that such embeddings are easily confounded by linguistic and stylistic similarities, making it difficult to distinguish genuinely distinct solution paths. To address this, we introduce Answer Probing, which probes the potential answer an LLM would reach from an intermediate reasoning path. We demonstrate that the hidden states of probed answers more effectively differentiate distinct solution paths than semantic embeddings, and the perplexity of probed answers serves as a practical proxy for reasoning correctness. Based on these findings, we propose Answer Probing-Guided Tree Search (APTS), which guides the tree search by the probed answers' hidden state similarity and perplexity. Experiments on three reasoning tasks across two LLMs show that APTS consistently enhances solution diversity, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

AI.tldr: APTS (Answer Probing-Guided Tree Search) improves LLM solution diversity by using probed answer hidden states instead of semantic embeddings to distinguish distinct reasoning paths during tree search.
AI.motivation: LLMs tend to converge on single high-confidence solutions during inference, limiting exploration of alternative valid solutions needed for applications like code-test generation and drug discovery. Existing methods use semantic embeddings to prune similar branches, but these embeddings are easily confounded by linguistic and stylistic similarities rather than true solution diversity.
AI.method: Introduces Answer Probing to probe potential answers an LLM would reach from intermediate reasoning paths. Uses hidden states of probed answers to differentiate distinct solution paths more effectively than semantic embeddings, and uses perplexity of probed answers as proxy for reasoning correctness. Combines these into APTS (Answer Probing-Guided Tree Search) that guides tree search using probed answer hidden state similarity and perplexity.
AI.result: Experiments on three reasoning tasks across two LLMs show that APTS consistently enhances solution diversity compared to existing methods, demonstrating effectiveness and robustness in promoting exploration of alternative valid solution paths.
AI.conclusion: Answer Probing effectively addresses limitations of semantic embeddings by using probed answer hidden states to distinguish genuinely distinct solution paths, and APTS provides a practical framework for improving LLM solution diversity in reasoning tasks.

title: The Safety Relay in Roleplay Jailbreaks: A Component-Resolved Causal Analysis of Harm Recognition and Refusal
summary:
Large language models are trained to follow instructions while refusing harmful requests. Jailbreaks exploit this balance to elicit content a model would ordinarily reject. Roleplay jailbreaks are especially concerning: the harmful request can remain visible inside a roleplay wrapper made of a persona, scenario, and task, yet the model may comply. We use mechanistic interpretability to determine how this context reverses refusal and which elements contribute to the reversal. Across two benchmarks, three model families, and four authored wrappers, we compare matched harmful and benign requests with and without this wrapper. We trace hidden-state contrasts from the request to the final prompt state, isolate wrapper operations through controlled counterfactuals, intervene on their activation directions in held-out evaluation requests, and decompose effective directions geometrically.
  Our analysis yields three findings. (1) Successful attacks retain the measured harmful-versus-benign distinction at the request, while its refusal-associated expression weakens where the answer begins, a pattern we call safety-relay attenuation. (2) Constructing the complete roleplay around the request and framing it within the scenario contribute causally: removing the associated activation changes restores refusal. (3) These effects largely share internal structure, and most repair is reproduced by components aligned with the model's ordinary refusal of harmful requests without roleplay; scenario framing retains a smaller, model-dependent component. Together, these findings explain how roleplay can produce compliance despite retained evidence of harm and identify a concrete target for future safeguards: maintaining the connection from harm recognition to refusal.

AI.tldr: Roleplay jailbreaks in LLMs work by weakening the connection between harm recognition and refusal through scenario framing, while maintaining harmful content recognition.
AI.motivation: Roleplay jailbreaks are concerning because they can make LLMs comply with harmful requests despite visible harmful content. Understanding the mechanistic basis of these attacks is crucial for developing better safeguards.
AI.method: Used mechanistic interpretability across two benchmarks, three model families, and four authored wrappers. Compared matched harmful/benign requests with/without wrappers, traced hidden-state contrasts, isolated wrapper operations via controlled counterfactuals, intervened on activation directions, and decomposed effective directions geometrically.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) Successful attacks retain harmful content recognition but weaken refusal expression at answer start (safety-relay attenuation). 2) Scenario framing and complete roleplay construction causally contribute to reversal. 3) Most repair aligns with model's ordinary refusal mechanisms, while scenario framing has smaller model-dependent components.
AI.conclusion: Roleplay jailbreaks exploit the weakening of connection between harm recognition and refusal. Future safeguards should focus on maintaining this connection rather than just recognizing harmful content.

title: Co-Annotator: Expert-Distilled ViT and VLM for Visual and Documentation Guidance in Age-Related Macular Degeneration
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. To appear in UIST '26: Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, November 02-05, 2026, Detroit, MI, USA. DOI: 10.1145/3830398.3830722
summary: Clinical AI often optimizes predictive performance without engaging how clinicians decide where to look and what to write. We present Co-Annotator, which distills expert gaze and dictation into two guidance components: a gaze-aligned Vision Transformer producing fixation-aligned areas of interest (AOIs), and an ontology-bounded vision-language model (VLM) that pre-fills editable biomarker summaries for retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT). We first collect expert gaze and dictations (US1) to train the models, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and biomarker generation. We then deploy the system with ophthalmology residents: a controlled resident study (US2) confirmed each modality is safe and independently beneficial, with AOI guidance producing lasting perceptual efficiency gains through post-guidance carryover and VLM guidance more than doubling biomarker documentation breadth. In a combined deployment across two academic institutions (US3), providing both modalities simultaneously produced efficiency gains that substantially exceeded either modality alone: correct diagnoses per minute increased by 40% and comment editing time fell by 67%, without compromising diagnostic accuracy. Notably, neither modality improved efficiency during guidance in US2, which makes the in-guidance efficiency gain under combined guidance in US3 the more striking result. Expert-distilled multimodal guidance can remove two distinct clinical workflow bottlenecks at once (visual search overhead and documentation burden) without compromising the diagnostic accuracy clinicians already achieve.

AI.tldr: Co-Annotator improves clinical AI by incorporating expert gaze and dictation patterns into two guidance components: gaze-aligned visual attention maps and ontology-bounded biomarker summaries for retinal OCT, substantially increasing diagnostic efficiency and documentation breadth without compromising accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current clinical AI often focuses solely on predictive performance without considering how clinicians actually work - where they look and what they document. There's a gap in AI systems that engage with clinicians' decision-making workflow processes.
AI.method: Developed Co-Annotator with two guidance components: 1) A gaze-aligned Vision Transformer producing fixation-aligned areas of interest (AOIs) from expert gaze data, and 2) An ontology-bounded vision-language model (VLM) pre-filling editable biomarker summaries for retinal OCT. Conducted three user studies: US1 collected expert gaze/dictations for training, US2 tested each modality separately with residents, US3 deployed combined system across two academic institutions.
AI.result: Significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and biomarker generation. Each modality independently beneficial: AOI guidance produced lasting perceptual efficiency gains through carryover effects; VLM guidance more than doubled biomarker documentation breadth. Combined deployment produced 40% increase in correct diagnoses per minute and 67% reduction in comment editing time without compromising diagnostic accuracy. Notably, efficiency gains only emerged during combined guidance.
AI.conclusion: Expert-distilled multimodal guidance can simultaneously address two clinical workflow bottlenecks (visual search overhead and documentation burden) while maintaining clinicians' existing diagnostic accuracy, representing a more clinically-relevant approach to AI system design.

title: State of Health Estimation using Convolutional and Bidirectional LSTM Neural Networks tuned by Bayesian Optimization
summary: In this research, a novel framework is proposed for the SOH estimation, which employs a hybrid deep learning architecture of a concatenation of a Convolution Neural Network (CNN) and a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) Neural Network (NN) with the integration of Bayesian Optimization-based hyperparameter tuning for the network. Three different deep learning architectures are being evaluated: standalone recurrent models, CNN-RNN architectures and CNN-RNN combinations enhanced with intermediate Fully Connected (FC) layers. Among the three, the model with the intermediate FC layers demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy. A comprehensive feature engineering approach combines capacity (Q), voltage (V), Incremental Capacity Analysis (ICA), and Differential Voltage Analysis (DVA), with systematic evaluation of multiple combinations to identify the optimal input representation. To validate the proposed method, three publicly available datasets were utilized, ensuring reproducibility of the results, two from external sources and one developed by the author of this study using a unique experimental setup. The comparison study was performed using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and the FLoating-point OPerations (FLOPs) as evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN-BiLSTM model with Bayesian hyperparameter tuning achieves superior SOH estimation accuracy, with optimal feature engineering combining capacity, voltage, ICA, and DVA features validated on three public datasets.
AI.motivation: To develop an accurate and efficient State of Health (SOH) estimation method for batteries using advanced deep learning techniques, addressing the need for reliable battery health monitoring in applications like electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
AI.method: Proposed a hybrid deep learning framework combining CNN and BiLSTM networks with Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter tuning. Compared three architectures: standalone RNNs, CNN-RNN combinations, and CNN-RNN with intermediate FC layers. Employed comprehensive feature engineering using capacity, voltage, ICA, and DVA features systematically evaluated in multiple combinations.
AI.result: The CNN-RNN architecture with intermediate FC layers demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy. The proposed method was validated on three publicly available datasets (two external, one internal) and evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and FLOPs metrics. The comprehensive feature engineering approach identified optimal input representations for SOH estimation.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid CNN-BiLSTM framework with Bayesian hyperparameter tuning and systematic feature engineering provides an accurate and efficient solution for battery SOH estimation, with the CNN-RNN-FC combination showing superior performance validated across multiple datasets.

title: Will the User Ever Know? Covert Indirect Prompt Injection on Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: As LLM agents take real-world actions through tools, indirect prompt injection (IPI) has emerged as a serious threat. The standard metric, Attack Success Rate (ASR), counts whether an injection succeeds but ignores what the user notices in the agent's final response. Looking at successful injection traces, we find two distinct outcomes: the agent executes the injection while returning an otherwise normal response, or reports the injected action in its final response, giving the user a chance to notice. We call these covert and overt successes. From the user's perspective, we decompose ASR into the Covert Success Rate (CSR), counting successes leaving no trace in the final response, and the Overt Success Rate (OSR), counting successes the user can detect. To understand what drives the gap, we analyze successful trajectories and find that the agent's behavior after the injection separates covert from overt: covert traces hand control back to the user task before ending, while overt traces end at the attack itself. This split follows from the ReAct format, where the final response summarizes the most recent action. Building on this observation, we propose ICoA (Induced Covert Attack), an IPI attack designed to induce covert outcomes by steering the agent back to the user task after executing the injection. Across four target models on AgentDojo, ICoA achieves the highest CSR, with gains of 3.79-12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new classification for indirect prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, distinguishing between covert and overt successes based on whether the attack leaves traces in the agent's final response visible to users.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks only measure attack success rate (ASR) but ignore whether users can detect the attack in the agent's final response, failing to capture the real security impact from a user's perspective.
AI.method: The authors analyze successful injection trajectories and decompose ASR into Covert Success Rate (CSR) and Overt Success Rate (OSR). They propose ICoA (Induced Covert Attack), an IPI attack designed to steer agents back to the user task after executing injections to create covert outcomes.
AI.result: ICoA achieves the highest CSR across four target models on AgentDojo, with gains of 3.79-12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline, demonstrating its effectiveness in creating undetectable attacks.
AI.conclusion: The covert/overt distinction provides a more nuanced understanding of IPI security risks, and the ICoA attack framework shows how adversaries can intentionally create covert attacks that are harder for users to detect.

title: PLC-DPO: Posterior Label Correction in Noisy and Ambiguous Preference Optimization
comment: Findings of EMNLP 2026; Code is available at https://github.com/VennTum99/PLC-DPO
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies alignment through pairwise comparisons but assumes all observed preferences are reliable. Real data often violates this assumption, leading to reversed, weak, or ambiguous labels that cause harmful policy updates. To address this, we propose Posterior Label Correction DPO (PLC-DPO) to robustly optimize preferences by routing each pair's training signal as a clean, flip, or tie case. The key idea is to use the calibrated policy-reference margin as online evidence to take appropriate correction actions. This reframes noisy preference learning as actively correcting supervision direction and strength rather than merely filtering suspicious examples. Across 57 dataset-model-benchmark cells, PLC-DPO obtains the best mean win rate against DPO (60.5 vs. 55.5 for the next-best method). Injected-noise and tie stress tests, human disagreement analysis, and self-confirmation diagnostics further show that the routing remains stable and distinguishes flipped from weakly directional pairs.

AI.tldr: PLC-DPO improves DPO by handling noisy preference data through intelligent routing of training pairs as clean, flipped, or tie cases based on online evidence.
AI.motivation: Standard DPO assumes all observed preferences are reliable, but real-world data often contains reversed, weak, or ambiguous labels that cause harmful policy updates during model alignment.
AI.method: Proposes Posterior Label Correction DPO (PLC-DPO) that reframes noisy preference learning as actively correcting supervision. It routes each training pair as clean, flip, or tie case using the calibrated policy-reference margin as online evidence to determine appropriate correction actions.
AI.result: Across 57 dataset-model-benchmark combinations, PLC-DPO achieves best mean win rate (60.5) against DPO compared to other methods (55.5 for next-best). The method shows stability in noise/tie stress tests, effectively distinguishes flipped from weakly directional pairs, and handles human disagreement well.
AI.conclusion: PLC-DPO successfully addresses noisy preference learning by actively correcting supervision direction and strength rather than merely filtering suspicious examples, making DPO-based alignment more robust to real-world data imperfections.

title: Augmenting Human Performance with an XR Agent Learning from Online Behavior and BCI Evidence
comment: To appear in ACM UIST 2026. 30 pages, 23 figures
summary: We present OLIVE, a framework for adapting a foundation model to provide real-time assistance in temporally demanding, high-stakes, and dynamic tasks. We show that passive EEG, fused online with behavioral evidence, can meaningfully extend the number of targets users detect and engage beyond their unaided action bandwidth. OLIVE learns from both explicit behavioral signals (the targets the user shoots down in an XR first-person shooter game) and implicit physiological signals (fixation-locked EEG) to provide timely guidance, continuously adapting a frozen vision-language model's inference on which items are task-relevant by jointly estimating per-source reliability without manual labels or offline training. Through three user studies, including two live deployments of an assistive agent driven by OLIVE in XR, we show that OLIVE Pareto-dominates prior test-time adaptation frameworks, achieving the highest convergence rate at comparable convergence speed. Combining implicit physiological and explicit behavioral signals, the OLIVE agent produces the largest and most reliable within-session improvement to a user's ability to detect and engage targets, largely independent of the individual's skill. When the target switches silently, the agent that uses both behavioral and physiological signals reconverges significantly faster than the behavior-only agent (1.27 times faster on average, p = .008), restoring trustworthy guidance at the moment the task changes, precisely when reliable assistance matters most.

AI.tldr: OLIVE is a framework that adapts foundation models for real-time assistance in high-stakes dynamic tasks using both explicit behavioral signals (user actions) and implicit physiological signals (EEG) to provide timely guidance without manual labels or offline training.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for real-time assistance in temporally demanding, high-stakes dynamic tasks where users have limited action bandwidth. Current approaches struggle to provide timely, trustworthy guidance that adapts to changing task conditions without requiring manual labels or extensive offline training.
AI.method: OLIVE combines passive EEG signals with behavioral evidence to continuously adapt a frozen vision-language model's inference. It learns from both explicit behavioral signals (user actions like shooting targets) and implicit physiological signals (fixation-locked EEG) to estimate per-source reliability automatically. The system performs online adaptation without manual labels or offline training.
AI.result: Through three user studies including two live XR deployments, OLIVE Pareto-dominates prior test-time adaptation frameworks with highest convergence rate at comparable speed. The agent combining both signals produces largest and most reliable within-session improvement to target detection and engagement, largely skill-independent. When targets switch silently, the combined-signal agent reconverges 1.27x faster than behavior-only (p = .008), restoring trustworthy guidance precisely when task changes.
AI.conclusion: OLIVE demonstrates that fusing implicit physiological signals (EEG) with explicit behavioral evidence can significantly enhance real-time assistance in dynamic tasks, providing timely guidance that adapts to changing conditions without manual intervention. The framework shows practical promise for high-stakes applications where reliable assistance matters most during task transitions.

title: MolLedger: An Additive Graph Neural Network with Chemically Grounded ADME Attributions
summary: Optimizing absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) is an important part of small molecule drug discovery. Many machine learning models have been built to predict ADME properties to facilitate this optimization process, but explaining model predictions is challenging. We propose a new graph neural network architecture with built-in meaningful per-atom attributions. Our model MolLedger outputs predictions that are the sum of per-atom scores.
