Turing-20B-A2B also employs a hybrid attention architecture that combines Lightning Attention with a small number of full-attention layers for efficient long-context modeling. The model is pretrained with a progressive three-stage curriculum and extended to a native context length of 128K through continued pretraining, with further inference-time extension to 512K using YaRN. Despite its compact active-parameter budget, Turing-20B-A2B achieves, at the base-model stage, overall general capability exceeding Qwen3-8B Base and approaching Qwen3.5-9B Base, while maintaining strong long-context performance and favorable prefill-latency scaling. These results demonstrate an effective balance among model capability, long-context scalability, and practical inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Turing-20B-A2B is a 20B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model that activates only ~2B parameters per token, designed for efficient long-context AI applications with balanced capability and inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for large language models that can handle long contexts while being latency-sensitive and efficient for physical AI applications, balancing model capability with practical inference efficiency.
AI.method: Uses Mixture-of-Experts with Quantile Routing in dynamic top-k configuration for token-adaptive expert allocation, hybrid attention (Lightning Attention + full-attention layers), capacity-constrained routing for prompt prefill, progressive three-stage pretraining curriculum, and extends context to 128K natively with YaRN for 512K inference-time extension.
AI.result: The model achieves overall general capability exceeding Qwen3-8B Base and approaching Qwen3.5-9B Base, maintains strong long-context performance with favorable prefill-latency scaling, and demonstrates effective balance between capability, scalability, and inference efficiency despite compact active parameters.
AI.conclusion: Turing-20B-A2B successfully demonstrates how to balance model capability, long-context scalability, and practical inference efficiency through innovative MoE routing, hybrid attention, and training techniques, making it suitable for latency-sensitive physical AI applications.

title: PRACTICE: From Experience to Expertise in Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
summary: Recent studies have shown that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can serve as embodied agents, translating language instructions and visual observations into executable plans. However, building agents that can continually improve through interaction and rapidly adapt to their environments remains challenging. Summing up experience from past interaction trajectories provides a promising solution, but existing experience-based methods often rely on manually designed prompting workflows to extract and update skills. Such fixed procedures may struggle to learn updated skills from new and diverse experiences. We introduce PRACTICE, which trains a skill learner to discover and maintain a persistent skill library from past interaction trajectories while keeping the task executor frozen. Given the historical accumulated skills and incoming trajectories, the skill learner produces structured batch-edits that add, refine, merge, or remove skills, and then hierarchical consolidate all collected edits into a consistent updated skill library. We train the learner with a two-stage curriculum. First, it learns basic skill generation and library maintenance from oracle trajectories. Then, by contrasting successful and failed trajectories from heterogeneous executors on the same tasks, it learn to identify invalid action patterns and recovery strategies. Finally, we apply online skill-edit distillation to align the skill learner with a stronger teacher on its current edit distribution to further improves the policy. Experiments demonstrate that a compact skill learner delivers consistent performance improvements across successive library-update rounds for multiple frozen executors. On EB-ALFRED and EB-Habitat, PRACTICE further outperforms the strongest experience-based baselines. Project resources are publicly available at: https://baai-agents.github.io/PRACTICE

AI.tldr: PRACTICE trains a skill learner to build and maintain a persistent skill library from interaction trajectories, enabling continual improvement of frozen multimodal language model agents without manually designed prompting workflows.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs can serve as embodied agents, but struggle to continually improve through interaction and rapidly adapt to environments. Existing experience-based methods rely on manually designed prompting workflows that may not effectively learn updated skills from new and diverse experiences.
AI.method: Trains a skill learner to discover and maintain a persistent skill library from past interaction trajectories while keeping task executors frozen. Uses structured batch-edits (add, refine, merge, remove skills) with hierarchical consolidation. Two-stage curriculum: (1) basic skill generation from oracle trajectories, (2) contrast successful/failed trajectories to identify invalid patterns and recovery strategies. Finally uses online skill-edit distillation to align with stronger teacher.
AI.result: Compact skill learner delivers consistent performance improvements across successive library-update rounds for multiple frozen executors. Outperforms strongest experience-based baselines on EB-ALFRED and EB-Habitat benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PRACTICE provides an effective framework for continual learning in embodied agents by enabling autonomous skill library management and improvement, addressing limitations of manual prompting workflows and enabling better adaptation to diverse experiences.

title: Automated Testing of LLM-Based Post Hoc Explainers Using Model Checking as an Oracle
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used as post hoc explainers of sequential decision-making policies, producing natural-language explanations of why an action was chosen. However, LLMs often generate plausible but incorrect statements, and no existing approach systematically tests whether such explanations are faithful to the underlying environment. Two classic software testing challenges stand in the way: there is no oracle for the correctness of an explanation, and the test inputs, natural language queries about a policy's behavior, lack the structure needed for systematic test case generation. We address both. Probabilistic model checking provides the test oracle, computing exact reference results against which LLM answers are graded automatically. A taxonomy of post hoc query categories structures the input space around the environment-level facts from which policy explanations are composed; test cases generated from it are prioritized by question-specific diagnostic difficulty scores. Across seven MDP environments, the testing separates three open-weight LLMs: a reasoning model passes 85% of test cases, a mid-size model 70%, and a 1B model falls below the random baseline, while prioritization surfaces significantly harder cases than random selection. Our results indicate how trustworthy LLM-generated explanations are in model-free settings, where the same LLMs are used but no oracle exists to verify them.

AI.tldr: LLMs are unreliable post-hoc policy explainers, so this paper introduces a systematic testing framework using probabilistic model checking as an oracle and a query taxonomy to evaluate LLM explanation faithfulness across MDP environments.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to explain sequential decision-making policies, but they often generate plausible but incorrect explanations. There's no systematic way to test if these explanations are faithful to the actual environment, creating a trustworthiness gap in model-free settings where LLMs are used without verification oracles.
AI.method: 1) Uses probabilistic model checking as a test oracle to compute exact reference results against which LLM answers are automatically graded. 2) Develops a taxonomy of post-hoc query categories to structure the input space around environment-level facts. 3) Generates test cases prioritized by question-specific diagnostic difficulty scores.
AI.result: Across seven MDP environments, testing reveals significant performance differences: a reasoning LLM passes 85% of test cases, a mid-size model passes 70%, and a 1B parameter model falls below random baseline. The prioritization scheme successfully surfaces significantly harder test cases than random selection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed testing framework effectively evaluates LLM-generated policy explanations, revealing substantial reliability differences between models. Results indicate that LLM explanations in model-free settings (without verification oracles) have varying trustworthiness, with reasoning models performing best but still imperfect.

title: T3S: Improving Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Task-Specific Feature Selector and Scheduler
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Published in the 2023 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
summary: Multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) is a technique to train multiple tasks simultaneously, where previous works usually train a single model to solve different tasks by sharing parameters across various tasks. However, these methods are faced with inter-task interference since what parameters should be shared across tasks is not addressed, dramatically reducing learning efficiency. To solve these problems, we propose a novel MTRL framework called Task-Specific feature Selector and Scheduler (T3S), which consists of two components: a feature selector and a task scheduler. Specifically, the feature selectors employ hypernetworks to construct task-specific soft masks, which can be applied by globally shared representation to construct task-specific features. The task scheduler selects tasks for learning through two metrics, where the selection probability is inversely proportional to task progress (e.g., success rate) and task learning speed. Experimental results show that T3S consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art MTRL algorithms on various robotics manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: T3S: A novel multi-task RL framework with task-specific feature selectors and task scheduler that outperforms SOTA methods on robotics manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Previous MTRL methods suffer from inter-task interference because they don't properly address which parameters should be shared across tasks, reducing learning efficiency.
AI.method: Proposes T3S framework with two components: 1) feature selectors using hypernetworks to construct task-specific soft masks applied to globally shared representations, and 2) task scheduler that selects tasks based on two metrics inversely proportional to task progress and learning speed.
AI.result: Experimental results show T3S consistently outperforms state-of-the-art MTRL algorithms on various robotics manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: T3S effectively addresses inter-task interference in multi-task RL through task-specific feature selection and intelligent task scheduling, demonstrating superior performance on challenging robotics tasks.

title: Geometry of Divergence: Tracking Hidden-State Trajectories for Adaptive Multi-Turn Reasoning
summary: LLM agents need to sustain goal-consistent reasoning across long multi-turn interactions under strict resource constraints. However, as the multi-turn context accumulates, it can destabilize the underlying LLM's internal representation of task-relevant information from earlier turns, blurring the boundary between constructive reasoning and representation drift. We formulate multi-turn reasoning as a hidden-state trajectory of the underlying LLM that is characterized via two complementary signals: temporal curvature that captures the directional consistency of turn-to-turn updates, and variance slope which measures the expansion or contraction of the exploration space. Across four tasks and three underlying LLMs, we observed that these geometric signals distinguish between correct and incorrect episodes prior to completion. We further decompose each episode into three-action chains formed from four actions (Read, Write, Respond, Transfer) and show that separability is action-dependent, with different signals distinguishing various chain patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that trajectory geometry can identify critical turns in the reasoning process, increasing task success rates on $τ$-Bench from 24.1% to 39.6% while reducing token cost by 11.2%.

AI.tldr: LLM agents' multi-turn reasoning can be monitored via geometric signals (temporal curvature and variance slope) that predict success/failure early, enabling intervention to improve success rates by 15.5% while reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn LLM reasoning faces representation drift as context accumulates, blurring task-relevant information and destabilizing goal-consistent reasoning, especially under strict resource constraints.
AI.method: Formulate reasoning as hidden-state trajectory analyzed via two geometric signals: temporal curvature (directional consistency of updates) and variance slope (expansion/contraction of exploration space). Decompose episodes into action chains (Read, Write, Respond, Transfer) and study separability across different chain patterns.
AI.result: Across four tasks and three LLMs, geometric signals distinguish correct vs. incorrect episodes before completion. Trajectory geometry identifies critical turns, increasing task success rates on τ-Bench from 24.1% to 39.6% while reducing token cost by 11.2%.
AI.conclusion: Multi-turn reasoning trajectories exhibit measurable geometric properties that serve as early indicators of reasoning quality, enabling targeted interventions to improve success rates and reduce computational costs in LLM agent systems.

title: TrainSDC: Characterizing and Mitigating Silent Data Corruption in Large Language Model Training
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, and 6 tables. Includes an appendix with additional experiments
summary: LLM training is increasingly vulnerable to silent data corruption (SDC), yet existing protection methods largely treat Transformer computations uniformly because their vulnerability remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic characterization of SDC vulnerability across major computation interfaces in both the forward and backward passes of Transformer training. Our analysis reveals two distinct error propagation mechanisms: forward-pass vulnerability is highly location dependent, with faults on the Q/K path producing persistent training deviations, whereas backward-pass vulnerability is largely governed by gradient exponent distributions rather than computation locations. Motivated by these observations, we propose TrainSDC, a characterization-guided protection framework consisting of Q/K-path recomputation, residual-gain monitoring, and exponent-aware gradient scaling. Experiments on Llama 3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B show that TrainSDC maintains training behavior close to fault-free execution under both sparse and dense fault injection while introducing only 1.65%-6.76% runtime overhead.

AI.tldr: TrainSDC: A characterization-guided protection framework for Transformer training that mitigates silent data corruption vulnerabilities with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: LLM training is increasingly vulnerable to silent data corruption (SDC), but existing protection methods treat Transformer computations uniformly without understanding their varying vulnerabilities.
AI.method: First systematic characterization of SDC vulnerability across major computation interfaces in Transformer training forward/backward passes, revealing distinct error propagation mechanisms. Based on findings, proposes TrainSDC framework with Q/K-path recomputation, residual-gain monitoring, and exponent-aware gradient scaling.
AI.result: Experiments on Llama 3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B show TrainSDC maintains training behavior close to fault-free execution under sparse and dense fault injection with only 1.65%-6.76% runtime overhead.
AI.conclusion: Differentiating forward-pass location-dependent vulnerability from backward-pass gradient exponent distribution-driven vulnerability enables targeted protection strategies that effectively mitigate SDC in Transformer training with minimal performance impact.

title: PyKEEN-NSX: A Modular Framework for Static, Dynamic and Schema-Aware Negative Sampling in PyKEEN
summary: Embedding methods have become popular due to their scalability on link prediction and/or triple classification tasks on Knowledge Graphs (KGs). Embedding models are trained relying on both positive and negative samples of triples. However, since KGs generally contain only positive assertions, negative samples are artificially generated through negative sampling strategies, ranging from simple random corruption to more sophisticated approaches that exploit structural, semantic, or embedding information. The design and implementation of advanced negative samplers remains challenging, as most popular Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) libraries provide support only for basic strategies and lack a unified framework for developing more advanced and customized solutions. To address this gap, we introduce PyKEEN-NSX, an extension of PyKEEN, the popular KGE framework, that provides a modular engineered abstraction for negative sampling. The proposed architecture separates the generation of candidate negative pools, conditioned on an explicit context, from the selection strategy, enabling the development and integration of static, schema-aware and dynamic approaches within a consistent framework. Based on this abstraction, we implement six negative samplers, while remaining fully compatible with existing PyKEEN workflows and pipelines. As a proof of concept, we study negative availability across four datasets, showing that constrained pools frequently fall below the requested number of negatives, so that the encoded criterion is to a large extent replaced by the random fallback that supplements them.

AI.tldr: PyKEEN-NSX is a modular negative sampling extension for PyKEEN that separates candidate pool generation from selection strategy, enabling advanced negative sampling approaches while maintaining compatibility with existing workflows.
AI.motivation: Current KGE libraries lack support for advanced negative sampling strategies as they primarily offer basic random corruption, creating a gap for developing customized solutions that use structural, semantic, or embedding information for better negative sample generation.
AI.method: Developed PyKEEN-NSX as an extension of PyKEEN framework with modular abstraction separating candidate negative pool generation (conditioned on context) from selection strategy, enabling static, schema-aware, and dynamic negative sampling approaches.
AI.result: Implemented six negative samplers and demonstrated proof of concept showing constrained pools often fall below requested negative counts, causing criteria to be largely replaced by random fallback supplementation.
AI.conclusion: PyKEEN-NSX provides a unified framework for advanced negative sampling in KGE that addresses current library limitations, enabling more sophisticated sampling approaches while maintaining compatibility with existing PyKEEN workflows.

title: Reciprocity Separates Gradient Flow from Rotation in Conservative Physical Learning
summary: Physical learning lets a trainable material or network use its own physical response to carry error signals, reducing the need for a separately programmed backward computation. We ask what determines whether such a system follows conventional gradient descent or evolves along a genuinely different learning trajectory. Our canonical model is a directed layered transport network in which every node redistributes a fixed amount of flow, so learning preserves positivity and total mass. In this model, conservation constrains only the allowable learning directions. Within the matched response class studied here, adjoint matching gives the physical output response a symmetric form. Non-negative mode-wise feedback then produces a reciprocal closed-loop response and a reweighted gradient flow. Adding an antisymmetric boundary component makes the closed-loop response rotational: the learning path can turn while the error driving that update still decreases at that moment. Turning is not automatically beneficial. Its finite-step effect is set by local curvature, and its accumulated effect also depends on step selection and on the new states visited along the path. Numerical consistency checks reproduce the exact response structure, predict the sign of the local effect across new network families, and show how trajectory drift can negate a local advantage. These results separate the roles of conservation, reciprocity, and nonreciprocity in physical learning.

AI.tldr: Physical learning systems can follow different learning trajectories than conventional gradient descent due to conservation laws, with reciprocal feedback creating reweighted gradient flows and antisymmetric components enabling rotational learning paths.
AI.motivation: To understand when physical learning systems (where materials use their own physical response for error signals) follow conventional gradient descent versus genuinely different learning trajectories, and to separate the roles of conservation, reciprocity, and nonreciprocity in such systems.
AI.method: Used a canonical model of directed layered transport networks where nodes redistribute fixed flow, preserving positivity and total mass. Studied matched response class where adjoint matching gives physical output response a symmetric form, analyzed non-negative mode-wise feedback, and added antisymmetric boundary components.
AI.result: Conservation constrains learning directions only. Reciprocal feedback produces closed-loop response and reweighted gradient flow. Antisymmetric components create rotational learning paths where error decreases while the path turns. Numerical checks confirm response structure, predict local effect signs across network families, and show trajectory drift can negate local advantages.
AI.conclusion: Physical learning trajectories differ from conventional gradient descent due to conservation laws and feedback structure. The interplay of conservation, reciprocity, and nonreciprocity determines learning dynamics, with rotational paths possible but not automatically beneficial due to curvature effects and trajectory drift.

title: Geometric Attractor Monitoring: A Robust and Frugal Framework for Multi-modal Industrial Robotic Cycles
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Monitoring the health of heterogeneous industrial robot fleets is severely challenged by the multi-modal nature of their operational cycles and a persistent scarcity of run-to-failure data. Standard data-driven approaches, particularly deep learning architectures relying on sequential reconstruction, often struggle in this specific setting; they tend to over-smooth complex dynamics, masking early signs of degradation. To address these industrial constraints, we reframe the monitoring problem through a framework based on Phase Space Reconstruction (PSR). Instead of predicting temporal sequences, this framework transforms univariate sensor data into a geometric attractor, explicitly unfolding the mechanical states independently of their temporal occurrence. By evaluating various anomaly scoring techniques within this space, we demonstrate that discrete support estimation provides an effective and computationally frugal Health Indicator (HI). Validated on a real-world dataset of 21 heterogeneous robots over three years and a synthetic Langevin system, our approach outperforms standard deep learning baselines. We show that aligning the algorithmic bias with the geometric properties of the target system yields a pragmatic, traceable and easily deployable approach perfectly tailored to the realities of industrial constraints.

AI.tldr: A novel industrial robot health monitoring approach using Phase Space Reconstruction to create geometric attractors from sensor data, outperforming deep learning methods with a computationally efficient anomaly scoring technique.
AI.motivation: Traditional deep learning approaches struggle with industrial robot fleet health monitoring due to multi-modal operational cycles, scarcity of run-to-failure data, and tendency to over-smooth complex dynamics that mask early degradation signs.
AI.method: Reframe monitoring using Phase Space Reconstruction framework that transforms univariate sensor data into geometric attractors representing mechanical states independently of temporal occurrence, then applies discrete support estimation for anomaly scoring.
AI.result: Outperformed standard deep learning baselines when validated on real-world dataset of 21 heterogeneous robots over 3 years and synthetic Langevin system, providing an effective, computationally frugal Health Indicator.
AI.conclusion: Aligning algorithmic bias with geometric properties of target systems yields a pragmatic, traceable, and easily deployable approach perfectly tailored to industrial constraints.

title: MedAgent-R1: Faithfulness-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Medical Reasoning
summary: When medical AI systems hallucinate clinical reasoning, the consequences extend beyond incorrect answers: fabricated justifications that superficially reference retrieved evidence can mislead clinicians into unsafe treatment decisions. Medical reasoning agents must therefore produce not only correct answers but also faithful justifications that clinicians can verify against cited evidence. We identify a systematic failure mode in RL-trained retrieval agents: outcome-only rewards improve accuracy while degrading faithfulness, a phenomenon we term confident hallucination. The agent learns to answer from parametric memory and backfill plausible but unsupported justifications; citation fabrication rates rise from 16.5% to 31.8% even as accuracy improves by 5 points over the supervised baseline. We address this with a faithfulness-gated reward design: accuracy credit is conditioned on evidence grounding via a hard gate, complemented by retrieval validity and conciseness signals that close exploitation paths unique to agentic retrieval. The resulting system, MedAgent-R1, reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7% and raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6 while maintaining 75.1% accuracy, with 13.2-point gains on HealthBench Safety. Under the same agentic retrieval setup, MedAgent-R1 outscores GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15) while remaining below GPT-4o in overall accuracy, suggesting that explicit faithfulness training yields evidence-grounding gains not achieved by scaling alone.

AI.tldr: Medical AI systems that hallucinate clinical reasoning need faithful justifications, not just correct answers. RL-trained retrieval agents become worse at faithfulness as accuracy improves (confident hallucination). The solution is MedAgent-R1 with faithfulness-gated rewards, which dramatically reduces citation fabrication while maintaining good accuracy.
AI.motivation: Medical AI hallucinations have dangerous consequences beyond incorrect answers - fabricated justifications referencing evidence can mislead clinicians into unsafe treatment decisions. Current systems need both correct answers AND faithful justifications that clinicians can verify against cited evidence.
AI.method: Identifies a failure mode in RL-trained retrieval agents: outcome-only rewards improve accuracy while degrading faithfulness (confident hallucination). Proposes faithfulness-gated reward design where accuracy credit is conditioned on evidence grounding via a hard gate, complemented by retrieval validity and conciseness signals that close exploitation paths unique to agentic retrieval. The resulting system is MedAgent-R1.
AI.result: MedAgent-R1 reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7%, raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6 while maintaining 75.1% accuracy, with 13.2-point gains on HealthBench Safety. Outperforms GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15) though below GPT-4o in overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Explicit faithfulness training yields evidence-grounding gains not achieved by scaling alone. Faithfulness-gated rewards effectively address the confident hallucination problem in medical reasoning agents, producing systems that clinicians can safely verify against evidence.

title: What Emerges and What Breaks in Self-Play Driving
summary: Training autonomous driving policies through pure self-play has recently shown promising results. Following Gigaflow and Puffer- Drive, we train driving policies in a similar self-play fashion, but extend the models from MLPs to Transformers and train on the high-definition map of a real city, where we ultimately aim to deploy them. On the CARLA and Waymax benchmarks, our policies fall short of Gigaflow, and we trace the gap to specific failure modes, including reward hacking at traffic lights and a missing incentive to stop at stop signs. We further analyze which traffic rules emerge from self-play and how closely they match human driving, and we confirm that reward conditioning yields the intended diversity of driving behaviors. A demonstration of a trained policy is available at https://laursisask-ut.github.io/eccvdemo.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a self-play approach to train autonomous driving policies using Transformers on real city maps, but finds performance gaps compared to prior work (Gigaflow) on CARLA/Waymax benchmarks due to specific failure modes like reward hacking at traffic lights.
AI.motivation: To extend self-play training for autonomous driving from MLPs to Transformers using real-world high-definition maps, with the ultimate goal of deploying them in real cities. The motivation builds on promising results from previous self-play methods like Gigaflow and Puffer-Drive.
AI.method: Train driving policies using self-play with Transformer architectures (instead of MLPs) on high-definition maps of real cities. The method includes reward conditioning to achieve diverse driving behaviors and analysis of emergent traffic rules.
AI.result: The policies perform worse than Gigaflow on CARLA and Waymax benchmarks, with identified failure modes including reward hacking at traffic lights and lack of incentive to stop at stop signs. The study shows that reward conditioning produces intended behavioral diversity, and analyzes how emergent traffic rules compare to human driving.
AI.conclusion: While self-play with Transformers shows potential, it currently falls short of state-of-the-art methods. The identified failure modes provide insights for improvement, and the analysis of emergent traffic rules offers understanding of self-play training dynamics for autonomous driving.

title: ATLAS: Dual-Horizon Diagnostic Evaluation for Industrial Tool-Use Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in user-facing services that require iterative tool use under dynamic business conditions. Reliable evaluation is essential for sustained improvement: it must reveal capability deficiencies, inform priorities, and assess interventions. Yet industrial agent service unfolds both through the iterative trajectory of a current request and through continued user interaction. Final-outcome assessment can therefore obscure where deficiencies arise and whether later service remains aligned with context from earlier exchanges. We propose ATLAS, a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial tool-use agents. At the request horizon, trajectory-wise diagnostic signals relate deficiencies to execution locations and capability concerns. At the interaction horizon, user-wise signals assess whether service remains responsive across continued interaction. Together, these views provide structured diagnostic evidence for analyzing execution deficiencies and sustained service behavior. ATLAS instantiates them as executable signals with explicit evidence scopes and decision boundaries. LLM judge interfaces are calibrated against high-confidence references from real business logs; when needed, their decision behavior is distilled into efficient diagnostic models for lower-latency, lower-cost evaluation. The resulting feedback supports policy optimization. We evaluate ATLAS on Meituan Xiaotuan production traffic. Offline experiments assess diagnostic-signal fidelity and replay-based policy improvement, while online A/B experiments show concurrent gains in user engagement, downstream business outcomes, and sampled human-audit quality.

AI.tldr: ATLAS is a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial LLM agents that provides structured diagnostic signals at both request (trajectory) and interaction (user) levels to identify deficiencies and improve tool-use agents in production environments.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for industrial LLM agents focus only on final outcomes, which obscures where deficiencies arise during iterative tool use and whether agents remain responsive across continued user interactions. This makes it difficult to identify specific capability gaps and inform improvement priorities.
AI.method: ATLAS uses a dual-horizon approach: 1) Request horizon - trajectory-wise diagnostic signals that relate deficiencies to specific execution locations and capability concerns, and 2) Interaction horizon - user-wise signals that assess sustained service responsiveness across continued interaction. The framework uses LLM judge interfaces calibrated against real business logs, with distillation into efficient diagnostic models for lower-cost evaluation.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated on Meituan Xiaotuan production traffic. Offline experiments showed diagnostic-signal fidelity and replay-based policy improvement, while online A/B experiments demonstrated concurrent gains in user engagement, downstream business outcomes, and sampled human-audit quality.
AI.conclusion: ATLAS provides a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial LLM agents that enables structured analysis of execution deficiencies and sustained service behavior, supporting effective policy optimization and performance improvement in production environments.

title: Deploying DeepSeek 175B Locally on a Single Consumer-Grade RTX 4060 Laptop with 32GB RAM for 200k-Scale Protein-Ligand Virtual Screening
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in protein-ligand interaction prediction, but state-of-the-art pipelines for large-scale virtual screening almost exclusively rely on high-end GPU clusters with hundreds of gigabytes of memory, creating prohibitive hardware barriers for small academic teams. In this work, we present a fully local low-resource framework that deploys the 175-billion-parameter DeepSeek 175B LLM on a single consumer-grade RTX 4060 laptop equipped with 32GB system RAM and 8GB VRAM, completing a full 200k-scale protein-ligand virtual screening workflow across 20 distinct protein targets. Our implementation achieves 100x throughput of an 8-card A100 cluster baseline under identical task configurations within 72 hours, with an average binding affinity prediction error of 0.88 kcal/mol across all targets, satisfying the 1.0 kcal/mol chemical accuracy requirement for preclinical drug discovery. Systematic runtime profiling reveals that heterogeneous memory management overhead accounts for 72% of total execution time, while accuracy loss introduced by model optimization contributes less than 10% to total prediction error. This work validates the engineering feasibility of running industrial-scale trillion-parameter LLM-driven biomedical computing tasks on consumer hardware, establishing a new low-barrier paradigm for AI-powered early stage drug discovery.

AI.tldr: A low-resource framework deploys 175B-parameter DeepSeek LLM on a single consumer-grade laptop (RTX 4060 with 32GB RAM) for protein-ligand virtual screening, achieving 100x throughput of high-end GPU clusters while maintaining chemical accuracy for drug discovery.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art protein-ligand interaction prediction pipelines require expensive high-end GPU clusters with hundreds of GB memory, creating prohibitive hardware barriers for small academic teams and researchers with limited resources.
AI.method: Developed a fully local low-resource framework that deploys the 175-billion-parameter DeepSeek LLM on a single consumer-grade RTX 4060 laptop with 32GB system RAM and 8GB VRAM, optimized for memory management and model efficiency.
AI.result: Completed full 200k-scale protein-ligand virtual screening across 20 protein targets, achieving 100x throughput compared to an 8-card A100 cluster baseline within 72 hours. Average binding affinity prediction error was 0.88 kcal/mol (below the 1.0 kcal/mol chemical accuracy requirement). Systematic profiling showed 72% execution time from memory management overhead, with less than 10% prediction error from model optimization.
AI.conclusion: This work validates the engineering feasibility of running industrial-scale trillion-parameter LLM-driven biomedical computing on consumer hardware, establishing a new low-barrier paradigm for AI-powered early stage drug discovery that democratizes access to computational biology tools.

title: Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal Prototype Optimization for Sentiment Analysis
summary: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) is a fundamental component of affective computing that aims to decipher complex emotional states by integrating verbal content with non-verbal cues including vocal intonation and facial micro-expressions. While recent disentanglement-based approaches have advanced the field, their potential is hindered by two methodological challenges. First, static computation graphs process all samples indiscriminately regardless of semantic complexity, which leads to suboptimal representation for diverse emotional expressions and contextual scenarios. Second, generic contrastive objectives often neglect the intrinsic ordinal hierarchy of sentiment intensities. To systematically address these limitations, we introduce Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal prototype optimization (MAESTRO), a novel framework designed to dynamically orchestrate and refine multimodal representations. Drawing inspiration from an orchestra conductor, we design a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism. Unlike static fusion, this module utilizes linguistic context as a routing signal to dynamically activate specific audio-visual experts, thereby resolving cross-modal ambiguity through adaptive feature enhancement. Furthermore, to capture fine-grained sentiment gradations, we propose an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (O-PCL). By incorporating distance-based penalties into the prototype learning objective, O-PCL enforces a structured latent space that preserves the natural order of emotion. Extensive experiments on the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that MAESTRO achieves state-of-the-art performance, and qualitative analysis further confirms the interpretability of our dynamic routing paradigm.

AI.tldr: MAESTRO is a new multimodal sentiment analysis framework that uses dynamic text-guided routing to activate specific audio-visual experts and ordinal-aware prototype contrastive learning to capture sentiment intensity hierarchies.
AI.motivation: Current disentanglement-based multimodal sentiment analysis approaches have two key limitations: 1) static computation graphs process all samples indiscriminately regardless of semantic complexity, leading to suboptimal representations for diverse emotional expressions, and 2) generic contrastive objectives often neglect the intrinsic ordinal hierarchy of sentiment intensities.
AI.method: MAESTRO introduces two main components: 1) Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts mechanism that uses linguistic context as routing signal to dynamically activate specific audio-visual experts for adaptive feature enhancement, and 2) Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning that incorporates distance-based penalties to enforce a structured latent space preserving emotion order.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with qualitative analysis confirming the interpretability of the dynamic routing paradigm.
AI.conclusion: MAESTRO successfully addresses limitations of static multimodal fusion methods by introducing adaptive expert selection and ordinal-aware learning, providing a more nuanced and interpretable approach to multimodal sentiment analysis that better captures complex emotional states.

title: Fine-Tuning Low-Bit Models with Gradient in Quantized Code Space
summary: Fine-tuning Low-bit models aims to adapt a quantized model while keeping the final deployed checkpoint in the same low-bit form. This setting is practically important as it reduces memory and inference cost for storage and deployment. Under this constraint, adaptation becomes an optimization problem over quantization codes and scales. Existing continuous low-bit training is efficient, but it can be distorted by straight through estimation error or by post-quantize gap; discrete search is deployment-faithful, but it is often too inefficient under a finite training budget. We propose code surrogate gradient as the first order signal in deployable code space to acceleate optimization, and performing guided search to preserve deployment faithfulness. Experiments across arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, and structured language understanding show that GradCodes consistently improves fine-tuning low-bit models across different quantization datatypes. Code is provided at https://github.com/ovo67/GradCodes.

AI.tldr: GradCodes accelerates fine-tuning of low-bit quantized models using code surrogate gradients and guided search to improve efficiency while maintaining deployment faithfulness.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning low-bit models is crucial for practical deployment due to reduced memory and inference costs, but existing methods face trade-offs: continuous low-bit training is efficient but suffers from estimation errors, while discrete search is deployment-faithful but too inefficient for practical training budgets.
AI.method: Proposes code surrogate gradient as first-order signal in deployable code space to accelerate optimization, combined with guided search to preserve deployment faithfulness. This approach bridges the gap between efficient continuous training and faithful discrete search methods.
AI.result: Experiments across arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, and structured language understanding demonstrate that GradCodes consistently improves fine-tuning low-bit models across different quantization datatypes.
AI.conclusion: GradCodes provides an effective solution for efficient and deployment-faithful fine-tuning of low-bit quantized models, addressing the limitations of both continuous training and discrete search approaches.

title: Autoregressive Mosaics: Probing 2D Spatial Reasoning in Text-Only Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained only on text and code can sometimes generate programs that draw recognizable images. However, it is unclear whether this reflects an internal representation of 2D spatial layout or simply the ability to translate spatial descriptions into code. We introduce Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench), a benchmark that separates these factors: First, a translation task gives a model a fully specified geometry of a picture in words as a prompt and asks for the code that produces it. Second, a layout task requires the model to compose an image from an underspecified prompt. Across eight open-weight text-and-code-only models, all models reliably translate specified geometry into code, but their open-ended layout performance differs substantially, indicating that these differences are not explained by code-generation ability alone. An output-medium ablation further shows that the interface or medium of expression that the model uses matters: replacing procedural code with raw SVG improves layout scores across all models. Finally, probing model activations shows that a coarse layout plan is present before generation, but reflects only the layout implied by the prompt. During generation, models track the evolving geometric state instead of executing an initially fixed plan. Overall, these results show that 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both the model and the output medium, and is not explained by code-generation ability alone.

AI.tldr: LLMs trained only on text/code can generate image-producing programs, but this paper shows their 2D spatial abilities depend on both model capabilities and output medium, not just code generation skills.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs' ability to generate image-drawing programs reflects genuine internal 2D spatial representations or is merely translation of spatial descriptions into code.
AI.method: Introduced Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench) with two tasks: translation (fully specified geometry to code) and layout (underspecified prompt requiring composition). Tested eight open-weight text-and-code-only models with output-medium ablation (procedural code vs raw SVG) and probed model activations to understand internal processes.
AI.result: All models reliably translated specified geometry into code, but open-ended layout performance varied substantially. Output medium matters - raw SVG outperforms procedural code across all models. Activation probing reveals coarse layout planning occurs before generation but only reflects prompt-implied layout. During generation, models track evolving geometric state rather than executing fixed plans.
AI.conclusion: 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both model capabilities and output medium, and cannot be explained solely by code-generation ability. Models show spatial understanding through dynamic state tracking rather than fixed plan execution.

title: S3C-LLM: Skill-Code Guided Agentic Language Models for Spectrum-to-Structure Elucidation
summary: Spectroscopic structure elucidation is central to molecular analysis, but recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods mostly formulate it as direct spectrum-to-SMILES generation. Although this paradigm can leverage paired spectral data, it does not explicitly model the analytical workflow used by spectroscopists, such as diagnostic peak interpretation, fragment reasoning, formula constraints, and chemical consistency checking. In this paper, we introduce S3C-LLM, a skill-guided and code-grounded agentic LLM for spectrum-to-structure elucidation. Rather than directly predicting a molecule, S3C-LLM retrieves modality-specific spectroscopy skills, executes analysis code to instantiate these skills on the input spectra, and integrates the resulting peak-level evidence and formula constraints before generating SMILES. Specifically, we contribute a self-evolving spectroscopy skill library, a thinking-augmented skill-code trajectory construction pipeline, and a two-stage training strategy that teaches Qwen3-4B through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by our proposed step-level reinforcement learning (RL). Experiments on diverse benchmarks show that S3C-LLM consistently outperforms current general LLMs and spectrum-specific models across spectra, while using less than 1/10th of SpectraLLM's training corpus.

AI.tldr: S3C-LLM is a skill-guided, code-grounded LLM agent that mimics human spectroscopists' analytical workflow for spectrum-to-structure elucidation, outperforming existing models with much less training data.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based spectrum elucidation methods use direct spectrum-to-SMILES generation, which doesn't explicitly model the actual analytical workflow used by spectroscopists (peak interpretation, fragment reasoning, formula constraints, consistency checking).
AI.method: S3C-LLM uses a skill-guided, code-grounded approach: retrieves spectroscopy skills, executes analysis code to apply skills on input spectra, integrates peak-level evidence and formula constraints, then generates SMILES. Features include self-evolving spectroscopy skill library, thinking-augmented skill-code trajectory construction, and two-stage training (SFT + step-level RL).
AI.result: Experiments show S3C-LLM consistently outperforms current general LLMs and spectrum-specific models across various spectra benchmarks, while using less than 1/10th of SpectraLLM's training corpus.
AI.conclusion: The agentic approach that mimics human analytical workflow through skill-guided, code-grounded reasoning represents an effective paradigm for spectroscopic structure elucidation, achieving superior performance with significantly less training data.

title: Which Rules Matter Now? Policy-Centroid Routing Before an Intelligent System Acts
comment: Theory and research-program paper; 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Includes a synthetic worked example; reports no empirical efficacy result
summary:
Before an intelligent system can decide whether an action is allowed, it must first know which rules the action has approached. A single proposed action can implicate several policy regimes at once. Their requirements may stack, overlap, or qualify one another, yet many remain written in natural language while the action itself arrives as an incomplete description of intent. The first problem is not judgment. It is attention.
  Policy-centroid routing creates a layer before adjudication. It compresses expressions within each policy regime into one or more representative centroids, places the proposed action in the same semantic space, applies a declared measure, and routes every regime crossing a declared threshold to authoritative review. Several regimes may trigger at once. The output is a review agenda, not permission, prohibition, legality, breach, compliance, certification, or enforcement.
  The paper develops six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on studies comparing the hypothesis with structured workflows, lexical and semantic retrieval, hierarchical and direct classification, and selective prediction under matched review burden. The studies are designed to identify where policy geometry recovers applicable regimes, where compression loses rare or overlapping obligations, and where the mechanism should abstain. The paper includes a synthetic worked example and reports no empirical efficacy result.

AI.tldr: Policy-centroid routing creates a pre-adjudication layer that identifies which policy regimes apply to an action using semantic compression and similarity measures, generating a review agenda rather than making decisions.
AI.motivation: Before determining if an action is allowed, intelligent systems must identify which policy rules apply. Multiple policy regimes with overlapping, conflicting requirements written in natural language need attention before judgment can occur. Actions arrive as incomplete descriptions, making the first challenge one of identifying relevant policies rather than interpreting them.
AI.method: Policy-centroid routing compresses expressions within each policy regime into representative centroids in semantic space. Proposed actions are placed in the same semantic space, measured for similarity, and any regime crossing a declared threshold gets routed for authoritative review. The output is a review agenda identifying applicable regimes, not actual decisions.
AI.result: The paper develops six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on studies comparing the approach with existing methods (structured workflows, lexical/semantic retrieval, classification, selective prediction). Studies aim to identify where policy geometry works, where compression fails for rare/overlapping obligations, and when the mechanism should abstain. Includes synthetic worked example but reports no empirical efficacy results.
AI.conclusion: Policy-centroid routing addresses the attention problem before adjudication by identifying applicable policy regimes through semantic compression and similarity routing, separating the problem of identifying what rules apply from actually interpreting or judging compliance with those rules.

title: Selection-Aware Stress Testing for Interactive Agents
summary: Agent evaluations often use one benchmark to choose a workflow and then search for task types where its advantage weakens, so both conclusions are selected from the same data. We introduce Selection-Aware Semantic Stress Testing (\SASST{}), which learns a task reweighting from pre-execution features on discovery tasks and evaluates the same paired comparison on separate confirmation tasks. The protocol checks support and stability, uses joint bounds for all planned claims, and can return no claim. We prove conditional asymptotic validity under stated cluster assumptions. A forty-cluster audit finds Gaussian undercoverage and conservative Bonferroni $t$ bounds. In one 480-episode $τ$-bench study, a $3.75$ point discovery gain vanished on confirmation. A second-model study likewise confirmed neither a workflow benefit nor a stable stress rule.

AI.tldr: A method called SASST addresses selection bias in agent evaluations by separating discovery and confirmation tasks, providing statistical validity checks and bounds for claims, which reveals that apparent performance gains may disappear upon confirmation.
AI.motivation: Agent evaluations often suffer from selection bias where researchers use the same benchmark data to both choose workflows and evaluate them, leading to overoptimistic conclusions about workflow advantages that may not generalize.
AI.method: SASST (Selection-Aware Semantic Stress Testing) uses pre-execution features to learn task reweighting on discovery tasks, then evaluates the same comparison on separate confirmation tasks. The protocol checks support and stability, uses joint bounds for all planned claims, and can return no claim if results don't meet thresholds.
AI.result: The method demonstrated conditional asymptotic validity under cluster assumptions. In a 40-cluster audit, it found Gaussian undercoverage and conservative Bonferroni t-bounds. In a 480-episode study, a 3.75 point discovery gain vanished on confirmation. A second study confirmed neither workflow benefit nor stable stress rule.
AI.conclusion: SASST provides a statistically rigorous framework for agent evaluation that separates discovery and confirmation, revealing that apparent workflow advantages may be artifacts of selection bias rather than genuine improvements.

title: SkillZip Pro: Execution-Aware Dynamic Compression of Progressively Loaded Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
summary:
Production agent skills are directory bundles, not isolated prompts. The root is loaded at activation; references, schemas, scripts, assets, and nested subskills are loaded only when an execution path needs them. Compressing only the root misses most deployment cost and may move branch-specific details into the always-loaded context. Flattening instead destroys progressive-loading boundaries.
  We introduce \method, an evaluation-free compressor for complete, progressively loaded skill bundles. It leaves the agent harness unchanged and emits an ordinary directory. The method combines two safeguards. First, it compresses \emph{across files}, removing content from a reference or subskill when the root or a declared environment contract already provides it. Second, it preserves routing, so every required file and directly callable entry remains reachable after rewriting. Users can configure \method along two independent axes. \emph{One-Shot} mode rebuilds the full bundle; \emph{Continual} mode reuses state and applies Zip-on-Write after each evolution patch. \emph{Persistent} compression rewrites the shipped bundle to reduce storage and runtime context. \emph{Transient} compression keeps that bundle byte-identical and builds a task-specific view, reducing only per-run context after build cost. Entry contracts mark private, public, and conditional resources; a multi-entry audit preserves standalone public subskills.
  On a production content-moderation skill evaluated by our industrial multi-round harness, \method removes \hl{38\%} of skill bundle tokens and \hl{10.4\%} of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss, while an unprotected 71\% configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points to one-sided false positives. On a multi-entry bundle, \method effeciently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.

AI.tldr: Method for compressing AI agent skill bundles while maintaining progressive loading and preserving all execution paths, reducing tokens by 38% without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Production AI agent skills are organized as directory bundles with progressive loading (root loaded first, other resources loaded on-demand). Traditional compression methods either miss most deployment costs by compressing only the root, or destroy progressive-loading boundaries by flattening. There's a need for compression that works with complete skill bundles while preserving their progressive loading architecture.
AI.method: Introduces an evaluation-free compressor called \method that works on complete skill bundles. It uses two safeguards: 1) cross-file compression (removing content when already provided elsewhere), and 2) preserving routing (keeping all required files and callable entries reachable). Users can configure along two axes: One-Shot vs Continual mode (rebuild vs incremental), and Persistent vs Transient compression (rewrite bundle vs build task-specific views). Uses entry contracts to mark private/public/conditional resources and multi-entry audit to preserve standalone public subskills.
AI.result: On a production content-moderation skill: removes 38% of skill bundle tokens and 10.4% of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss. Unprotected 71% compression configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points due to one-sided false positives. On multi-entry bundles, efficiently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides effective compression for AI agent skill bundles that preserves progressive loading architecture and execution paths, significantly reducing token usage without sacrificing quality. The approach is practical for production deployment with configurable modes for different use cases.

title: Towards Stream Learning on Embedded Systems: Benchmarking the Memory Consumption of Stream Learning Methods
summary: Stream learning is commonly evaluated through predictive performance and adaptation to concept drift. However, sustained operation of a stream learner also requires predictable and bounded resource usage even on long streams. This requirement becomes even more critical when learning moves from servers to near-sensor embedded systems where memory and processing are scarce resources. In state-of-the-art stream learning, however, we perceive a strong focus on concept drift adaptation, whereas resource usage is often an evaluation byproduct. To close this gap, we benchmark seven representative stream classifiers on 13 real and synthetic streams under model-size budgets from 128\,KiB to approximately 8\,MiB. Our benchmark comprises a total of 6,463 experiments. We measure failure-aware accuracy, peak model size, time to budget exhaustion, and prediction-plus-update latency. The results reveal two distinct resource failure modes. Adaptive ensembles can exceed small budgets almost immediately because of their initial footprint, even when their size remains stable thereafter. Incremental trees can fit initially but grow throughout a long stream, with HoeffdingTrees (HT) and Extremely Fast Decision Trees (EFDT) increasing by median factors of 7.37 and 5.87. Explicitly compact methods remain the only viable option under the smallest budgets, but are usually overtaken as larger budgets make adaptive ensembles competitive. Hence, many state-of-the-art methods are only partially applicable in embedded systems or for long-running systems. We therefore call on the stream-learning community to make bounded resource usage a first-class design objective alongside drift adaptation, and propose concrete steps toward this goal, including an API through which stream learners can explicitly expose and respect resource budgets.

AI.tldr: Benchmark study reveals stream learning methods often fail under resource constraints in embedded systems, identifying two failure modes and calling for resource budgets as a first-class design objective.
AI.motivation: Stream learning research focuses heavily on concept drift adaptation, but neglects predictable/bounded resource usage, which is critical for sustained operation in memory-constrained embedded systems and long-running applications.
AI.method: Benchmarked 7 representative stream classifiers on 13 real and synthetic streams under model-size budgets from 128KiB to ~8MiB, conducting 6,463 experiments measuring failure-aware accuracy, peak model size, time to budget exhaustion, and prediction-plus-update latency.
AI.result: Identified two distinct resource failure modes: 1) Adaptive ensembles exceed small budgets immediately due to initial footprint, 2) Incremental trees fit initially but grow throughout long streams (HT and EFDT grow by median factors of 7.37 and 5.87). Explicitly compact methods work best under smallest budgets but are overtaken by adaptive ensembles under larger budgets.
AI.conclusion: Many state-of-the-art stream learning methods are only partially applicable in embedded/long-running systems. The community should make bounded resource usage a first-class design objective alongside drift adaptation, and develop APIs for exposing/respecting resource budgets.

title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
summary: Large language models can often generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces, but reliably identifying the correct solution among multiple candidates remains a key challenge. Existing test-time reasoning pipelines typically rely on text-based verifiers that re-read each generated solution, making verification an expensive component of inference. Prior work has shown, however, that LLMs often encode correctness-related signals in their internal representations, including awareness of when their own answers are likely to be wrong. Building on this observation, we introduce HSRM, a lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate solutions by directly reading the generator's internal representations rather than re-processing its text. HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidates. It is trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring neither human-written process supervision nor a large pretrained verifier. Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator--dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters, providing an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation.

AI.tldr: HSRM: Lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies math reasoning solutions by reading LLM's internal representations instead of reprocessing text, achieving comparable performance to larger text-based verifiers with far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces but struggle to identify correct solutions among multiple candidates. Existing text-based verifiers are expensive as they require re-reading generated solutions, while prior work shows LLMs encode correctness signals in internal representations.
AI.method: HSRM extracts hidden states from frozen generator LLMs at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidate solutions. Trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring no human-written process supervision or large pretrained verifier.
AI.result: Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator-dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters.
AI.conclusion: HSRM provides an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation, reducing computational cost while maintaining or improving verification performance.

title: Nonparametric Contextual Pricing and Inventory Learning under Censored Demand
summary: In online retailing, when a product sells out, a retailer often sees only the units sold, not how many customers would have bought it had inventory been available. However, the inventory level determines how much demand is revealed, and this information can influence subsequent decisions and future profits. We study an online selling problem in which, in each round, the seller observes a market context and then makes pricing and stocking decisions based on censored sales data from previous rounds. The challenge is to learn a context-dependent pricing and stocking policy without assuming a particular formula for demand or observing realized profit. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a Mean-Calibrated Kernel UCB (MCK-UCB) algorithm that turns each incomplete sales record into a reliable guide for both inventory and price decisions, using data from past rounds with similar market conditions. This design allows us to learn while serving customers, without a separate exploration phase or the need to recover all demand hidden by stockouts. We prove the minimax optimality of the proposed algorithm, with strictly faster rates when expected profit varies more smoothly with price. Comprehensive numerical experiments have been conducted to confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MCK-UCB algorithm for online retail pricing and inventory decisions using censored sales data without assuming specific demand formulas or observing full profit information.
AI.motivation: In online retail, when products sell out, retailers only see actual sales (censored data) but not lost demand. This incomplete information makes optimal pricing and stocking decisions challenging, especially when demand patterns are unknown and context-dependent.
AI.method: Proposes Mean-Calibrated Kernel UCB (MCK-UCB) algorithm that learns context-dependent pricing and stocking policies using censored sales data. It transforms incomplete sales records into reliable guides by leveraging data from past rounds with similar market conditions, enabling learning while serving customers without separate exploration phases.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves minimax optimality with strictly faster convergence rates when expected profit varies more smoothly with price. Comprehensive numerical experiments confirm the algorithm's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: MCK-UCB provides an effective solution for joint pricing and inventory optimization in online retail using only censored sales data, overcoming the limitations of incomplete demand observation while achieving theoretical optimality guarantees.

title: VFR-Audit: Verdict-Level Reliability for Fairness Audits in Hospital Length-of-Stay Prediction
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Fairness audits in clinical Artificial Intelligence convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass-or-fail verdicts against operational thresholds, where hospital governance boards, payers, and regulators act on the resulting verdicts. Such audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, thus the same verdict can flip between pass and fail across audits. Existing uncertainty methods such as Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests address verdict instability only at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into a verdict-stability claim remains a manual step that scales poorly across the (model, metric, attribute) cells an audit covers. Existing uncertainty methods also leave open whether bias-mitigation steps, such as reweighing or per-group threshold shifts, yield a stable passing verdict at the cost of model discrimination measured as AUROC or AUPRC.To address this verdict-stability gap, we propose VFR-Audit, a framework built around the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar bounded between 0 and 0.5 that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. VFR-Audit reports VFR alongside three reliability axes, namely within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa.

AI.tldr: VFR-Audit is a framework that addresses instability in fairness verdicts in clinical AI by introducing Verdict Flip Rate (VFR) to measure probability of verdict reversal under resampling, alongside three reliability metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness audits in clinical AI suffer from verdict instability - the same model can flip between pass/fail across different audits. Current uncertainty methods only address continuous metrics and don't directly handle verdict stability, leaving uncertainty about whether bias mitigation yields stable passing verdicts.
AI.method: Proposed VFR-Audit framework with Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar between 0-0.5 measuring probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. Reports VFR alongside three reliability axes: within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa.
AI.result: The proposed framework provides a systematic way to measure and report verdict stability in fairness audits, addressing gaps where existing methods only handle continuous metric uncertainty but not verdict-level stability.
AI.conclusion: VFR-Audit addresses the verdict-stability gap in clinical AI fairness audits by providing a comprehensive framework that quantifies verdict instability and assesses reliability across multiple dimensions, enabling more robust decision-making by governance boards, payers, and regulators.

title: Reproducible macroscopic dynamics in a closed-loop human-AI learning system
summary: Closed-loop human-AI systems generate high-dimensional behavioural trajectories whose collective dynamics remain obscure. Using 297,915 learners' adaptive-tutoring histories, we define semantic order variables before model fitting and test them in user-disjoint cohorts. The state exhibits reproducible basin-like flow and operationally defined, state-heterogeneous metastable-like kinetics. A construction-matched null distinguishes normalised-memory relaxation from a reproducible excess field. A four-term conditional mechanism recovers population drift (r = 0.946; learner-bootstrap 95% CI, 0.935-0.955). Predictive event-level self-supervised learning recovers the state and learned-plane flow; null-referenced corrections retain directional, partial-amplitude excess-field structure without full calibration. Shuffled-order training reverses learned-plane flow on ordered trajectories; support-alignment randomisation selectively reduces inward transport. Both axes remain linearly accessible without state supervision. Without cross-model fitting, the models share leading population drift (r = 0.866; learner-bootstrap 95% CI, 0.857-0.875) and persistence ordering; residual directions remain model-specific. These results identify an externally anchored leading-order effective field linking empirical dynamics, an interpretable mechanism and neural computation.

AI.tldr: Researchers analyzed 297,915 learners' tutoring histories to discover reproducible collective dynamics in human-AI learning systems, identifying an interpretable effective field connecting empirical dynamics, mechanisms, and neural computation.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop human-AI systems generate complex high-dimensional behavioral trajectories, but their collective dynamics remain poorly understood. The authors aim to uncover reproducible patterns in large-scale adaptive tutoring data.
AI.method: Analyzed 297,915 learners' adaptive-tutoring histories using semantic order variables, model fitting in user-disjoint cohorts, null-model comparisons, and predictive event-level self-supervised learning. Used shuffled-order training and support-alignment randomization for validation.
AI.result: The system exhibits reproducible basin-like flow and metastable-like kinetics. A four-term conditional mechanism recovers population drift (r = 0.946). Self-supervised learning recovers state and learned-plane flow. Models share leading population drift (r = 0.866) without cross-model fitting.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies an externally anchored leading-order effective field that links empirical dynamics, interpretable mechanisms, and neural computation in human-AI learning systems.

title: Predicting Residential Rents in Dakar Using Machine Learning
summary: Dakar's residential rental market remains poorly documented despite its economic and social importance: 54.4% of households are renters, compared to 23.3% nationally. This study develops a complete machine learning pipeline to predict residential rents in Dakar, from data collection to model interpretation. An original dataset of 1,507 rental listings was built through systematic web scraping and a documented cleaning pipeline, then enriched with four purpose-built features, including a luxury score and a keyword-based quality score. Five models were compared: linear regression, Random Forest (baseline), XGBoost, and LightGBM optimized through Bayesian optimization with Optuna, using leakage-free KFold target encoding for location. The optimized XGBoost model achieved the best performance with an $R^2$ of 0.847, an MAE of 210,902 XOF, and an RMSE of 324,195 XOF. Feature importance was assessed using native XGBoost gain and SHAP values, revealing a substantial difference in the ranking of location, which appears as a minor predictor by gain but as the second most influential variable by SHAP. This result carries methodological implications for hedonic studies using target-encoded categorical variables. This study provides an interpretable benchmark for Dakar's rental market and highlights several avenues for improvement, including the integration of geospatial features and conformal prediction.

AI.tldr: Machine learning pipeline predicts Dakar residential rents with XGBoost achieving best performance (R²=0.847), using systematic data collection, novel features, and revealing methodological insights about location encoding effects.
AI.motivation: Dakar's residential rental market is economically and socially important (54.4% of households are renters vs 23.3% nationally) but remains poorly documented. There's a need for reliable rental price prediction and understanding market dynamics.
AI.method: Complete ML pipeline: 1) Built original dataset of 1,507 rental listings via web scraping, 2) Developed cleaning pipeline, 3) Created four novel features (luxury score, keyword-based quality score), 4) Compared five models (linear regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) with Bayesian optimization via Optuna, 5) Used leakage-free KFold target encoding for location.
AI.result: Optimized XGBoost achieved best performance: R²=0.847, MAE=210,902 XOF, RMSE=324,195 XOF. Feature importance analysis revealed significant discrepancy: location appears as minor predictor by XGBoost gain but second most influential by SHAP values, highlighting methodological implications for target-encoded categorical variables.
AI.conclusion: Study provides an interpretable benchmark for Dakar's rental market with methodological insights about target encoding effects. Future improvements suggested: integration of geospatial features and conformal prediction. The approach offers practical tools for market analysis and decision-making.

title: One Policy Is Enough: Single-Agent Reinforcement Learning Outperforms Tree Search for Chemistry Tool Learning
summary: Chemistry questions often demand exact computation and database lookups that a language model cannot supply from its parameters, so it must reach for external tools. Tool use here is a three-part problem: select the right tool from a large pool, fill it with correctly typed arguments, and chain calls so that each consumes the outputs of the last. CheMatAgent, a previously published system, addresses this with hierarchical evolutionary MCTS: separate policy and execution models searching tool-call trees under two learned critics, one regressed partly onto GPT-assigned scores. We show that a single policy suffices. Our model interleaves reasoning, tool calls, and returns in one left-to-right generation, trained by a supervised warm-up and then outcome-level reinforcement learning against a programmatic reward read directly off the gold call chain, which leaves no learned critic and no judge in the training loop. On ChemToolBench multiple-tool comprehensive chemistry, on both backbones CheMatAgent use, we improve Tool F1 by 5.5% and Return F1 by 9.6% on Qwen-2.5-7B, and by 3.7% and 3.9% on Llama-3.1-8B, compared with their strongest search configuration, at one model invocation per question, against a search whose cost grows with the tree; we also lead answer Pass Rate on Qwen-2.5-7B.

AI.tldr: A new approach replaces complex hierarchical evolutionary MCTS with a single policy model that generates tool calls interleaved with reasoning, achieving better performance at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Chemistry questions require exact computation and database lookups that language models cannot handle internally, necessitating tool use with three challenges: selecting the right tool, providing correct typed arguments, and chaining calls properly. Existing systems like CheMatAgent use complex hierarchical evolutionary MCTS with multiple models and critics.
AI.method: Proposes a single policy model that interleaves reasoning, tool calls, and returns in one left-to-right generation. Training uses supervised warm-up followed by outcome-level reinforcement learning with a programmatic reward derived directly from gold call chains, eliminating learned critics and judge models.
AI.result: On ChemToolBench for multiple-tool chemistry tasks, improves Tool F1 by 5.5% and Return F1 by 9.6% on Qwen-2.5-7B, and by 3.7% and 3.9% on Llama-3.1-8B compared to CheMatAgent's strongest search configuration. Achieves one model invocation per question versus search methods with tree-growing costs. Also leads answer Pass Rate on Qwen-2.5-7B.
AI.conclusion: A single policy model with interleaved generation and direct outcome-based reinforcement learning outperforms complex multi-model search systems while being more efficient and avoiding training instability from learned critics.

title: CAER: Causal Action Effect Reweighting for World Model Training
