summary: World models are becoming core infrastructure for embodied intelligence, with action-conditioned video generation providing controllable predictions of how scenes evolve after agent interventions. Yet existing models are commonly trained with space-time-uniform mean squared error, allowing abundant background tokens to dominate the gradient while sparse interaction dynamics remain under-optimized; such uniform fitting rewards reconstructing appearance rather than learning how actions change the world. We introduce Causal Action Effect Reweighting (CAER), a general training paradigm that redistributes supervision toward the tokens whose predicted future is causally affected by the action. CAER contrasts the model's own predictions with and without action conditioning to localize these tokens online, then normalizes the resulting effect map into a weight that preserves the total coefficient mass and changes only where it is spent. This online signal requires no external annotations or offline preprocessing, avoids additional data-processing time, and scales naturally with model and dataset size. Experiments across heterogeneous action-conditioned world-model tasks show that CAER converges to better solutions than uniform MSE training, with consistent improvements in the physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality of generated videos.

AI.tldr: CAER is a training paradigm for action-conditioned world models that reweights supervision toward tokens causally affected by actions, improving video prediction quality and physical consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing world models use uniform MSE loss that emphasizes background reconstruction over learning action effects, causing sparse interaction dynamics to be under-optimized while abundant background tokens dominate gradients.
AI.method: CAER (Causal Action Effect Reweighting) contrasts model predictions with and without action conditioning to localize causally affected tokens online, then normalizes the effect map into a weight that preserves total coefficient mass and redistributes supervision to action-relevant regions.
AI.result: CAER converges to better solutions than uniform MSE training across heterogeneous action-conditioned world-model tasks, with consistent improvements in physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality of generated videos.
AI.conclusion: CAER provides a general, scalable training paradigm for world models that focuses learning on action-relevant scene changes without needing external annotations or offline preprocessing, enabling better prediction of how actions change the world.

title: Singular Curvature in ReLU Training:Differentiation and the Gradient-Flow Limit Need Not Commute
summary: Gradient descent (GD) is explicit Euler for gradient flow, but a state-accurate continuous-time surrogate need not remain accurate after differentiation. At every fixed nonresonant step size, ordinary automatic differentiation exactly differentiates the executed hard-ReLU GD program. We prove that, over a fixed finite horizon, the GD states converge and these exact discrete derivatives approach an event-free regional propagator, whereas the derivative of the limiting flow also contains speed-normalized activation-event transfers. A prepoint Stieltjes representation separates the absolutely continuous regional Hessian from atomic interface curvature; one nonzero gradient jump produces an exactly rank-one endpoint discrepancy, and global convexity prevents complete multi-event cancellation whenever an event is strict. Nevertheless, a standard family of globally 1-strongly convex residual-ReLU squared-loss risks realizes arbitrarily large reciprocal sensitivity ratios on open initialization sets, with a uniform transversality margin. The same discrete-versus-flow decomposition extends to parameters and reverse-mode adjoints; resolved smoothing in the scalar or autonomous-normal regime and consistent event localization recover the flow sensitivity. The results concern deterministic full-batch, finite-horizon dynamics with a stable finite itinerary of separated same-direction transverse events; they are consistency theorems, not prevalence claims for large-scale training.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the discrepancy between gradient descent's exact discrete derivatives and the derivative of its limiting continuous-time gradient flow, showing that activation events in ReLU networks create fundamentally different sensitivity structures that cannot be fully canceled even in convex settings.
AI.motivation: Gradient descent (GD) can be viewed as explicit Euler discretization of gradient flow, but the exact discrete derivatives computed by automatic differentiation may not match the derivative of the limiting continuous flow, particularly when activation events (like ReLU switches) occur during optimization.
AI.method: The authors prove convergence results for GD states and their exact discrete derivatives over finite horizons, using a prepoint Stieltjes representation to separate continuous Hessian components from atomic interface curvature at activation events. They analyze deterministic full-batch dynamics with stable finite itineraries of separated transverse events.
AI.result: 1) Exact discrete derivatives approach an event-free regional propagator while flow derivatives include event transfers. 2) Nonzero gradient jumps produce rank-one endpoint discrepancies. 3) Global convexity prevents complete multi-event cancellation for strict events. 4) Globally 1-strongly convex ReLU squared-loss risks can exhibit arbitrarily large sensitivity ratios on open initialization sets. 5) The decomposition extends to parameters and adjoints, with smoothing recovering flow sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes fundamental consistency theorems showing the structural differences between discrete GD derivatives and continuous flow derivatives due to activation events in ReLU networks, emphasizing that these are deterministic consistency results rather than prevalence claims for large-scale training.

title: Responsible Integration of AI in Cancer Genomics: Barriers, Risks, and Pathways to Trustworthy Clinical Translation
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly used to extract, integrate, and interpret biomedical knowledge relevant to cancer genomics, yet their translation into routine clinical oncology has been comparatively slow. The central challenge is not computational capability alone, but trustworthy integration into clinical workflows. This review examines how NLP and AI support the cancer genomics pipeline, from literature mining and automated variant interpretation to clinical trial matching, knowledge graph construction, and multimodal data integration. We identify four interrelated translational failure domains: evidence inconsistency, explainability and uncertainty, data governance and reproducibility, and interoperability. Rather than considering these challenges in isolation, we take a systems-level view, focusing on their interaction across the translational pathway. We propose a conceptual framework and roadmap for addressing these domains through rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle. Progress toward routine clinical use will depend less on further improving model capability than on systematically addressing these interacting failure domains from development through deployment and post-deployment monitoring.

AI.tldr: This review examines challenges in translating AI/NLP for cancer genomics into clinical oncology, identifying four failure domains and proposing a systems-level framework for trustworthy integration.
AI.motivation: AI and NLP are increasingly used for cancer genomics but face slow translation into routine clinical oncology. The main challenge is trustworthy integration into clinical workflows, not just computational capability.
AI.method: The paper examines how NLP/AI support the cancer genomics pipeline (literature mining, variant interpretation, clinical trial matching, knowledge graphs, multimodal integration) and identifies four translational failure domains through a systems-level review.
AI.result: Identified four interrelated translational failure domains: 1) evidence inconsistency, 2) explainability and uncertainty, 3) data governance and reproducibility, and 4) interoperability. Proposed a conceptual framework addressing these through validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and human oversight.
AI.conclusion: Progress toward routine clinical use depends less on improving model capability and more on systematically addressing these interacting failure domains across the AI lifecycle from development through deployment and monitoring.

title: A Universal Context-Reuse Layer for Cross-Model KV Sharing
summary: Modern large language model (LLM) serving systems increasingly operate over repeated or shared context, yet each model typically performs its own prefill computation even when another model has already processed the same input. Existing KV-cache reuse mechanisms substantially reduce redundant computation within a single model, but generally assume that the producer and consumer of a cache are identical. We study \emph{cross-model KV sharing}, which translates the KV state produced by a source model into a representation that can be consumed by a different target model, including models that differ in scale, architecture, attention configuration, tokenizer, and model family. We evaluate the approach in both within-family and cross-family settings. For Qwen2.5-7B $\rightarrow$ Qwen2.5-1.5B, translated KV states improve LongBench2 accuracy from 27.59\% to 34.48\%, a gain of 6.89 percentage points over the native 1.5B baseline, while reducing handoff cost relative to native target prefill. For the cross-family Qwen2.5-1.5B $\rightarrow$ Gemma-2-2B setting, KV handoff reduces target-side prefill cost by up to 67.05\% at 4K context length while maintaining decoding perplexity close to native-model baselines. In a more heterogeneous Llama3.1-70B $\rightarrow$ Qwen2.5-7B setting, cross-family handoff achieves 44.0\% accuracy compared with 45.7\% for native Qwen2.5-7B inference, while reducing measured latency from 899ms to 138ms. These results provide initial evidence that KV states can serve as transferable computational representations rather than strictly model-local caches, and motivate \emph{context mobility} as a systems abstraction for reducing redundant prefill across heterogeneous LLM and multi-agent inference workflows.

AI.tldr: Cross-model KV sharing enables reuse of precomputed KV states across different LLMs, reducing redundant computation while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Current LLM serving systems waste computation by repeating prefill for shared context across different models, even when KV-cache reuse only works within the same model.
AI.method: Cross-model KV sharing translates KV states produced by a source model into representations consumable by different target models, handling differences in scale, architecture, attention, tokenizer, and model family.
AI.result: Substantial performance improvements: Qwen2.5-7B→1.5B gains 6.89pp accuracy on LongBench2; Qwen2.5-1.5B→Gemma-2-2B reduces prefill cost by 67.05%; Llama3.1-70B→Qwen2.5-7B reduces latency from 899ms to 138ms while maintaining comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: KV states can serve as transferable computational representations across heterogeneous models, motivating "context mobility" as a systems abstraction to reduce redundant prefill in multi-agent LLM workflows.

title: CARVE: Verified Expansion for Variable-Length Generation in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models predict tokens from a partially observed response canvas, enabling bidirectional conditioning and parallel token refinement. Yet standard masked-diffusion decoders use a rigid inference interface: the number of masked positions allocated to the answer is fixed before generation begins. Choosing this length is difficult. A short canvas can truncate reasoning or code, while a long canvas wastes computation and can perturb denoising. We introduce CARVE (Counterfactual-Aware Reveal with Verified Expansion), a training-free variable-length algorithm for masked diffusion LMs. Starting from a shorter canvas, CARVE can grow the response during decoding by inserting additional [MASK] positions. Rather than keeping every insertion, CARVE tests a candidate expanded canvas and asks a counterfactual question: would the model make similar predictions for the unresolved positions in the original canvas if the extra masked space were present? The inserted masks are kept only when they induce low Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence on aligned unresolved positions. This makes length growth a verified stability decision rather than a pure confidence heuristic. CARVE applies without retraining to both full-canvas and blockwise diffusion decoders. Across code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CARVE consistently improves average performance over fixed-length baselines across all evaluated model families. Crucially, CARVE achieves these accuracy gains while reducing inference cost, reaching half the FLOPs of fixed-length decoding in some settings.

AI.tldr: CARVE is a training-free variable-length algorithm for masked diffusion language models that dynamically expands the response canvas during decoding using counterfactual verification, improving performance while reducing inference costs.
AI.motivation: Standard masked-diffusion decoders require fixing the response canvas length before generation, which is problematic: choosing too short truncates reasoning/code, while too long wastes computation and can disrupt the denoising process.
AI.method: CARVE starts from a shorter canvas and dynamically grows it by inserting additional [MASK] positions. It tests candidate expansions using counterfactual verification - measuring Jensen-Shannon divergence between predictions in original vs expanded canvases for unresolved positions, keeping inserts only when divergence is low.
AI.result: CARVE consistently improves average performance over fixed-length baselines across code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks for all evaluated model families, while reducing inference costs (reaching half the FLOPs of fixed-length decoding in some settings).
AI.conclusion: CARVE provides an effective training-free solution for variable-length generation in masked diffusion LMs, transforming canvas length determination from a fixed pre-generation decision to a verified stability decision during decoding.

title: A Human-in-the-Loop Autonomous Agent for Industry Time Series Forecasting
summary: Real-world time-series forecasting is rarely a one-shot model invocation: practitioners must formulate tasks, connect data and models, incorporate domain expertise, assess prediction plausibility, and communicate uncertainty. Specialized forecasting models provide strong numerical predictions but usually operate in fixed pipelines, while general-purpose large language model (LLM) agents often lack forecasting-specific checks, constraints, and stopping rules. We present CastClaw, a human-in-the-loop autonomous forecasting system built through forecasting-oriented harness engineering. CastClaw connects data, specialized models, analytical tools, user input, and a versioned execution record in one runtime. Users specify the target, horizon, constraints, and hypotheses in natural language. Starting from a supplied or model-generated forecast, CastClaw checks temporal patterns and user constraints; when evidence is missing, it retrieves context, runs an analysis or another model, or asks the user. It then keeps, revises, or escalates the result under explicit stopping conditions. The output contains the final forecast and an execution report recording inputs, evidence, actions, and revisions. In this five-dataset electricity-price setting, CastClaw reports the lowest point-estimate MSE and MAE among 16 baselines. A Nord Pool case demonstrates the inspectable workflow. CastClaw was also validated offline on provincial electricity-load data from North China covering January--June 2026.

AI.tldr: CastClaw is a human-in-the-loop autonomous forecasting system that combines specialized forecasting models with LLM agents through forecasting-oriented harness engineering, enabling natural language specification and iterative refinement of forecasts with checks, constraints, and stopping rules.
AI.motivation: Real-world forecasting requires more than just one-shot model invocation - it involves task formulation, data/model connections, domain expertise incorporation, prediction plausibility assessment, and uncertainty communication. Specialized forecasting models operate in fixed pipelines, while general LLM agents lack forecasting-specific checks, constraints, and stopping rules.
AI.method: CastClaw uses forecasting-oriented harness engineering to connect data, specialized models, analytical tools, user input, and versioned execution records. Users specify targets, horizons, constraints, and hypotheses in natural language. The system starts with a forecast, checks temporal patterns and constraints, retrieves context when evidence is missing, runs analyses or other models, or asks users, then keeps/revises/escalates results under explicit stopping conditions.
AI.result: In a five-dataset electricity-price setting, CastClaw reports the lowest point-estimate MSE and MAE among 16 baselines. A Nord Pool case demonstrates the inspectable workflow, and offline validation on provincial electricity-load data from North China covering January-June 2026 shows the system's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: CastClaw successfully bridges the gap between specialized forecasting models and general LLM agents by creating a human-in-the-loop autonomous forecasting system with built-in checks, constraints, and stopping rules, providing both accurate forecasts and transparent execution reports for real-world forecasting applications.

title: Learning Action Models with Conditional and Quantified Effects via Uncertainty-Guided Exploration
summary: Accurate action models are critical for effective planning. Existing action-model learning methods largely assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when learning conditional and quantified effects. We present Online Hypothesis-Driven Conditional Action Model Learning (OHCAM), an online approach for learning action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited interactions with the environment. OHCAM maintains a belief over hypothesized action models and actively selects informative actions to reduce uncertainty by maximizing disagreement among competing hypotheses, while being robust to noisy observations. To enable scalability, OHCAM begins with a small set of simple action model hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when the current hypotheses become inconsistent with the data. Experiments on six benchmark planning domains demonstrate that OHCAM is sample efficient in learning action models that solve substantially more tasks than baselines, even with observation noise. We validate OHCAM on two tasks using a Kinova Gen3 robot, demonstrating the real-world applicability of our approach.

AI.tldr: OHCAM is an online algorithm that efficiently learns action models with conditional and quantified effects by maintaining hypothesis beliefs and actively selecting informative actions, demonstrating sample efficiency and real-world applicability even with observation noise.
AI.motivation: Existing action-model learning methods either assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when learning complex conditional and quantified effects, creating a need for scalable online learning approaches that can handle real-world complexity from limited environment interactions.
AI.method: OHCAM maintains a belief over hypothesized action models and actively selects informative actions to reduce uncertainty by maximizing disagreement among competing hypotheses. It starts with simple action model hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when current hypotheses become inconsistent with data, ensuring scalability.
AI.result: Experiments on six benchmark planning domains show OHCAM is sample efficient in learning action models that solve substantially more tasks than baselines, even with observation noise. Validation on Kinova Gen3 robot tasks demonstrates real-world applicability.
AI.conclusion: OHCAM provides an effective online approach for learning complex action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited interactions, offering both theoretical sample efficiency and practical real-world applicability for robotic systems.

title: Sparse Competition during Training For the Emergence of Specialized Modules
summary: Modularity in deep neural networks has been proposed as a means of improving both interpretability and training by promoting disentangled representations and reducing redundancy. In this work, we study the emergence of modular structure through competition dynamics between groups of neurons during training. We introduce a method that (i) maintains near-baseline accuracy, (ii) induces usage-based modularity by sparsely routing inputs to neuron groups, and (iii) encourages specialization of these modules, such that their activations are correlated with input classes. We evaluate the proposed approach on ImageNet-100 and CIFAR-100 and show that with it, specialized modules emerge without module-level supervision. These modules capture a meaningful high-level structure in the data, with individual modules responding to semantic categories (e.g., dogs or vehicles). We also study the emergence of a hierarchical partition of sub-tasks depending on the number of modules. Our results suggest that competitive dynamics can serve as a simple mechanism for inducing functional modularity in standard architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a competition-based method that induces modular structure in neural networks without explicit supervision, enabling specialized modules that respond to semantic categories while maintaining near-baseline accuracy.
AI.motivation: Modularity in deep neural networks is desirable for improving interpretability and training efficiency by promoting disentangled representations and reducing redundancy. The paper aims to study how modular structure can emerge through competitive dynamics rather than being explicitly designed.
AI.method: The proposed method uses competition dynamics between groups of neurons during training. It features: (i) sparse routing of inputs to neuron groups to induce usage-based modularity, (ii) encouragement of module specialization such that activations correlate with input classes, and (iii) maintenance of near-baseline accuracy. The approach operates without module-level supervision.
AI.result: When evaluated on ImageNet-100 and CIFAR-100, specialized modules emerged automatically, capturing meaningful high-level semantic structure (e.g., individual modules responding to categories like dogs or vehicles). The method also showed hierarchical partitioning of sub-tasks depending on the number of modules, demonstrating emergent functional organization.
AI.conclusion: Competitive dynamics can serve as a simple yet effective mechanism for inducing functional modularity in standard neural network architectures, potentially offering benefits for interpretability and training efficiency without requiring complex architectural changes or extensive supervision.

title: MNIST-PRO: MNIST is Back as a Partially Observable World for AI Agents
summary: AI agents in partially observable environments need to coordinate active sensing with working memory to maintain an evolving perceptual state. However, existing benchmarks struggle to isolate this perceptual-state construction and interpretation capability because they introduce physical and control complexities. We address this with MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that isolates agentic perception by converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. We evaluate ten multimodal models across four memory representations, including raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas. While models excel under full observability, partial observability exposes a clear performance gap. We identify three distinct bottlenecks. First, perceptual-state construction and interpretation present a challenge, as agents struggle to integrate fragmented glimpses. Second, agents often stop exploring before they see the full sequence. Third, models often fail to revise early, incorrect beliefs even when faced with subsequent contradictory evidence. These results show that simply acquiring visual evidence is not enough. Agents must also be able to build and update a reliable perceptual state.

AI.tldr: MNIST-PRO is a benchmark isolating agentic perception by converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints, revealing that current multimodal models struggle with perceptual-state construction and interpretation under partial observability.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks struggle to isolate perceptual-state construction and interpretation capabilities because they introduce physical and control complexities. There's a need to specifically evaluate how AI agents coordinate active sensing with working memory to maintain evolving perceptual states in partially observable environments.
AI.method: Created MNIST-PRO benchmark that converts MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. Evaluated ten multimodal models across four memory representations: raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and consolidated visual canvas.
AI.result: Models excel under full observability but show clear performance gap under partial observability. Three bottlenecks identified: 1) Difficulty with perceptual-state construction and interpretation from fragmented glimpses, 2) Premature exploration stopping before full sequence observation, 3) Failure to revise incorrect early beliefs despite contradictory evidence.
AI.conclusion: Simply acquiring visual evidence is insufficient; agents must build and update reliable perceptual states. Current multimodal models need improved capabilities for constructing, interpreting, and revising perceptual states from sequential, partial observations.

title: Controlling Refusal Behavior of LLMs via Stiefel-Constrained Rotation Steering
summary: Activation steering has emerged as a lightweight approach for controlling model refusal at inference time. A growing line of research explores trainable rotations of activations to develop geometrically principled intervention mechanisms. However, existing techniques rely on auxiliary constructs, such as refusal vectors, to define these rotations. In our work, we develop a self-contained methodology for learning parameter-efficient rotational transformations based on Riemannian optimization. We empirically validate the proposed scheme, demonstrating its superiority in intervention efficiency. An extensive ablation study highlights the importance of key design choices in our method. Our results identify the proposed rotation-based steering scheme as a promising direction for more reliable control over the behavior of LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-contained Riemannian optimization method for learning parameter-efficient rotational transformations to steer LLM activations, showing superior intervention efficiency compared to existing refusal vector approaches.
AI.motivation: Current activation steering methods for controlling model refusal rely on auxiliary constructs like refusal vectors to define rotations, which adds complexity and may not be geometrically optimal. There's a need for a more self-contained, principled approach to rotational transformations.
AI.method: Develops a self-contained methodology for learning parameter-efficient rotational transformations using Riemannian optimization. This approach avoids relying on auxiliary refusal vectors and instead learns rotations directly through geometrically principled optimization on manifolds.
AI.result: The proposed scheme demonstrates superior intervention efficiency compared to existing methods. Extensive ablation studies highlight the importance of key design choices, showing the rotation-based steering scheme effectively controls LLM behavior.
AI.conclusion: The Riemannian optimization-based rotation steering scheme represents a promising direction for more reliable control over LLM behavior, offering a geometrically principled and parameter-efficient alternative to refusal vector approaches.

title: Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents
summary: Agent working memory is heterogeneous. Objects such as instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, and agent-generated state play different semantic roles and exhibit different size, retention, and representation profiles. Recent work has begun to explore memory-management mechanisms that account for such heterogeneity. This work focuses on semantic heterogeneity and studies how it should shape the management and evaluation of working memory in coding agents. Across 55 archived coding-agent trajectories, we find that semantically different working-memory objects exhibit distinct retention and compression behavior. This heterogeneity motivates semantically informed memory management. We study two semantically informed strategies: an object-aware compression policy and a retrieval-based policy. Their evaluation shows that calibration gains may not transfer to held-out tasks, and that equal token budgets do not imply equal delivered context or management cost. A real-system replay further exposes serving limits that nominal budgets alone do not capture. Together, these results show why semantic structure matters for agent working memory and why evaluating memory-management strategies requires more than a nominal token budget. We organize these lessons into four levels: stored state, delivered context, management work, and task or process outcome.

AI.tldr: Agent working memory has semantic heterogeneity where different objects (instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, etc.) have distinct retention/compression patterns, requiring semantically-aware memory management strategies.
AI.motivation: Recent work explores memory-management mechanisms for heterogeneous agent working memory, but focuses specifically on how semantic heterogeneity should shape the management and evaluation of working memory in coding agents.
AI.method: Analyzed 55 archived coding-agent trajectories to understand retention/compression behavior, then studied two semantically informed strategies: object-aware compression policy and retrieval-based policy. Conducted evaluation with calibration gains, token budget analysis, and real-system replay.
AI.result: Found semantically different working-memory objects exhibit distinct retention/compression behavior. Semantically informed strategies showed calibration gains don't always transfer to held-out tasks, equal token budgets don't imply equal delivered context or management cost, and real-system replay reveals serving limits not captured by nominal budgets.
AI.conclusion: Semantic structure matters for agent working memory, and evaluating memory-management strategies requires going beyond nominal token budgets. Proposed four-level evaluation framework: stored state, delivered context, management work, and task/process outcome.

title: Language-Informed Flow Matching for Trend-Guided Structure-Based 3D Molecular Generation
summary: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) requires ligands that satisfy both 3D target affinity and 1D chemical validity. Existing controllable generation methods often rely on task-specific fine-tuning or externally imposed sampling-time guidance, adding cost and potentially conflicting with evolving 3D geometric constraints. We propose LiFT, a language-informed cross-modal framework built on Flow Matching for trend-guided 3D molecular generation across both de novo design and scaffold hopping. LiFT uses a "Sense-Evolve-Assemble" agent to generate target-aware SMILES as intermediate chemical conditions, from which a pre-trained chemical foundation model extracts continuous semantic priors. These priors are integrated into geometric generation through a lightweight semantic projector with zero-initialized adaptive normalization for stable cross-modal conditioning. We further introduce a Self-Conditioned Decoupled Router (SCDR), which modulates the velocity field according to intermediate structural states during ODE integration. Experiments on Cross-Docked2020 show that LiFT achieves competitive distribution matching while improving medicinal chemistry metrics and maintaining competitive structural validity under task-steering settings without additional generator fine-tuning. Our results suggest that language-derived chemical priors provide effective trend-level guidance for 3D molecular generation. Code and released artifacts are available at https://github.com/kasurl/LiFT.

AI.tldr: LiFT is a framework for 3D molecular generation using language-informed cross-modal conditioning through Flow Matching, achieving competitive performance without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing SBDD methods often require task-specific fine-tuning or external sampling-time guidance, which adds cost and can conflict with evolving 3D geometric constraints. There's a need for more efficient and stable 3D molecular generation.
AI.method: LiFT uses a "Sense-Evolve-Assemble" agent to generate target-aware SMILES as intermediate chemical conditions. A pre-trained chemical foundation model extracts continuous semantic priors from these, which are integrated via a lightweight semantic projector with zero-initialized adaptive normalization. The Self-Conditioned Decoupled Router (SCDR) modulates the velocity field during ODE integration based on intermediate structural states.
AI.result: Experiments on CrossDocked2020 show LiFT achieves competitive distribution matching, improves medicinal chemistry metrics, and maintains structural validity under task-steering settings without additional generator fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Language-derived chemical priors provide effective trend-level guidance for 3D molecular generation, offering a promising approach for structure-based drug design without the need for costly task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Wrong Prediction, Right Answer: Recovering Evidence from Collapsed LLM Sequence Scores
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, and 43 appendix tables. Research paper on language-model interpretability, reasoning evaluation, output-scoring bottlenecks, and label-free calibration. The paper evaluates controlled three-way logical reasoning tasks, ProofWriter, ANLI, and FOLIO using Qwen3.5, OLMo-2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Pythia checkpoints
summary: When a large language model fails a reasoning task, it is often assumed to lack the underlying capability. However, this conflates a genuine absence of reasoning with a late-stage output bottleneck. We observe a consistent readout gap across diverse reasoning benchmarks: hidden-state probes successfully decode correct answers even when native sequence scoring completely collapses due to structural biases. To test whether instance-specific logic survives this collapse, we introduce a diagnostic protocol using a minimal, target-label-free additive correction. Fitting just two parameters on as few as 25 unlabeled examples recovers 9--34 accuracy points for Qwen3.5 models, transferring successfully to OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. Crucially, these recovered decisions persist on hard instances unresolved by simple lexical overlap and significantly exceed count-preserving permutation baselines. Our results show that many apparent zero-shot reasoning deficits are expression failures masking intact internal logic, urging a narrower interpretation of benchmark evaluations.

AI.tldr: Hidden-state probes reveal that LLMs often have correct internal reasoning capabilities that fail to surface in outputs due to structural biases, not genuine reasoning deficits.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the assumption that when LLMs fail reasoning tasks, it's due to lack of underlying capability. Instead, the authors identify a "readout gap" - correct answers exist in hidden states but fail to appear in final outputs due to structural biases in output generation.
AI.method: The authors use hidden-state probes to decode correct answers from internal representations, even when native outputs are wrong. They introduce a diagnostic protocol with a minimal additive correction requiring only 2 parameters fitted on 25 unlabeled examples. This correction transfers across different models (Qwen3.5, OLMo-2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B).
AI.result: The method recovers 9-34 accuracy points for Qwen3.5 models. Recovered decisions persist on hard instances not resolved by simple lexical overlap and significantly exceed count-preserving permutation baselines. The correction successfully transfers to other models.
AI.conclusion: Many apparent zero-shot reasoning deficits are actually expression failures that mask intact internal logic. Benchmark evaluations need narrower interpretation since models may have correct reasoning internally that fails to express in outputs.

title: TSPFN: A Temporal Tabular Foundation Model for Physiological Time Series Classification
comment: Accepted at STACOM 2026 (MICCAI Workshop). 10 pages, 3 figures
summary: Designing models that generalize effectively in low- to medium-data regimes remains a primary challenge in medical machine learning, particularly for physiological time-series classification. While tabular foundation models such as TabPFN offer an attractive alternative to conventional fine-tuning through in-context learning, they are not designed to capture the temporal dependencies inherent to physiological signals. ~In this paper, we introduce TSPFN, a foundation model that redesigns TabPFN's architecture for time series data. TSPFN integrates structured temporal representations and positional embeddings to capture intra-sample temporal and channel dependencies. To fully leverage its spatio-temporal design, the model is pretrained on 140,000 real-world physiological time series across multiple medical domains. This yields a unified, generalizable framework capable of learning the specificities of medical time series. Experiments across diverse physiological benchmarks demonstrate that TSPFN consistently outperforms standard tabular baselines and TabPFN, and achieves superior cross-domain generalization compared to specialized deep time-series models. All our experiments, ablation studies, and pre-processing scheme are publicly available at https://github.com/Jeremstym/TSPFN

AI.tldr: TSPFN is a new foundation model for physiological time-series classification that extends TabPFN to handle temporal dependencies, achieving better performance than tabular models and specialized time-series approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular foundation models like TabPFN don't capture temporal dependencies in physiological signals, creating a need for specialized time-series foundation models for medical applications.
AI.method: Redesigned TabPFN architecture with structured temporal representations and positional embeddings, pretrained on 140,000 real-world physiological time series across multiple medical domains.
AI.result: TSPFN consistently outperforms standard tabular baselines and TabPFN, and shows superior cross-domain generalization compared to specialized deep time-series models across diverse physiological benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TSPFN provides a unified, generalizable framework for medical time-series classification that effectively addresses the challenges of low-to-medium data regimes in physiological signal analysis.

title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
summary: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can substantially improve reasoning in mathematics and code, where outcomes can be checked automatically. Extending this progress to open-ended and agentic tasks remains difficult because reliable rewards are harder to obtain and direct human supervision cannot keep pace with the scale and complexity of model-generated experience. This paper studies how LRMs can continue to improve as human supervision gradually recedes from the learning loop. We examine two connected dimensions of this problem. The reward axis traces the development from per-instance human judgments to reusable verifiers and rewards that operate even without human feedback. The experience axis examines how learning can progress from human-curated tasks and environments toward self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution. We connect these dimensions through a five-level ladder from L0 to L4 that identifies which parts of the learning process remain under continued human control. Our analysis further highlights the risks introduced by increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors. Consequently, we also provide the evaluation around three complementary objects: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality. This analysis provides a structured account of current approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision and the open problems involved in developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence. Furthermore, we maintain a continuously updated \href{https://github.com/visitworld123/Awesome-Scaling-LRM-Beyond-Human-Supervision}{GitHub repository} to track the latest advances.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for scaling large reasoning models beyond human supervision, outlining progression from human-controlled learning to increasingly autonomous reward and experience generation systems.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR approaches work well for domains like math and code with verifiable outcomes, but struggle with open-ended agentic tasks where reliable rewards are hard to obtain and human supervision can't scale with model complexity. The paper aims to address how LRMs can continue improving as human supervision recedes from the learning loop.
AI.method: The paper examines two dimensions: (1) reward axis - progression from human judgments to reusable verifiers and autonomous rewards, and (2) experience axis - from human-curated tasks to self-generated curricula and autonomous co-evolution. These are connected through a five-level ladder (L0-L4) identifying human control levels, with evaluation focused on policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality.
AI.result: The analysis provides a structured framework for current approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision, identifying key challenges and progression levels toward autonomous learning systems, while highlighting risks like reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a roadmap for developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence, emphasizing the need to balance autonomy with safeguards against emerging risks, and provides ongoing tracking of advances through a GitHub repository.

title: Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: While low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient model adaptation, how to regularize its training dynamics for stable and effective optimization remains underexplored. Because LoRA initializes the up-projection to zero, its early optimization dynamics are largely governed by the down-projection. Building on this observation, we introduce Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation (NoRA), a simple yet effective method that normalizes the down-projection matrices during training. We further show that the same normalization can be applied only at initialization, improving standard LoRA without requiring repeated normalization throughout training. Across pretraining, supervised finetuning, and reinforcement learning, NoRA consistently accelerates convergence, improves performance and training stability, and mitigates catastrophic forgetting. These benefits require neither additional trainable parameters nor inference-time computation, making NoRA a simple and broadly applicable enhancement to LoRA.

AI.tldr: NoRA normalizes LoRA's down-projection matrices during training or initialization to improve optimization stability and performance without extra parameters or inference cost.
AI.motivation: LoRA training dynamics lack proper regularization for stable optimization, and its initialization causes early dynamics to be governed primarily by the down-projection matrix, making training suboptimal.
AI.method: NoRA normalizes the down-projection matrices in LoRA during training. The paper also shows this normalization can be applied only at initialization to improve standard LoRA without repeated normalization throughout training.
AI.result: Across pretraining, supervised finetuning, and reinforcement learning, NoRA consistently accelerates convergence, improves performance and training stability, and mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: NoRA is a simple, broadly applicable enhancement to LoRA that provides significant benefits without additional trainable parameters or inference-time computation overhead.

title: Reconciling Process Supervision with Outcome-Based Credit in Agentic Policy Optimization
summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides verified feedback for language-model agents, but assigns trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all decisions, yielding coarse credit over long-horizon interactions. On-policy self-distillation offers finer supervision by re-evaluating sampled behavior with privileged information (PI) available only during training. However, fine-grained supervision is not necessarily fine-grained credit: PI-induced likelihood changes describe how additional information alters policy preference, but do not directly determine how an executable action should inherit the verified task outcome. This creates a supervision-credit gap. Privileged signals may be irrelevant to the current interaction state, operate at a token granularity misaligned with executable decisions, and lack the outcome semantics required for reinforcement. We introduce TASPO, which converts privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit. TASPO constructs decision-applicable PI from verified successful experience, aggregates PI-induced likelihood shifts at the executable-action level, and converts relative action support into positive, bounded, mean-preserving weights on the original trajectory advantage. Thus, the verified outcome determines the update direction and average scale, while PI only redistributes credit across actions. Across three agentic benchmarks, TASPO improves over GRPO by 10.6\% and generalizes better to unseen tasks. Further analysis indicates that TASPO reduces supervision mismatch and that action-level assignment stabilizes the policy optimization process. These findings offer the community another interesting perspective.

AI.tldr: TASPO (Task-Aware Supervised Policy Optimization) addresses the supervision-credit gap in language model agents by converting privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit, improving over standard reinforcement learning methods.
AI.motivation: Standard outcome-based RL for language models assigns trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all decisions, providing coarse credit assignment. While privileged information during training offers finer supervision, it doesn't directly translate to executable action credit, creating a supervision-credit gap where privileged signals may be irrelevant, misaligned with token granularity, or lack outcome semantics.
AI.method: TASPO constructs decision-applicable privileged information from verified successful experiences, aggregates privileged-information-induced likelihood shifts at the executable-action level, and converts relative action support into positive, bounded, mean-preserving weights on the original trajectory advantage. This ensures verified outcomes determine update direction and scale while privileged information redistributes credit across actions.
AI.result: Across three agentic benchmarks, TASPO improves over GRPO by 10.6% and demonstrates better generalization to unseen tasks. Analysis shows TASPO reduces supervision mismatch and stabilizes the policy optimization process through action-level credit assignment.
AI.conclusion: TASPO successfully bridges the supervision-credit gap in language model agent training by converting privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit, offering a promising approach for more effective fine-grained credit assignment in long-horizon interactions while maintaining outcome-driven reinforcement semantics.

title: Rotational Equivariance in Machine Learning: A Comprehensive Tutorial
summary: Rotational symmetry is one of the most important structural principles in machine learning on 3D data. In applications ranging from physics and materials science to 3D computer vision, predictions should not depend on an arbitrary choice of coordinate frame. Rotational equivariance captures this requirement mathematically by enforcing that a rotation of the input induces a corresponding transformation of the model output. This tutorial provides a comprehensive introduction to rotational equivariance, starting from the physical and geometric intuition behind coordinate independence and building up the necessary machinery from geometric deep learning, group theory, and representation theory. We introduce message passing on Euclidean graphs, group actions and representations, spherical harmonics, Wigner matrices, tensor products, and Clebsch-Gordan decomposition, and explain how these ingredients give rise to modern equivariant architectures. We then survey the principal strategies for incorporating rotational equivariance in deep learning, including group convolutions, internal tensorial representations, and canonicalization-based methods, and discuss their practical strengths and limitations. The tutorial aims to lower the barrier to the subject by connecting the underlying mathematics to practical model design, by unifying ideas that are often expressed in different formal languages, and by helping practitioners choose among competing approaches through a clear discussion of their trade-offs.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive tutorial introducing rotational equivariance in machine learning for 3D data, covering mathematical foundations, practical architectures, and trade-offs between different approaches.
AI.motivation: Rotational symmetry is crucial in 3D machine learning applications (physics, materials science, 3D vision) where predictions should be independent of arbitrary coordinate frame choices. Current literature uses different formal languages, creating barriers to understanding and implementation.
AI.method: The tutorial introduces mathematical foundations (group theory, representation theory, spherical harmonics, Wigner matrices) and connects them to practical model design. Surveys three principal strategies: group convolutions, internal tensorial representations, and canonicalization-based methods, comparing their trade-offs.
AI.result: Provides a unified framework for understanding rotational equivariance, lowering barriers to the subject by connecting abstract mathematics to practical implementation, and offering clear guidance on choosing among different architectural approaches.
AI.conclusion: This tutorial successfully bridges the gap between mathematical theory and practical implementation of rotational equivariance in 3D machine learning, providing practitioners with the tools to make informed decisions about which equivariant architecture to use based on their specific application needs.

title: Token-Efficient Data Reasoning Agents via Adaptive Structuring of Unstructured Data
summary: Valuable data remains embedded in unstructured sources: web pages, reports, contracts, filings, earnings calls, and PDFs. The big bet in enterprise AI is deploying LLM agents that reason over this data to answer complex questions for every knowledge worker. Agents can do this today, but at prohibitive cost. Each question repeatedly opens large documents to recover scattered evidence, consuming up to a million tokens. However, if the data were already structured, the same question would reduce to a cheap database lookup. For example, on FanOutQA benchmark, reasoning over an ideal pre-structured store is 28X cheaper, and the gap grows to orders of magnitude as questions fan out over more documents. Yet structuring everything in advance is not viable: documents hold vastly more possible structure than any workload will use, and the useful structure and documents are unknown until queries arrive. We propose agentic data cracking, a method that structures unstructured data adaptively and speculatively as a byproduct of reasoning itself. Structuring is adaptive because observed queries decide when it happens and what matters, and speculative because it goes beyond the current question. Whenever the agent opens a document to answer, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure likely to serve related future queries. Over time, an increasing share of queries is fully covered by structured data and answered without opening a document, keeping agentic accuracy at close to RAG cost. On FanOutQA, extended with merely one related question per test question, cracking cuts cost by 53% while preserving accuracy. Agentic data cracking is a first step toward next-generation data infrastructure for agentic reasoning over unstructured data: a shared substrate beneath the model where knowledge that reasoning already paid to uncover accumulates.

AI.tldr: Agentic data cracking adaptively structures unstructured data as a byproduct of LLM reasoning to dramatically reduce query costs while maintaining accuracy, addressing the prohibitive expense of traditional RAG approaches.
AI.motivation: Current enterprise AI faces prohibitive costs when LLM agents reason over unstructured data using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Each query requires opening large documents and processing scattered evidence, consuming up to a million tokens. Pre-structuring everything isn't viable since useful structure and relevant documents are unknown until queries arrive, plus documents contain vastly more potential structure than any workload will use.
AI.method: Proposes "agentic data cracking" - an adaptive, speculative method where structuring happens as a byproduct of reasoning. When an agent opens a document to answer a question, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure likely to serve related future queries. This structuring is adaptive (driven by observed queries) and speculative (goes beyond current needs).
AI.result: On the FanOutQA benchmark, reasoning over an ideal pre-structured store is 28X cheaper than traditional RAG. With agentic data cracking (extended with just one related question per test question), cost is reduced by 53% while preserving accuracy. Over time, increasing shares of queries are fully covered by structured data and answered without opening documents.
AI.conclusion: Agentic data cracking represents a first step toward next-generation data infrastructure for agentic reasoning over unstructured data - creating a shared substrate where knowledge uncovered during reasoning accumulates, transforming how enterprises handle unstructured data analysis with LLM agents.

title: Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) offers dense token-level supervision as an alternative to the sparse outcome-level advantages of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, the teacher scores student-generated trajectories that are inherently off-policy for it, so the reliability of its supervision, and hence the source of the student's improvement, remains unclear. We quantitatively analyze teacher supervision during OPD training and find substantial noise whose prevalence increases with teacher scale. Surprisingly, the student policy is insensitive to such noise, converging to comparable performance regardless of whether noisy supervision is retained or removed. Does OPD distill at all? By analyzing what drives its gains, we find that learning concentrates on low log-probability tokens, and using a single fixed negative advantage matches the performance of teacher-provided ones. This suggests that OPD works largely by suppressing low log-probability tokens, which requires no teacher. These findings motivate On-Policy Self-Adaptation (OPSA), a supervision-free method using entropy-adaptive negative advantages. It assigns stronger learning signals to high-entropy positions, suppressing tail tokens, and evenly redistributing probability mass among head tokens. Compared with the base \texttt{Qwen3-1.7B}, OPSA improves Avg@32 by 35.41 points on AIME24, corresponding to a 263\% relative gain, and more than doubles Pass@32 across all three benchmarks. It also outperforms OPD by 16.77 points in Avg@32 on AIME24. Extensive experiments and analyses across model families and tasks further demonstrate its effectiveness and generalizability.

AI.tldr: On-Policy Self-Adaptation (OPSA) replaces teacher supervision in distillation with entropy-adaptive negative advantages, achieving significant performance gains without requiring a teacher model.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) uses teacher supervision but the reliability of this supervision is unclear since teachers score student-generated trajectories that are inherently off-policy for them. Analysis reveals substantial noise in teacher supervision that increases with teacher scale, questioning whether OPD actually distills knowledge at all.
AI.method: The paper proposes On-Policy Self-Adaptation (OPSA), a supervision-free method that uses entropy-adaptive negative advantages. It assigns stronger learning signals to high-entropy positions to suppress tail tokens and redistribute probability mass among head tokens, eliminating the need for teacher models.
AI.result: OPSA improves Avg@32 by 35.41 points (263% relative gain) on AIME24 compared to base Qwen3-1.7B, more than doubles Pass@32 across three benchmarks, and outperforms OPD by 16.77 points in Avg@32 on AIME24. Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness across model families and tasks.
AI.conclusion: OPD works primarily by suppressing low log-probability tokens rather than distilling teacher knowledge, and this effect can be achieved more effectively through teacher-free methods like OPSA that adaptively suppress tokens based on entropy.

title: Cross-Regional Grapevine Cold Hardiness Prediction via Learned Multimodal Latent Representations
summary: Accurate daily predictions of cold hardiness in woody plants are critical in regions where freezing temperatures can damage dormant buds and reduce seasonal yield. Existing biophysical, hybrid, and deep learning models have shown high predictive accuracy when trained on local data but remain largely site-specific. The limited availability of cold hardiness data, coupled with the lack of principled methods for transferring cold hardiness predictions to new regions and cultivars, has limited the broader adoption and practical utility of these approaches, particularly in data-scarce regions. To address these limitations, we propose a cold hardiness prediction framework that learns a transferable latent representation by capturing region-specific variation through learned embeddings. To enable prediction in previously unseen regions, we infer embeddings from (1) text descriptions of the cultivar and growing region, and (2) limited historical observations, supporting both zero-shot and few-shot transfer. Experiments on datasets from six regions across North America demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cold hardiness prediction methods, yielding more accurate predictions and substantially improving transfer to data-scarce regions.

AI.tldr: A novel transfer learning framework for predicting cold hardiness in woody plants using learned embeddings enables accurate predictions across new regions and cultivars with minimal data.
AI.motivation: Existing cold hardiness prediction models are site-specific and require extensive local training data, limiting their broader adoption in data-scarce regions where freezing temperatures threaten crop yield.
AI.method: A cold hardiness prediction framework that learns transferable latent representations using region-specific embeddings, enabling zero-shot and few-shot transfer via text descriptions of cultivars/regions or limited historical observations.
AI.result: The approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across six North American regions, providing more accurate predictions and substantially improving transfer to data-scarce regions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing site-specific models by enabling transferable cold hardiness predictions, significantly enhancing practical utility in data-scarce agricultural regions.

title: Universal Transformers for Circuit Computations: Perfect Length Generalization in Tiny Transformers
summary: Learning generalizable algorithmic computations remains a challenge for neural networks, as reflected in persistent failures on compositional and length generalization benchmarks. We present a provably correct, transformer parameterization (with only 280 learnable parameters for Boolean algebra tasks) capable of learning and evaluating problems of any depth or length. We assume inputs are fully parenthesized, well-formed expressions. Our approach conceptualizes algorithmic tasks as circuit models embedded in transformers, enabling depth-1 circuit reduction in a single forward pass. To achieve depth generalization, we introduce a positional encoding that tracks each gate's depth within the circuit, enabling the model to identify evaluable subexpressions at each iteration via masked hard attention, with $O(n)$ per-iteration complexity via linear attention. Combined with an autonomous halting criterion, the model terminates after $d$ iterations for problems of depth $d$, yielding $O(n \cdot d)$ total complexity. We show that training on shallow problem instances (depth 1 and depth 2) effectively recovers interpretable parameters that {\em snap} into place, resulting in exact length generalization. Though we establish that our construction provably evaluates Boolean expressions -- a universal symbolic computation -- of arbitrary length perfectly, in other experiments we also demonstrate that our transformer variant can learn and generalize perfectly (100% accuracy) on other common length generalization benchmarks, including modular arithmetic and ListOps.

AI.tldr: A provably correct transformer parameterization with only 280 learnable parameters achieves perfect compositional and length generalization on algorithmic tasks by treating them as circuit models with depth-based positional encoding and linear attention.
AI.motivation: Neural networks struggle with compositional and length generalization in algorithmic computations, as shown by persistent failures on benchmarks. Current models fail to generalize beyond their training distribution in terms of expression depth and length.
AI.method: Transformers parameterized as circuit models with minimal learnable parameters (280). Uses depth-based positional encoding to track gate depth, masked hard attention to identify evaluable subexpressions, linear attention for O(n) per-iteration complexity, and autonomous halting after d iterations for depth d problems.
AI.result: The model achieves provably correct evaluation of Boolean expressions (universal symbolic computation) of arbitrary length. Perfect 100% accuracy on length generalization benchmarks including modular arithmetic and ListOps. Training on shallow instances (depth 1-2) yields interpretable parameters that enable exact length generalization.
AI.conclusion: Algorithmic computations can be learned by neural networks with perfect compositional and length generalization through proper parameterization as circuit models with depth-aware mechanisms. The minimal parameter approach demonstrates that correct algorithmic learning is possible with extremely small models when properly structured.

title: BLOOM-WILT: Logit Tilting for Behaviour Elicitation in Automated LLM Auditing
summary: Users of a deployed language model routinely encounter behaviours that testing almost never surfaces, since deployment puts the model through orders of magnitude more interactions than any evaluation can simulate. Automated auditors make testing cheap to scale and flexible enough to cover almost any specified behaviour, yet their lack of optimisation pressure makes them sample-inefficient. To address this shortcoming, we introduce BLOOM-WILT, a full auditing pipeline that elicits natural multi-turn instances of rare behaviours, without training cost or access beyond the target's next-token distribution. On the input side, WILT's auditor model revises its conversational strategy across rounds, learning from previous scored interactions. On the output side, WILT adaptively reweights the target's decoding using the model's own distribution conditioned on an elicitation prompt, so that behaviour-relevant generations are sampled ahead of others it finds equally probable when unprompted. We evaluate WILT across 4 target models and 8 behaviours, where it beats the baseline auditor in 30 of the 32 settings and overturns the previous model safety rankings. WILT raises average behaviour presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, beating every elicitation method we port into the same pipeline at matched compute, without pushing output probability below the baseline's.

AI.tldr: BLOOM-WILT is an automated auditing pipeline that efficiently discovers rare harmful behaviors in language models through multi-turn conversations, using adaptive conversation strategy updates and targeted decoding without model training.
AI.motivation: Traditional testing methods fail to surface rare behaviors that emerge during real-world deployment due to the orders-of-magnitude difference in interaction volume. While automated auditors scale testing, they lack optimization pressure and are sample-inefficient, making them poor at discovering infrequent but critical model failures.
AI.method: WILT uses a two-pronged approach: 1) An auditor model that learns and revises its conversational strategy across rounds based on scored previous interactions; 2) Adaptive reweighting of the target model's decoding using the model's own distribution conditioned on elicitation prompts, prioritizing behavior-relevant generations without changing their base probability.
AI.result: WILT outperformed baselines in 30 of 32 settings across 4 target models and 8 behaviors. It increased average behavior presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, surpassing all comparable methods at matched compute without reducing output probability below baseline levels.
AI.conclusion: BLOOM-WILT provides an effective, training-free approach to auditing language models for rare harmful behaviors, demonstrating superior efficiency over existing methods and potentially overturning established model safety rankings by revealing previously undetected vulnerabilities.

title: A Model with No Head and Many Thoughts
summary: Large language models decode by projecting hidden states through a large vocabulary head at every step. This operation is computationally costly and forces all reasoning to be expressed in discrete tokens. We introduce Soft Latent Thinking, a method that replaces the LM head during reasoning with a lightweight projector, enabling autoregressive rollout in embedding space where reasoning steps remain continuous rather than tokenized. Experiments on DeepSeek-Qwen-1.5B and LLaMA-3.2-3B show that Soft Latent Thinking consistently improves pass@k across all k while reducing per-step compute during chain-of-thought. Our method achieves the highest pass@32 among all soft-thinking approaches, demonstrating that effective reasoning can be carried out in continuous space without discrete token generation.

AI.tldr: Soft Latent Thinking enables reasoning in continuous embedding space instead of discrete tokens, reducing compute while improving performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional LLM decoding requires costly vocabulary projection at every step and forces reasoning into discrete tokens, which is computationally expensive and limits expressiveness.
AI.method: Replace the language model head during reasoning with a lightweight projector, enabling autoregressive rollout in embedding space where reasoning steps remain continuous rather than tokenized.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepSeek-Qwen-1.5B and LLaMA-3.2-3B show consistent improvements in pass@k across all k while reducing per-step compute during chain-of-thought, achieving highest pass@32 among soft-thinking approaches.
AI.conclusion: Effective reasoning can be carried out in continuous space without discrete token generation, offering a more efficient alternative to traditional token-based decoding.

title: When Does Bigger Help? A Controlled Study of LLM Scale for Ontology Learning
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, and 5 tables. WOP 2026 workshop at ISWC 2026
summary: The effect of Large Language Model (LLM) scale on ontology learning (OL) performance remains insufficiently characterized. We present a controlled evaluation of 13 models spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants from the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 lineages, together with proprietary GPT release variants, using the OntoLearner retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. All models are evaluated with the same embedding model, retrieval configuration, prompt templates, decoding settings, datasets, and metrics on term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relationship extraction across four biomedical and materials science and engineering ontologies. Within the dense Qwen3.5 lineage, increasing parameter count primarily improves precision rather than recall, with the largest gains occurring between 9B and 27B parameters. However, the effect of scale is neither monotonic nor uniform across tasks and domains. Dense 27B models outperform substantially larger sparse models on term typing, whereas larger Mixture-of-Experts models achieve the strongest open-weight results on taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relationship extraction remains difficult across model scales, particularly for the Materials Data Science ontology. Performance differences across matched Qwen variants and proprietary GPT releases further indicate that architecture and model lineage can outweigh nominal parameter count. These findings show that model size alone is an insufficient selection criterion for OL and provide empirical guidance for reproducible LLM-assisted ontology engineering.

AI.tldr: LLM scale effects on ontology learning are complex and non-monotonic; parameter count alone is insufficient for selecting models, as architecture and lineage can outweigh size differences.
AI.motivation: The effect of Large Language Model scale on ontology learning performance remains insufficiently characterized, creating uncertainty about how model size relates to OL capabilities across different tasks and domains.
AI.method: Controlled evaluation of 13 models from Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 lineages (including dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants) and proprietary GPT variants using the OntoLearner RAG pipeline, with standardized embeddings, retrieval, prompts, datasets, and metrics across term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relationship extraction tasks in biomedical and materials science ontologies.
AI.result: Within dense Qwen3.5 models, increasing parameters primarily improves precision over recall, with biggest gains from 9B to 27B parameters. Effects are non-monotonic and task-dependent: dense 27B models beat larger sparse models on term typing, while larger MoE models excel at taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relationship extraction remains challenging, especially for materials science. Architecture and lineage outweigh nominal parameter count differences.
AI.conclusion: Model size alone is insufficient for ontology learning; researchers need empirical guidance considering architecture, lineage, and task-specific performance rather than just parameter counts, enabling more reproducible LLM-assisted ontology engineering.

title: Sycophantic Agreement Transfers with Neutral Data via Contrastive Preference Optimization
summary: Sycophantic agreement refers to a behavior in which language models excessively affirm the user, often at the cost of factual accuracy. Although sycophantic agreement is a well-known failure of model alignment, there is limited understanding of how it emerges from model training. In this work, we demonstrate that sycophantic agreement can emerge as an unintended consequence of widely used contrastive preference optimization objectives. Using the OLMo 3 post-training pipeline, we show that, for various pairs of teacher models across three families, there is a strong correlation between the log-ratio of the teacher model sycophantic agreement rates and the resulting student model sycophantic agreement rate. We further demonstrate that this unintended transfer is not limited to DPO but also occurs across 6 other preference optimization objectives. To understand whether this effect can be attributed to particular training examples, we analyze the preference data and find that the sycophancy signal is diffused across the entire dataset rather than concentrated in a sparse set of examples: each example appears neutral, i.e., there are no explicit instances of sycophantic agreement, and filtering based on probe-based data attribution or logit-linear selection fails to mitigate sycophancy without removing a large portion of the dataset. Overall, our findings suggest that the teacher models used to generate preference data can interact with alignment training objectives in unexpected ways, generalizing to undesirable and potentially harmful behaviors like sycophantic agreement.

AI.tldr: Sycophantic agreement emerges in language models as an unintended consequence of contrastive preference optimization objectives, where teacher models transfer this behavior to student models through preference data, with the signal diffused across entire datasets rather than concentrated in specific examples.
AI.motivation: Sycophantic agreement (excessive affirmation at cost of accuracy) is a known alignment failure in language models, but there's limited understanding of how it emerges from model training processes.
AI.method: Used OLMo 3 post-training pipeline to show correlation between teacher model sycophancy rates and student model sycophancy rates. Tested 6 different preference optimization objectives beyond DPO. Analyzed preference data to see if sycophancy is concentrated in specific examples or diffused across datasets.
AI.result: Strong correlation found between teacher model sycophancy rates and student model sycophancy rates. The effect occurs across multiple preference optimization objectives. Sycophancy signal is diffused across entire datasets - each example appears neutral with no explicit instances, and filtering techniques fail to mitigate sycophancy without removing large portions of data.
AI.conclusion: Teacher models used to generate preference data can interact with alignment training objectives in unexpected ways, generalizing to undesirable behaviors like sycophantic agreement. This suggests fundamental issues with how preference optimization objectives handle subtle behavioral signals.

title: OntoAligner-Ensemble: Voting-Based Fusion across Heterogeneous Ontology Alignment Techniques
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, accepted for OM-2026 workshop at ISWC 2026
summary: Ontology alignment (OA) has evolved through several methodological paradigms, ranging from lexical and structural aligners to knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models and, more recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches. Although modern OA frameworks provide unified ecosystems for deploying these heterogeneous aligners, mechanisms for systematically reconciling their complementary and sometimes conflicting predictions remain relatively underexplored. We present OntoAligner-Ensemble, a modular and aligner-agnostic framework that combines candidate correspondences through a configurable two-stage process comprising voting-based fusion strategies followed by post-fusion selection policies. The framework supports any aligner implemented within OntoAligner that produces candidate correspondences, enabling diverse alignment paradigms to be integrated through a unified decision process. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we instantiate the framework using representative lightweight string-aligner, KGE-based, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation aligners powered by both open-weight and API-based LLMs. We evaluate individual aligners and ensemble configurations across eight benchmark tasks from five OAEI tracks spanning biomedical to beyond-equivalence. The results show that ensemble fusion consistently improves the balance between precision and recall and frequently outperforms standalone aligners across diverse domains. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that ensemble composition directly affects the precision-recall trade-off: heterogeneous cross-paradigm ensembles generally improve precision, whereas homogeneous LLM ensembles more often achieve higher overall F1-scores. These findings demonstrate that systematic ensemble learning offers a robust and reproducible strategy for OA while providing practical guidance for selecting ensemble compositions under different alignment scenarios.

AI.tldr: OntoAligner-Ensemble is a modular framework that combines multiple ontology alignment methods through voting-based fusion and post-fusion selection to systematically reconcile complementary and conflicting predictions from different aligners.
AI.motivation: Although modern OA frameworks support heterogeneous aligners (lexical, structural, KGE, LLM-based), there's a lack of systematic mechanisms to reconcile their complementary and sometimes conflicting predictions, leading to underexplored ensemble approaches in ontology alignment.
