AI.method: A modular, aligner-agnostic framework with configurable two-stage process: 1) voting-based fusion strategies to combine candidate correspondences, and 2) post-fusion selection policies. The framework supports any aligner that produces candidate correspondences within OntoAligner.
AI.result: Ensemble fusion consistently improves balance between precision and recall, frequently outperforming standalone aligners across 8 benchmark tasks from 5 OAEI tracks. Heterogeneous cross-paradigm ensembles improve precision, while homogeneous LLM ensembles achieve higher overall F1-scores.
AI.conclusion: Systematic ensemble learning offers a robust and reproducible strategy for ontology alignment, with practical guidance for selecting ensemble compositions under different alignment scenarios based on precision-recall trade-offs.

title: Stress-Testing Efficient Responsible-AI Evaluation: When Compute Savings Change Benchmark Conclusions
summary: Efficient evaluation changes the protocol used to support claims about model behavior, yet it is rarely tested whether those claims remain stable after the evaluation itself is made cheaper. We stress-test conclusion robustness in responsible-AI benchmarking by evaluating three dense and mixture-of-experts models on BBQ and BBQ-V under seven conditions spanning batching, quantization, benchmark reduction, and their combinations. Rather than treating preserved aggregate accuracy as sufficient, we compare accuracy, bias severity and prevalence, reasoning quality, subgroup behavior, subset-membership stability, runtime, and measured GPU energy against a full-benchmark BF16 baseline. Larger batching keeps accuracy within 0.35 percentage points of baseline and produces comparatively small subgroup changes, while reducing energy in five of six model--dataset settings. INT8 largely preserves quality but uses 1.79--4.26$\times$ baseline energy. INT4 causes larger, model- and context-dependent changes. Reduced benchmarks provide the most consistent savings, but very small subsets are substantially more sensitive to which items are retained. Efficient evaluation should therefore be treated as a measurement intervention whose validity must be checked across the conclusions the benchmark is intended to support. Our project website is https://vectorinstitute.github.io/sustainable-rai-evaluation/ and the code is available at https://github.com/VectorInstitute/sustainable-rai-evaluation.

AI.tldr: Efficient evaluation methods (batching, quantization, benchmark reduction) can significantly change conclusions about model behavior in responsible-AI benchmarking, requiring careful validation across multiple metrics beyond just aggregate accuracy.
AI.motivation: While efficient evaluation methods make testing cheaper, it's rarely tested whether the conclusions drawn about model behavior remain stable when evaluation itself is made cheaper. There's a need to stress-test conclusion robustness in responsible-AI benchmarking under various efficiency conditions.
AI.method: The paper evaluates three dense and mixture-of-experts models on BBQ and BBQ-V datasets under seven efficiency conditions: batching, quantization (INT8, INT4), benchmark reduction, and their combinations. They compare multiple metrics against a full-benchmark BF16 baseline, including accuracy, bias severity/prevalence, reasoning quality, subgroup behavior, subset-membership stability, runtime, and GPU energy consumption.
AI.result: Larger batching keeps accuracy within 0.35 percentage points of baseline with small subgroup changes, while reducing energy in 5/6 model-dataset settings. INT8 quantization largely preserves quality but uses 1.79-4.26× baseline energy. INT4 causes larger, model- and context-dependent changes. Reduced benchmarks provide consistent savings, but small subsets are sensitive to which items are retained.
AI.conclusion: Efficient evaluation should be treated as a measurement intervention whose validity must be checked across all the conclusions a benchmark is intended to support, not just aggregate accuracy. Different efficiency methods have varying impacts on different metrics, and careful validation is needed when using cheaper evaluation methods.

title: On the Complexity of the Compatibility Problem for Succinctly Encoded Conditional Distributions
summary: The motivation for this paper is the investigation of the trade-offs implicit in probabilistic models used in machine learning. Models are often used to make predictions in the form of conditional probabilities. However, a pair of conditional distributions p(x|y) and p(y|x) may not be compatible with any joint distribution p(x,y). Given two such conditionals, determining if there exists a compatible joint is known as the compatibility problem. For discrete random variables, when the conditionals are encoded as probability tables, the compatibility problem has a known solution, which is computationally tractable. In this paper, we formalise and study a succinct version of the problem, encoding conditional distributions as arithmetic circuits. This is applicable to practical applications of probabilistic modelling in high-dimensional settings, including neural network models. We show that, for succinct circuit representations of conditionals, the compatibility problem is intractable. In the case that all probabilities are non-zero, the problem is co-NP-complete. In the case that probabilities can be zero, we give examples to demonstrate that several notions of compatibility can be distinguished, and we prove that multiple versions of the problem are PSPACE-complete. Furthermore, we show that, assuming the polynomial hierarchy does not collapse, there exist compatible succinct conditionals whose joint cannot be expressed succinctly. Implications of these results for probabilistic modelling and machine learning are discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that determining if two conditional probability distributions (represented as succinct arithmetic circuits) are compatible with any joint distribution is computationally intractable - co-NP-complete for non-zero probabilities and PSPACE-complete when zeros are allowed.
AI.motivation: To investigate trade-offs in probabilistic models used in machine learning, specifically examining when conditional distributions p(x|y) and p(y|x) are compatible with any joint distribution p(x,y), particularly for practical applications in high-dimensional settings including neural networks.
AI.method: Formalizes and studies a succinct version of the compatibility problem by encoding conditional distributions as arithmetic circuits instead of probability tables, analyzing computational complexity across different scenarios.
AI.result: For succinct circuit representations: 1) The compatibility problem is intractable; 2) With non-zero probabilities, it's co-NP-complete; 3) With zero probabilities, multiple problem versions are PSPACE-complete; 4) There exist compatible succinct conditionals whose joint cannot be expressed succinctly (assuming polynomial hierarchy doesn't collapse).
AI.conclusion: The computational complexity results reveal fundamental limitations in probabilistic modeling, showing that verifying consistency between conditionals in succinct representations is computationally hard, with implications for the design and verification of probabilistic models in machine learning applications.

title: Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations
summary: Many parameter-efficient methods generate the parameters of a large neural network from a low-dimensional latent representation. Given an architecture $Φ$ with $P_Φ$ parameter slots, we write $\boldsymbolθ_f=\mathcal{G}(\boldsymbolξ_f)$, where $\mathcal{G}\colon\mathbb{R}^M\to\mathbb{R}^{P_Φ}$ is a parameter generator and $\boldsymbolξ_f\in\mathbb{R}^M$ is a latent representation of the target function $f$. The architecture $Φ$ and the generator $\mathcal{G}$ are shared across the entire target class, while each target $f$ is represented by its own latent vector $\boldsymbolξ_f$, with $Φ_{\mathcal{G}(\boldsymbolξ_f)}$ approximating $f$. This framework encompasses hypernetworks, low-dimensional parameterizations, parameter-efficient adaptation, and model compression. Understanding the tradeoff between the latent dimension $M$ and the network budget $P$ is therefore fundamental to characterizing the expressive efficiency of these methods. We study this tradeoff for affine generators and fully connected ReLU architectures. More precisely, optimizing jointly over architectures $Φ$ satisfying $P_Φ\leq P$ and affine generators $\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^M\to \mathbb{R}^{P_Φ}$, we prove that the optimal worst-case uniform approximation error over the unit ball of $α$-Hölder functions on $[0,1]^d$, where $0<α\leq1$, has the sharp order $ \bigl(P\min\{M,P\}\bigr)^{-α/d}. $ In particular, our result shows that even a fixed-dimensional latent space suffices to achieve vanishing approximation error as the network budget increases.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes sharp approximation error rates for parameter-efficient neural network methods using affine generators, showing optimal tradeoffs between latent dimension M and network budget P for approximating Hölder functions.
AI.motivation: Many parameter-efficient methods (hypernetworks, low-dimensional parameterizations, adaptation, compression) generate network parameters from low-dimensional latent representations. Understanding the fundamental tradeoff between latent dimension M and network budget P is crucial for characterizing expressive efficiency.
AI.method: Study affine parameter generators 𝒢:ℝᴹ→ℝᴾ with fully connected ReLU architectures Φ. Jointly optimize over architectures satisfying PΦ≤P and affine generators to analyze worst-case uniform approximation error over the unit ball of α-Hölder functions.
AI.result: Prove the optimal worst-case uniform approximation error has sharp order (P·min{M,P})^{-α/d}. Shows even fixed-dimensional latent space suffices for vanishing approximation error as network budget increases.
AI.conclusion: Provides theoretical foundation for parameter-efficient methods by precisely quantifying the tradeoff between latent dimension and network budget, demonstrating that modest latent dimensions can achieve optimal approximation rates for function classes.

title: Constant Individual Regret in General Games
summary: Uncoupled no-regret dynamics provide a decentralized route to equilibrium, but prior guarantees for individual regret retain a polylogarithmic dependence on the horizon. We remove this dependence for every finite $N$-player normal-form game under full-information feedback. We introduce \emph{ECHO-OFTRL}: optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (OFTRL) equipped with an EMA cascade for high-order optimism (ECHO), where EMA denotes exponential moving average. The algorithm is deterministic and fully uncoupled. If $m_{\max}$ denotes the largest action-set size, then, simultaneously for every horizon $T\geq1$, it guarantees that each of the $N$ players in the game incurs regret upper bounded by $O(\textrm{poly}(N, \log m_{\max}))$. Our algorithm leverages a new form of optimism inspired by modern filter design.

AI.tldr: ECHO-OFTRL algorithm removes logarithmic dependence on horizon in uncoupled no-regret dynamics, guaranteeing constant regret bounds independent of time horizon for all finite N-player normal-form games under full-information feedback.
AI.motivation: Prior uncoupled no-regret algorithms for decentralized equilibrium learning had regret bounds with polylogarithmic dependence on the time horizon T. The authors aim to remove this dependence and achieve constant regret bounds that don't grow with time.
AI.method: Proposes ECHO-OFTRL: optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (OFTRL) equipped with an EMA cascade for high-order optimism (ECHO), where EMA stands for exponential moving average. The algorithm is deterministic, fully uncoupled, and uses a novel optimism approach inspired by modern filter design.
AI.result: Simultaneously for every horizon T≥1, each of the N players incurs regret upper bounded by O(poly(N, log m_max)), where m_max is the largest action-set size. This eliminates the polylogarithmic T dependence present in prior work.
AI.conclusion: The paper achieves a significant breakthrough in uncoupled no-regret dynamics by removing horizon dependence from regret bounds through the novel ECHO-OFTRL algorithm with filter-inspired optimism, providing constant regret guarantees for all finite normal-form games.
